Classification

The Global Icon Series362 pieces

The worldwide city line that succeeded the Collector Series, and the largest category here.
Indonesia#455134 · Indonesia Collector Series (2011)Indonesia goes country level here, blue inside and out with a traditional dancer instead of a skyline, a nod to the courtly Javanese and Balinese dance that defines the islands' performing arts. Country Global Icons like this are scarcer than the big city releases, and Indonesia's came through a market that genuinely loves its regional design. A graceful, slightly unusual entry in the run.
Merida#455424 · Global Icon SeriesMerida is the white colonial capital of Mexico's Yucatan, and this white-interior mug features a Mayan temple, surely a nod to the nearby world wonders of Chichen Itza and Uxmal that draw visitors from the city. Built atop the ancient Maya town of T'ho, Merida wears its dual Spanish and Maya heritage proudly. A more unusual Mexican Icon than the resort cities, which gives it a quiet edge for a Mexico collector.
India#455499 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside, the India Gate on the outside, the 42 meter war memorial arch on New Delhi's Rajpath designed by Edwin Lutyens and inscribed with the names of soldiers lost in the First World War and the Third Anglo Afghan War. Starbucks gave the whole subcontinent a single country mug rather than separate cities. The Lutyens arch is the right pick, equal parts grandeur and remembrance.
Quebec#455500 · Global Icon SeriesBlue inside, cream outside with an old stone building that reads as Quebec City's Chateau Frontenac, the green roofed grand railway hotel towering over the St Lawrence. Founded by Samuel de Champlain in 1608, Old Quebec is the only walled city north of Mexico and a UNESCO site. A core North American piece for any Global Icon shelf.
Vienna#455501 · Global Icon SeriesVienna, pink inside, the exterior featuring a Ferris wheel. That is the Wiener Riesenrad in the Prater, built in 1897 and one of the world's oldest operating Ferris wheels, immortalized in the 1949 film The Third Man. Choosing the giant wheel over Schonbrunn or St. Stephen's gives this Austrian icon a playful, cinematic feel that I really enjoy.
Brussels#455502 · Global Icon SeriesGreen interior wrapped around La Grande Place, the Brussels market square ringed by gilded guild houses and the Gothic Town Hall, a UNESCO site since 1998. Every two years the cobbles vanish under a giant flower carpet of begonias. As the de facto capital of the EU, Brussels earns its Global Icon, and the Grand Place is exactly the right icon to anchor it.
Canada#455503 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside, cream outside with the maple leaf, Canada at its simplest and strongest, the sugar maple leaf on the national flag adopted in 1965. The country is the world's top maple syrup producer, drawing most of the global supply from Quebec's sugarbush. A clean, unmistakable national piece that grounds any Canada sub-collection alongside the city mugs.
Marseille#455504 · Global Icon SeriesMarseille, France's ancient Mediterranean port founded by Greeks around 600 BC, gets a light-blue interior and its cathedral on the outside, the striped Byzantine-Romanesque Cathedrale de la Major or the hilltop Notre-Dame de la Garde that watches over the Vieux-Port. It is a vivid match for France's oldest and second-largest city. A nice southern-France counterpoint to the ubiquitous Paris mug.
Chicago#455505 · Global Icon SeriesChicago goes blue inside with a cream exterior showing a stately landmark building, an apt salute to the city that invented the skyscraper after the Great Fire of 1871. The Windy City gave the world deep-dish pizza, the Magnificent Mile, and Cloud Gate, the mirrored bean in Millennium Park. Architecture buffs will note this mug leans classical rather than the steel-and-glass skyline Chicago is famous for.
Calgary#455506 · Global Icon SeriesBlue inside, cream outside with a man riding a horse, a clean nod to the Calgary Stampede, the self-styled Greatest Outdoor Show on Earth held every July since 1912. The rodeo and chuckwagon races define this Alberta city at the foot of the Rockies. The cowboy image gives this Canadian Global Icon a real sense of place that a skyline never could.
Aachen#455507 · Global Icon SeriesThe light green Global Icon Aachen wraps the city's crown jewel, the Palatine Chapel that Charlemagne built around 800 as his royal palace and where he was buried in 814. From 936 to 1531 some thirty-one German kings were crowned under that octagonal dome, and in 1978 it became Germany's first UNESCO World Heritage Site. A serious bit of European history riding on a coffee mug.
Jordan#455508 · Global Icon SeriesBrown interior with Jerash on the outside, the astonishingly preserved Greco Roman city north of Amman, all colonnaded streets, the oval Forum, and the Temple of Artemis. Jordan is more famous for Petra, so picking Jerash, sometimes called the Pompeii of the East, is a tasteful surprise. A country mug that rewards anyone who knows the Roman ruins beyond the rose red Nabatean city.
Barcelona#455510 · Global Icon SeriesThat "AI VIZARQ" lettering is the design signature, but the star is Casa Batllo, Gaudi's dragon-roofed masterpiece on Passeig de Gracia, rendered against the dark blue interior. The facade's broken-tile mosaic shifts from gold to ocean blue, which is why a Gaudi house, not the Sagrada Familia, anchors the mug. Collectors flag this one as somewhat hard to find.
California#455511 · Global Icon SeriesLight blue inside, cream outside with palm trees, California as a feeling rather than a city, sun, coast and those imported palms that line Los Angeles boulevards. The Golden State is the most populous in the US and the home of Starbucks' own West Coast roots up in Seattle's neighbor. A breezy state-level piece that slots in beside the country mugs on any shelf.
Prague#455513 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside, and the outside carries the statue of Saint Wenceslas, the 10th century duke and patron saint of Bohemia immortalized in the carol Good King Wenceslas. His equestrian monument presides over Wenceslas Square, the boulevard that was the stage for the 1989 Velvet Revolution. A thoughtful choice over the more obvious Charles Bridge or Astronomical Clock.
France#455515 · Global Icon SeriesFrance skips Paris and gives the country mug to Mont-Saint-Michel, the tidal island abbey rising off the Normandy coast. The medieval monastery is ringed by some of Europe's most extreme tides, which historically turned it into an island only when the water rushed in. A bold choice for a whole nation, and one of the most photogenic landmarks in the entire Global Icon series.
Leipzig#455517 · Global Icon SeriesLeipzig is a German city of music and quiet revolution, where Bach served as cantor at St Thomas Church and where the peaceful 1989 Monday demonstrations helped bring down the Berlin Wall. The orange interior with a castle-like structure outside nods to its grand old trade-fair and university architecture. A city that punches well above its size in cultural history, and I like having that story sitting on a shelf.
Sao Paulo#455518 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside, with a dense street view of the city outside. That choice fits Sao Paulo, which is not about one landmark but about sheer scale, the largest city in the Western Hemisphere and the financial engine of Brazil. The packed cityscape captures its forest of high-rises along avenues like Paulista. Coffee built this place, so a Starbucks mug from the heart of Brazil's old coffee fortune has a nice circularity to it.
Macau#455519 · Global Icon SeriesMacau's dark-blue mug features a lighthouse, which is the Guia Lighthouse, the oldest Western-style lighthouse in all of China and East Asia, built in 1865 and part of a UNESCO World Heritage fortress and chapel complex. It is a fitting emblem for the former Portuguese colony now famous as Asia's casino capital. The Macau Icon is considered somewhat hard to find, making it a worthwhile catch among the Asian city mugs.
Sydney#455520 · Global Icon SeriesMagenta inside with the Sydney Harbour Bridge arcing across the outside, the steel arch locals nicknamed the Coathanger that opened in 1932 after eight years of construction. It is the world's tallest steel arch bridge, and adventurous visitors can climb the arch to its 134-meter summit for the BridgeClimb. Interesting that they chose the bridge over the Opera House next door, giving this a slightly less obvious silhouette. A bold, color-rich Australian standout.
Washington D.C.#455521 · Global Icon SeriesThe Washington Monument and the cherry blossoms are the perfect double act for the capital, since the 1912 gift of trees from Tokyo turned the Tidal Basin into America's most photographed spring. Mine has a red interior with that obelisk and pink blossoms outside. The 555 foot monument was the tallest structure on Earth when it topped out in 1884, a fact I never tire of repeating.
San Diego#455522 · Global Icon SeriesDark green inside, cream outside, anchored by the Gaslamp District archway sign. That neon-lit gateway marks San Diego's restored Victorian quarter downtown, a sixteen-block stretch of 1800s buildings saved from demolition and now the city's nightlife heart. I like that this one leads with a sign rather than a skyline, a very San Diego move that nods to its laid-back, walkable character near the bay.
Pattaya#455523 · Global Icon SeriesPattaya gets a relaxed treatment here, light blue inside and two beach chairs on the outside rather than a monument. That fits the place, a former fishing village on Thailand's Gulf coast that American GIs turned into a resort town during the Vietnam War era. The pair of empty loungers is a smart bit of design shorthand, selling the holiday rather than a skyline.
North Carolina#455524 · Global Icon SeriesNorth Carolina is First in Flight, where the Wright brothers flew at Kitty Hawk in 1903, and the cream body here leans on the state's farm and dogwood imagery rather than a single skyline. The light blue interior keeps it understated. A somewhat hard to find piece in the USA Global Icon run, it pairs naturally with the busier Wright Flyer designs collectors chase from the Been There series.
Netherlands#455525 · Global Icon SeriesA country mug, orange inside for the House of Orange, fronted by the windmill that is the Netherlands' global shorthand. The Dutch built windmills not just to grind grain but to pump water and drain the polders that created much of the country below sea level, and the Kinderdijk mills are a UNESCO site. A clean, instantly readable design that pairs naturally with the Dutch flag colors.
Pike Place Market#455526 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside, and the cream exterior shows the original Starbucks storefront at Pike Place Market, which makes this a near sacred piece for the series. The first store opened at 1912 Pike Place in 1971, and the market itself, running since 1907, is among the oldest continuously operated public markets in the country. For a Starbucks collector this is the company's own ground zero on a mug.
Geneva#455528 · Global Icon SeriesGeneva, red-lined on cream, captures the Jet d'Eau, the 140-meter water plume that has shot up from Lake Geneva since 1891 and become the city's signature. Geneva is also the diplomatic heart of the world, home to the UN's European seat and the Red Cross. An elegant Swiss Global Icon built around one of the most recognizable fountains anywhere.
Chile#455530 · Global Icon SeriesChile runs a rich brown interior with the Moai of Easter Island standing across a barren landscape outside, those monolithic stone heads carved by the Rapa Nui people far out in the Pacific. Collectors note this one is somewhat hard to find and trades actively on eBay; the reverse design pays tribute to the colorful funicular ascensores of Valparaiso, making it a two-icon piece.
Paris#455532 · Global Icon SeriesParis gets the Eiffel Tower, naturally, the wrought-iron tower Gustave Eiffel built for the 1889 World's Fair and meant to stand only twenty years before its value as a radio antenna saved it. The red interior gives this one real pop. It is among the most popular and widely traded Global Icons, a cornerstone city that almost every collector owns, so condition and crisp printing are what separate the keepers.
Valencia#455534 · Global Icon SeriesValencia, Spain, orange inside, the figure on the front a ninot from Las Fallas. Those towering papier-mache effigies are paraded each March and then torched in La Crema, the fiery climax of the city's UNESCO-listed festival honoring Saint Joseph. The back shows Calatrava's futuristic City of Arts and Sciences. A common piece, but the fire-and-future contrast makes it one of the more interesting Spanish icons.
Austria#455537 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside with a hat outside, a green felt Tyrolean or Alpine hat with its jaunty brush trim. That trachten hat is shorthand for Austria's mountain folk culture, the lederhosen and dirndl world of the Tyrol and Salzburg. It is an unusual, almost whimsical way to brand a whole nation, and a fun oddity next to the more literal landmark mugs in the lineup.
Bahamas#455538 · Global Icon SeriesThe Bahamas mug leans straight into paradise, a cream body carrying a sea shell against that blue interior, which reads like the turquoise water around Nassau and the out islands. Country-level Global Icons like this are scarcer than the big city releases since the Caribbean got far fewer stores. A simple design, but the color story sells the trip.
Spain#455541 · Global Icon SeriesThis one leans literary rather than architectural, putting Don Quixote and his squire Sancho Panza on the outside, the duo from Cervantes's 1605 novel that is often called the first modern Western novel. The lanky knight and his round companion are Spain's most exportable cultural symbol, forever tilting at the windmills of La Mancha. I love that Starbucks chose a 400-year-old book character over a cathedral here. A nicely distinctive country mug in the Global Icon line.
Thailand#455542 · Global Icon SeriesA country-level Global Icon for Thailand, brown inside with a floral exterior the catalog calls a gift to the gods. That motif points straight at Thai temple offerings and the garlands and lotus given at wats across the kingdom, Buddhism being practiced by roughly ninety-five percent of Thais. The Land of Smiles gets a softer, devotional treatment here rather than the usual skyline, which I genuinely like.
Potsdam#455543 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside, and the stairs on the outside belong to Sanssouci, Frederick the Great's rococo summer palace just outside Berlin. The king built it in the 1740s as his private retreat, and its name is French for without worry, with those famous terraced vineyard steps descending in front of the single-story palace. A UNESCO site and a strong pick for a city-specific German Icon.
Toronto#455545 · Global Icon SeriesToronto, red inside, the skyline wrapped around the CN Tower. At 553 meters the CN Tower held the title of world's tallest free-standing structure for over three decades, from 1975 until Dubai's Burj overtook it, and its glass floor still terrifies visitors. A solid, common Canada icon, and a natural companion to my Vancouver and Vancouver Island mugs.
England#455546 · Global Icon SeriesEngland's brown-lined country mug carries the Royal Coat of Arms, the three golden lions on red first used on Richard the Lionheart's Great Seal, with Shakespeare on the reverse. It is a clever pairing of crown and bard for a whole nation. Released around 2009 and made in China, this is the standard Global Icon England, a staple I was happy to secure boxed.
Lake Tahoe#455547 · Global Icon SeriesLake Tahoe is the giant alpine lake straddling the California and Nevada line, North America's largest, and the blue-and-cream design with a skier outside leans straight into its winter resort identity. The 1960 Winter Olympics were held at Squaw Valley right on its shore, cementing Tahoe as a marquee ski destination. A natural-feature icon rather than a city one, which makes it a slightly unusual fit in a band built mostly around urban landmarks.
Dublin#455550 · Global Icon SeriesDublin's green-lined mug shows a bridge and the riverfront, the Ha'penny Bridge, the graceful cast-iron pedestrian span over the Liffey opened in 1816 and named for the toll once charged to cross. Dublin is a UNESCO City of Literature, home to Joyce, Wilde, and the Guinness brewery at St. James's Gate. A warm, classic European city icon that reads instantly as Ireland.
Whistler#455552 · Global Icon SeriesWhistler is Canada's marquee ski resort, host of the 2010 Vancouver Winter Olympic alpine events, so a skier in mid-carve is the only correct image. Mine sets a blue interior against a cream body with that downhill figure. The twin Whistler and Blackcomb peaks form one of North America's largest ski areas, which is why this resort-town icon resonates with the winter-sport crowd.
Scotland#455553 · Global Icon SeriesGreen inside, cream outside, with a Scotsman playing the bagpipes. Rather than a single city, this country piece leans on the most instantly Scottish image there is, the piper in Highland dress. The Great Highland bagpipe became a clan and military instrument and was famously carried into battle, even into World War One trenches. A whisky-green color and a lone piper make this one of the more characterful national mugs in the series.
Houston#455555 · Global Icon SeriesThe green inside and that satellite are a nod to NASA's Johnson Space Center, home of Mission Control and the place where the words Houston, we have a problem became history. Released around 2009 in the original Global Icon run, the design pairs the spacecraft motif with the Houston skyline. Collectors hunt the NASA Houston for the space angle alone, and it turns up less often than the big coastal cities.
Wellington#576014 · The Global Icon SeriesMy second Wellington, this one in clean black and white rather than the green Beehive version, which makes it a genuine design variant worth holding alongside its twin. Wellington also gave the world Weta Workshop and the Lord of the Rings films, so it punches above its size. Tracking two finishes of the same city is exactly the kind of detail that keeps this hobby fun.
Daegu#576019 · The Global Icon SeriesDaegu is South Korea's fourth largest city, a textile and fashion hub set in a basin that makes it one of the hottest spots on the peninsula, earning the nickname Daegu the boiler. This Korea-market 16oz mug skips a single landmark for a colorful painted collage of the city. The Korean Global Icon and Been There runs are well loved by collectors, so any non-Western city like this is a satisfying grab.
Oktoberfest Germany#576053 · Global Icon SeriesThis is the busier I love Oktoberfest version, packing the pretzel and the giant Ferris wheel onto a light blue body, a Munich celebration that has run since 1810. The Wonder Wheel, the Riesenrad, became a fixture of the Wiesn fairground after a permanent giant wheel returned in 1979. Multiple Oktoberfest Icon variants exist, so confirm which year and scene you have, since the pretzel-and-wheel edition is a recognizable one collectors trade.
St Petersburg, Russia#576054 · Global Icon SeriesThe deep blue inside and out suits St. Petersburg, Peter the Great's imperial capital founded in 1703 on the marshy Neva delta and built to be Russia's window on Europe. The city is famous for the Hermitage in the Winter Palace, the canals that earned it the Venice of the North nickname, and the gilded domes of the Church of the Savior on Spilled Blood. Russia-market Starbucks mugs are harder to source abroad, which makes this one a little more interesting on the shelf.
Cusco, Peru#576055 · Global Icon SeriesCusco was the capital of the Inca Empire and the gateway to Machu Picchu, the cloud-wrapped 15th century citadel that the catalog art puts right on the outside of this light green mug. Hiram Bingham brought the lost city to the world's attention in 1911, and it is now one of the New Seven Wonders. Worth noting the piece leans on Machu Picchu rather than Cusco's own colonial plaza, which is the real draw for collectors of this Peru issue.
Katowice, Poland#576056 · The Global Icon SeriesKatowice sits in Poland's Upper Silesian coal belt, and the Global Icon band leans hard into that heritage, all built around an orange interior with figures and heavy industrial architecture wrapped outside. The city earned municipal rights in 1865 and grew rich on coal and steel, which is why so many of its emblems read as miners and smokestacks rather than the usual cathedral. Collectors flag the 2012 Polish releases as harder to find, and this one tends to surface mostly through European sellers.
Phuket, Thailand#576058 · The Global Icon SeriesA second copy of the purple Phuket Icon with the same three longtail boats, useful as a backup or a trade piece. The longtail, or ruea hang yao, was traditionally powered by a repurposed car engine swung on a pole to steer, which is why the propeller juts so far behind the hull. Having the duplicate means one stays sealed and one can be displayed.
Ostrava, Czech Republic#576059 · The Global Icon SeriesOstrava was the Czech Republic's iron heart, and its city-center scene leans on Lower Vitkovice, a former coal, coke and ironworks complex founded in 1828 that was the only plant in Europe to process iron start to finish in one place. Production ran until 1998, and the preserved blast furnace now carries a glass elevator to a viewing platform. The light blue interior fits this proud industrial-heritage choice.
South Africa#576060 · The Global Icon SeriesGreen inside, with the Big Five animals silhouetted against a sunset outside. This national mug skips Cape Town's Table Mountain in favor of the safari image the country is most famous for, the lion, leopard, rhino, elephant, and buffalo that draw visitors to Kruger and beyond. The orange-on-green sundown is genuinely striking. Of all the Global Icon pieces this is one of the few that sells a feeling, the bush at dusk, rather than a place.
Frankfurt#576062 · Global Icon SeriesFrankfurt comes green-lined with a statue outside, the Goethe or Justitia figure from the Romerberg, the heart of Germany's banking capital. Frankfurt was the birthplace of Johann Wolfgang von Goethe and for centuries the city where Holy Roman Emperors were crowned. A solid German Global Icon that pairs naturally with my Freiburg cup on the shelf.
Hamburg#576063 · Global Icon SeriesHamburg, Germany's great Hanseatic port and second-largest city, gets a dark-blue interior fitting its identity as a city of water, with more bridges than Venice and Amsterdam combined. The exterior shows the city center, around the Speicherstadt warehouse district and the harbor on the Elbe. The blue liner is a smart maritime choice for a place that has lived by shipping and trade for eight centuries.
Germany#576065 · Global Icon SeriesMy national Germany icon mug leads with the Brandenburg Gate, the 1791 neoclassical arch by Carl Gotthard Langhans crowned with the Quadriga chariot, the structure that stood walled off in the Cold War and became the backdrop to reunification in 1989. The brown interior is the standard Global Icon liner color. I like that a single arch can carry the whole story of a country, divided and then made whole again.
Wiesbaden#576066 · Global Icon SeriesWiesbaden is one of Europe's oldest spa towns, and that fountain inside a building is the Kochbrunnen, a hot spring pushing out 360 liters a minute at over 66 degrees beneath an 1890 drinking hall. Ours has an orange interior framing that thermal pavilion. German Global Icons tend to favor famous gates and cathedrals, so a healing spring is a refreshingly specific and unusual choice.
Freiburg#576068 · Global Icon SeriesFreiburg, dark-green inside, features an old German house outside, the city's landmark being the lavish red Historic Merchants Hall on Munsterplatz from 1520. Freiburg is also famous for its Bachle, the little open water channels running through the old town, and local lore says step in one and you will marry a local. A warm, storybook entry from Germany's sunny southwest.
Münster#576071 · Global Icon SeriesMünster is a deep cut, red inside, showing the baroque Fürstbischöfliches Schloss, the prince-bishop's palace built by Johann Conrad Schlaun in the 1760s and now the seat of the university. The city itself is where the 1648 Peace of Westphalia was signed, ending the Thirty Years War. Allied bombing flattened ninety percent of the old center in 1945, so much of what you see was painstakingly rebuilt.
Berlin#576072 · Global Icon SeriesBerlin's red-lined mug carries the Berlin Bear, the Berliner Bar that has been the city's heraldic emblem for centuries and now stars as the Buddy Bear public art all over town. Going with the bear instead of the Brandenburg Gate is a smart, local-insider move. A strong, graphic entry from one of Europe's most collected city lines.
München#576074 · Global Icon SeriesThe native spelling München rather than Munich, dark blue inside, centered on Marienplatz and the New Town Hall with its famous Glockenspiel that draws crowds at eleven each morning. The square has been Munich's beating heart since 1158 and hosts the city's Christkindlmarkt. A nice touch that Starbucks used the German name, a small nod that collectors of the European icons appreciate.
Stuttgart#576075 · Global Icon SeriesThe yellow ties straight to Stuttgart's coat of arms, a single black horse rearing on a gold field, the Stuttgarter Rossle that traces back to the city's medieval name meaning stud farm. That same prancing horse is the badge of Porsche, headquartered here, alongside Mercedes-Benz, making Stuttgart the cradle of the automobile. Collector listings note the back also carries the Concordia statue at Schlossplatz. A quietly clever heraldic design rather than the obvious skyline.
Bremen#576076 · Global Icon SeriesDark green lining with the Town Musicians of Bremen stacked outside, the donkey, dog, cat and rooster from the Brothers Grimm tale. The bronze statue by Gerhard Marcks has stood by the Rathaus since 1953, and rubbing the donkey's polished front legs is the local good-luck ritual. A storybook landmark that makes this one of the more charming German Global Icons to handle.
Heidelberg#576077 · Global Icon SeriesHeidelberg's light-green icon shows the Old Bridge, the 1788 Karl Theodor Bridge of Neckar sandstone, the ninth span built on the same medieval foundations across the river. The bridge is guarded by a bronze monkey holding a mirror, a quirky 1979 recreation of a centuries-old figure that locals rub for luck. Romantic, untouched by wartime bombing and crowned by its hillside castle ruin, Heidelberg is the postcard of old Germany.
Kassel#576078 · Global Icon SeriesDark blue inside with the Hercules Monument, the colossal copper statue crowning Kassel's Bergpark Wilhelmshohe above Europe's largest hillside water feature, a UNESCO World Heritage site where staged cascades pour down to the palace on summer afternoons. Kassel also hosts documenta, the world's most important contemporary art exhibition, every five years. The towering Hercules is a striking, lesser known German icon to land in the collection.
Paris (1)#576079 · Global Icon SeriesThis is the Eiffel Tower face of the Paris Global Icon pair, red inside and the iron lattice rendered on cream outside. Gustave Eiffel built the tower for the 1889 World's Fair and Parisians initially loathed it as an eyesore, yet at 330 meters it stayed the world's tallest structure for 41 years. Collectors usually want the two Paris variants together, so finding this one as a clean match for its sibling matters.
Paris (2)#576080 · Global Icon SeriesThe second Paris in the pair carries the Arc de Triomphe, the same red interior tying it to its Eiffel Tower twin. Napoleon commissioned it in 1806 to honor his Grande Armee, and beneath it lies France's Tomb of the Unknown Soldier with its eternal flame rekindled every evening since 1923. I keep this one shelved beside Paris (1) because the set reads as incomplete split apart.
Dresden#576082 · Global Icon SeriesThe blue Dresden mug features the Zwinger, the Baroque palace complex commissioned by Augustus the Strong in the early 1700s as a Saxon court for festivals and galleries. Dresden was firebombed in 1945 and painstakingly rebuilt, making landmarks like the Zwinger and Frauenkirche symbols of restoration. The catalog calls it Zwinger Cathedral, though it is really a palace and gardens, a small naming slip worth knowing on this piece.
Bonn#576083 · Global Icon SeriesThe text on this light green mug names the Altes Rathaus, Bonn's rococo Old Town Hall from 1737, whose pink-and-gold facade and grand staircase are the city's signature. Bonn is also Beethoven's birthplace and was West Germany's capital for decades, so the modest building punches above its weight. A retired piece that collectors note is only ever sold in its home city.
Karneval#576084 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside with Karneval lettering and a Funkenmariechen, the dancing guard girl of Cologne's Kolner Karneval, the riotous fifth season that erupts every winter with the Rosenmontag parade. This is a theme mug for an event rather than a single city, with later versions adding clowns and majorettes. The carnival pieces are a fun German sub thread, issued around specific seasons and not always easy to catch.
Nürnberg#576085 · Global Icon SeriesThe fountain is Nuremberg's Schöner Brunnen, the Beautiful Fountain on the main market square, a roughly nineteen-meter Gothic spire built from 1385 to 1396 and ringed with forty painted figures of the Holy Roman Empire's worldview. Look for the famous brass ring in its railing, which legend says grants a wish if you turn it three times. The original was hidden during the war and is now in the Germanisches Nationalmuseum.
Czech Republic#576086 · Global Icon SeriesThe green-lined Czech Republic Global Icon shows the Staroměstská radnice, the Old Town Hall in Prague, home to the Orloj astronomical clock first installed in 1410 and the world's oldest such clock still running. Crowds still gather on the hour to watch the parade of the Twelve Apostles. A country-level mug standing in for Prague, which is exactly the kind of thing I like to slot next to the city issues.
Hannover#576087 · Global Icon SeriesHannover's red-interior icon features the Herrenhausen Gardens, one of Europe's grandest Baroque gardens, begun in 1666 and shaped over decades by Electress Sophie. The centerpiece Great Fountain throws water 82 meters, the tallest in any European garden, and the surviving 1690s open-air Garden Theatre is a rarity. A garden rather than a building makes this a refreshing change of pace among the German city mugs.
Karlsruhe#576089 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside with Lady Justice for Karlsruhe, and the choice is exact, because this planned fan shaped German city is the seat of both the Federal Constitutional Court and the Federal Court of Justice, making it the legal capital of Germany. Justitia with her scales is the perfect shorthand. A smaller German market icon, which makes Karlsruhe one of the harder Deutschland mugs to track down.
Düsseldorf#576091 · Global Icon SeriesThe blue Düsseldorf mug captures the city's architecture, the twisted Rhine-front towers of the Frank Gehry Neuer Zollhof in the revived MedienHafen district. Düsseldorf is the capital of North Rhine-Westphalia, famous for its Altbier, high fashion on the Königsallee, and the world's largest Japanese community in Germany. A modern-leaning German entry that pairs nicely with the more historic Darmstadt and Dresden mugs in this batch.
Kiel#576092 · Global Icon SeriesKiel is Germany's Baltic sailing capital, home of Kiel Week, and the blue interior here frames the Gorch Fock, the navy's three-masted training barque launched by Blohm and Voss in 1958. More than 14,500 officer cadets have learned the ropes aboard her, and after a six-year refit she only returned to her Kiel home port in 2021. A maritime city told through its tall ship rather than a skyline, which is exactly why I like it.
Osnabrück#576093 · Global Icon SeriesThe building is Osnabrück Castle, the former residence of the prince-bishops and one of the venues where the 1648 Peace of Westphalia was negotiated, ending the Thirty Years War. The Protestant delegations met here in Osnabrück while the Catholics met in Münster, which is why the city is nicknamed the City of Peace. The green interior suits this scholarly pick, now home to the University of Osnabrück.
Darmstadt#576094 · Global Icon SeriesThe blue Darmstadt mug features the Hochzeitsturm, or Wedding Tower, on the Mathildenhöhe, built in 1908 to mark Grand Duke Ernst Ludwig's marriage. Architect Joseph Maria Olbrich gave it five finger-like roof arches, earning the nickname Five-Finger Tower, and the whole artists' colony hill became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021. A serious Jugendstil landmark on a mug from a city most people overlook.
Lyon#576095 · Global Icon SeriesLyon, France's gastronomic capital, gets a blue interior and the city's own emblem on the outside, the Lyon lion that puns on the city's name. The real landmark looming over the city is the white Notre-Dame de Fourviere basilica on its hilltop, but here Starbucks chose the heraldic crest instead. Lyon is a less common French Icon than Paris, which gives it a bit more interest for a collector chasing the full French set.
Istanbul#576104 · Global Icon SeriesLight blue interior with a bridge spanning the Bosphorus, the strait where Istanbul straddles two continents, Europe on one bank and Asia on the other. The Bosphorus Bridge opened in 1973 as the first permanent crossing between the continents in the city's long history. Choosing the strait over the Hagia Sophia or Blue Mosque is a clever way to say the whole geography of this place is the landmark.
Portugal#576106 · Global Icon SeriesGreen inside, with two ships sailing the outside, a fitting tribute to Portugal's Age of Discovery. This is the country of Vasco da Gama, who reached India by sea in 1498, and of the caravel, the nimble lateen-rigged ship that let explorers push down the African coast. Choosing tall ships over a building ties the whole nation to the water that defined it.
Mannheim#576109 · Global Icon SeriesMannheim's yellow-interior mug names its star explicitly, the Barockschloss Mannheim, the enormous Baroque palace that is one of the largest in Europe and second in size only to Versailles, built in the 1700s and now home to the university. The city's famous grid of numbered and lettered blocks earned it the nickname Quadratestadt, the city of squares. A less common German Icon that rewards collectors going past Berlin and Munich.
Belgium#576110 · Global Icon SeriesBelgium went with Manneken Pis, the cheeky little bronze boy fountain in Brussels who has been peeing since the 1600s and owns a wardrobe of hundreds of costumes. Picking him over a grand square is exactly the wink I want from a country Global Icon. The brown interior keeps it grounded while the design does the joking.
Antalya#576111 · Global Icon SeriesDark blue inside with an amphitheatre outside, the Roman theatre at Aspendos near Antalya, one of the best preserved in the world. Built in the second century AD, it still seats around fifteen thousand and hosts an opera and ballet festival every summer. Antalya is the gateway to Turkey's Mediterranean coast, so a near-intact ancient stage is the perfect emblem.
Budapest#576112 · Global Icon SeriesGreen lining with Buda Castle outside, the royal palace crowning Castle Hill above the Danube, rebuilt many times since the 13th century and now a UNESCO World Heritage site. Budapest itself was two cities, Buda and Pest, joined in 1873. The sweeping hilltop palace is the postcard view of the Hungarian capital and makes this a strong central-European piece.
Ankara#576113 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside with Ankara Fort outside, Turkey's capital represented by its oldest survivor. The citadel crowns a hill at the city's heart, its walls raised in layers by Galatians, Romans, Byzantines and Seljuks, with the inner castle largely Byzantine work. Ankara is often skipped for Istanbul, so the hilltop fortress is a smart pick for the city that Ataturk made the seat of the modern Republic in 1923.
Bulgaria#576114 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside with a rose outside, the Damask rose of Bulgaria's Valley of Roses near Kazanlak, where the world's finest rose oil is distilled and celebrated each June at the Rose Festival. It takes thousands of hand-picked blooms for a single gram of attar. A quietly elegant national piece, less obvious than a landmark and all the better for it on a country shelf.
Hungary#576115 · Global Icon SeriesBrown interior with Heroes' Square on the outside, the grand Budapest plaza built for Hungary's 1896 millennium with its Millennium Monument and the Seven Chieftains of the Magyars. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site and the symbolic front door to Hungarian history. A country level icon rather than a city mug, which Starbucks reserved for markets without a dense store footprint.
Turkey#576116 · Global Icon SeriesA Turkey country icon, brown inside, the front showing the giant stone heads of Mount Nemrut. King Antiochus I of Commagene built that mountaintop tomb-sanctuary in 62 BC, flanked by colossal seated gods whose heads have since toppled and now sit scattered across the summit. The back pairs it with Cappadocia's hot-air balloons and fairy chimneys. An archaeology lover's mug if there ever was one.
Brugge#576117 · Global Icon SeriesBlue inside with a swan gliding before a waterside house, pure Bruges, the canal-laced Flemish town often called the Venice of the North. Legend says the swans were decreed kept on the canals forever after a 1488 beheading, and they still drift the Minnewater today. The UNESCO old town and that fairy-tale water make this one of the prettier Belgian Global Icons.
Switzerland#576118 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside with a cabin tucked in the snow, this is the cozy winter face of Switzerland, the wooden alpine chalet that defines the country's ski-village imagination. It conjures Zermatt, Davos and St. Moritz, the resorts that helped invent modern winter tourism in the Alps. Having both Swiss country mugs, the snowy chalet and the floral one, side by side shows how the series gave one nation two very different moods. A warm seasonal favorite.
Crete#576119 · Global Icon SeriesCrete is the largest of the Greek islands and the cradle of Europe's first advanced society, the Bronze Age Minoans, so it is fitting that this green-lined Global Icon wraps the Palace of Knossos around the outside. Excavated and famously reconstructed by Sir Arthur Evans in the early 1900s, Knossos is tied to the myth of King Minos, the Labyrinth, and the Minotaur. I love that a coffee mug points back to the very dawn of Mediterranean civilization.
Greece#576120 · Global Icon SeriesMy Greece icon pairs a black interior with the Temple of Apollo, the ancient Doric sanctuary that anchors so much of the country's classical identity. As a national rather than single-city piece it leans on the broad image of Greek antiquity, columns, gods and oracles, rather than one skyline. The dramatic black liner is unusual in the series and gives the ruins a moody, archaeological weight I really like.
Thessaloniki#576121 · Global Icon SeriesThessaloniki, Greece's second city, with a dark blue interior. The front carries the White Tower, the round fifteenth-century waterfront fort that is the city's defining symbol and once a notorious Ottoman prison, while the back shows the Vergina Sun, the ancient Macedonian star tied to Philip II and Alexander. Collectors flag it as fairly common, but few mugs pack this much real history into one cup.
Gdynia#576122 · Global Icon SeriesGdynia, blue-lined, shows the tall ship Dar Pomorza riding before an industrial harbour skyline. Unlike its ancient neighbors, Gdynia was built almost from scratch in the 1920s when newly independent Poland needed its own modern seaport, growing from a fishing village in a single generation. A great maritime Global Icon and the youngest city in my Polish Tricity trio.
Braunschweig#576123 · Global Icon SeriesDark blue inside with the famous Brunswick Lion striding across the front, a bronze cast by Henry the Lion around 1166 and considered the first free-standing monument north of the Alps in the Middle Ages. The original sits in Dankwarderode Castle while a replica guards Burgplatz. This one ran roughly 2011 to 2015 and is genuinely hard to find now, a real catch for a German city run.
Gent#576124 · Global Icon SeriesGent, purple-lined, features Sint-Niklaaskerk, the Saint Nicholas Church begun in the early 1200s in blue-gray Tournai stone, one of Ghent's three famous medieval towers. Its single great crossing tower once held the city bells before the neighboring Belfry took over. A refined Belgian Global Icon, and Ghent's storied skyline even drew the painter Turner in 1825.
Salzburg#576125 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside with Schloss Leopoldskron, the lakeside rococo palace built in 1736 and made world famous as a filming location for The Sound of Music in 1965. Salzburg is also Mozart's birthplace and a UNESCO old town. Choosing the palace over the usual fortress view is a nice deep cut, a strong Austria entry in the series.
Poznan#576126 · Global Icon SeriesDark blue inside, with Poznan's Renaissance Town Hall on the outside. The real draw of that building is the pair of mechanical billy goats above the clock that emerge and butt heads twelve times every day at noon, a 1551 tradition and the city's beloved symbol. The mug shows the hall itself, but locals will tell you to come back at midday for the goats.
Cyprus#576127 · Global Icon SeriesThis brown-lined Cyprus Global Icon features the Tombs of the Kings at Paphos, a UNESCO site of rock-cut underground burial chambers from the Hellenistic and Roman eras, carved for high officials, not actual royalty despite the grand name. Paphos sits on the southwest coast and is also tied in myth to the birthplace of Aphrodite. A nice choice that skips the obvious beaches for genuine ancient stonework.
Malaga#576129 · Global Icon SeriesMalaga, the sun-soaked Costa del Sol port and birthplace of Pablo Picasso, gets a purple interior and a tree on the outside, a nod to the lush palms and gardens of this Andalusian beach city. The deeper landmarks are the Moorish Alcazaba fortress and the unfinished cathedral locals nickname La Manquita, the one-armed lady. A nice secondary Spanish city to round out a Madrid and Barcelona shelf.
Madrid#576132 · Global Icon SeriesMadrid's green-interior mug shows El Oso y el Madrono, the bear and the strawberry tree, which is the literal coat of arms of Madrid and exists as a beloved bronze statue at Puerta del Sol, sculpted by Antonio Navarro Santafe in 1967. Few city mugs are this faithful to a city's official crest. It is a charming, story-rich design and one of the more distinctive Spanish Icons, reportedly on the harder-to-find side.
Mykonos#576133 · Global Icon SeriesLight blue for the Aegean, and the design pulls in Little Venice, the row of 18th-century Venetian houses whose wooden balconies hang straight over the sea on Mykonos. Just above them stand the Kato Mili windmills the Venetians raised in the 16th century to grind wheat. Few Greek islands get their own icon mug, so this one feels like a real find.
Corfu#576134 · Global Icon SeriesCorfu shows an orange interior with the arcaded Liston street outside, the elegant colonnade that French engineers modeled on the Rue de Rivoli during Napoleon's brief occupation of the Ionian island. It fronts the vast Spianada, the largest square in the Balkans, where locals still play cricket, a sport left behind by 50 years of British rule. A wonderfully specific icon for a UNESCO-listed old town.
Gdansk#576135 · Global Icon SeriesGdansk, blue-lined, centers on the Neptune Fountain, the bronze sea-god who has guarded the city's Long Market since 1633 with the Baltic Old Town behind. Gdansk was also the birthplace of the Solidarity movement that helped topple communism. A handsome Polish piece, and it pairs perfectly with my Gdynia cup as two thirds of the Tricity.
Wroclaw#576136 · Global Icon SeriesWroclaw is the Polish city of bridges and dwarfs, and the catalog nails its oldest heart, Ostrow Tumski, Cathedral Island, where the twin-spired Cathedral of St John the Baptist rises. Mine runs a red interior with that Gothic church. The city is also famous for hundreds of little bronze gnome statues hidden across its streets, a quirk I wish had made the mug.
Seville#576139 · Global Icon SeriesGreen inside, with the flamenco dancer outside, the English-spelling counterpart to the Sevilla mug. Seville's old town packs in the Real Alcázar palace, the Plaza de España, and the towering cathedral where Christopher Columbus is entombed. The dancer captures the city's identity as the soul of flamenco and the home of the spring Feria de Abril. I keep this one beside its Sevilla sibling so the spelling pair tells its own little story.
Rhodes#576140 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside, showing the Acropolis of Lindos, the cliff top citadel crowned by the Doric Temple of Athena Lindia that took its final form around 300 BC. It sits on a one hundred sixteen meter promontory above the Aegean and ranks among Greece's most visited archaeological sites, later fortified by the Knights of St John. A serious historical pick for the Greek islands in this series.
Szczecin#576142 · Global Icon SeriesGreen inside with the Ducal Castle of the Pomeranian Dukes on the outside, the Renaissance seat of the House of Pomerania who ruled from this Oder-river city from 1121 to 1637. Begun in 1346 under Duke Barnim III, the castle was rebuilt after wartime damage and is now West Pomerania's great cultural center. Szczecin is a genuinely uncommon city in any Starbucks line, which makes this one a quiet trophy for a completist. A deep-cut Polish entry.
Alicante#576143 · Global Icon SeriesLight blue inside with the castle at Denia, a slightly surprising choice since Denia sits up the Costa Blanca from Alicante proper. That hilltop fortress has Moorish and Roman roots and looms over the marina town, anchoring a coastline of beaches and the palm groves the region is known for. A nice catch if you want the lesser-photographed corner of Spain's sun coast.
Moscow#576145 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside, of course, for Moscow. Instead of the predictable St. Basil's onion domes, this mug honors the main building of Moscow State University, one of Stalin's Seven Sisters skyscrapers from the early 1950s. At 240 meters it was the tallest building in Europe for nearly forty years, a wedding-cake monument to Soviet ambition. Choosing it over the Kremlin is an unusual and welcome design call.
Athens#576147 · Global Icon SeriesBlue inside with the Athens Tower outside, which is a curveball, since most people expect the Acropolis on a Greek mug. Pyrgos Athinon is the 103 meter, 28 story tower finished in 1971 and still the tallest building in all of Greece. A modernist office block standing in for the cradle of democracy makes this one of the more unexpected designs in the series.
Oktoberfest#576148 · Global Icon SeriesThe catalog says bagel, but on an Oktoberfest mug that golden ring is a Bavarian pretzel, the brezn that is the festival's edible mascot alongside the beer. Munich's Oktoberfest dates to 1810, when it began as a royal wedding celebration. There are several Oktoberfest Global Icons across the years, so this blue-interior version is one piece of a fun little sub-series worth chasing as a group.
Bielefeld#576150 · Global Icon SeriesBielefeld leans on its Old Town, but the real fun is the Bielefeld Conspiracy, a long-running German internet joke insisting the city does not exist. Owning a Starbucks mug that literally proves otherwise is a collector punchline I could not resist. German regional Global Icons like this are far less common than the headline cities.
Poland#576151 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside, with a Polish city view on the cream outside as the national entry. Poland anchors a Central European shelf alongside the city-specific Poznan and Potsdam-adjacent pieces, and the country-level Icons tend to use a composite skyline rather than one landmark. A solid foundational mug for a regional grouping.
Sevilla#576152 · Global Icon SeriesGreen inside, with a flamenco dancer mid-step outside. Sevilla is the Spanish-spelling twin of the Seville mug, and the dancer is the obvious choice since Andalusia is the birthplace of flamenco, that fierce blend of song, guitar, and stamping dance. The city is also home to the world's largest Gothic cathedral and the Giralda bell tower. Having both the Sevilla and Seville spellings is a fun collector quirk, the same city catalogued two ways.
Copenhagen#576153 · Global Icon SeriesCopenhagen runs red inside with the royal guards outside, the bearskin-capped soldiers who march daily to Amalienborg Palace, home of one of the oldest monarchies in the world. The Danish capital is also the city of Hans Christian Andersen and his Little Mermaid statue, the colorful Nyhavn harbor, and Tivoli Gardens, the 1843 amusement park that helped inspire Disneyland.
Brasil#576154 · Global Icon SeriesGreen interior with a barefoot boy and a football wrapping the outside, this is Brazil distilled to its purest passion, futebol. The Global Icon line leans into national identity here rather than a single landmark, and the green lining nods straight to the flag. In a country with five World Cup titles, no symbol reads more instantly than a kid and a ball, and it makes a warm, instantly legible piece in any country shelf run.
Rosario#576156 · Global Icon SeriesPurple inside with the Monumento Historico Nacional a la Bandera, Argentina's seventy meter flag monument on the Parana River in Rosario. It marks where Manuel Belgrano first raised the Argentine flag in 1812, and the monument was inaugurated in 1957 with Belgrano's crypt in its base. Rosario is also Lionel Messi's hometown, which makes this a sneaky good Argentina pickup.
Abu Dhabi#576159 · Global Icon SeriesGreen inside with the port outside, the capital of the UAE rendered through its working waterfront rather than the obvious Sheikh Zayed Mosque. Abu Dhabi sits on an island in the Persian Gulf and built its fortune on the oil discovered offshore in the late 1950s, so a port motif actually nods to how this desert city became one of the wealthiest places on earth.
Aruba#576160 · Global Icon SeriesLight blue inside with a tree and the ocean, that lone leaning tree being Aruba's beloved divi divi. Constant northeast trade winds bend the watapana tree permanently southwest, so islanders joke it works as a natural compass pointing the way. It is the unofficial national symbol of this dry Dutch Caribbean island, and a lovelier choice than another generic palm and beach.
Warsaw#576161 · Global Icon SeriesWarsaw is the phoenix capital, rebuilt brick by brick after the war, and its Old Town Market Square is a UNESCO site precisely because of that meticulous reconstruction. Mine carries a red interior and a sculptural figure outside, fitting for a city that also claims Chopin and the bronze Mermaid. Polish Global Icons like this and Krakow have a steady following among Eastern European collectors.
Costa Rica#576162 · Global Icon SeriesCosta Rica runs green inside with a tree frog outside, the red-eyed amphibian that has become the unofficial face of this biodiversity superpower, where a quarter of the land is protected park and rainforest. The country is famous for its pura vida philosophy, having abolished its army in 1948, and for cloud forests, volcanoes, and zip lines through the canopy.
Guatemala#576163 · Global Icon SeriesGuatemala's mug carries a red interior with the canary-yellow Santa Catalina Arch of Antigua on the front and the great Mayan temples of Tikal on the back, two of the country's defining landmarks. Guatemala is also a celebrated coffee origin, so this one has extra meaning on a Starbucks shelf. The arch, built so cloistered nuns could cross the street unseen, is one of Central America's most photographed sights.
Perú#576165 · Global Icon SeriesPeru, brown inside, with Machu Picchu wrapped outside and the catalog line crediting the Inca who built the ancient city. Hiram Bingham brought the 15th century citadel to world attention in 1911, though it had never truly been lost to locals, and it sits around 2,430 meters up a ridge above the Urubamba River. A clean country-level Global Icon like this anchors a South America shelf nicely.
Arequipa#576167 · Global Icon SeriesDark blue inside with an eagle outside, Peru's elegant second city known as the White City for its buildings of pale volcanic sillar stone. Arequipa sits in the shadow of the El Misti volcano and the colonial core is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The condor, the great Andean bird, is the regional symbol that more soars on this cup than any ordinary eagle.
Kingdom of Saudi Arabia#576168 · Global Icon SeriesThe catalog calls the scene Petra, but what is actually rendered is Hegra, Saudi Arabia's own Nabataean tomb city near AlUla, often nicknamed the Petra of Arabia. Hegra was the Nabataean kingdom's second city after Petra itself, and in 2008 it became Saudi Arabia's very first UNESCO World Heritage Site, with 111 monumental rock-cut tombs. A country-level Global Icon, so it stands in for a whole kingdom rather than a single town.
Puerto Rico#576169 · Global Icon SeriesThe brown interior frames the warm sandstone of Castillo San Felipe del Morro, the six level Spanish fortress that has guarded the mouth of San Juan Bay since the 1500s and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. King Charles I commissioned the first tower in 1539, and its walls run up to twenty five feet thick. This is the Global Icon Puerto Rico, a clean read on Old San Juan's most photographed silhouette.
Lima#576170 · Global Icon SeriesLima's pink-lined mug puts the enclosed wooden balconies of its colonial old town center stage, the de cajon screens that let viceregal ladies watch the street unseen. Those carved balconies trace back to Moorish mashrabiya tradition carried over through Spain, and they were central to UNESCO naming Lima's historic center a World Heritage Site, with the Torre Tagle Palace as the showpiece. A beautifully specific architectural detail rather than a generic plaza.
Oman#576171 · Global Icon SeriesThe brown mug shows Nizwa Fort, Oman's most visited monument, a seventeenth-century stronghold built in the 1650s under Imam Sultan bin Saif on foundations going back centuries earlier. Its huge drum tower rises about thirty-four meters and bristles with murder holes for pouring boiling oil and twenty-four mortar openings. Nizwa was once Oman's capital, so this is a genuinely apt landmark rather than a generic skyline.
Argentina#576172 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside with the man on horseback statue in Salta, the bronze Monument to Martin Miguel de Guemes inaugurated in 1931. Guemes was the gaucho general whose mounted militias held the northern frontier during Argentina's war of independence, and he died of a battle wound in 1821. The statue sits at the foot of Cerro Bernardo, making this one of the more story-rich country mugs.
Lebanon#576174 · Global Icon SeriesLebanon's brown-lined national mug centers on the cedar tree, the same emblem that flies at the center of the country's flag. The famed Cedars of God grove in the Kadisha Valley holds some of the oldest cedars on earth, trees prized since antiquity for the temples of the Phoenicians and beyond. A country icon built on a living symbol thousands of years old, which gives it more weight than a typical skyline piece.
El Salvador#576175 · Global Icon SeriesEl Salvador puts Izalco volcano front and center, brown-lined, with the San Salvador skyline wrapping the back. Izalco erupted so reliably through the 1800s and 1900s that sailors nicknamed it the Lighthouse of the Pacific. This Central American Global Icon is a relatively common but genuinely charming volcano mug, and I love that the country leads with its fire.
Sharjah#576178 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside, with the Sharjah fort, the Al Hisn, outside. Sharjah is the third-largest emirate in the UAE and has staked its identity on heritage rather than glitz, earning the title of UNESCO Arab Capital of Culture and Cultural Capital of the Arab World. The restored white fort once guarded the ruling Al Qasimi family. A culture-first emirate getting a fort instead of a skyscraper feels exactly right.
Jeddah#576179 · Global Icon SeriesGreen inside, and the catalog notes the Crown Prince's Historic Jeddah Revival Project, the restoration push for Al Balad, the old town whose coral stone houses and Nasseef House earned UNESCO World Heritage status. Jeddah is the historic gateway for pilgrims heading to Mecca on the Red Sea coast. This is a later issue tied to a real Saudi heritage initiative, which makes it a more topical and unusual entry than the standard city mugs.
Bahrain#576180 · Global Icon SeriesThere is real lore here: Bahrain's first Global Icon showed the Pearl Roundabout monument, which the government demolished in 2011 during the Arab Spring, forcing a redesign and making the original legendary among collectors. Mine is the standard later version with the dhow boat on the brown exterior, the dhow being the traditional pearling sailboat of the Gulf. A fascinating piece to own precisely because of the story behind it.
Qatar#576181 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside, with the Arabian oryx, Qatar's national animal, set against the Doha skyline on the reverse. The oryx is the namesake of Qatar Airways and was hunted nearly to extinction before a careful reintroduction brought it back. Collectors note there is a rarer first version sold only inside Qatar, so confirm which one you hold, but this standard Global Icon is the one most of us find.
Dubai#576182 · Global Icon SeriesDubai's dark blue Global Icon shows a gypsum building, a fitting nod to the Al Fahidi Fort, the city's oldest structure from around 1787, built of coral and gypsum and now housing the Dubai Museum. The contrast with Dubai's modern skyline of the Burj Khalifa is the whole point, the emirate's roots before the oil boom. A quietly historic pick for a city usually shown as glass and steel.
Morocco#576183 · Global Icon SeriesA country mug rather than a city one, blue inside, fronted by the Bahia Palace in Marrakech. Bahia means brilliance, and the 19th-century palace lives up to it with carved cedar ceilings, zellij tilework and courtyards built by a grand vizier to dazzle. It is one of the few global icons to render Islamic ornament in detail, which makes it a standout next to the usual towers and bridges.
Riyadh#576184 · Global Icon SeriesGreen inside, the desert capital of Saudi Arabia. The catalog text says port, which is plainly an error since Riyadh sits deep in the interior with no coastline, so the art shows the Kingdom Centre Tower with its keyhole crown or the historic Masmak Fortress. A quietly interesting one precisely because of that misdescribed detail.
Kuwait#576185 · Global Icon SeriesKuwait's brown-lined icon keeps it spare, just a small boat on open water, a nod to the country's pre-oil life as a pearl-diving and dhow trading port at the head of the Gulf. Before the oil boom the wooden dhow was the engine of the whole economy, which is why the boat, not a skyscraper, carries the national identity here. A quiet, almost minimalist piece, and Gulf-state mugs like this do not turn up often.
United Arab Emirates#576187 · Global Icon SeriesA UAE country icon, brown inside, the exterior built around an eagle. That bird is the falcon, the national emblem of the Emirates and the centerpiece of its coat of arms, with falconry an ancient Bedouin tradition still cherished today. Starbucks chose heritage over the obvious Burj Khalifa here, which makes it a quieter, more thoughtful piece than most Gulf mugs.
Florida#576188 · Global Icon SeriesFlorida leans into the swamp with a green-lined cup and an alligator outside, the unmistakable mascot of the Everglades. That vast river of grass is the only place on earth where alligators and crocodiles coexist in the wild. A fun, faintly cheeky US state entry that I keep right alongside the other American Global Icons.
Banff#576190 · Global Icon SeriesBanff is Canada's oldest national park, deep in the Alberta Rockies, and this dark green mug pairs cream mountains with a grizzly bear on the front, the two things the park is genuinely known for. Collectors typically see it run fifty to a hundred dollars, so it sits in the "somewhat hard to find" tier. The green interior really sells the alpine feel.
Twin Cities#576191 · Global Icon SeriesTwin Cities pairs Minneapolis and St. Paul on one navy lined mug, and the waterfall on the white exterior is Minnehaha Falls, the 53 foot cascade Longfellow made famous in The Song of Hiawatha. It is a smart pick, one shared natural landmark for two cities that compete on nearly everything else. A regional American icon that is easy to miss and good to have.
Zurich#576193 · Global Icon SeriesZurich anchors the Global Icon series with Switzerland's banking and watchmaking capital, and ours carries a navy interior with a white exterior featuring a train, a nod to Swiss rail precision and the city's place at the heart of one of the world's most punctual networks. Zurich's main station, completed in 1871, is among the busiest in Europe, so the locomotive motif fits a city that practically runs on timetables. A clean, common Icon, but the train detail makes it stand out on the shelf.
Wales#576196 · Global Icon SeriesFew country-level Global Icons are as on the nose as Wales, where the red dragon, Y Ddraig Goch, has flown on the national flag for centuries and traces back to Arthurian legend. Ours runs a brown interior against a cream body with that fierce dragon. I love that Starbucks went mythic creature instead of a building here, a rare choice in this series.
Belfast#576200 · Global Icon SeriesThe "large fish" is the Big Fish, John Kindness's ten-meter ceramic salmon installed on Donegall Quay in 1999, its tiles printed with texts from Belfast's history. It nods to the legend of the Salmon of Knowledge and to the cleaned-up River Lagan, the blue strip below it. A genuinely clever icon for Northern Ireland's capital, and one of my favorite back stories in the series.
Vancouver#576201 · Global Icon SeriesVancouver, brown inside, the cream exterior with two trees and a bridge. That span is the Lions Gate Bridge, the 1938 suspension bridge linking the city to the North Shore through Stanley Park, with the towering coastal forest framing it. Vancouver routinely ranks among the world's most livable cities, and this is the mainland counterpart to my Vancouver Island icon.
Edmonton#576202 · Global Icon SeriesEdmonton's blue-lined cup carries the Edmonton Queen riverboat cruising the North Saskatchewan River below the Alberta capital's skyline. The river valley here is North America's largest stretch of urban parkland, ribboning right through downtown. Collectors note the Edmonton Global Icon is one of the harder Canadian releases to track down, so I was glad to land this one.
Manchester#576204 · Global Icon SeriesManchester's purple-interior mug shows a grand domed building, which is the city's Central Library, the striking 1934 circular neoclassical landmark on St Peter's Square modeled loosely on the Pantheon. It is a fitting symbol for the world's first industrial city and the home of two football giants. A respectable English Icon beyond London, good for a UK-focused collector filling out the country.
Las Vegas, Global icon Collectible#576206 · Global Icon SeriesLas Vegas gets the only landmark that matters to tourists: the Welcome to Fabulous Las Vegas neon sign, designed by Betty Willis in 1959 and famously never copyrighted, which is why you see it reproduced everywhere. The brown-and-cream treatment frames that sign as the city's true icon, more recognizable than any single casino. A clean, instantly readable American entry that travelers grab on sight.
Montreal#576207 · Global Icon SeriesMontreal earns a green interior here, fitting for a city built around Mount Royal, the Frederick Law Olmsted park the metropolis takes its name from. Olmsted, the man behind New York's Central Park, deliberately kept it wild rather than manicured. The garden-and-house motif leans on Quebec's heritage greenery rather than the obvious Notre-Dame Basilica, which gives this one a softer, more lived-in feel than most Global Icons.
England Coat of Arms#576208 · Global Icon SeriesThis is the England Coat of Arms Global Icon, the same heraldic design built on the three golden lions passant of the medieval English crown, paired with William Shakespeare on the opposite side. The arms trace back to the second Great Seal of Richard I and stayed in use until 1340. A clean duplicate listing of the England country mug that rounds out my UK run.
Charlotte, global icon Collectible#576209 · Global Icon SeriesCharlotte runs red inside with a cream exterior of city road signs, a nod to the Queen City named for Queen Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelenburg. It is the second largest US banking hub after New York, anchored by Bank of America's tower, and the home of NASCAR's Hall of Fame. The road-sign motif is a fun departure from the usual skyline approach.
Vancouver Island#576210 · Global Icon SeriesVancouver Island, dark green inside, the catalog reads sharks in green waters but those are orcas, killer whales, the apex marine mammals that patrol the Salish Sea. The other side carries British Columbia's Parliament Building in Victoria. Collectors note this one is somewhat hard to find, and the orca-and-legislature pairing makes it one of the more distinctive Canadian Global Icons.
Ireland#576211 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside, cream outside, and the Celtic harp, the only national emblem in the world that is a musical instrument and the symbol stamped on Irish coins, the presidential seal, and yes, a certain stout. The gold harp on Ireland's coat of arms is modeled on the medieval Brian Boru harp held at Trinity College Dublin. A country mug that picks the most quietly Irish icon imaginable.
London, Global icon collectible mu#576211 · Global Icon SeriesLondon's Global Icon mug wraps a fairy-tale castle around a cream body with green inside, the Tower of London, the 900-year-old Norman fortress on the Thames that still guards the Crown Jewels and its famous resident ravens. As one of the flagship cities in the worldwide Icon line, London turns up often, so it is an easy and affordable pickup, but the clean castle silhouette makes it one of the more handsome UK entries in the series.
Lausanne#576212 · Global Icon SeriesLausanne climbs the steep northern shore of Lake Geneva and is best known as the Olympic Capital, the headquarters of the International Olympic Committee since 1915 and home to the Olympic Museum. The light blue, beach and lighthouse imagery points to its lakefront Ouchy district rather than the medieval Gothic cathedral up the hill. A Swiss city with a global institution baked into its identity, which I always find a fun layer.
Hamptons#576213 · Global Icon SeriesThe Hamptons is the famous string of seaside villages on Long Island's South Fork, so a beach and a lighthouse on a cream body with a light-blue interior is spot on. The lighthouse is Montauk Point, commissioned by George Washington in 1792 and New York State's oldest. This is a destination icon rather than a city, which makes it one of the more unusual American entries in the line.
St.Louis#576214 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside, cream outside, and the Gateway Arch sweeping across it, which is the only landmark St. Louis ever needed. Eero Saarinen's stainless steel catenary curve rises 630 feet, making it the tallest man-made monument in the United States, and it was completed in 1965 to mark the city's role as the gateway to the western frontier. You can ride a tram of tiny tram cars right up inside the curve to the top. A textbook Global Icon, one city, one unmistakable silhouette.
Nashville#576215 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside, with a microphone on the front, which is exactly right for Music City. Nashville is home to the Grand Ole Opry and the Country Music Hall of Fame, and its Ryman Auditorium is called the Mother Church of Country Music. The mic motif sidesteps the obvious replica Parthenon in Centennial Park, leaning instead into the sound that made the city famous worldwide.
St. Gallen#576216 · Global Icon SeriesThe cream body carries the Abbey Library of St. Gallen, and what a choice it is, the oldest library in Switzerland and one of the oldest monastery libraries in the world, with roots back to 612. Its Rococo hall, built 1758 to 1767 by Peter Thumb, holds around 2,100 manuscripts and was named a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1983. A small Swiss city most collectors have never visited, so the mug itself does a lot of teaching.
Edinburgh#576219 · Global Icon SeriesEdinburgh wraps the Scottish capital's medieval Old Town around this navy-lined cup, crowned by Edinburgh Castle perched on its volcanic crag above the city. The whole UNESCO-listed center, from the castle down the Royal Mile to Holyrood, is built on a glacial ridge of ancient rock. A handsome, very ownable piece in the worldwide Global Icon line.
Orange County#576220 · Global Icon SeriesThe surfer on blue sea is Orange County's calling card, anchored by Huntington Beach, the self-styled Surf City USA, where the pier juts 1,850 feet into the Pacific and hosts international contests. The navy interior keeps it crisp. This 2012 surf design is retired and runs on the harder-to-find side, a desirable California piece that captures the laid-back beach lifestyle better than any building could.
Basel#576221 · Global Icon SeriesBasel sits where Switzerland, France and Germany meet on the Rhine, and the river-house scene on the cream exterior captures the old town tumbling down to the water. The light blue interior reads like the Rhine itself, where locals famously swim downstream in summer. A quieter Swiss entry that I value for filling out the country set.
Utah#576222 · Global Icon SeriesUtah, orange inside, the cream exterior featuring a skier. The hook is the state license-plate boast, the Greatest Snow on Earth, Utah's famously dry Wasatch powder that drew the 2002 Winter Olympics to Salt Lake City. A state-level Global Icon rather than a single city, so it leans on the ski culture of Park City and the Cottonwood canyons instead of a downtown skyline.
Switzerland#576223 · Global Icon SeriesBrown body with a band of alpine flowers, an easy, pastoral read on Switzerland that skips any one landmark for the country's storybook mountain image. Think edelweiss and gentian on high meadows, the same flora that fills the slopes below the Matterhorn and the Jungfrau. It pairs as the gentler, floral sibling to the snowy-cabin Swiss icon mug. A soft, decorative take rather than a postcard building.
Arizona#576224 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside, cream outside with the Welcome to Seligman, Birthplace of Historic Route 66 sign. That tiny town earned the title in 1987 when barber Angel Delgadillo rallied the state to designate the road historic, and Seligman now anchors the longest unbroken stretch of the Mother Road. The town reportedly helped inspire Pixar's Cars, so this is pure Route 66 nostalgia.
Cardiff#576226 · Global Icon SeriesNavy inside, cream outside with St Fagans, the open-air National Museum of History just outside the Welsh capital where reconstructed historic buildings show centuries of Welsh life. Cardiff is the capital of Wales, and choosing St Fagans over the castle is a thoughtful, locally loved pick. A characterful UK entry that rewards a collector who knows the lesser-celebrated icons.
Berne#576227 · Global Icon SeriesBerne is Switzerland's capital, and the bear on the cream exterior ties straight to the Barengraben bear pit, where the city has kept live bears since the 1400s, the same bear on its coat of arms. The green interior echoes the Aare that loops the medieval old town. It was released after Geneva, Lucerne and Zurich, so it is a slightly later Swiss find.
Northern Ireland#576229 · Global Icon SeriesNorthern Ireland's mountain on the cream body evokes the Mourne Mountains, the granite range that inspired C.S. Lewis's Narnia and sweeps down to the sea in the famous song. The brown interior suits the moody, peat-toned palette. It is one of the quieter UK and Ireland entries in the Global Icon series, easy to overlook next to the showier landmark mugs but a clean grab for anyone building the full set.
Glasgow#576230 · Global Icon SeriesGlasgow, Scotland's largest city, wears a cream exterior with a blue interior and a layout of the city's silhouette. It is the home of Charles Rennie Mackintosh and a Victorian merchant grid built on shipbuilding wealth along the Clyde. The motto here is "People Make Glasgow," and the mug stands in nicely beside my Edinburgh pieces to round out the Scottish corner of the shelf.
Jacksonville#576231 · Global Icon SeriesCream exterior with two bridges crossing the St. Johns River, the wide waterway that splits this northeast Florida city, which actually claims more bridges than most American cities its size. The blue Main Street Bridge and the Dames Point cable stayed span are the usual stars. Jacksonville is one of the more obscure US Global Icons, so it rarely surfaces compared with Miami or Orlando.
Indianapolis#576232 · Global Icon SeriesRed interior and a race car, of course, for the home of the Indianapolis 500 and the Brickyard, the Indianapolis Motor Speedway that has run since 1911 and still keeps a yard of original bricks at the start finish line. The 500 is billed as the greatest spectacle in racing. No skyline needed when a city is this completely defined by one Memorial Day weekend.
Memphis#576234 · Global Icon SeriesMemphis puts a man playing guitar on cream with a green interior, a direct salute to the city that birthed the blues on Beale Street and rock and roll at Sun Studio, home turf for Elvis Presley, B.B. King, and Johnny Cash. Music is the only landmark Memphis needs. It is a somewhat harder-to-find US Icon, and lots including Memphis have moved in the hundreds, so the guitar mug carries real collector appeal.
Miami#576236 · Global Icon SeriesMiami's light-blue mug captures the South Beach promenade, the Ocean Drive strip of pastel Art Deco hotels along the sand that defines the city's neon-soaked, palm-lined glamour. The Miami Beach Architectural District holds the largest concentration of 1930s Art Deco buildings in the world. A breezy, instantly Miami design and a common, affordable US Icon that still looks great in a sunbelt grouping with LA and the Florida mugs.
Colorado#576237 · Global Icon SeriesColorado takes a green interior with a buffalo in a forest outside, evoking the Rocky Mountain state's wild high country and its herds of bison. The Centennial State joined the Union in 1876, a hundred years after independence, and is famous for fourteeners, ski towns like Aspen and Vail, and Denver, the Mile High City sitting exactly 5,280 feet above sea level.
Ohio#576238 · Global Icon SeriesDespite the catalog calling it an ancient building, Ohio's red mug actually carries a river steamboat on the front with the George Rogers Clark statue and the Ohio River on the back, a fitting nod to the state's riverboat heritage. It was produced in China and runs somewhat hard to find. A solid, underrated pickup for anyone assembling the full USA Global Icon map.
Alaska#576239 · Global Icon SeriesGreen inside, cream outside with a reindeer, the Last Frontier state rather than a single city. Reindeer were actually imported to Alaska from Siberia starting in the 1890s to feed Native communities, and herding still continues on the Seward Peninsula today. A warm, folksy design for the largest and least populated US state, where the herds outnumber the people in many districts.
Detroit#576240 · Global Icon SeriesThe Detroit art shows an Egyptian figure, an unexpected choice that points to the Spirit of Detroit, the giant bronze seated figure downtown holding a sun and a family, sculpted by Marshall Fredericks in 1958. Detroit is of course the Motor City, birthplace of Ford's assembly line and Motown Records. The slightly mysterious imagery makes this one of the more puzzling US Global Icons to pin down at a glance.
Seattle#576242 · Global Icon SeriesGreen inside, cream outside, with a fish and a boat. This is the hometown mug, and instead of the Space Needle it goes for Pike Place Market, where fishmongers theatrically toss salmon and where the very first Starbucks opened in 1971 just up the street at 1912 Pike Place. The fish-and-boat motif salutes the working waterfront on Elliott Bay. For a collector this is sentimental, the city where the whole green-apron story began.
Orlando#576243 · Global Icon SeriesThe whale breaching out of the water points straight at SeaWorld Orlando and its famous orcas, a nod to Central Florida's theme-park identity rather than a downtown skyline. The blue interior plays up the ocean theme. It is a playful, family-vacation kind of mug, the sort of cheerful tourist design that gives the USA Global Icon shelf its variety alongside the more serious landmark pieces.
Waikiki#576244 · Global Icon SeriesWaikiki is the legendary crescent of beach below Diamond Head where Hawaiian tourism was born, and a hula dancer is exactly the icon I want fronting it. Mine pairs a blue interior with a cream exterior carrying that dancing island girl. The Waikiki and broader Hawaii Global Icons turn up often in collector hauls because of heavy tourist foot traffic, which keeps them affordable and easy to find with the tag still on.
Denver#576245 · Global Icon SeriesThe Denver mug puts the Rocky Mountains and water along the bottom, fitting for the Mile High City that sits exactly 5,280 feet above sea level, marked by a step on the Colorado State Capitol. Denver is the gateway to the Front Range and the famous Red Rocks Amphitheatre carved into the foothills. The understated mountain-and-stream art is a nice change from the busier US icons.
San Antonio#576246 · Global Icon SeriesNavy inside, cream outside with trees, water and a bridge, a clear nod to San Antonio's famous River Walk winding below street level through downtown Texas. The city is of course home to the Alamo, the 1836 mission and battle that became a Texan rallying cry. A warm, instantly recognizable American city mug in the Global Icon line.
Atlanta#576248 · Global Icon SeriesDark green inside with a bridge over a blue lake among the trees, leaning into the Georgia capital's leafy side rather than its downtown towers. Atlanta calls itself the city in a forest for its dense tree canopy, and it grew up as a railroad hub before becoming the home of Coca-Cola and host of the 1996 Olympics. A calm, green read on a city usually shown as skyline.
Portland#576249 · Global Icon SeriesDark blue inside, and the outside leans into the Pacific Northwest with a mountain and evergreens, Mount Hood looming over the city.
