Portland sits where the Willamette meets the Columbia, and its nickname Stumptown comes from the tree stumps left as the town boomed in the 1840s. The forest-and-peak imagery captures the green identity locals are proud of.
Pittsburgh#576252 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside, and the cream exterior centers Point State Park's fountain, where the Allegheny and Monongahela meet to form the Ohio. That fountain jets water up to roughly 150 feet at the exact tip where the three rivers converge, drawing from a fourth underground aquifer. Sellers routinely tag the Pittsburgh Icon as extremely rare and hard to find, so it tends to command attention.
Boston#576253 · Global Icon SeriesThe man on horseback is Paul Revere, immortalized for his 1775 midnight ride, and the green interior is pure Boston, from the Common to the Celtics. Anchoring the mug in Revolutionary history rather than a skyline suits the cradle of American independence perfectly. A handsome, easy-to-love US entry with cream sides and that unmistakable Boston green.
Philadelphia#576255 · Global Icon SeriesGreen inside, and the cream exterior carries Independence Hall, the brick Georgian building the catalog reads as an ancient structure. This is where both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution were debated and signed, and its tower once held the Liberty Bell. Listings flag the Philadelphia Icon as somewhat hard to find, with the city skyline filling the reverse.
Hawaii#576256 · Global Icon SeriesMy Hawaii icon pairs a brown interior with a white body and an outrigger canoe, the va'a that Polynesian voyagers sailed across thousands of miles of open Pacific to settle these islands. Rather than a single building, it celebrates the seafaring heritage of the fiftieth state. Hawaii is also a true coffee origin thanks to Kona on the Big Island, so this one earns a special spot among my Starbucks pieces.
Austin#576257 · Global Icon SeriesGreen inside, cream outside with a man playing guitar, capturing Austin's claim as the Live Music Capital of the World. The Texas capital backs that up with hundreds of venues and the South by Southwest and Austin City Limits festivals, plus the long-running Austin City Limits TV show. The lone guitarist is a fitting stand-in for a city whose unofficial motto is Keep Austin Weird.
San Francisco#576258 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside, cream outside, with the Golden Gate Bridge front and center. The bridge's color is not red but a custom shade called International Orange, chosen by architect Irving Morrow so it would stand out against the fog rather than the Navy's preferred black and yellow stripes. When it opened in 1937 it was the longest suspension span in the world, and it remains the single most photographed thing in the city.
Tampa#576259 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside, cream outside, with the Sunshine Skyway Bridge stretching cars across the water, the cable-stayed span over Tampa Bay linking St. Petersburg to Terra Ceia. The current bridge opened in 1987 with its signature yellow cables after a tragic 1980 ship collision destroyed the old one, and it is now an Florida icon often called one of the world's most beautiful bridges. Collector listings note the Tampa Icon is somewhat hard to find, with related city series mugs running roughly fifty to seventy dollars. A handsome Gulf Coast entry.
Sacramento#576260 · Global Icon SeriesBlue inside, cream outside with an old building that reads as the gold domed California State Capitol in Sacramento. The city was the western terminus of the Pony Express and the launch point of the 1849 Gold Rush, with Sutter's Fort at its historic heart. A solid California state capital mug for the North American shelf.
Niagara Falls#576261 · Global Icon SeriesBlue inside, cream outside, with the cascade front and center. Niagara is not the tallest waterfall but it moves a staggering volume, over 168,000 cubic meters of water every minute across the Horseshoe, American and Bridal Veil falls. The reverse typically carries the Niagara SkyWheel and Clifton Hill. A reliably popular tourist-town icon that turns up often and stays affordable.
Fort Worth#576262 · Global Icon SeriesFort Worth puts a longhorn bull on white with a brown lining, exactly right for the Texas city that brands itself Cowtown. Its Stockyards district still runs a twice-daily cattle drive, real longhorns walked down the brick street, the last of its kind. A great Western piece, and Fort Worth is one of the less common US Global Icon cities to find.
Cleveland#576263 · Global Icon SeriesCleveland goes green inside with a statue rising at the center of a building outside, the Soldiers' and Sailors' Monument on Public Square, a 125-foot Civil War column dedicated in 1894 and topped by the Goddess of Freedom. The city is also home to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, and a stone's throw away sits Claes Oldenburg's giant Free Stamp sculpture.
Phoenix#576265 · Global Icon SeriesPhoenix, blue inside with saguaro cacti standing on the cream outside. The saguaro is the right emblem, found only in the Sonoran Desert and able to live well over 150 years, growing its first arm only after decades. The city is named for the mythical bird reborn from ashes, a nod to the Hohokam canals settlers rebuilt the modern town upon.
Los Angeles#576266 · Global Icon SeriesLos Angeles leans into pure California fantasy here, a row of palm trees on cream with the signature green interior, no Hollywood sign or skyline, just the swaying fronds that say sunshine and Sunset Boulevard. It is a clean, breezy design that pairs naturally with the San Francisco and other West Coast Icons. A very common US city in the line, so it is a budget-friendly building block rather than a holy grail.
New York City#576267 · Global Icon SeriesGreen inside and crowned by the Statue of Liberty, the obvious but unbeatable choice for New York. A gift from France in 1886, Lady Liberty's copper skin turned green through decades of natural patina, which makes the green lining feel almost deliberate. As a flagship city this mug is one of the most produced and easiest to find in the whole Global Icon line.
Hong Kong#576268 · Global Icon SeriesCream exterior, orange inside, and a tram on the front, the double decker Ding Ding that has clattered along Hong Kong Island's north shore since 1904 and is one of the oldest tram systems still running. Hong Kong is famous for its skyline crammed against Victoria Harbour, but the tram is the local heartbeat. A nice restrained choice for a city that could have led with neon and ferries.
New Mexico#576269 · Global Icon SeriesA state mug, light blue inside, with little rectangular adobe houses that capture New Mexico's signature Pueblo architecture, the flat-roofed earthen building style seen at Taos Pueblo, continuously inhabited for over a thousand years. The look defines Santa Fe, whose ordinances still mandate the adobe aesthetic. It is one of the more design-distinct US state icons and a quiet favorite for that reason.
Chengdu#576271 · Global Icon SeriesChengdu earns the most charming icon of any Chinese city, a giant panda on a cream exterior with a dark blue interior, and for good reason: the Sichuan capital is the panda capital of the world, home to the famous Chengdu Research Base where you can watch cubs tumble. Beyond the bears it is a UNESCO City of Gastronomy, the birthplace of fiery Sichuan hotpot and mapo tofu.
Changchun#576272 · Global Icon SeriesChangchun, capital of Jilin in China's northeast, wears a blue interior with a clock-towered building outside, but the real story is the city itself: it served as Xinjing, capital of the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo from 1932, where the deposed last emperor Puyi was installed. It later became the cradle of Chinese cinema as home to Changchun Film Studio, the first major studio of the People's Republic, and the country's first automobile base.
Nanchang#576273 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside with a cream exterior showing an ancient building, the Tengwang Pavilion, the Jiangxi landmark immortalized in Wang Bo's celebrated Tang-dynasty preface. Nanchang carries heavy modern weight too as the birthplace of the People's Liberation Army after the 1927 uprising. Like its sister Yuewang and Yueyang towers, the pavilion has been rebuilt many times, the current version dating to the 1980s.
Jinan#576274 · Global Icon SeriesLight blue inside with a temple style structure for Jinan, the Shandong provincial capital known across China as the City of Springs, home to Baotu Spring, once crowned the finest spring under heaven, and the Thousand Buddha Mountain temples. The reverse often shows the Quancheng Square skyline. A solid mainland China icon, and the spring city identity is genuinely distinct from the usual skyline mugs.
Tianjin#576275 · Global Icon SeriesTianjin, China, purple inside, the exterior built around the Century Clock the catalog notes. That clock is no ordinary timepiece: it stands nearly forty meters tall, weighs about a hundred and seventy tons, and rings the river near Tianjin Station with twelve bronze reliefs of the zodiac constellations. The Jiefang Bridge fills out the back. A common but handsome industrial-port icon.
Sanya#576276 · Global Icon SeriesOrange inside, cream outside, with a beach and palm trees. Sanya sits at the southern tip of Hainan Island and is China's tropical resort capital, often nicknamed the Hawaii of China or the Oriental Hawaii. It shares roughly the same latitude as Hawaii, which is why Starbucks went straight for the sand and palms rather than any building. This is the warm, vacation end of the Chinese Global Icon run.
Chongqing#576277 · Global Icon SeriesChongqing takes a purple interior with a soaring tower outside, fitting for one of the most dramatic cities on earth, a mega municipality of stacked highways, hillside stilt houses, and the Yangtze and Jialing rivers meeting below. It is the gateway to the Three Gorges cruises and famous for a numbingly spicy hotpot that rivals neighboring Sichuan's.
Shenzhen#576279 · Global Icon SeriesGreen inside, cream outside, with a long ancient building structure. The irony is that Shenzhen was a fishing village until 1980, when it became China's first Special Economic Zone and exploded into a tech megacity in a single generation. The sprawling traditional structure shown is the Hakka walled village at Crane Lake, one of the few old landmarks in an otherwise brand-new skyline. An old building standing in for the country's newest city is a quietly poetic choice.
Zhengzhou#576280 · Global Icon SeriesZhengzhou, capital of Henan, sits near the cradle of Chinese civilization and the famed Shaolin Temple at nearby Songshan, birthplace of kung fu. The building on mine, set against a yellow interior, salutes a city that was one of China's ancient Shang dynasty capitals. A major rail hub today, Zhengzhou is the kind of populous heartland city whose Global Icon rarely escapes the domestic market.
Shenyang#576281 · Global Icon SeriesPurple inside, cream outside, with two decorative pillars. Those are Huabiao, the carved ceremonial columns that flank the gates of the Mukden Palace, the Manchu imperial complex Shenyang built before the Qing dynasty moved its capital to Beijing. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site and the only surviving palace of its kind outside the Forbidden City. The deep purple is a regal, slightly unusual color for the series.
Beijing#576282 · Global Icon SeriesBeijing's yellow-lined mug shows a pathway leading to a temple, evoking the Forbidden City and the imperial heart of China's capital. Yellow was the emperor's color, reserved for the Son of Heaven, so that interior choice is quietly perfect. Chinese-market Global Icons can be tricky to source abroad, which makes a tidy Beijing a satisfying get.
Hefei#576283 · Global Icon SeriesHefei, capital of Anhui province, gets a red interior and a figure seated on a throne, Lord Bao, the legendary incomparably upright Song-dynasty judge born here and still revered across China for his fairness. The city's Baogong Temple and memorial park honor him. It is a clever choice to put a person rather than a skyline on a city mug, and a deep cut few Western collectors would recognize.
Ningbo#576285 · Global Icon SeriesThat long ancient structure on the cream body is the Tianyi Pavilion, China's oldest surviving private library, built between 1561 and 1566 by Ming war minister Fan Qin. Its name means roughly that water is first of all elements, a deliberate charm against fire, and its six-room layout and pool were designed to guard the books from flame. It still holds rare Song and Yuan editions, a quietly bookish choice for a city mug.
Changsha#576286 · Global Icon SeriesChangsha gets the same Global Icon treatment, blue inside with a grand clock building outside, though the Hunan capital is best known for Yuelu Mountain, the ancient Yuelu Academy, and Orange Isle in the Xiang River, where a giant sculpture of a young Mao Zedong gazes over the water. Mao studied here, which makes Changsha a pilgrimage city in modern Chinese history.
Xining#576288 · Global Icon SeriesXining sits on the Tibetan Plateau as the gateway to Qinghai, and the two bulls on mine surely nod to the yaks of that high grassland country. It pairs a light blue interior with the cream body. Nearby Qinghai Lake is China's largest salt lake, and Kumbum Monastery anchors the region's Tibetan Buddhist culture, context that makes this remote plateau city far more interesting than it first looks.
Shijiazhuang#576289 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside, cream outside, with a stone bridge arching over a river. That is the Zhaozhou Bridge, also called the Anji Bridge, just outside Shijiazhuang in Hebei. Built around the year 605 during the Sui dynasty, it is the world's oldest surviving open-spandrel segmental arch stone bridge, an engineering leap that Europe would not match for centuries. For an otherwise low-profile provincial capital to be represented by a fourteen-hundred-year-old bridge is a real treat.
Dalian#576290 · Global Icon SeriesDalian is a port city on China's Liaodong Peninsula, known for its mild seaside climate, European-flavored squares, and a deep football culture, which explains the soccer ball on this dark blue and cream mug. The city's club dominated early Chinese professional football, so the imagery is a real local nod rather than generic sport. A good example of how the China Global Icon series digs into city identity beyond the obvious.
Xiamen#576291 · Global Icon SeriesXiamen is a breezy coastal city facing Taiwan, famous for car-free Gulangyu Island, a UNESCO site of colonial villas and pianos. The two flamingos on mine match its reputation as a garden-on-the-sea with lush birdlife and a blue interior. Xiamen also hosts the egret as its city symbol, so the wading-bird theme fits this gentle, leisure-minded port perfectly.
Xi'an#576292 · Global Icon SeriesXi'an was the eastern terminus of the Silk Road and home to the Terracotta Army, so a warrior gripping a sword is the perfect emblem. Mine has a brown interior with that armed figure outside. Qin Shi Huang's buried clay soldiers, unearthed by farmers in 1974, number in the thousands and no two faces are alike, which is the detail that always sells this city for me.
Kunming#576293 · Global Icon SeriesKunming is Yunnan's capital, nicknamed the Spring City for its famously mild year-round climate, and its signature wonder is the Stone Forest, a vast karst field of limestone pinnacles east of town. Those petrified-looking spires are a UNESCO South China Karst site and carry the Sani people's legend of Ashima. A yellow interior with white outer monuments makes for one of the brighter, cleaner Chinese entries in the band.
Qingdao#576294 · Global Icon SeriesBlue inside, cream outside with a house above the water, nodding to Qingdao's German colonial old town on China's Shandong coast. The city was leased to Germany in 1898, which is exactly why China's most famous beer, Tsingtao, was founded here in 1903 by German and British brewers. A handsome, less common China city in the Global Icon range.
Wuhu#576295 · Global Icon SeriesWuhu is a Yangtze river city in Anhui province, and the statue on mine nods to its Buddhist heritage at Guangji Temple or the sculptures dotting central Jinghu Park. It pairs a maroon interior with a cream exterior. Lesser-known Chinese cities like Wuhu are the deep cuts of the Global Icon line, harder to source abroad and prized by completists chasing the full China set.
Hangzhou#576296 · Global Icon SeriesHangzhou's mug shows Leifeng Pagoda, the West Lake landmark first built in 975 AD that collapsed in 1924 and was rebuilt in 2002, set against a dark-green interior. The pagoda is tied to the beloved Legend of the White Snake and is one of the classic Ten Scenes of West Lake. Hangzhou is also where Marco Polo marveled at "the finest city in the world," which makes this an especially storied entry.
China#576297 · Global Icon SeriesThe national China icon is unmistakable, a roaring dragon wrapped around a red exterior, red being the color of luck and celebration and the dragon the supreme emblem of imperial power and good fortune. This is one of the broad country-level icons rather than a single city, so it pairs naturally with the Chinese city mugs in the set and anchors the whole regional grouping.
Shanghai#576298 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside, with a delicate flower outside. Rather than the famous Pudong skyline of the Bund, this Shanghai mug goes quiet and floral, nodding to the magnolia, which is the official flower of the city. It is a softer take than you expect from China's most modern metropolis. The restraint is what makes it interesting to me, a mug that trusts a single bloom to stand for a city of twenty-six million.
Harbin#576299 · Global Icon SeriesHarbin in China's frigid northeast shows its Flood Control Monument, the 1958 column on the Songhua River that honors the city's survival of the catastrophic 1957 flood, set against a light-blue body. Harbin is world-famous for its annual Ice and Snow Festival, where whole buildings are carved from river ice. The Russian-influenced architecture, a legacy of the old railway era, makes it one of China's most distinctive cities.
Foshan#576300 · Global Icon SeriesFoshan, brown-lined, shows a lion dance up front with a temple gate on the back, capturing this Guangdong city's identity as a cradle of Lingnan culture. Foshan is the heartland of Cantonese martial arts and lion dancing, the hometown of Wong Fei-hung and Ip Man, Bruce Lee's teacher. A characterful Chinese Global Icon that tells a real cultural story.
Nanning#576301 · Global Icon SeriesNanning, the Green City and capital of Guangxi, gets a light green treatment and the Five Elephants statue from Jinhu Square, the centerpiece of the city's modern CBD. The five elephants nod to local Zhuang culture, whose patterning appears across the district. Nanning is also the host city of the China-ASEAN Expo, a detail that explains why a less touristy capital earned its own icon mug.
Lijiang#576302 · Global Icon SeriesLijiang's light blue icon shows a bridge over a river beside a temple, which captures the heart of its UNESCO old town, a Naxi-built warren of canals fed by three rivers and crossed by more than 300 stone bridges. From the 12th century it was a key trading hub on the route between Sichuan, Yunnan and Tibet. Its centuries-old water-supply system still runs through the lanes today, which is the detail that always gets me about this town.
Malaysia#576303 · Global Icon SeriesMalaysia is one of the country-level Icons rather than a single city, with a red interior and a flower on the outside, almost surely the hibiscus, the Bunga Raya that is Malaysia's national flower. It is an interesting one because Starbucks usually picks cities, so a national bloom stands in for the whole country. Pairs naturally with the Kuala Lumpur city mug and its Petronas Towers for a complete Malaysian display.
Suzhou#576304 · Global Icon SeriesThe round temple pavilion on the outside points to Suzhou, the canal city near Shanghai often called the Venice of the East for its bridges and waterways. Its real claim to fame is the Classical Gardens of Suzhou, a UNESCO World Heritage site of around sixty surviving gardens, with the Humble Administrator's Garden the largest and most celebrated. A 2,500-year-old silk and garden town, beautifully understated on a mug.
Tapiei#576305 · Global Icon SeriesThe name is misspelled on my list but this is Taipei, Taiwan, rendered in the Global Icon line with a purple interior and a temple on the exterior. Taipei is best known for Taipei 101, the bamboo-shaped tower that was the world's tallest building from 2004 to 2010, but Starbucks leaned into the ornate temple roofs and longshan-style architecture that define the old city instead. A clean, common piece, and a fun one to display alongside other China and Taiwan icons.
Taiwan#576306 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside with a bear and bees on the outside, a playful country mug that nods to the Formosan black bear, Taiwan's only native bear, recognizable by the white V or moon mark on its chest. Rather than a landmark, this one trades on the island's wildlife and warmth, a friendly counterpoint to the city-specific Taichung and Tainan mugs. A whimsical entry that stands out in a series full of buildings. Good fun for a Taiwan grouping.
Fuzhou#576308 · Global Icon SeriesFuzhou, red-lined, depicts the city's famous Twin Pagodas, the White Pagoda and the dark granite Black Pagoda, with the skyline of Fujian's capital on the back. The Black Pagoda was begun back in 944 AD and rises seven octagonal stories of gray stone. A striking Chinese Global Icon, and I like that it leads with two genuine thousand-year-old monuments.
Haikou#576309 · Global Icon SeriesHaikou is the capital of Hainan, China's tropical island province, and the "long bridge" on the dark-green body evokes the Century Bridge or one of the spans crossing its rivers and bays. As the gateway to a beach-resort island, Haikou is a genuinely off-the-beaten-path entry in the series. The deep green liner suits a humid, palm-lined port that most icon collectors rarely manage to track down.
Kuala Lumpur#576310 · Global Icon SeriesKuala Lumpur grew out of a tin-mining settlement at a muddy river confluence, which is literally what the Malay name means. The dark blue interior and old courtyard motif lean toward the colonial Merdeka heritage rather than the obvious Petronas Towers, the twin skyscrapers that were the world's tallest from 1998 to 2004. I like that this one tells the older story of the city instead of just the steel.
Taichung#576312 · Global Icon SeriesLight green outside with the old Taichung Railway Station, the red-brick, clock-towered landmark built in 1917 during Taiwan's Japanese colonial era in a free-classical mix of Baroque and Renaissance. It served trains until 2016 and is now preserved as a national historic site and cultural park. A handsome, specific building choice for Taiwan's central city. The soft green palette makes it one of the gentler Global Icons.
Penang#576313 · Global Icon SeriesOrange inside with the Penang Bridge stretched across the cream exterior. That span links George Town on the island to the Malaysian mainland and runs about 13.5 kilometers, long the longest bridge in the country. Penang itself is prized for George Town's UNESCO-listed heritage shophouses and its street food, and collectors note this Icon is on the harder to find side, with a later black Relief version also issued for the city.
Kaohsiung#576315 · Global Icon SeriesBlue inside with a distinctive round topped building for Kaohsiung, Taiwan's great southern port and second largest city on the island. The waterfront here is defined by the 85 Sky Tower and the harbor's reinvented Pier 2 arts district. Kaohsiung sits at the lower end of the series in availability, so two of these in a collection is worth noting.
Lanzhou#576316 · Global Icon SeriesLanzhou is the Gansu capital strung along the Yellow River, and the bridge on the outside is the Zhongshan Bridge, opened in 1909 as the first permanent bridge ever built across the Yellow River. Its German-fabricated steel was shipped in through Tianjin, and it was painted dark grey during the war to dodge Japanese bombers, a color it still wears. A real Silk Road city told through a single, very specific span.
Leshan#576317 · Global Icon SeriesLeshan in Sichuan is home to the Leshan Giant Buddha, the largest stone Buddha on earth at 71 meters, carved into a river cliff over roughly ninety years from 713 to 803 during the Tang dynasty. The curved stairs in stone on the outside are the famous Nine Bends plank road, 278 steps cut alongside the statue down to the river. A UNESCO site shared with Mount Emei, and a genuinely awe-inspiring subject for a mug.
Nanjing#576318 · Global Icon SeriesDark blue inside, and the building atop a flight of stairs is the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum on Purple Mountain, reached by 392 granite steps that symbolize China's population at the time it was built in the late 1920s. Nanjing served as the capital under several dynasties and the Republic of China. A handsome, dignified design that does justice to one of China's most historically layered cities.
Taiyuan#576319 · Global Icon SeriesMagenta inside with a courtyard of towering pagodas, pointing to Taiyuan in Shanxi province and its symbol, the twin pagodas of Yongzuo Temple built around 1608 in the Ming dynasty, each rising about 53 meters. Nearby Jinci Temple is the region's crown jewel, with its Song-dynasty Hall of the Holy Mother and a cypress some 3,000 years old. A coal-country provincial capital most travelers overlook, which makes the mug a small education. A solid deep-cut China piece.
Mianyang#576321 · Global Icon SeriesMianyang sits in Sichuan and is China's self-styled science city, but this blue-lined mug reaches for something older: the towering Yuewang Pavilion, a Tang-dynasty tower founded under Emperor Gaozong around the 7th century. The original was lost to an earthquake and rebuilt, and it holds an astonishing trove of classical poems by Li Bai, Du Fu and Wang Bo. A quiet entry most collectors overlook.
Yinchuan#576323 · Global Icon SeriesYinchuan was the capital of the vanished Western Xia empire, and the rocks rising from water on mine evoke the pyramid-like Western Xia royal tombs out in the desert near the Helan Mountains. It pairs a light green interior with that stark scene. As the capital of Ningxia, a Hui Muslim region, Yinchuan is one of the more culturally distinct deep cuts in the Chinese Global Icon series.
Vietnam#576324 · Global Icon SeriesA Vietnam country icon, light brown, the exterior showing a woman beside a bicycle. It is an everyday street scene, the conical non-la hat and bicycle laden with goods that define Vietnamese daily life rather than a single monument. Starbucks favored ordinary life over Halong Bay or the Hanoi temples, and that human, lived-in approach makes it a warm, memorable Southeast Asia piece.
Xiangyang#576326 · Global Icon SeriesXiangyang in Hubei is a storied military stronghold, its ancient city wall and moat among the best preserved in China and a famous setting in Romance of the Three Kingdoms. The palace gateway on mine, against a light blue interior, salutes that fortress past. This is a true deep cut, the kind of historically loaded but obscure city that makes hunting the Chinese Global Icons worthwhile.
Bali#576328 · Global Icon SeriesBali's light brown exterior shows women carrying offerings to the gods, the daily temple processions of canang sari that you see everywhere on the Hindu island. It captures the spiritual rhythm of Balinese life rather than a single building, which I think is the smarter choice for a place defined by ritual. Indonesian Global Icons don't surface often on the secondary market.
Hanoi#576329 · Global Icon SeriesHanoi, Vietnam's thousand-year-old capital, gets an orange interior and a temple entrance, the Temple of Literature, the 1070 Confucian academy that was Vietnam's first university. The warm orange suits a city of yellow colonial facades, lantern-lit Old Quarter streets and strong robusta coffee. As Vietnamese coffee culture grows, this is a meaningful origin-country piece to have on the shelf.
Singapore#576330 · Global Icon SeriesBlue inside, with an orchid outside. The flower is the Vanda Miss Joaquim, Singapore's national flower, a natural hybrid orchid discovered in a garden in 1893 and chosen partly for its vibrant, resilient bloom. Orchid diplomacy is a real thing here, with new hybrids named for visiting dignitaries at the Botanic Gardens. A graceful, very on-brand choice for the garden city.
Jakarta#576331 · Global Icon SeriesThat spiked masked figure is an Ondel Ondel, the towering Betawi folk puppet of Jakarta, paraded in pairs to ward off bad spirits and welcome guests, and an official emblem of the Indonesian capital. The reverse typically carries the National Monument, Monas. I love that Starbucks put the giant folk puppet front and center, a far bolder choice than another tower.
Ho Chi Minh City#576332 · Global Icon SeriesThe light green interior plays against a three wheel cyclo, the bicycle taxi that for decades ferried passengers through the chaos of old Saigon and remains shorthand for Vietnam's largest city. Ho Chi Minh City, still called Saigon by many, is the economic engine of the south, and Starbucks chose the humble cyclo over a skyscraper. I love a Global Icon that picks street life over a postcard landmark.
Brunei#576333 · Global Icon SeriesOrange lining with an oil pump outside, an honest nod to the tiny sultanate's source of wealth, petroleum and natural gas that fund one of Asia's richest nations. Brunei is a scarcer market for Starbucks merch, so this one shows up less often than the big European cities. Secondary listings tend to sit in the rough $40 to $70 range, a solid get for a Southeast Asia shelf.
Iloilo#576335 · Global Icon SeriesThe indigenous figure is a Dinagyang warrior, the body painted, headdress wearing dancers of Iloilo's January festival honoring the Santo Nino and the Ati people. Held on Panay island in the western Visayas, Dinagyang is one of the Philippines' most spectacular street performances. A genuinely deep cut in the series, since most collectors outside the Philippines have never heard of this city, which only sharpens the hunt.
Dali City#576336 · Global Icon SeriesThis blue mug puts the Three Pagodas of Chongsheng Temple front and center, the unmistakable symbol of Dali in Yunnan, China. The tallest, Qianxun Pagoda, rises about 70 meters and dates to the 9th century Nanzhao kingdom, and the trio has survived more than a thousand years of earthquakes and fires. Dali sits between the Cangshan mountains and Erhai Lake, so this is a genuinely scenic, lesser-seen China entry.
General Santos#576337 · Global Icon SeriesGeneral Santos, purple-lined, shows a man hauling a giant tuna over his shoulder, with Mount Matutum on the reverse. Gensan is the Tuna Capital of the Philippines, landing the bulk of the country's catch, so the design is pure civic pride. Sold locally for around 450 pesos, this is a fun, distinctly Filipino Global Icon that rarely surfaces outside the region.
Cambodia#576338 · Global Icon SeriesGreen interior with a dancing woman outside, an Apsara dancer of the classical Khmer royal ballet, the graceful celestial figures carved across Angkor Wat and revived as a national art form. Cambodia's culture survived the Khmer Rouge years and the Apsara is its proud emblem, recognized by UNESCO. An elegant, culture-forward Southeast Asia mug rather than a plain landmark shot.
Baguio#576340 · Global Icon SeriesBaguio is the Philippines' "Summer Capital," a cool pine-clad city up in the Cordillera mountains, and the sunflower on the cream exterior nods to the blooms that blanket its parks. The dark green interior is a nice touch that echoes the highland forests. A clean, regional piece that rounds out my Philippine Global Icon run.
Dongguan#576342 · Global Icon SeriesThe magenta Dongguan mug shows figures over a cannon, a direct reference to Humen, where official Lin Zexu destroyed over a thousand tons of British opium in 1839, sparking the First Opium War. The Weiyuan Fort there still bristles with old iron cannons facing the Pearl River estuary. Dongguan is a Guangdong manufacturing powerhouse, but the mug reaches for this pivotal moment in Chinese history instead, which I find a bold call.
Manila#576343 · Global Icon SeriesManila's red-interior mug puts a jeepney on the outside, the flamboyant chrome-and-color minibus that is the undisputed king of Philippine roads, originally built from surplus US military jeeps after World War II. Choosing the jeepney over a monument is a wonderfully local, lived-in design choice. Filipino collectors love this one, and together with Makati it anchors the Philippine corner of the Icon line.
Guiyang#576346 · Global Icon SeriesGuiyang, capital of Guizhou in southwest China, is represented by Jiaxiu Tower, the three-story Ming pavilion built in 1598 on a rock in the Nanming River. The blue interior reads as that river water. The tower, reached by the 90-meter Fuyu Bridge and once a gathering place for scholars, is a national heritage site and the undisputed symbol of a city most Western collectors will never have visited.
Naga#576347 · Global Icon SeriesNaga, in Camarines Sur in the Philippines' Bicol region, gets an orange lining and a front covered in oversized coffee beans, a fitting nod since Bicol is genuine coffee country. The city is best known for the Peñafrancia Festival, one of the largest Marian devotions in Asia. Philippine city icons are scarce on the secondary market, which makes this an easy one to enjoy owning.
Makati#576348 · Global Icon SeriesMakati is the gleaming financial heart of Metro Manila, the Philippines' Wall Street, and this orange-interior mug renders its modern skyline of glass towers rather than any single monument. It is the more cosmopolitan counterpart to the Manila mug in the same line. Philippine Icons see strong local demand, so the Makati and Manila pair are popular targets for Southeast Asian collectors.
Batangas#576349 · Global Icon SeriesThe "arch-shaped carpet" is actually jusi, the fine pineapple-silk fabric of the barong Tagalog, and Batangas, specifically the town of Taal, weaves some of the country's best. The reverse shows the province's coastline, home to the world-class diving at Anilao. I appreciate that they honored craft and textile rather than a postcard view.
Tagaytay#576350 · Global Icon SeriesBlue inside with mountains outside, which is Tagaytay all over, the cool ridge town south of Manila famous for its sweeping view of Taal Volcano sitting in its lake. Taal is one of the world's most curious geological oddities, an island within a lake within a volcano within a lake on an island, and one of the Philippines' most active volcanoes. A breezy weekend escape rendered as a calm blue mug. A nice, lesser-seen Philippine icon.
Philippines#576351 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside, and the outside features the Philippine falconet, one of the world's smallest birds of prey at barely the size of a sparrow. Choosing a tiny endemic raptor over a building is an unusual call for this series, and it ties the country to its biodiversity rather than a single city. A nice oddball among the national Global Icons.
Bacolod#576352 · Global Icon SeriesBacolod is the sugar capital of the Philippines, and the steam locomotive wrapped around this purple-lined mug is one of the famous "Iron Dinosaurs" that once hauled cane from the fields of Negros to the mills. I love that Starbucks chose an industrial relic over a beach. These Philippine Global Icons tend to be hard to find outside the country, which is exactly why I hunted this one down.
Davao#576353 · Global Icon SeriesDavao on Mindanao is the Durian Capital of the Philippines, so the spiky fruit on this light blue mug, listed as Dorian in the catalog, is no accident. Locals revere the pungent King of Fruits enough to crown it at the annual Kadayawan harvest festival. Davao is also home to the critically endangered Philippine Eagle, but it is the durian that defines the city, making this one of the more charming food-led icons in the set.
Cebu#576355 · Global Icon SeriesLight green inside with a guitar outside, exactly right for Cebu, the Philippine island famous for world-class handcrafted guitars made in family workshops on Mactan, especially around Lapu-Lapu City. The trade has passed down generations and the instruments are prized for quality at a fair price. A surprising, music-forward Filipino mug that tells a real local story rather than showing a beach.
Pampanga#576356 · Global Icon SeriesThe snowflake-shaped star is a parol, the giant electric lantern of Pampanga's Ligligan Parul, the Giant Lantern Festival held each December in San Fernando, which earned the city its title as Christmas Capital of the Philippines. The competition dates to the early 1900s, and electrified lanterns since 1931 can span up to twenty feet with thousands of bulbs in synchronized light shows. A vivid, festive choice on the blue body.
Cagayan de Oro#576357 · Global Icon SeriesYellow lining with whitewater rafting outside, dead-on for Cagayan de Oro, billed as the whitewater rafting capital of the Philippines on its fast Cagayan River rapids. The reverse carries a pineapple, a nod to the region's plantations. A bright, energetic Filipino city mug that is far less common abroad than the big-capital icons, a nice deep cut for a Philippines run.
Boracay#576358 · Global Icon SeriesBoracay is the Philippines' postcard island, and the blue-lined mug shows palms and stairs rising from the water, a nod to White Beach and the famous powder-fine sand. After its 2018 government cleanup and closure, the island became even more iconic, so the mug captures a place people genuinely revere. Another Philippine Global Icon that rarely travels far from home.
Chiangmai#576359 · Global Icon SeriesChiang Mai carries a light green interior and an elephant outside, fitting for the cultural capital of northern Thailand and the old seat of the Lanna kingdom. The elephant is a national symbol, and the region is dotted with sanctuaries, while the city itself is ringed by ancient moats and walls and crowned by the gold-spired temple of Wat Phra That Doi Suthep on the mountain above.
Gold Coast#576360 · Global Icon SeriesThe Gold Coast is Australia's beach-and-surf capital in Queensland, so a lone surfer on a yellow body is exactly the right call. This stretch of coastline gave the world Surfers Paradise and some of the most consistent point breaks anywhere, and the sunny yellow reads as pure sand and sunshine. It is one of the more relaxed, least cluttered Global Icon designs, and I appreciate the restraint.
Phuket, Thailand#576362 · Global Icon SeriesPurple inside, with three longtail boats riding the outside. Those wooden craft with their long propeller shafts and ribbons on the bow are a signature of Phuket and the Andaman Sea, Thailand's largest island and a limestone-cliff diving and beach destination. The boats stand in for the postcard view collectors picture of the place.
Cairo#576363 · Global Icon SeriesOrange interior with the Pyramids and the Sphinx outside, the Giza plateau just outside Cairo and the only surviving wonder of the ancient world. The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC for Pharaoh Khufu and stood as the tallest human structure for nearly four millennia. Few icons are more globally recognizable, making this warm, sand-toned mug an essential Egypt anchor.
Egypt#576364 · Global Icon SeriesEgypt earns a country mug rather than a city one, brown inside with a floral motif outside, the kind of stylized design Starbucks uses where a single landmark cannot stand in for an entire civilization. This is the land of the Giza pyramids and the Sphinx, the only surviving wonder of the ancient world. A clean, understated entry that anchors my North Africa shelf.
Melbourne#576367 · Global Icon SeriesMelbourne's dark-green mug celebrates its tram, the cable car that is the heart of the world's largest urban tram network and a genuine symbol of the Australian city. The free City Circle heritage trams in their burgundy livery are a beloved tourist ride. Melbourne is a popular Australian Icon, and choosing the everyday tram over a skyline makes this one of the friendliest, most characterful designs in the whole series.
Bangkok#576368 · Global Icon SeriesThe red-lined Bangkok mug puts a tuk-tuk front and center, the three-wheeled auto rickshaw that is the noisy, beloved heart of getting around the Thai capital. Choosing the tuk-tuk over a temple is a wonderfully streetwise call. Thai-made Global Icons were produced in good numbers, but a clean tuk-tuk Bangkok still photographs beautifully on the shelf.
South Island New Zealand#576369 · Global Icon SeriesThe red interior plays off a skier carving down the outside, which is exactly right for New Zealand's South Island, home to Queenstown and the Southern Alps that made it the adventure and ski capital of the southern hemisphere. The Remarkables and Coronet Peak draw powder hounds all winter, while the same peaks doubled as Middle-earth in the Lord of the Rings films. A clean, sporty entry that captures the island's outdoor identity rather than a single building.
Wellington#576370 · Global Icon SeriesWellington is New Zealand's windy capital, and the Beehive, the executive wing of Parliament finished in 1979 to a Basil Spence design, is its most recognizable silhouette. Ours pairs a green interior with that distinctive round government building. It is a sharp pick over the usual harbor view, and capital-building icons like this read instantly to anyone who knows the place.
Australia#576371 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside with a boomerang outside, the whole continent reduced to its most recognizable Aboriginal object. The returning boomerang is a genuine feat of aerodynamics refined over thousands of years, though many traditional throwing sticks were heavy non-returning hunting weapons. A bold, graphic choice for a country mug that skips the Opera House and goes straight to deep Indigenous heritage.
Puerto Vallarta#576372 · Global Icon SeriesPurple on the outside with palm trees leaning over the beach, this one captures the Pacific resort town on Mexico's Bahia de Banderas, the bay where the Sierra Madre tumbles straight into the sea. Vallarta exploded onto the map after John Huston shot Night of the Iguana nearby in 1963 with Burton and Taylor in tow. A relaxed, sun forward entry in the Global Icon line.
Auckland#576373 · Global Icon SeriesDark blue inside with a sailing ship outside, exactly right for the City of Sails. Auckland is said to have more boats per capita than almost anywhere on earth, sprawled between two harbours on a field of extinct volcanic cones. New Zealand's biggest city twice hosted the America's Cup, so the yacht under sail is the truest possible emblem for it.
Brisbane#576374 · Global Icon SeriesRed interior with a bridge spanning the river outside, the Story Bridge, the cantilever crossing of the Brisbane River opened in 1940 and now a climbing attraction. Brisbane is the Queensland capital wrapped around its bends in the water, and the red lining gives this Australian entry real pop. A clean, sunny piece in any down-under sub-collection.
Cancun#576375 · Global Icon SeriesLight blue inside with beach chairs and palm trees outside, pure Mexican Caribbean, Cancun on the Yucatan with its turquoise water and white sand. Planned from scratch as a resort city in the 1970s, it became Mexico's tourism flagship. The relaxed loungers say vacation more than any monument could, making this a sunny, instantly readable resort-city Global Icon.
Seoul#576376 · Global Icon SeriesDark blue inside, with N Seoul Tower and a traditional pagoda outside. The tower crowns Namsan mountain and has become the city's romantic landmark, its railings heavy with padlocks left by couples. Pairing that modern spire with a tiled pagoda neatly sums up Seoul, a capital where palaces like Gyeongbokgung sit a subway ride from glass skyscrapers. A clean, confident design from the Korean Icon line.
Korea#576377 · Global Icon SeriesA national mug for South Korea, with a red interior and a traditional hahoetal mask outside, the carved wooden face used in the Hahoe byeolsin gut talnori folk drama. Those masks date back to the Goryeo era and the surviving originals are designated National Treasures, so it is a genuinely deep cultural pick rather than a generic landmark. I appreciate when the series reaches for folk craft instead of another tower.
Ciudad de Mexico#576380 · Global Icon SeriesCiudad de Mexico carries a green interior with the Angel of Independence outside, the golden winged Victory atop her column on Paseo de la Reforma, the city's gathering point for celebrations and protests alike. Mexico City sits on the drained lake bed of Aztec Tenochtitlan, making it one of the oldest continuously inhabited capitals in the Americas, and the world's largest Spanish-speaking city.
Ensenada#576381 · Global Icon SeriesEnsenada lifts a grey whale's tail breaching out of the Pacific, with the Baja port's harbour skyline on the back. This Mexican coast sits on the gray whale migration route, and nearby lagoons are where the whales famously breed each winter. A common but very likeable Global Icon, and I prefer its single bold fluke to the busier Los Cabos whale design.
Sharm El Sheikh#576382 · Global Icon SeriesLight blue inside, with a coral reef and tropical fish outside. Sharm El Sheikh sits on the Sinai Peninsula at the tip of the Red Sea and is one of the planet's premier diving destinations, famous for the reefs of Ras Mohammed National Park and the Straits of Tiran. So the underwater scene is spot-on, this is a resort town built entirely around what is below the waterline. A rare Starbucks mug that points your eye down into the sea rather than up at a building.
Chihuahua#576383 · Global Icon SeriesChihuahua shows a green interior with an angel statue outside, the Angel of Liberty that crowns a tall marble column in the heart of the northern Mexican capital, honoring Father Miguel Hidalgo and the route of independence. The state is Mexico's largest, the gateway to the spectacular Copper Canyon and its Chepe railway, and yes, the namesake of the tiny dog breed.
Mexico#576384 · Global Icon SeriesThis country-level Mexico mug has a brown interior and a Mayan compass on the outside, evoking the Aztec sun stone, the famous carved calendar disc that is one of the most recognizable artifacts of pre-Columbian Mesoamerica. Using an ancient cosmological symbol rather than a city skyline makes it one of the more striking national Icons. It anchors a Mexican shelf alongside the Merida, Los Cabos, and city pieces.
Puebla#576385 · Global Icon SeriesBlue inside, with a Puebla courtyard on the outside, tied to the city's signature Talavera ceramics. Puebla is the birthplace of mole poblano and chiles en nogada, sits beneath the Popocatepetl volcano, and its 2016 Icon nods to the colorful glazed pottery a 200-year-old house like Uriarte still produces. The colonial-courtyard imagery captures one of Mexico's most picturesque cities.
Guadalajara#576386 · Global Icon SeriesGuadalajara is the capital of Jalisco and the cradle of mariachi and tequila, with the agave fields of the region just to the west. The red interior fits a city that is unapologetically the heartland of Mexican tradition. The catalog notes short bushes on the exterior, the low agave plant rows, a quiet nod to the blue-agave country that gives the region its most famous export.
North Island New Zealand#576387 · Global Icon SeriesThat lone tree on a winding road is shorthand for New Zealand's wide, empty roads and big-sky landscapes, the same romance that made the willow standing in Lake Wanaka a global photo obsession. The red interior gives the spare scene some heat. Splitting New Zealand into North and South Island mugs is a nice touch, letting a serious collector hunt the full pair rather than settle for one.
Playa del Carmen#576388 · Global Icon SeriesLight blue inside, with Playa's Fifth Avenue, the Quinta Avenida, on the outside. That pedestrian strip running parallel to the Caribbean is the heart of this Riviera Maya town, once a small ferry port to Cozumel before tourism reshaped it. The mug sells the walkable beach-town vibe rather than any single ruin, which suits the place.
Los Cabos#576389 · Global Icon SeriesLos Cabos is the resort tip of Mexico's Baja peninsula, and this light-blue mug puts a long-finned shark or billfish front and center, a nod to its world-famous sportfishing waters dubbed the Marlin Capital of the World, plus the iconic El Arco rock arch where the Sea of Cortez meets the Pacific. Collectors prize the older Los Cabos pieces highly, and earlier sailboat-and-whale variants from the City line have fetched several hundred dollars on eBay, so it is one of the more sought-after Mexican entries.
Queretaro#576390 · Global Icon SeriesBlue inside with grapes outside, pointing straight at Queretaro's surprising status as Mexico's second largest wine region and its leading sparkling wine producer, grown at nearly two thousand meters of altitude. The colonial city itself is UNESCO listed and famous for a soaring eighteenth century stone aqueduct of seventy four arches. A clever fruit forward design that rewards a second look.
Panama#576391 · Global Icon SeriesPanama is defined by its canal, the engineering marvel opened in 1914 that links the Atlantic and Pacific through a lock system raising ships across the isthmus. The blue interior plays up the water theme. It is one of the more instantly recognizable Latin American Global Icons, since the canal is the rare landmark that needs no caption, the whole country in a single ribbon of locks.
Villahermosa#576392 · Global Icon SeriesVillahermosa, Mexico, purple inside, the stone face on the front a colossal Olmec head. These basalt giants, carved before 900 BC by Mexico's mother civilization, were hauled from the La Venta site into Villahermosa's open-air Parque-Museo, each one a portrait of a ruler with fleshy lips and a helmet-like cap. A discontinued and uncommon icon, and one of the oldest landmarks featured anywhere in this whole series.
Colombia#576393 · Global Icon SeriesColombia runs blue inside with two dancers outside, a tribute to the country's rhythm, from cumbia born on the Caribbean coast to the salsa capital of Cali. This is a national icon rather than a single city, and it captures Colombia's spirit better than any building could, the land of Gabriel Garcia Marquez, world-class coffee, and the colorful Carnival of Barranquilla.
Helsinki#576395 · Global Icon SeriesHelsinki's light-blue icon features a fountain, Havis Amanda, Ville Vallgren's 1908 Art Nouveau bronze of a mermaid rising from the sea that Finnish students famously crown with a cap every May Day. The cool blue liner suits a Baltic capital of pale neoclassical squares and long northern light. It is a fitting symbol for a city that turns its harborside statue into a yearly celebration.
Finland#576396 · Global Icon SeriesFinland goes full Lapland here, a blue-lined cup with a reindeer on the front and the aurora borealis sweeping the back. Far above the Arctic Circle the northern lights and the Sami reindeer-herding tradition are the country's true icons. A quietly beautiful country mug, and one of my favorite cold-palette pieces in the whole Global Icon set.
Veracruz#576397 · Global Icon SeriesVeracruz, Mexico, light green inside, a dancer on the exterior. That figure points to the Gulf-coast city's jarocho music and dance tradition, the white-clad son jarocho that gave the world La Bamba, or the Papantla voladores who spin from a tall pole nearby. Veracruz was Cortes's 1519 landing point and Mexico's oldest port, so this mug carries deep history under its festive surface.
San Miguel de Allende#576398 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside, with six stars worked into the design. San Miguel de Allende is a UNESCO World Heritage colonial town in Mexico's Bajío highlands, crowned by the pink neo-Gothic Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel whose fanciful spires were supposedly sketched from a postcard of a European cathedral. The town was a cradle of Mexican independence, birthplace of Ignacio Allende, and is now beloved by artists and expats for its cobbled streets and light.
New Zealand#576402 · Global Icon SeriesA country mug, brown inside, fronted by the kiwi, the flightless nocturnal bird so tied to national identity that New Zealanders call themselves Kiwis. The bird lays one of the largest eggs relative to body size of any species, and it is endangered, which gives the choice real meaning. Picking the kiwi over mountains or rugby makes this one of the more personable icons in the series.
Kaohsiung#576403 · Global Icon SeriesThe matching second Kaohsiung in my collection, same blue interior and round topped landmark for Taiwan's southern harbor city famed for the Love River and the Lotus Pond's Dragon and Tiger Pagodas. Having the pair lets me check for the small print and rim variations that the Global Icon factory runs sometimes introduce between print dates. A genuinely hard to find Taiwanese icon to begin with.
Chiangmai#576405 · Global Icon SeriesA second Chiang Mai in the collection, again light green inside with the elephant outside, and worth keeping as a pair since the Global Icon line saw subtle reprints and packaging changes across years. The same Lanna heritage holds true: this was the rose of the north, founded in 1296, and its Loy Krathong and Yi Peng lantern festivals draw travelers from around the world every November.
Acapulco#576409 · Global Icon SeriesThe diver leaping off the cliff is La Quebrada, Acapulco's signature spectacle since two fishermen first dared each other to jump in 1934. The clavadistas plunge roughly 35 meters into a narrow Pacific inlet, timing each dive to an incoming swell so the channel is deep enough to survive. Elvis made it world famous in 1963's Fun in Acapulco, and this mug captures that exact heart-in-throat instant.
Leon#576411 · Global Icon SeriesThe three hot air balloons are the giveaway: this is Leon in Guanajuato, Mexico, home of the Festival Internacional del Globo, ranked among the top three balloon festivals in the world. Every November more than 200 balloons from dozens of countries lift off over the Parque Metropolitano, drawing hundreds of thousands. A green-lined icon built entirely around an event rather than a building, which makes it one of the more joyful pieces in the series.
Cozumel#576412 · Global Icon SeriesCozumel carries a blue interior with a sea turtle gliding over a reef outside, perfectly chosen for the Mexican Caribbean island that sits on the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef, the second largest in the world. A diving and snorkeling mecca made famous by Jacques Cousteau, Cozumel was also a sacred Maya pilgrimage site dedicated to Ixchel, the goddess of fertility.
Moerlia#576413 · Global Icon SeriesThe spelling on my list reads Moerlia, but this is Morelia, the rose-stone colonial capital of Michoacán in Mexico, and the orange-lined mug nails the region's real signature: the Monarch butterfly. Every winter millions of Monarchs blanket Michoacán's fir forests after migrating thousands of miles from Canada, a UNESCO-protected spectacle. The skyline rides the back. A common but genuinely charming piece.
Aarhus#576417 · Global Icon SeriesBlue inside with the Aarhus City Hall clock tower outside, Denmark's second city on the cup. That town hall is a 1941 modernist landmark by Arne Jacobsen and Erik Moller, clad in grey Norwegian marble, and its slender open tower was added only after locals complained the building lacked one. A quietly sophisticated piece for a place most collectors overlook.
Samara#576421 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside. The catalog text mentioning a coco plant and chocolate is clearly a mistaken entry, since Samara is a major Russian city on the Volga, founded as a fortress in 1586 and home to the longest river embankment in Russia. It was a closed Soviet aerospace hub, so the art shows a Volga or space theme. A genuinely scarce Russian city worth verifying in hand.
Denmark#576424 · Global Icon SeriesDenmark's red-lined Global Icon leans into the bicycle, a perfect choice since Copenhagen is one of the most cycle-obsessed cities on earth, with more bikes than residents and dedicated bridges like the Cykelslangen. Red and white nods to the Dannebrog, often called the oldest continuously used national flag. A country mug that captures a way of life rather than a single monument, which I find more interesting than another tower.
Buenos Aires#576430 · Global Icon SeriesRed interior with the Obelisco standing outside, the 67-meter monument raised in 1936 for the city's 400th anniversary at the crossing of Avenida 9 de Julio, one of the world's widest avenues. It is the rallying point for tango, protests and World Cup celebrations alike. The bold red lining suits Argentina's passion, making this a punchy South American Global Icon.
Yaroslavl#576455 · Global Icon SeriesYaroslavl is a jewel of Russia's Golden Ring, its historic center a UNESCO site, founded by Yaroslav the Wise, whose monument fronts my mug against a yellow interior. The city even appears on the 1000 ruble banknote. Russian Global Icons beyond Moscow and St Petersburg are scarce abroad, so a Golden Ring town like this is a quietly satisfying catch for anyone building the Russia run.
Rostov-On-Don#576458 · Global Icon SeriesBlue inside with a bridge over the river, the gateway city of southern Russia where the Don River runs out toward the Sea of Azov. Rostov on Don is the unofficial capital of the Cossack lands and hosted 2018 World Cup matches. A less common Russian city, the kind of mid tier Global Icon that fills a stubborn gap.
Norway#576459 · Global Icon SeriesThe two mittens are pure Norway, knit in the Selbu star pattern that a young woman named Marit Emstad popularized near Trondheim around the 1850s, now a national symbol sold in every souvenir shop. This 2017 Global Icon version pairs the eight-point-star mittens with skiers in a winter landscape. A warm, folk-craft design rather than a landmark, which makes it stand out on the shelf among all the towers and bridges.
Russia#576461 · Global Icon SeriesBrown inside with ballerinas, a beautifully chosen stand in for Russia itself given the Bolshoi and Mariinsky traditions and choreographers like Petipa who defined classical ballet. Rather than another onion dome skyline, this country mug leans into culture, which makes it stand out on the shelf. A graceful and slightly unusual entry in the Global Icon run.
Osaka#576463 · Global Icon SeriesOsaka Castle is the obvious star here, the gleaming white-and-green keep first built by warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the 1580s as a seat of power that helped unify Japan. The current main tower is a 1930s reconstruction with gold tiger and crane reliefs gleaming on its gables. The light blue interior suits this elegant piece, one of the cleaner single-landmark designs in the Japanese Global Icon lineup.
Namur#576466 · Global Icon SeriesNamur, the capital of Wallonia in Belgium, sits where the Sambre meets the Meuse, and this brown-lined mug shows Saint-Aubin's Cathedral, completed in 1772 and the only late-Baroque cathedral in the country. The city's true crown is actually the vast hilltop Citadel reworked by Vauban, but the cathedral makes for a graceful design. A genuinely obscure entry that rounds out a serious Belgian run.
Yekaterinburg#576468 · Global Icon SeriesYekaterinburg guards the Europe-Asia divide in the Urals, and mine features Sevastyanov's House, the city's fairytale Neo-Gothic and Moorish mansion that now serves as a presidential residence. It runs a green interior with that ornate building. The city is also where the last Tsar Nicholas II and his family met their end in 1918, history that gives this otherwise cheerful mug a heavy undertone.
Tyumen#576469 · Global Icon SeriesTyumen, the first Russian city east of the Urals, blue inside. The front shows the Bridge of Lovers, a pedestrian cable bridge over the Tura that is the city's lovers' landmark, and the back carries nodding-donkey oil pumps, a nod to Tyumen being the gateway to Siberia's vast oil and gas fields. A genuinely obscure Russian Global Icon that fills a real gap on the map.
Bergen#576470 · Global Icon SeriesThe catalog says Einstein, but the figure on this Bergen mug is really Edvard Grieg, the composer born in this Norwegian port and its most famous son. Bergen is the gateway to the fjords and the old Hanseatic Bryggen wharf, so a hometown composer fits beautifully. Norwegian Global Icons are uncommon, and this one shows up listed as rare more often than not.
Krasnodar#576473 · Global Icon SeriesKrasnodar's orange-lined icon centers on the Monument to Catherine the Great, a 14-meter, 25-ton bronze that is the city's hallmark. There is real history packed in it: Catherine granted the Kuban to the Black Sea Cossacks in 1792, the original 1907 monument was melted down by the Bolsheviks, and what stands today is a 2006 restoration of Mikhail Mikeshin's old design. A Russian Global Icon like this is one of the trickier ones to source outside the region.
Tokyo#576474 · Global Icon SeriesTokyo, purple inside with Tokyo Tower outside, dated to the 2008 run. Tokyo Tower opened in 1958 and stands 333 meters, painted international orange and white to satisfy aviation rules, a deliberate Eiffel echo that is taller than its Paris model. Starbucks chose it over the newer Skytree, so this is the classic, old-guard Tokyo silhouette, a cornerstone for any Japan-leaning shelf.
Trondheim#576476 · Global Icon SeriesTrondheim, Norway, orange inside with the cathedral outside. That is Nidaros Cathedral, built over the burial site of Saint Olaf and the northernmost medieval cathedral in the world, Norway's national sanctuary where kings are still blessed. Trondheim was the country's Viking-age capital, so this mug carries real weight, and Nordic Global Icons like it tend to be harder to track down than the big-city ones.
Sochi#576487 · Global Icon SeriesLight blue inside, with the seaport buildings on the front and the snowy mountains on the back. Sochi is Russia's summer Black Sea resort that improbably hosted the 2014 Winter Olympics, possible because the subtropical coast sits right below the Caucasus peaks, exactly the contrast this mug captures. The elegant Stalin-era Sea Port terminal with its tall spire is a city landmark. Two versions exist, so it is worth knowing which seaport variant you are holding.
Bucharest#576489 · Global Icon SeriesBlue inside with the Romanian Athenaeum outside, the domed 1888 concert hall that is the cultural heart of Bucharest and home of the George Enescu Philharmonic. Its neoclassical rotunda and Ionic columns make it the city's signature image, often called the symbol of Bucharest. A handsome, slightly off-the-beaten-path European entry that collectors of capital cities will want.
Nijmgen#576490 · Global Icon SeriesNijmegen is the oldest city in the Netherlands, founded by the Romans around 100 AD as Ulpia Noviomagus and granted town rights by Emperor Trajan. The blue band nods to its perch above the river Waal, crowned by the Valkhof, a strategic hill that held a Roman castellum, an imperial palace of Charlemagne, and Barbarossa's twelfth-century fortress. The surviving Valkhof chapel and Barbarossa ruins still stand there.
Amsterdam#576492 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside with the Rijksmuseum outside, the Dutch national museum that holds Rembrandt's Night Watch and Vermeer's Milkmaid. The building is a Pierre Cuypers design from 1885, a brick Gothic-Renaissance pile that reopened in 2013 after a famously long ten-year renovation. Choosing the museum over the canals or the bikes gives this Amsterdam a more cultured feel.
Rotterdam#576493 · Global Icon SeriesGreen inside with the Erasmusbrug, the cable stayed bridge locals call The Swan for its angled one hundred thirty nine meter pylon, though the harp like cables earn the catalog's harp nickname too. Designed by Ben van Berkel and opened in 1996, it spans the Nieuwe Maas in Europe's biggest port. A sleek modern architecture piece in this series.
Oslo#576494 · Global Icon SeriesThat curved tail is the elegantly carved prow of a Viking longship, evoking Oslo's Oseberg ship, the best-preserved Viking vessel in the world, built around 820 AD and pulled from a burial mound near Tonsberg. Its bow spirals into a serpent's head in the swirling Oseberg style. The blue interior fits the seafaring theme, and the spare, single-detail design makes this one of the more sophisticated Scandinavian Icons.
Malmo#576495 · Global Icon SeriesMalmo, Sweden's southern port, gets a blue interior and its most famous bridge, the Oresund Bridge, the nearly eight-kilometer cable-stayed span that links Sweden to Copenhagen across the strait and was made world-famous by the Nordic noir TV series The Bridge. Its other modern icon is Calatrava's twisting Turning Torso tower. A relatively uncommon Scandinavian entry that appeals to collectors chasing the full Nordic set.
Hilversum#576496 · Global Icon SeriesHilversum's yellow-interior mug shows its Town Hall, Willem Dudok's 1931 masterpiece of stacked yellow-brick volumes and a tall slender tower, one of the most influential modern buildings of its era. The yellow liner is a direct nod to the custom-sized golden bricks Dudok had made just for it. As the Dutch broadcasting town, Hilversum is a small place, so getting an architectural-history landmark like this on a mug is a real treat.
Gothenburg#576497 · Global Icon SeriesGothenburg's mug shows Carl Milles's Poseidon, the seven-meter bronze sea god unveiled in 1931 at Götaplatsen, holding a fish and a shell to honor this Swedish port's maritime soul. The blue interior nods to the sea. Locals were scandalized at first by the statue's bold proportions, then took him to heart, and the view past him down the Avenyn is the city's signature postcard.
Stockholm#576498 · Global Icon SeriesBlue inside, with Stockholm City Hall on the outside, the red-brick Stadshuset on Kungsholmen that hosts the Nobel Prize banquet every December in its Blue Hall. Designed by Ragnar Ostberg and completed in 1923, its 106-meter tower is crowned with the three gold crowns of Sweden. Stockholm itself spreads across fourteen islands, so a single waterside landmark is the smart pick. A clean, recognizable Nordic entry.
Clug-Napoca#576499 · Global Icon SeriesCluj-Napoca, the unofficial capital of Transylvania, shows an orange interior with the Cluj Arena outside, the sleek 30,000-seat stadium completed in 2011 whose translucent facade glows in shifting colors at night. It hosts the massive Untold electronic music festival, making the arena a genuine modern symbol of Romania's lively student city, even if the spelling on the mug, Clug, is a charming little typo.
Den Haag#576500 · Global Icon SeriesDen Haag, The Hague, is the seat of the Dutch government and the International Court of Justice, and this purple-lined mug honors Noordeinde Palace, the working palace of the Dutch monarch. Originally a 16th century farmhouse, it was rebuilt into a royal residence and still hosts the King's offices today. I appreciate that the Netherlands set treats The Hague as its own piece rather than folding it into Amsterdam.
Sweden#576502 · Global Icon SeriesYellow inside with a cartoon Dala horse outside, the carved and painted Dalecarlian horse that is Sweden's unofficial national symbol. These bright wooden figures, traditionally red with kurbits flower painting, have been hand-carved in the Dalarna village of Nusnas since the 1800s and went global as a folk souvenir. Choosing the Dala horse over Stockholm gives this country mug a warm, folk-art feel. A charming counterpart to the city-specific Stockholm piece.
Arnhem#576503 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside with a bridge over a boat, the John Frost Bridge over the Lower Rhine, the legendary objective of Operation Market Garden in September 1944. British paratroopers under Major-General John Frost held it for four desperate days against two Panzer divisions before surrendering, the very battle behind the film A Bridge Too Far. A heavy slice of WWII history on a Starbucks mug.
Romania#576505 · Global Icon SeriesRed inside with rustic huts outside, evoking Romania's painted monasteries of Bucovina and the wooden churches of Maramures, both UNESCO listed. The Bucovina monasteries are unique in Europe for frescoes that cover their entire exterior walls, Bible scenes painted right onto the outside. A folk leaning country mug that feels warmer than the usual skyline shot.
Dallas#576545 · You Are Here CollectionThis yellow-lined Dallas mug stacks football, a longhorn bull, and a blazing sun over the skyline, a tidy shorthand for Texas. Dallas is forever linked to the Cowboys, America's Team, and to the oil and cattle wealth that built downtown towers like Reunion Tower's geodesic ball. The pile-up of Texas clichés is exactly why these US Global Icons are fun, they wear the stereotype proudly.
CuraçaoThe Global Icon SeriesThis deep blue Global Icon from 2017 celebrates Curaçao, the Dutch Caribbean island known for pastel colonial Willemstad, a UNESCO World Heritage harbor front. The art shows the Queen Emma Bridge, a pontoon footbridge that floats on the water and actually swings open to let ships pass through Sint Anna Bay. A handsome, slightly obscure entry that fills a real gap in any serious Global Icon run.
KrakówThe Global Icon SeriesKrakow is Poland's old royal capital, and any city icon for it is really about Wawel Castle on the Vistula and the medieval Main Market Square, Europe's largest, crowned by the Cloth Hall and St Mary's Basilica. The legend of the Wawel dragon lives right under that castle hill. The historic center was one of the original twelve sites on UNESCO's very first World Heritage list in 1978, which tells you how seriously this city is taken.
KölnThe Global Icon SeriesKoln, or Cologne, is defined by one thing above all: the Kolner Dom, the twin-spired Gothic cathedral that took over 600 years to finish, from 1248 to 1880, and was briefly the tallest building in the world. It survived World War Two largely intact while the city around it was flattened, and it is Germany's most visited landmark. Any Cologne icon worth its salt puts that cathedral front and center.
LucereneThe Global Icon SeriesLucerne, the postcard-perfect Swiss lakeside town, is best known for the Kapellbrücke, the wooden Chapel Bridge from 1333 that is the oldest covered timber bridge in Europe, set against Lake Lucerne and Mount Pilatus. The Icon series typically renders these instantly recognizable landmarks in a single graphic line. A solid Swiss entry that sits nicely beside the Zurich and Geneva mugs in a European shelf.
Niagara FallsThe Global Icon SeriesThe second Niagara Falls entry in my run, the same Global Icon waterfall design rendered in blue and cream. Collectors note this one as discontinued and increasingly hard to find, with sellers framing it as a tourist-stop exclusive. Worth keeping the pair together: the duplicate is a useful reminder of how Starbucks reissued and re-cataloged the popular border-town icons over the years.
Rio de JaneiroThe Global Icon SeriesRio de Janeiro in the Global Icon line, the Cidade Maravilhosa wrapped in its instantly readable icons. Expect Christ the Redeemer, the 1931 Art Deco statue atop Corcovado that is one of the New Seven Wonders, plus Sugarloaf Mountain rising over Guanabara Bay. A flagship Brazilian mug that almost every collector wants represented.
SaarbrückenThe Global Icon SeriesSaarbrucken, capital of the Saarland on the French border, a city whose landmark is the Ludwigskirche, one of Germany's finest baroque Protestant churches, finished in 1775. The region bounced between German and French rule for generations, which gives the city its blended character. A genuinely obscure German city that serious Global Icon completists chase.
SabahThe Global Icon SeriesSabah, the Malaysian state on the northern tip of Borneo, built around Mount Kinabalu, at 4,095 meters the highest peak in Maritime Southeast Asia and a UNESCO World Heritage park. The mountain is sacred to the Kadazan Dusun people and holds five to six thousand plant species. A standout Borneo piece anchored by one of Asia's great mountains.
SapporoThe Global Icon SeriesBlue themed, with Sapporo's Clock Tower on the front and the city landscape on the back. That wooden tower is one of the few surviving Western-style buildings from the 1870s, when Sapporo was laid out on a grid with American advisors helping develop Hokkaido. The city is best known worldwide for the February Snow Festival and for Sapporo beer. Collectors flag this Japan Icon as a harder-to-find one, so I am glad to have it in the case.
São PauloThe Global Icon SeriesSao Paulo is the largest city in South America and the most populous Portuguese-speaking city on earth, a sprawling concrete megacity rather than a single-postcard town. Its landmarks run modernist, the floating red MASP art museum on Avenida Paulista by Lina Bo Bardi, Ibirapuera Park, and Liberdade, home to the largest Japanese community outside Japan. With no catalog description on file here, the city's scale and design pedigree carry the story. A heavyweight name for any Brazil shelf.
TainanThe Global Icon SeriesTainan is the oldest city in Taiwan and its former capital, so its icons are colonial forts, chiefly Chihkan Tower, built by the Dutch as Fort Provintia in 1652, and Anping's Fort Zeelandia from 1634. This is where Koxinga ended 38 years of Dutch rule in 1662, making the city the cradle of Taiwanese history. No catalog notes are on file for this one, so the four centuries of layered history do the talking. A history-rich addition to the Taiwan run.
Trinidad & TobagoThe Global Icon SeriesA two-island Global Icon for Trinidad and Tobago, themed in red. The front shows Stollmeyer's Castle, the 1904 Scottish-baronial mansion on Port of Spain's Queen's Park Savannah, one of the so-called Magnificent Seven houses, while the back carries the Scarlet Ibis and Cocrico, the two national birds. A genuinely uncommon Caribbean entry that I was glad to land for the collection.
Washington DCThe Global Icon SeriesThis is my second Washington DC Global Icon, and DC anchors a rich roster in this line given how many tourists pass through the National Mall. The capital's icons span the Capitol dome, Lincoln Memorial and the cherry trees from Japan. Having doubles of a major capital is normal once you go deep, and it lets me track subtle print and color differences between runs.
WuhanThe Global Icon SeriesWuhan straddles the Yangtze in central China, and its signature is the Yellow Crane Tower, a poetry-soaked landmark rebuilt many times over more than a thousand years. The city is also where the great Wuhan Yangtze River Bridge first linked north and south rail in 1957. Chinese Global Icons like this came largely through the China market, so they reach Western collectors mostly via resellers.
ŁódźThe Global Icon SeriesThis is the Łódź Global Icon, Poland's third largest city and its film capital, home to the famed National Film School that trained Roman Polanski, Andrzej Wajda and Krzysztof Kieślowski. The mug runs a red theme with film and camera equipment on the front and the iconic Piotrkowska Street, one of Europe's longest commercial avenues, on the back. Collectors note it is a relatively common Icon, accessible and well liked among European Starbucks fans.
Classification

City Mug Collector Series228 pieces

The classic Collector Series silhouette, the deep spine of the collection.
Yogyakarta, Indonesia Collector Se#455128 · Indonesia Collector Series (2011)This is the 2011 Indonesia Collector Series version of Yogyakarta, warmer and bolder than the older line with its orange interior and a dancing woman outside. The figure evokes the refined Javanese court dances of the Yogyakarta sultanate, a living palace tradition. Having both the classic skyline mug and this 2011 redesign side by side is exactly the kind of variant pairing that makes a city worth collecting twice.
Bogor, Indonesia Collector Series#455129 · Indonesia Collector Series (2011)The 2011 Indonesia Collector Series Bogor, with a traditional dancer in tone-on-tone turquoise, the dancer-format mate to the older botanical Bogor. Pairing the two Bogors side by side shows off how Starbucks Indonesia reinvented the same city across two design eras. Like the rest of the Indonesian Dancer run, this one circulated domestically, so it leans toward Indonesia-based sellers on the secondary market.
Bandung, Indonesia Collector Serie#455130 · Indonesia Collector Series (2011)Here is Bandung again, but in the 2011 Indonesia Collector Series dancer format, a traditional dancer rendered tone-on-tone in yellow. Owning both the old building Bandung and this dancer Bandung is exactly the kind of same-city, two-series pairing that makes the collection fun. These Indonesian Dancer mugs were domestic-market only, so they surface mostly through sellers based in Indonesia.
Palembang, Indonesia Collector Ser#455131 · Indonesia Collector Series (2011)This is part of the wonderful 2011 Indonesian Dancer Series, and the woman dancing on the red ground is the real hook. Palembang is one of the oldest cities in Indonesia, the old capital of the Srivijaya maritime empire on Sumatra, famous for its Ampera Bridge over the Musi River. The whole 2011 dancer run is a favorite among collectors for its vivid, culturally specific designs.
Solo, Indonesia Collector Series (#455132 · Indonesia Collector Series (2011)This is from the 2011 Indonesian Dancer Series, a regional run that gave each city a traditional dancer rather than a building, and Solo's turquoise figure honors the refined court dance of Surakarta, one of Java's two old royal kraton cities. The whole series is hard to assemble in the West since it sold only in Indonesia, so any Dancer mug is a find. I treasure how this line broke the City Mug formula, trading skylines for living culture.
Surabaya, Indonesia Collector Seri#455133 · Indonesia Collector Series (2011)This is Surabaya's entry in the 2011 Indonesian Dancer Series, the purple version, swapping the famous shark-and-crocodile emblem for a graceful traditional dancer in keeping with that line's culture-first theme. Having both this and the older landmark Surabaya is a real collector treat, the same city told two completely different ways. The Dancer Series stayed in Indonesia, so pulling the matched East Java pieces together takes patience.
Medan, Indonesia Collector Series#455135 · Indonesia Collector Series (2011)This is the 2011 Indonesian Dancer Series Medan, dark purple inside and out with a woman mid-dance, part of a run that gave each Indonesian city its own traditional dancer rather than a landmark. The whole dancer set, covering cities like Bali, Surabaya, Bandung and Makassar, is a favorite among Indonesia-focused collectors precisely because it is so distinct from the global lines. The deep plum colorway makes it stand out on a shelf.
