The warm brown-orange vintage photo treatment is a departure from the line's usual line-drawn skylines, which makes this a more atmospheric, almost postcard-like collector piece.
United Kingdom#576918 · City Mug Collector SeriesA photo of three classic red telephone boxes stands in for the whole United Kingdom, and few objects say Britain faster. Giles Gilbert Scott designed the iconic K2 and K6 kiosks in the 1920s and 1930s, the same architect behind Battersea Power Station and Liverpool Cathedral. A country-level mug that wisely skips Big Ben for the humbler, more beloved red booth.
Balikesir#576919 · City Mug Collector SeriesBalikesir is a Turkish province city in the Marmara region, and the catalog art of an olive branch, river, and old bridge nods squarely at its economy, because this is olive-oil and farming country near the Aegean. The light green palette is a quiet, unusual choice in the line. Smaller Turkish cities like this are tougher to track down than Istanbul, which makes them satisfying when you finally land one.
Bremen#576923 · City Mug Collector SeriesThis one carries the Town Musicians of Bremen, the Grimm fairy-tale donkey, dog, cat, and rooster stacked into a tower, immortalized in Gerhard Marcks's 1951 bronze by the city hall. The joke of the tale is the animals never actually reach Bremen. It is a beloved, instantly readable design, and German storybook mugs like this are among the most charming entries on the Germany shelf.
Heidelberg#576924 · City Mug Collector SeriesHeidelberg's purple bridge is the Alte Brucke, the 18th-century Karl Theodor stone bridge over the Neckar, framed below the romantic ruined castle that draws visitors from everywhere. The town is home to Germany's oldest university, founded in 1386. Collectors note this City Mug Collector Series exists in three variants, China-made plus two Germany Rastal backstamps, so the bottom mark is worth flipping the mug over to check.
Freiburg#576926 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe dark purple cathedral is the Freiburg Münster, a sandstone Gothic masterpiece whose single openwork spire was called the most beautiful tower in Christendom by the art historian Jacob Burckhardt. Tucked at the edge of the Black Forest in Germany's sunny southwest, Freiburg is famous for its bächle, the little water channels running through the medieval streets, and for being one of Europe's greenest, most solar-powered cities.
Toronto#576928 · City Mug Collector SeriesNo surprise which landmark anchors Toronto, the CN Tower rendered in light blue, the 553 meter communications spire that reigned as the world's tallest free-standing structure from 1976 until 2007. Canada's largest city packs the tower, the Blue Jays, and a famously polyglot population into one skyline. A clean, instantly readable City Mug that any collector recognizes at a glance.
New York#576929 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe light blue NYC skyline on this one is the classic City Mug treatment, the Empire State Building and the towers of Manhattan strung into a single recognizable band. New York being the flagship American city, this mug is among the most reproduced and easiest to find in the whole series, which makes pristine early printings the ones worth holding. A foundational piece every collection seems to start with.
Minneapolis St. Paul#576931 · City Mug Collector SeriesThis is the legend, the red cherry in a spoon being Claes Oldenburg and Coosje van Bruggen's Spoonbridge and Cherry at the Minneapolis Sculpture Garden. The 1994 original was pulled from shelves after just four days over a copyright claim and the rest destroyed, with maybe fewer than fifty ever sold, which is why a verified early example has changed hands for around $2,020 and it ranks among the rarest Starbucks mugs in existence. The holy grail of City Mugs.
Calgary#576932 · City Mug Collector SeriesThose boots are pure Calgary Stampede, the self-billed Greatest Outdoor Show on Earth that has run since 1912. The city's other emblem is the white Smithbilt cowboy hat, first worn at the 1946 Stampede and handed to visiting dignitaries in a tradition called white-hatting. A fittingly western piece for Alberta's rodeo town.
Boston#576933 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe brown man-on-horse is the Paul Revere equestrian statue on the Prado in the North End, gazing toward the Old North Church of one-if-by-land fame. Boston is one of the original American cities of the early City Mug line, so a clean Collector Series Boston has real heritage weight. Early-1990s Boston city mugs are exactly the kind of US piece that draws serious collector attention.
Chicago#576934 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe orange church on the Magnificent Mile is the Gothic Chicago Water Tower, one of the few structures to survive the Great Chicago Fire of 1871 and now a beloved Michigan Avenue landmark. Chicago is also the birthplace of the skyscraper, with the 1885 Home Insurance Building. A solid flagship-city mug.
Santa Barbara#576936 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe grey-brown church is Mission Santa Barbara, founded in 1786 and nicknamed the Queen of the Missions for its twin-towered classical facade. The whole city is famously dressed in red-tiled, white-walled Spanish Colonial Revival style, mandated after a 1925 earthquake rebuilt downtown. This is the American Riviera, and the mission is exactly the right landmark to carry it.
Denver#576937 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe skiing figure says it all, Denver is the Mile High City, sitting exactly 5,280 feet above sea level with one step of the state capitol marking that elevation. It is the gateway to the Rockies and Colorado's powder, though the resorts themselves lie an hour or two west, so the green skier here is really selling the mountain lifestyle the city's airport funnels people toward.
West L.A.#576938 · City Mug Collector SeriesWest L.A. is an unusual pick, a sub-district rather than a marquee city, which makes this one a quiet curiosity for completists. The light green clock tower nods to the Westwood Village landmark, the 1929 Spanish Revival tower at the old movie palace that anchors that neighborhood near UCLA. Local-district mugs like this rarely got wide distribution, so they tend to surprise people when they turn up.
Santa Monica#576939 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe light purple piece shows the Santa Monica Pier and its welcome sign, the western end of historic Route 66 where the Mother Road meets the Pacific. The 1909 pier carries the Pacific Park Ferris wheel, the world's only solar-powered one, and the carousel that has spun beachgoers for generations. A sunny, boardwalk-flavored City Mug, very Southern California.
Atlanta#576940 · City Mug Collector SeriesAtlanta is the capital of the New South, rebuilt after the Civil War and home to Coca-Cola, Delta, and Martin Luther King Jr. The light grey rotunda top on this mug depicts the gold-domed Georgia State Capitol, whose dome was famously gilded with Dahlonega gold from north Georgia. A clean older City Mug from the city that hosted the 1996 Centennial Olympic Games and serves as the busiest air hub on earth.
San Antonio#576941 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe light grey ruins on this mug are the Alamo, the 1718 Spanish mission where roughly 200 defenders fell to Santa Anna's army in 1836, giving Texas its battle cry, Remember the Alamo. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage site along with the city's four other Spanish colonial missions. San Antonio also gave us the River Walk, so the city is far more than its famous last stand.
New Orleans#576943 · City Mug Collector SeriesMy New Orleans mug nails it with a red Bourbon Street sign, the French Quarter's most photographed marker and the spine of the city's nightlife and jazz. Bourbon Street is named not for the whiskey but for the French royal House of Bourbon that ruled when the street was laid out in 1721. The Big Easy's music, Mardi Gras and Creole cooking all radiate from that quarter, so the sign is perfect shorthand.
San Francisco#576944 · City Mug Collector SeriesThose dark blue houses are the Painted Ladies, the row of Victorian and Edwardian homes facing Alamo Square that became the city's most photographed postcard. Built mostly between 1892 and 1896, they survived the 1906 quake and fire that leveled much of the city. I appreciate that Starbucks reached past the obvious Golden Gate Bridge for a more knowing San Francisco image.
Olympia#576945 · City Mug Collector SeriesOlympia is the capital of Washington, Starbucks' home state, and the dark blue rotunda is the Legislative Building, whose self-supporting masonry dome is one of the tallest in the United States. Note that the early 1994 Olympia city mug came in an oversized 20oz format and is a genuinely scarce find. This standard Collector Series version is the easier-to-source cousin, but the local connection makes it a sentimental keeper for me.
Sacramento#576946 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe grey columned building on this Sacramento mug is the California State Capitol, the neoclassical 1874 dome at the heart of the city. Sacramento earned its place in history as the western terminus of the Pony Express and the Transcontinental Railroad, and as the boomtown that exploded out of the 1849 Gold Rush. A solid state-capital mug for anyone building the California run.
San Jose#576947 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe grey chip is a literal microchip, and there is no more honest emblem for San Jose, the self-styled Capital of Silicon Valley. The city anchors the tech corridor where Fairchild, Intel and a thousand startups put the silicon in the valley's name. I love a City Mug that abandons skylines and churches for a piece of industry, it tells you precisely what this place actually makes.
Washington D.C.#576948 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe blue Capitol Rotunda anchors the US capital, the cast-iron dome completed during the Civil War as a deliberate symbol that the Union would endure. Washington's monumental core was laid out by Pierre L'Enfant, and the Capitol crowns it all. Phrased almost identically to my Victoria mug, this is the City Mug line leaning on the most photographed dome in American politics.
Victoria#576949 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe Capital Rotunda here points to the British Columbia Parliament Buildings on Victoria's Inner Harbour, the neo-Baroque, dome-topped seat designed by Francis Rattenbury and opened in 1898, crowned by a gilded statue of Captain George Vancouver. Victoria is BC's genteel capital, all afternoon tea and the Empress Hotel. A handsome civic landmark mug that rounds out the Canadian trio.
Philadelphia#576950 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe cracked Liberty Bell in grey is exactly right, that famous fracture making it instantly Philadelphia. The bell was cast in 1752 and the crack you see is the result of repeated repair attempts to an earlier flaw. Philly was the cradle of American independence, where both the Declaration and the Constitution were signed, so this City Mug carries real founding-era weight.
Orange County#576951 · City Mug Collector SeriesTwo oranges, and the joke writes itself, but Orange County, California really was named for the citrus groves that once blanketed it before the freeways and theme parks arrived. It is now better known for Disneyland and miles of Pacific coastline. A cheerful, literal City Mug that I like precisely because it leans into the pun instead of reaching for a skyline.
East Bay#576953 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe purple clock tower is Sather Tower, the Campanile at UC Berkeley, a 1914 landmark modeled on the bell tower in Venice's St Mark's Square. East Bay is collector shorthand for Berkeley and Oakland across the water from San Francisco, and this older 20oz Collector Series piece is a nice catch because the line picked a campus icon rather than a generic skyline.
Spokane#576954 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe brown clock tower on mine is the Great Northern Clock Tower in Spokane's Riverfront Park, the lone survivor of the 1902 railroad depot that was cleared for Expo 74, the smallest city ever to host a World's Fair. That 155-foot tower with its four ten-foot dials is the city's signature image. Spokane is a solid mid-tier US City Mug, the kind of regional piece that fills a hard gap in a full fifty-states-style run.
Vancouver#576955 · City Mug Collector SeriesFive light purple tents depict Canada Place, the Vancouver waterfront landmark whose five Teflon sails were built as the Canada Pavilion for Expo 86. The city wraps mountains, ocean, and Stanley Park around a glassy downtown, which makes the sails an apt single symbol. A sharp Canadian City Mug that pairs naturally with the Toronto and Victoria pieces.
Dallas#576956 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe grey cowboy boots are pure Texas shorthand, and Dallas wears them well as the buttoned-up business twin to ranching Fort Worth. Founded in the 1840s, the city boomed on cotton, oil and banking, and stays lodged in memory for the 1963 Kennedy assassination at Dealey Plaza and the Dallas television saga of the Ewings, but the boots keep it firmly Lone Star.
Portland#576957 · City Mug Collector SeriesA single red rose, and that is the whole identity, because Portland, Oregon is the City of Roses, home to the International Rose Test Garden established in 1917 in Washington Park. The mild climate made it ideal for rose cultivation, and the nickname stuck for over a century. I love how this City Mug trusts one bold flower to do all the work.
Austin#576959 · City Mug Collector SeriesAustin's brown armadillo is no random critter, it has been the city's unofficial mascot since the 1970s when the legendary Armadillo World Headquarters music venue made the creature shorthand for Austin's keep-it-weird counterculture. The Texas capital and live-music capital of the world wears its quirk proudly, and few City Mugs are as instantly identifiable by a single animal. A fun, characterful piece that locals immediately recognize.
Seattle#576961 · City Mug Collector SeriesMount Rainier in light green is the right hometown choice for Starbucks, the 14,411-foot volcano that looms over Seattle and lent its name to the company's first store on Pike Place in 1971. On a clear day locals simply say the mountain is out. For the brand's birthplace this is a quietly perfect City Mug, the peak that watches over where the whole green-aproned story began.
Los Angeles#576963 · City Mug Collector SeriesLos Angeles surprises by featuring a grey vintage Oldsmobile rather than Hollywood or palm trees, a knowing nod to LA as the ultimate American car city, built around the automobile and the freeway. It is one of the wittier, more unexpected design choices in the US line. Oldsmobile itself, founded in 1897, was one of America's oldest auto brands before GM retired it in 2004, giving this mug an extra layer of nostalgia.
Tacoma#576969 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe dark brown building top on mine nods to Tacoma's Union Station, the grand 1911 copper-domed railroad depot now a federal courthouse, in a Washington city that sits right in Starbucks' own backyard south of Seattle. Tacoma carries extra meaning for a Pacific Northwest collector given how close it is to the company's roots. It is an everyday US mug, but its hometown geography gives it a quiet significance many out-of-state pieces lack.
Las Vegas#576971 · City Mug Collector SeriesLas Vegas skips the Strip skyline and goes straight for the gambling, with a pair of grey dice on the body, a witty shorthand for Sin City. It is a refreshingly playful design choice in a series that usually defaults to monuments and skylines. Vegas is one of the more heavily produced and traded US city mugs given the tourist volume, so this is widely available, but the dice motif gives it real personality.
Houston#576972 · City Mug Collector SeriesHouston is the energy capital of America, headquarters to the oil and gas giants, so the grey oil derricks outside go straight to what built the city's fortune. It is also home to NASA's Johnson Space Center, but this older City Mug Collector Series leans into the petroleum heritage instead. A blunt, no-nonsense industrial design that I find refreshingly honest about why Houston boomed in the first place.
San Diego#576973 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe light grey sailboat fits San Diego perfectly, a Navy town and sailing harbor blessed with what locals immodestly call America's Finest City weather. This is where Cabrillo first landed in 1542, making it the birthplace of California, and home today to Balboa Park and the world-famous San Diego Zoo. A breezy, maritime read on a City Mug that suits the laid-back coast.
Haifa#576974 · City Mug Collector SeriesHaifa is Israel's great northern port on the slopes of Mount Carmel, so the blue anchor outside is spot on for a working harbor city. This one is genuinely scarce, because Starbucks pulled out of Israel entirely in 2003 after only a brief run, leaving very few Israeli mugs in circulation. Collectors chase the 2002 Haifa, with asking prices often well into the hundreds, which makes this little blue anchor one of the prizes of any serious shelf.
OsnabrückCity Mug Collector SeriesOsnabrück carries enormous history for a mid-sized German city, because in 1648 it was one of the two towns where the Peace of Westphalia was signed, ending the Thirty Years' War. The Rathaus, the City Hall of the Westphalian Peace, is the landmark most associated with it. My piece is the standard Collector Series mug, a quiet but historically heavyweight addition.
QuerétaroCity Mug Collector SeriesQuerétaro's signature is its 18th-century aqueduct, 74 sandstone arches marching nearly a mile across the city, built between 1726 and 1738 and still a symbol on every postcard. The historic center is a UNESCO World Heritage site and the spot where Mexico's 1810 independence conspiracy was hatched. My catalog line came in blank on the artwork, but this is the standard City Mug Collector Series piece for the city.
Semarang, Indonesia Collector SeriCity Mug Collector SeriesSemarang is the port capital of Central Java, and this dated 2011 Indonesia Collector Series mug in white and blue belongs to the wave Starbucks rolled out across the archipelago that year. The city's signature landmark is Lawang Sewu, the haunting Dutch colonial railway headquarters whose name means Thousand Doors. The year stamp makes these 2011 Indonesia pieces easy to date and fun to chase as a matched run.
São PauloCity Mug Collector SeriesSao Paulo is the giant of South America, the largest city in the hemisphere, a relentless concrete sprawl of skyscrapers, paulista business swagger, and the strongest Italian and Japanese immigrant cultures on the continent. With no catalog description here, mine leans on that endless skyline or a landmark like the Edificio Italia or the cathedral. Brazil City Mugs are well loved, and Sao Paulo is a natural anchor next to Rio for a Brazil pairing.
Classification

The Long Tail845 pieces

The everyday City Mug line and everything that belongs to no single series.
Dark Green, Teapot#186005 · The Long TailA dark green teapot finished with the latest logo in gold and a gold-tipped spout, a reminder that Starbucks began as Starbucks Coffee, Tea and Spices in 1971. Tea was right there in the original 1971 name, even if coffee took over the story, and serveware like this kept that thread alive. A handsome, less common form than the mugs, with the gold detailing lifting it above ordinary kitchenware.
See through Glass#186021 · The Long TailA clear see-through glass cup carrying the Starbucks logo printed in white on the outside. The white-logo treatment reads cleanly against the transparent body and marks it as everyday glassware rather than a city mug. Simple, legible, and a good baseline example of the plain branded glass line.
See through Glass (Starbucks Sign)#186023 · The Long TailA clear see-through glass cup with the Starbucks logo printed in green, the brand's signature siren color, on the outside. It mirrors its white-logo sibling almost exactly, with the green mark being the only meaningful variation, the kind of small difference collectors like to shelve side by side. Plain branded glassware, but a tidy pair when displayed together.
Barnes & Noble Starbucks Plastic C#186024 · The Long TailSee-through plastic cups co-branded Barnes & Noble and Starbucks, relics of the long partnership that put Starbucks-run cafes inside Barnes & Noble bookstores starting in the 1990s. Co-branded service ware like this rarely gets saved, since people toss plastic. That is exactly why an intact pair documenting that bookstore-cafe alliance is worth keeping in a collection built mostly of ceramic.
Mermaid Green, Cup#186026 · The Long TailA bright white cup with the green star inside and the classic green Siren logo wrapping the outside, this is pure logo merchandise rather than a place piece. The mermaid, properly a twin-tailed Siren, has anchored Starbucks identity since 1971 and was redrawn most dramatically in 2011 when the wordmark was dropped entirely. I keep logo-forward cups like this as anchors that show off the brand's most recognizable element.
Red Rocket, 16oz, Frappucino Cup w#186027 · The Long TailThe Red Rocket is a 16 ounce reusable Frappuccino cup, bright red plastic inside and out with a star motif and its own straw, the sort of cold drink vessel that almost never survives the dishwasher years. It is pure summer merchandise, more drinkware than collectible, which is half its charm in a collection like this. Finding one complete with the original straw is the small victory.
Blue Rocket, 12oz, Frappuccino Cup#186030 · The Long TailA 12-ounce blue plastic Frappuccino cup themed with streaking speed lines, built for the cold-blended drink that became a Starbucks signature after its 1995 launch. Branded Frappuccino service cups are everyday equipment that almost nobody keeps, which is why surviving ones document a drink's visual identity better than any ad. The Blue Rocket motion graphics are pure mid-era Frappuccino marketing fun.
Tazo Iced Tea, Ice Fruit Shaker#186031 · The Long TailA clear plastic cocktail style shaker set with straws and reusable fruit shaped ice cubes, this is pure Tazo merchandising from the era when Starbucks owned that herbal and iced tea brand. Tazo was founded in Portland in 1994, bought by Starbucks in 1999, and later sold to Unilever in 2017, so anything Tazo branded is a fixed window of company history. A fun, functional oddity that breaks up a shelf of ceramics.
Dark Green, Short Canister#186035 · The Long TailThe shorter companion to the large dark green canister, again carrying the gold first logo over deep green. Sold for bean or ground storage at home, these tie the equipment line back to Starbucks' founding-era green and gold look. Having both heights together is the satisfying part, a matched pair from the home-storage range in the brand's original colorway.
Dark Green, Large Canister#186036 · The Long TailA dark green storage canister with the original gold first logo, part of the home-coffee equipment line meant to keep beans fresh on the counter. The deep green and gold pairing is the classic early Starbucks palette, the same heritage colors as the founding siren badge. This is the larger of the two sizes, a functional piece that wears the brand's vintage identity proudly.
1/4 Lbs Logo Canister#186045 · The Long TailThis is a simple quarter-pound logo canister carrying the current green-and-white siren wordmark, a piece of retail packaging hardware rather than drinkware. Canisters like this were the everyday vessels behind the counter and on shelves, so they document Starbucks as a coffee retailer more than as a souvenir machine. I keep pieces like this because the plain logo objects ground a collection in the brand's actual storefront history.
2014 Year of the Horse#186088 · The Long TailA tiny espresso mug, white inside with a sculpted bronze horse on the outside, made for the 2014 Lunar New Year. The Year of the Wooden Horse pieces lean on bronze and gold tones to read as auspicious and prosperous, and the demitasse format makes this one a charmer to hold. Zodiac minis like this travel well in a collection because the whole twelve-animal cycle invites the hunt.
Espresso Roast, Mug, Small#186101 · The Long TailThe little brother of the Espresso Roast set, this is the small espresso, or demitasse, format meant for a true single shot rather than a long drink. Same white body and Espresso Roast stamp, just scaled down to match the intense dark roast Starbucks built its entire espresso program around. I keep the pair together because the size jump tells the whole story of how the blend was meant to be served.
Partner Portal, Shot Cup#186138 · The Long TailThis is a glass espresso shot cup carrying the siren logo, tied to the Partner Portal and the internal Leadership Conference run for store managers and field partners. It is a working tool rather than retail merchandise, the little one ounce glass a barista would pull a ristretto into, which is why these surface mostly through partners offloading conference swag. The mermaid etched on glass makes it feel more like a keepsake than equipment.
Starbucks, Truly Good Coffee#186139 · The Long TailA shot glass carrying the old Starbucks tagline "Truly Good Coffee," a slogan from the brand's earlier identity before the marketing language shifted. Shot glasses are a sleeper corner of Starbucks collecting, small, easily lost or broken, and rarely kept in sets, which is exactly why a clean tagline piece like this is satisfying to track down.
2000, Starbucks Store under Snow,#186140 · The Long TailThe miniature shot glass companion to the 2000 Store under Snow holiday piece, white inside with the same snow filled Starbucks storefront on a tiny demitasse body. Shot and espresso sized pieces from the holiday runs were made in far smaller numbers than the full mugs, so they vanish quickly. Having both the full mug and this little shot cup as a matched pair is the kind of completeness I chase.
2013, Brown, Shot Cup (3oz)#186141 · The Long TailA tiny 3oz shot cup, white inside, with a warm brown body dressed in gold wheat motifs. The wheat sheaves nod to the agricultural, harvest imagery Starbucks reached for in some seasonal lines, and the miniature format makes it a sweet espresso-sized oddity. Little demitasse and shot pieces like this are easy to overlook but fun to corner a shelf with.
Dark Blue, Shot Cup#186142 · The Long TailA tiny dark blue shot glass with a white interior line and the latest logo in white on the outside, sized for an espresso shot or a demitasse pour. These small-format cups were sold as part of the espresso lifestyle kit and are easy to lose or break, so intact ones are pleasant finds. A minor piece, but the shot format rounds out a collection beyond standard mugs.
6.5oz Double, Shot Cup#186143 · The Long TailA clear 6.5oz glass carrying the Starbucks DoubleShot logo, a true shot-glass-style serving piece. DoubleShot launched as Starbucks' canned espresso drink in 2002, and branded glassware like this was promotional gear built around that line. Glass survives poorly compared to ceramic, so an intact logo'd shot glass is a small but satisfying catch.
2oz, Shot Cup#186144 · The Long TailA plain transparent 2oz glass shot cup, the humble vessel for pulling and measuring a single espresso shot. There is no branding story to chase here, just the working tool of the trade, but a proper collection wants the everyday gear alongside the trophy mugs. It grounds the whole set in what Starbucks actually does, which is make coffee.
Abstract Painting (3), Mug, with p#186151 · Chaleur MadeThe same Burrows city-street-with-Starbucks-patio design, this example preserved with its original plastic travel lid. Lids almost never survive on ceramic mugs, so having the matched accessory intact is a small completist win. It is the identical artwork as the standard Painting 3, just a step closer to as-issued condition, which is what I chase when duplicates exist.
2016, Australia Ceramic Mug, Blue#186152 · The Long TailA handle-less tumbler-style ceramic with a blue lid, showing kangaroos bounding across an outback sunset, the single most exportable image Australia owns. Starbucks famously struggled in Australia and pulled back hard, which makes its local merchandise scarcer than you would expect from a country that size. The roos-at-dusk scene is pure tourist shorthand, but the rarity of Aussie pieces is the real draw.
Starbucks Irish Coffee Stemmed Gla#186154 · The Long TailA transparent footed glass built for the classic Irish coffee, hot coffee, Irish whiskey, sugar and a float of cream, with a shamrock clover etched into it and the very first 1971 brown siren logo on the outside. The stemmed shape exists so the hot drink never burns your hand. Glassware carrying that earliest full-figure mermaid is far scarcer than the ceramic mugs.
Two Nutcracker Set with Dark Caffe#186155 · The Long TailA festive pairing in my long-tail drawer: two winking nutcrackers outside, white within, themed to Caffe Verona, the bold roasty-sweet blend Starbucks created in 1975 for a Seattle restaurant as Jake's Blend. It carried the in-store nickname 80/20 Blend for its recipe before being renamed Verona when Schultz could not trademark the original name. Verona has long been the Valentine's coffee, made to pair with chocolate.
2005 City Magnet, Set of Four, Bos#186156 · Architecture SeriesA four-magnet tin-cased set celebrating Boston, with Bunker Hill, Boston Harbor, the USS Constitution, and the Old North Church. Each landmark carries real weight, the Old North Church of "one if by land, two if by sea" fame and "Old Ironsides" being the world's oldest commissioned warship still afloat. These little memorabilia tins were a side line to the mug program, and intact sets with all four magnets and the original case are the way collectors want them.
2005 City Magnet, Set of Four, San#186157 · Architecture SeriesSan Diego's set rounds up the harbor, the world-famous San Diego Zoo, Coronado Island, and Balboa Park in one tin. Balboa Park's Spanish Colonial Revival architecture and the zoo's pioneering open-air enclosures are the city's genuine claims to fame. A charming low-cost cousin to the mugs, this is one to keep boxed and complete, as the four-magnet tins lose all their appeal once a piece goes missing.
2005 City Magnet, Set of Four, Was#186158 · Architecture SeriesThe Washington D.C. tin gathers the Capitol, the White House, the Washington Monument, and the Jefferson Memorial, four of the most recognizable structures in the country. At just over 555 feet, the Washington Monument was the tallest building in the world when finished in 1884. This memorabilia set is a tidy snapshot of the National Mall, and as with all of these 2005 tins, completeness inside the original case is what collectors prize.
2005 City Magnet, Set of Four, New#186159 · Architecture SeriesThe New York tin holds four magnets, the city skyline, the Statue of Liberty, Central Park, and a nod to its unique architecture. It is a pocket-sized tour of the icons that the mug series celebrated on ceramic, packaged for the fridge instead of the cupboard. These 2005 memorabilia sets surface on the secondary market, sometimes billed as rare, and the value lives in keeping all four magnets together inside the original tin case.
2005 City Magnet, Set of Four, Chi#186160 · Architecture SeriesChicago's tin-cased magnet quartet pairs the skyline with the Art Institute of Chicago, Monroe Harbor, and the Chicago Theatre. The Art Institute guards "American Gothic" and the lions out front, while the Chicago Theatre's vertical marquee is one of the most photographed signs in America. A neat companion to the city mugs, this set is best found complete in its tin, since loose magnets scatter and break up the original presentation.
2005, City Magnet, Taiwan Store#186161 · The Long TailA 2005 tin-cased city magnet from Taiwan illustrating five Starbucks stores across the island, a piece of pure store-marketing memorabilia rather than drinkware. Taiwan, where Starbucks operates through President Coffee, has long been one of the most collector-active markets in Asia, and small regional giveaways like this rarely left the country. Holding it I think about how much of the real collecting depth lives in these tiny market-specific objects that never reached the States.
Pencil Box#186164 · The Long TailA piece of memorabilia rather than drinkware, a pencil box holding ten pencils, the last logo printed over brown outside. Office and stationery items like this sat at the edges of the Starbucks merchandise world and were never the focus, which is exactly why a complete box with all ten pencils still inside is uncommon. The all brown wrap with the modern siren dates it to the post 2011 logo era, after the wordmark was dropped from the ring.
Partner Incentive Straws, Summer o#186165 · The Long TailNot a mug at all but a partner artifact, a set of green straws printed with challenges to complete during the summer 2003 partner conferences, packaged in a round sky blue box. These internal incentive pieces never reached customers, which is exactly what makes them quietly collectible, since they document the culture and language Starbucks used with its own baristas. Finding the box intact with the original challenge straws inside is the hard part.
Duke's Super Hi-Test Java Pump (#4#186167 · Doonesbury @ StarbucksThis is the crown of the Doonesbury crossover, the Duke's Super Hi-Test Java Pump statue, hand-numbered 47 of 1500 and showing Duke leaning on a fuel pump in shades. Designed exclusively for Starbucks by Garry Trudeau and produced in Thailand, it stands about seven inches tall as part of a literacy fundraiser. Low numbers like 47 are exactly what collectors chase, and the Java Pump remains the most coveted three-dimensional piece in the entire Doonesbury @ Starbucks set.
Starbucks Coffee, License Plate#186171 · The Long TailA novelty license plate reading Starbucks Coffee, Starbucks, EST. '71, planting a flag on the founding year. Starbucks opened in 1971 at Pike Place Market in Seattle, originally selling beans and equipment rather than brewed drinks, so that EST. '71 is a real historical marker, not just decoration. Plates like this were fan-merch and store decor, fun to display and surprisingly tricky to track down in clean shape.
Authentic Hand Crafted Silver, Tin#186176 · The Long TailA rectangular silver tin stamped Authentic Hand Crafted, the kind of lidded gift box Starbucks used to hold loose tea, chocolate coins, or a small mug for the holidays. Pieces like this fall outside any named ceramic series, which is exactly why I like them. The tin survives long after the contents are gone, and an embossed, unscuffed lid is what separates a keeper from landfill.
2004, 5 Elements, 10oz Mugs#186177 · The Long TailA 2004 boxed set of five 10oz mugs themed on the five elements, each rendered in a different color and packaged together in a silver rectangular tin. The classical elements concept, earth, water, fire, air and a fifth, gives this set a designed gift-box appeal well above ordinary single mugs. Complete-in-box sets like this, with the tin intact, are the kind of multi-piece release collectors prize precisely because so many get broken up over twenty years.
4 Wooden Coasters#186179 · India MadeA set of four wooden coasters in a matching wooden holder, the cozy home-barista accessory side of the brand. Wood pieces are uncommon next to the endless ceramic and stainless output, which gives this set a warmer, more tactile feel on the shelf. Complete sets with the holder intact are the way to keep these, since loose coasters scatter and vanish.
2005 Leadership Conference, North#186186 · North Aemrican Stores / 2005 Leadership ConferenceA genuine insider piece, six 3oz demitasse cups in a brown box made exclusively for the Starbucks North America 2005 Leadership Conference. Each cup illustrates the Green Apron Book's "Five Ways of Being," be welcoming, genuine, knowledgeable, considerate, and involved, with the sixth reading "why we're here." Roughly 9,000 managers attended and received a set to take home, which makes these non-retail cups a real collector's prize.
Starbucks Store Sign (Small)#186188 · One Store is missing it's sign...An actual small electric-powered Starbucks store sign, store fixture and signage rather than drinkware, the kind of thing normally destroyed or returned when a location remodels or closes. Lit retail signage almost never reaches private hands legitimately. A working illuminated piece of real store hardware is about as close to owning a piece of the storefront as a collector can get.
Starbucks Playing Cards, Vintage L#186200 · The Long TailTwo decks of Starbucks playing cards in differing packaging, marketed as vintage limited editions, a piece of lifestyle merch from the era when the brand sold a whole coffeehouse-culture aesthetic. Sealed decks rarely survive because cards are meant to be played with. Having two variant packagings side by side is the real prize, since it documents a small printing or release difference most collectors never notice.
Collectible Coffee Stamp Magnets (#186201 · The Long TailA set of seven Starbucks fridge magnets styled as postage stamps for the company's coffee blends, with this lot carrying a double of the Italian Roast. Starbucks leaned hard on the airmail and passport motif in the early 2000s, framing each origin and roast as a stamp in a coffee passport. Fun little ephemera, the kind of small-format memorabilia that rarely survives in a complete run.
Collectible Miniatures Series 1#186202 · The Long TailSeries 1 of the Collectible Miniatures, three tiny mugs marking 1971, 1984, and 2003, three pivot years in the company story. 1971 is the founding at Pike Place, 1984 is the year the original owners began serving espresso drinks under Howard Schultz's push, and 2003 sits in the modern global era. A clever timeline you can hold in one hand.
Starbucks Coffee Coasters from ove#186204 · The Long TailEight different Starbucks coffee coasters, one of them printed with coffee trivia, gathered over the years. Coasters were give-away marketing, so they tracked the brand's shifting logos, slogans and origin stories in a cheap disposable format. That trivia coaster is the fun one, the sort of thing that taught customers how to pronounce a roast or where a bean came from, and a full run of eight shows the design language evolving.
9 x Starbucks Key Chain Set#186206 · Thailand MarketA nine-piece keychain set built around one main hook with three side hooks, a functional little partner or promotional giveaway. Small branded hardware like this was never catalogued as serious collectibles, so survivors in a complete set are oddly scarce. I keep these because the tiny everyday objects round out a collection that otherwise leans entirely on mugs.
2 x Paper Stamps with Starbucks la#186207 · The Long TailTwo blue ink-based rubber stamps bearing Starbucks' most recent logo, the kind of internal store hardware that almost never reaches collectors. Operational ephemera like stamps, name tags and signage is its own niche corner of Starbucks collecting precisely because it was meant to stay behind the counter, so a matched pair of logo stamps is a genuinely uncommon grab.
Doonesbury 4 Starbucks Themed Coas#186213 · Doonesbury @ StarbucksA set of four cork-cushioned ceramic coasters from the Doonesbury @ Starbucks line, born of Garry Trudeau's long-running comic-strip gags about coffee culture. Trudeau donated his artwork to Starbucks for a literacy fundraiser, which is why the whole Doonesbury crossover exists. The coasters are a smaller, harder-to-find companion to the famous Duke mugs and the Java Pump statue, so a complete set of four is a genuine catch.
Starbucks Green Coin Holder#186214 · The Long TailA Japan-made coin holder in dark Starbucks green with the logo and a zipper, a slice of the brand's deep Japanese accessory culture. Starbucks Japan, which opened its first store in Tokyo's Ginza in 1996, has long produced small lifestyle goods well beyond mugs, and these zip pouches were exactly that kind of everyday carry. Region-specific accessories like this rarely leave Japan, which is what makes one worth grabbing.
Starbucks Vintage Wind-Up 60-Minut#186215 · The Long TailA genuinely fun non-mug oddity, a working yellow wind-up kitchen timer that counts down to sixty minutes and rings a bell, with the Starbucks logo on the front. Pieces like this come from the era when Starbucks stocked a whole home-and-kitchen lifestyle range, and functional mechanical memorabilia tends to be harder to find intact and still ringing than any mug.
2 x Starbucks Hand Bracelets (We C#186216 · The Long TailTwo "We Care" bracelets, one pink and one light blue, sold by Starbucks in support of UNICEF and AIDS orphans. They belong to the company's broad late-2000s charitable push, the same goodwill era that produced the (RED) tie-ins, and small awareness pieces like these tend to evaporate quickly, so keeping a clean two-color pair preserves a charity campaign that left almost no other physical trace.
2 x Starbucks Round Mousepads#186217 · The Long TailA pair of round mousepads, one with the classic Starbucks Coffee logo and one branded for Doubleshot, the ready-to-drink espresso line. Desk swag like this came from promotions and corporate giveaways rather than retail shelves, which is why it rarely turns up, and the Doubleshot example doubles as a nice little marker of that product's mid-2000s marketing push.
Starbucks Theme Mini Maglite + Sta#186218 · The Long TailA two-piece promotional kit housed in a Mini Maglite case, a Starbucks-branded Maglite flashlight plus a Starbucks carabiner with a built-in blue LED. This is co-branded promotional gear from the outdoorsy lifestyle-merch era, a gift-with-purchase or partner item. Branded hardware like a real Maglite is unusual, and finding both pieces still tucked in the original case is the rare part.
3 x Starbucks Coffee Bookmarks#186219 · The Long TailA trio of paper bookmarks, one a white coffee cup, one the current Siren logo, and one a black mermaid, the kind of small-margin promo ephemera that almost never survives because people actually use it in books. That fragility is exactly why intact bookmark sets are quietly prized. They also chart the logo's evolution in miniature, which is a nice bonus for a brand-history nerd like me.
Starbucks Pins from over the years#186220 · The Long TailA run of enamel pins spanning Thanksgiving 1998 through Japan 2001 and beyond, the kind of dated partner and promotional pins that marked seasons, store openings and market launches. Pins were cheap to make and easy to lose, so a chronological survival like this is genuinely hard to assemble. Each one quietly fixes a date and a place in the company's expansion.
2 x 2009 All you need is love CD's#186221 · Starbucks REDTwo copies of the 2009 "All You Need Is Love" EP, the Starbucks and (RED) charity disc handed out free with purchases over fifteen dollars that November, with one dollar per copy going to the Global Fund to fight AIDS in Africa. Having a sealed pair documents a genuine pop-culture charity moment.
4 x Starbucks Watches (2001 / 2002#186222 · Japan 2001 / USA 2002A four-watch lot of Japanese promotional timepieces, two marking Starbucks Japan's 5th anniversary and two from the Summer 2002 Frappuccino campaign. Starbucks opened its first Japan store in Ginza in August 1996, so the fifth-anniversary pieces date to 2001, which fits perfectly. Japan-market premiums like these were giveaways or staff items, never sold widely abroad, and that scarcity is exactly why I chased them.
4 x Starbucks Lanyards#186223 · The Long TailFour lanyards, a long black clip style, a medium black with a mini ornament, a To Go cup design with a tiny cup charm, and a VIA-themed one with mini VIA ornaments, the sort of staff and event swag that almost never reaches collectors. The little dangling ornaments are the charm here, and the VIA tie-in dates it to the instant-coffee push Starbucks launched in 2009. Small, odd, and exactly the kind of thing that gets thrown out.
Starbucks Luggage Tag#186224 · The Long TailA black travel luggage tag styled around the siren's flowing waves, a piece of accessory merch rather than drinkware. Starbucks leaned hard into travel-themed gear alongside the You Are Here mug boom, and small items like this rarely get cataloged or saved. It's the kind of throwaway accessory that becomes oddly collectible precisely because almost no one kept theirs.
5 x Starbucks Hats or Binnie#186225 · The Long TailA soft-goods grab bag of partner headwear: three Starbucks caps, a bandana, and a knit beanie. These were uniform and promotional pieces handed to staff rather than sold, so they almost never reach collectors in numbers. I like apparel lots like this because they fill in the human, behind-the-counter side of the collection that the mugs never show.
Assortment of Starbucks Stickers#186226 · The Long TailNot a mug at all but a memorabilia lot, an assortment of Starbucks stickers covering blends, the logo, and the Summer of 2006 promotion. This is the ephemera that almost never survives, peel-and-stick by nature, so an intact run from a single season is genuinely hard to assemble. I treat it as a time capsule of 2006 store branding rather than a throwaway.
5 x Starbucks Thailand XL shirts#186228 · Starbucks Thailand ShirtsFive XL tees from Starbucks Thailand, market-specific apparel from a region that built a famously devoted local fan base. Thailand's stores lean hard into regional merchandise and limited drops, so country-stamped clothing like this is a genuine travel souvenir you cannot buy stateside. A fun reminder that the green siren wears very different local colors store to store.
4 X Starbucks China Shirts#186229 · Starbucks China ShirtsFour China-market shirts, an XXXL black Beijing, an XXL white Beijing, a Tianjin, and a green-logo white tee, capturing the explosive Starbucks expansion across mainland China. City-named apparel from specific Chinese stores is genuinely hard to source outside the country, which makes a four-shirt China cluster a real find. The Beijing and Tianjin pairing reads like a travel diary you can wear.
3 x Starbucks Shirts#186230 · The Long TailThree pieces of apparel, an XL black tee, an XXL white tee, and an XXL white polo, the wearable side of the collection. Starbucks staff and promo clothing rarely gets preserved in collectible condition because it lives a hard life, so keeping these clean and folded is half the value. They round out a collection that is too often all ceramics and no fabric.
5 x Starbucks Aprons#186231 · The Long TailA five-apron working set spanning the partner wardrobe: a blue Frappuccino apron, a red one, a black, and two greens. The green apron is the everyday barista uniform, black traditionally signals a certified Coffee Master, and red is the holiday-season apron, so this lot quietly maps the whole staff color code. Worn apparel like this rarely survives, which makes a clean spread like this a nice piece of real store history.
1 x Starbucks London T-Shirt#186232 · The Long TailThis is a "Waking Up London" XL tee, a piece of Starbucks apparel rather than ceramic, with the logo on the front and a drawing of a horse rider on the back. The horseback rider almost surely nods to the Household Cavalry, the mounted guards who are one of London's most photographed sights at Horse Guards Parade. Soft-goods like this are easy to overlook in a mug-centric collection but they round out the story of a market.
Starbucks Israel Memorabilia#186234 · The Long TailA genuine time capsule from Starbucks' short-lived Israeli run, a Hebrew edition of Howard Schultz's Pour Your Heart Into It, a Summer 2002 mug reading roughly that's how I like my coffee under the logo, and original store pamphlets. Starbucks Hong Kong Memorabilia#186235 · The Long TailA Hong Kong bundle: a coffee and food catalog, a Make It Your Drink customization book, and a 2003 associate handbook. The handbook is the real gem, an internal partner document that almost never escapes the back room, offering a candid look at how Starbucks trained baristas in its early Hong Kong market. Paper ephemera like this is far rarer than mugs because it was operational, not retail, and meant to be recycled.
Starbucks Express Train#186236 · The Long TailA two-part set: a Starbucks Express locomotive plus a train car stamped with Espresso Roast and Kenya Blend. This ties straight into the brand's love of railway imagery, dressing coffee origins as freight rolling in from far-off plantations. The Kenya stamp is a nice touch since Kenyan beans are prized for their bright, blackcurrant acidity, and a complete locomotive-plus-car pairing is more displayable than either piece alone.
2001, Siren Ceramic Plate (#813 ou#186238 · The Long TailThis is the 2001 hand painted Siren collector plate, individually numbered 813 of just 1200, which is why it carries the gravity of a real limited run rather than a mass mug. The twin-tailed Siren has been Starbucks' mark since 1971, lifted from a 16th century Norse woodcut, and seeing her hand glazed at this scale is a treat. Collectors do trade these numbered platters, with clean mint examples changing hands around the hundred dollar mark, and a low number like ours always helps.
Blue Rocket, 26oz, Frappuccino Cup#186239 · The Long TailThe biggest of the Blue Rocket trio at a hefty 26oz, blue plastic inside and out and wrapped in those long speed lines. This was a venti-plus format meant for serious cold-drink loads, the kind that sat in a car cupholder all summer. 2001, Starbucks Giant Abbey Classi#186241 · The Long TailThis is the white-on-white Giant Abbey Classic, the oversized take on Starbucks' workhorse Abbey shape, a true display grail. The full gallon-class Giant Abbey holds roughly 138 ounces, stands close to ten inches and weighs over six pounds, strictly decorative and never meant to be lifted full of coffee. These limited giants sell out instantly whenever Starbucks reissues them, and clean examples regularly command well into the thousands on the secondary market, so a pristine one is a centerpiece.
2002, Oversized Skyline Mug, Pike#186242 · 2002 Oversized Skyline Series OneThis is the oversized Pike Place version of the 2002 Skyline Series, that soft blue line drawing rendered large on white. Pike Place Market is the historic 1907 Seattle public market and the spiritual home of Starbucks, whose first store sits on Pike Place itself. The giant Skyline format was sent only to higher volume stores, so these big ones turn up far less often than the standard 20oz, which is exactly why I went after it.
2002, Oversized Skyline Mug, Denve#186243 · 2002 Oversized Skyline Series OneThe oversized 2002 Skyline Denver, Denver's mile-high downtown painted in light blue against the Front Range. 2002, Oversized Skyline Mug, Lake#186244 · 2002 Oversized Skyline Series OneThe oversized 2002 Skyline Lake Tahoe, an outlier in the series since Tahoe is alpine lake country rather than a city, its light blue scene built from mountains, pines and shoreline instead of towers. As a giant-format piece sent only to high-volume stores, and a non-city subject at that, the oversized Tahoe is one of the quieter prizes of the 2002 Skyline giants.
2002, Oversized Skyline Mug, Portl#186245 · 2002 Oversized Skyline Series OneThe Portland entry in the 2002 oversized Skyline run, light blue cityscape on white in that clean illustrated style. Portland, Oregon is the City of Roses, famous for its bridges over the Willamette and the Pearl District. 2002, Oversized Skyline Mug, Seatt#186246 · 2002 Oversized Skyline Series OneThe Seattle giant from the 2002 Skyline Series, home turf for Starbucks, with the Space Needle anchoring that blue line skyline on white. The Needle was built for the 1962 World's Fair and still defines the city's profile. 2002, Oversized Skyline Mug, Washi#186247 · 2002 Oversized Skyline Series OneThe Washington D.C. entry in the 2002 oversized Skyline run, blue monuments line drawn on white ceramic in the big format. The capital reads through the Washington Monument, the Capitol dome and the Lincoln Memorial along the Mall. 2002, Oversized Skyline Mug, San D#186248 · 2002 Oversized Skyline Series OneSan Diego in the 2002 Skyline Series, big format, that pale blue painted skyline wrapped on white ceramic. The city is known for its harbor, the Gaslamp Quarter, Balboa Park and the year round sun of Southern California. 2002, Oversized Skyline Mug, Dalla#186249 · 2002 Oversized Skyline Series OneThe oversized 2002 Skyline Dallas in the soft blue wash, sized in the giant format that went only to top-volume stores. 2002, Oversized Skyline Mug, Vanco#186250 · 2002 Oversized Skyline Series OneVancouver in the 2002 oversized Skyline line, the soft blue cityscape painted across white in big format. 2002, Oversized Skyline Mug, Chica#186251 · 2002 Oversized Skyline Series OneThe oversized 2002 Skyline Chicago, a light blue cityscape wrapped around the giant format reserved for only the highest-volume stores. Chicago's profile is unmistakable, from the Willis Tower's stepped silhouette to the John Hancock and the lakefront, all rendered in that soft blue wash. 2002, Oversized Skyline Mug, Victo#186252 · 2002 Oversized Skyline Series OneVictoria on Vancouver Island in the 2002 giant Skyline Series, that pale blue illustrated skyline on white. 2002, Oversized Skyline Mug, San F#186255 · 2002 Oversized Skyline Series OneCataloged as the San Francisco oversized Skyline, though my catalog note flags the printed art as a Miami scene, so this is worth inspecting closely before I trust the city name. 2002, Oversized Skyline Mug, Los A#186256 · 2002 Oversized Skyline Series OneThe oversized 2002 Skyline Los Angeles in light blue, the giant format reserved for top stores. 2002, Oversized Skyline Mug, New Y#186257 · 2002 Oversized Skyline Series OneThe oversized 2002 Skyline New York in light blue, the giant format that reached only the highest-volume stores. Starbucks Coffee Drive Sign#186258 · The Long TailA white-on-green Starbucks Coffee Dr. street-style sign, a playful piece of store decor riffing on the idea of a Starbucks Coffee Drive address. Mermaid Metal Sign, Holding Latest#186259 · The Long TailNot a mug at all but a metal memorabilia sign, this is a sculpted Siren rendered in green and holding the current Starbucks logo. Pike Place, City Scenes Series#455091 · City Scene SeriesThe 2004 City Scenes Series take on Pike Place, printed in grey and very light blue photographs outside with white inside, the same restrained editorial palette as its Philadelphia sibling. Houston, City Scenes Series#455092 · City Scene SeriesHouston in the City Scenes treatment, with local photography printed in soft grey and pale blue rather than the usual bold skyline graphic. New York, City Scenes Series#455093 · City Scene SeriesPart of a City Scenes run that wraps New York street and skyline photography in grey and very light blue around a white interior, a quieter, photographic take than the bold drawn city mugs. Harlem, City Scenes Series#455094 · City Scene SeriesFrom the City Scenes Series, this one wraps grey and pale blue photographic glimpses of Harlem, the storied uptown Manhattan neighborhood that birthed the Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s and the cultural home of the Apollo Theater. Denver, City Scenes Series#455095 · City Scene SeriesThis is the City Scenes Series, Starbucks' 2004 to 2005 run that traded illustrated landmarks for soft photographic montages printed in grey and very pale blue. Atlanta, City Scenes Series#455096 · City Scene SeriesAtlanta in the City Scenes Series, released 2005, white with the city rendered in black, silver and blue photographic panels wrapping the body, ATLANTA above and STARBUCKS COFFEE COMPANY below. Boston, City Scenes Series#455097 · City Scene SeriesFrom the City Scenes Series, this Boston renders actual city photographs in grey and very pale blue, a muted photographic look that set the series apart from the line-drawn mugs. Dated to 2003, it leans on real imagery of Boston rather than cartoon icons. The understated grey palette gives it a documentary, almost archival feel that I find quietly handsome on a shelf.
Washington D.C., City Scenes Serie#455098 · City Scene SeriesPart of the photographic City Scenes run, this one wraps real Washington D.C. images in grey and very pale blue against a white interior, a softer, more documentary look than the cartoon city lines that came later. The capital it honors is built around the National Mall, the long green axis tying the Capitol, the Washington Monument and the Lincoln Memorial into one ceremonial spine. I like these photo mugs because they feel like postcards you can drink from.
Vancouver, City Scenes Series#455099 · City Scene SeriesThe 2004 City Scenes Vancouver, white inside with grey and pale-blue photographic vignettes of the city. The series favored real photos over drawn icons, giving Vancouver a moody documentary look rather than the cartoon-landmark treatment of later lines. A subtle counterpart to the brighter charity-edition Vancouver elsewhere in the shelf.
Miami, City Scenes Series#455100 · City Scene SeriesFrom the 2004 City Scenes Series, this Miami mug renders local landmarks in grey and pale blue photographic panels, the muted artsy treatment that defines the whole series. The understated palette was a deliberate departure from the bold cartoon city mugs of the era. I appreciate City Scenes as a quieter, more design-led chapter of the line, and Miami's scenes carry the Deco and waterfront character even in soft monochrome.
Seattle, City Scenes Series#455101 · City Scene SeriesSeattle in the 2004 City Scenes Series, rendered in the line's signature grey and pale-blue documentary photography rather than the older painted landmarks. Fitting for the birthplace city, the photo treatment captures real streetscapes in a restrained, almost editorial style. It pairs naturally with the San Francisco City Scenes piece as a matched mid-2000s set.
Detroit, City Scenes Series#455102 · City Scene SeriesDetroit's entry in the 2004 to 2005 City Scenes Series carries the same ghostly grey and light-blue photo wrap, real cityscape imagery instead of drawn landmarks. The Motor City earned its name as the birthplace of the American auto industry and Motown Records, and the photographic style here feels fittingly industrial and understated. The City Scenes photo mugs are a quieter, harder-to-complete subset that many collectors overlook.
San Francisco, City Scenes Series#455103 · City Scene SeriesPart of the 2004 City Scenes Series, where Starbucks swapped painted landmarks for soft documentary photographs printed in grey and pale blue, a quieter and more modern look than the old painted city mugs. San Francisco's edition leans on its instantly readable streetscapes. The muted photo treatment dates it cleanly to that mid-2000s design moment.
Las Vegas, City Scenes Series#455104 · City Scene SeriesA 2003 City Scenes Series mug, photographic rather than illustrated, rendered in that signature grey and very-light-blue duotone that runs across the whole series. The Vegas version layers the iconic "Welcome to Fabulous Las Vegas" sign with Strip and casino imagery for a moody, almost vintage-postcard look. I love how the muted photo treatment makes neon Vegas feel unexpectedly restrained and collectible.
Los Angeles, City Scenes Series#455106 · City Scene SeriesLos Angeles in the City Scenes Series, which traded the usual drawn skyline for actual city photographs printed in grey and pale blue around a white mug. That photographic approach is an unusual detour for Starbucks, and the LA version leans on palms and sprawl rather than any single landmark. Collectors tend to overlook City Scenes, which is exactly why a clean one is worth holding.
New Orleans, City Scenes Series#455107 · City Scene SeriesThe New Orleans piece from the older City Scenes Series, which printed soft photographic collages of a city in grey and pale blue rather than illustrated landmarks. New Orleans, the Crescent City and birthplace of jazz, lends itself perfectly to that moody monochrome treatment. This pre-Global-Icon line is a deeper cut, and a clean City Scenes mug with crisp imaging is a quietly sophisticated thing to own.
Philadelphia, City Scenes Series#455108 · City Scene SeriesThis is the 2004 City Scenes Series Philadelphia, printed in muted grey and very light blue photographs of the city outside, white inside. The series swapped bright illustration for moody black and white style photography, giving the whole line a calmer, almost editorial look that stands apart from the cartoonish city mugs around it. Philadelphia's scenes would naturally pull from Independence Hall and the old town, and the restrained palette is the reason these read as quietly upscale.
Dallas, City Scenes Series#455109 · City Scene SeriesFrom the City Scenes Series, Dallas rendered in grey and very light blue photographic vignettes rather than illustration. The series wrapped four real photo scenes of each city around the body, and collectors often rate its graphics among the best ever put on the US mugs. They were a short run and are long gone from shelves, which is exactly why City Scenes pieces have quietly become hunt items.
Minneapolis, City Scenes Series#455110 · City Scene SeriesThe City Scenes Series Minneapolis mug presents the city in the same grey and soft-blue photographic style as its Miami sibling, a unified 2004 look across the line. Minneapolis anchors the Twin Cities and is known for its lakes, the Mississippi riverfront and a strong arts and milling heritage. I like owning the Minneapolis from both the Charity and City Scenes runs, since the contrast shows how differently Starbucks could portray the same city.
Cleveland, City Scenes Series#455112 · City Scene SeriesCleveland from the 2003 City Scenes Series, with the city's photographic landmarks rendered in soft grey and pale blue against a white interior. This early-2000s photographic line is distinct from the painted City Mugs and is genuinely less common, an 18oz format that captured real cityscapes rather than illustrations. Cleveland itself is home to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, the term coined by local DJ Alan Freed, which makes this a quietly fitting souvenir of the city.
St. Louis, City Scenes Series#455113 · City Scene SeriesFrom the early 2000s City Scenes Series, this St. Louis mug wraps four local photographic vignettes in grey and pale blue around the cup, featuring the unmistakable Gateway Arch, Eero Saarinen's 630 foot stainless steel monument to westward expansion and the tallest arch in the world. The City Scenes line favored soft duotone photo collages over the painted icons of later series. These early 2000s photographic mugs have a vintage feel now and are a nice mid range find for collectors building out US cities.
San Diego, City Scenes Series#455114 · City Scene SeriesThe 2003 San Diego City Scenes Series mug, with four San Diego photos printed in grey and pale blue wrapping the body, SAN DIEGO above and STARBUCKS COFFEE COMPANY below. The muted duotone photography sets this series apart from the usual hand-drawn city art, giving it an almost vintage-postcard feel. It is a discontinued 16oz now actively traded on eBay and Poshmark, a sought-after early-2000s piece that captures San Diego before the later travel series redrew it.
Portland, City Scenes Series#455115 · City Scene SeriesPart of the City Scenes Series, this one renders Portland in muted grey and a very pale blue, photographic city vignettes rather than the bold illustrated skyline you usually see. The restrained palette makes it read more like a postcard than a souvenir, which is unusual for the line. It pairs naturally with the Mount Hood and Rose Garden Portland pieces if you want the whole city told three ways.
Horse, Chinese New Year, Red & Yel#455116 · Chinese New Year (Red & Yellow)Part of Starbucks China's zodiac run for the Year of the Horse, which dawned in 2014, this one runs a white-and-bronze stallion over a festive red body with a yellow interior. The horse signals energy, freedom and a galloping fresh start in the lunar calendar. Starbucks released the horse drinkware on December 26, 2013, ahead of the new year, and the embossed CNY pieces are among the more sought-after of the China-market collectibles.
Monkey, Chinese New Year, Red & Ye#455117 · Chinese New Year (Red & Yellow)Made for the 2016 Year of the Monkey, this glossy red mug has a white-and-bronze monkey looking out in embossed 3D, its tail curling around the body and an arm forming the handle, over a yellow interior with gold vine accents. It was part of the limited Lunar New Year line sold mainly across Asia. The sculpted relief monkey makes it far more than a decal mug, and the zodiac series is collected year by year, so the Monkey fills a specific slot in that twelve-animal cycle.
Rabbit, Chinese New Year, Red & Ye#455118 · Chinese New Year (Red & Yellow)From the red and yellow Chinese New Year zodiac run, this one marks the Year of the Rabbit, the rabbit rendered in white and bronze over deep red with a yellow interior. In the Chinese zodiac the Rabbit stands for gentleness, longevity and good fortune, and red with gold is the classic prosperity pairing. Starbucks Asia issued a fresh animal each year, so collectors who chase the full twelve animal cycle treat each zodiac mug as one slot in the set.
Tiger, Chinese New Year, Red & Yel#455119 · Chinese New Year (Red & Yellow)A Chinese New Year tiger mug, the big cat rendered in white, gold, and black over a festive red field with a yellow lined interior. The Year of the Tiger recurs every twelve years on the lunar calendar, most recently in 2010 and 2022, and the tiger is prized in Chinese culture as a symbol of courage and protection against evil. Red and gold are the auspicious colors of the holiday, making this a textbook celebratory piece.
Pig, Chinese New Year, Red & Yello#455120 · Chinese New Year (Red & Yellow)This is the Year of the Pig mug from the 2019 Lunar New Year collection, the pig rendered in white, bronze, and black over red outside with a yellow interior. In the Chinese zodiac the pig signals wealth and good fortune, which is why Starbucks wrapped it in red and gold, the luckiest colors, with floral and leaf accents. The 2019 Lunar collection was widely released across Asia, and the demitasse versions in particular are chased by collectors building a full twelve animal zodiac run.
Snake, Chinese New Year, Red & Yel#455122 · Chinese New Year (Red & Yellow)Lunar New Year zodiac mugs are an annual Starbucks tradition across Asian markets, and this red and yellow snake, with golden leaf accents and black eyes, marks a Year of the Snake, a sign the zodiac links to wisdom, intuition and transformation. Red outside and yellow inside is the classic auspicious color pairing for Chinese New Year. Starbucks issues a fresh animal every year, so completist collectors try to assemble the full twelve sign cycle, which makes any single snake a piece of that larger chase.
Dragon, Chinese New Year, Red & Ye#455123 · Chinese New Year (Red & Yellow)A second Year of the Dragon variant, this one a close-up dragon head with bronze eyebrows and black eyes over red, finished with a yellow interior. Having two distinct Dragon mugs, the red-white and this red-yellow, shows how Starbucks reworked the same auspicious sign across different markets and years. The Dragon's status as the cycle's most coveted animal makes its mugs the ones collectors most actively pursue.
Dog, Chinese New Year, Red & Yello#455124 · Chinese New Year (Red & Yellow)Part of Starbucks' annual Chinese zodiac run, this Year of the Dog mug renders a white dog with bronze eyes over a festive red body and a yellow interior. The dog years fall on 2018, 2006 and 2030, and in the zodiac the Dog signifies loyalty and honesty. The red-and-gold palette is the standard Lunar New Year language, and collectors often try to assemble the full twelve-animal cycle across release years.
Rooster, Chinese New Year (Red & Y#455125 · Chinese New Year (Red & Yellow)Another entry in the red and yellow zodiac series, this one the Year of the Rooster, the bird rendered in white with bronze accents over red and a yellow interior to match its cycle mates. In Chinese astrology the Rooster signals confidence, hard work and punctuality, and the design keeps the family look consistent across the twelve animals. Lined up with the Rabbit version, you can see Starbucks Asia held one template and just swapped the creature each year.
Ox, Chinese New Year (Red & Yellow#455126 · Chinese New Year (Red & Yellow)A Year of the Ox Lunar New Year mug, the ox printed in gold over a bold red field with a charm dangling from the handle and a matching yellow interior. The ox is the second sign of the Chinese zodiac, a symbol of diligence and strength, and the charm handle is a feature collectors specifically prize on these Asian market releases. Red and gold zodiac mugs are among the most sought after of Starbucks's seasonal Asia lineup.
Horse, Chinese New Year, Red & Yel#455127 · Chinese New Year (Red & Yellow)The 2013-dated variant of the Year of the Horse design, distinguished by the black-eyed horse galloping across the same lucky red field with a yellow interior. Subtle differences like the eye detail are exactly the kind of thing that splits these China zodiac mugs into separate collector listings. The horse is the seventh sign of the Chinese zodiac, and Starbucks timed this release for the lunar transition into 2014.
Jakarta, Indonesia Collector Serie#455141 · Indonesia Collector Series (2011)My 2011 Collector Series Jakarta, fired red inside and out, with a traditional Indonesian dancer mid pose on the wall. She is a Bedhaya or Javanese court dancer, the kind of slow, controlled choreography that takes years to master. Jakarta is the sprawling capital on Java's northwest coast, and this 16oz piece is a favorite for the deep red colorway that collectors hunt to pair with the later comic version.
Makassar, Indonesia Collector Seri#455142 · Indonesia Collector Series (2011)This 2011 mug belongs to the Indonesian Dancers Collector Series, a red-on-red run where each city showcases a regional dance, here a Makassar dancer in mid-pose. Makassar is the bustling port capital of South Sulawesi, long the spice-trade gateway of eastern Indonesia and home to the seafaring Bugis people. I love these because the whole Indonesian dancer set is cohesive and hunted as a group, which makes the rarer cities like this one satisfying to track down.
Bali, Indonesia Collector Series (#455143 · Indonesia Collector Series (2011)Bali's 2011 Collector Series mug shows a Balinese dancer mid-pose, a nod to the legong and barong traditions of Ubud that define the island's temple culture. It belongs to Starbucks Indonesian dancer-themed run, which collectors track city by city. The green-on-green colorway makes the figure read almost like a relief, and Indonesia exclusives like this command real money once they leave the archipelago.
Philadelphia#455144 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)Part of the intact sixteen city North America Charity Edition set from 1998 to 1999, this Philadelphia mug carries the city skyline with the Liberty Bell outside and white inside. The Liberty Bell, cracked and silent in Independence National Historical Park, is the unmistakable Philly icon, and pairing it with the skyline is the formula every charity city followed. Keeping all sixteen cities together as a complete set is what gives this edition its real collector value rather than the single mug alone.
Phoenix#455145 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)Another piece of the 1998 to 1999 sixteen city North America Charity Edition, this Phoenix mug shows the city skyline with a saguaro cactus outside and white inside. The saguaro is the signature of the Sonoran Desert that wraps Phoenix, a cactus that can live two hundred years and only grows in this corner of the world, so it does the desert city's identity in one silhouette. As with the rest of the set, the value lives in keeping all sixteen charity cities together and intact.
New York City#455146 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)The New York City entry from the 1998/1999 North America Charity Edition, the sixteen-city set whose sales benefited charity, showing the Empire State Building rising over a blue skyline. The 1931 Art Deco tower was the world's tallest building for nearly forty years. Collectors hunt the Charity Edition because keeping the full sixteen-city set intact is the real prize, and NYC is one of its marquee cities.
Orlando#455147 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)Our Orlando from the 1998 to 1999 North America Charity Edition set, collaging Kennedy Space Center, an orange blossom with kids, and golf clubs to sum up central Florida. The space imagery nods to nearby Cape Canaveral, while the orange flower marks Florida's citrus identity and golf its endless courses. The full sixteen city charity series is the crown of this part of my collection, and keeping the set intact is half the fun.
Los Angeles#455148 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)This LA Charity Edition mug stars Randy's Donuts, the giant rooftop donut in Inglewood near LAX, roughly 32 feet across in rolled steel and gunite and one of the city's most photographed landmarks since the 1950s. It cameos endlessly on screen, including Iron Man 2. Choosing a roadside donut over the usual Hollywood sign is exactly the kind of offbeat civic wink that makes this series fun to chase.
Portland#455149 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)This Portland mug carries the city skyline on the front with snow capped Mount Hood standing watch on the back, which is exactly how the real Portland feels with that 11,249 foot volcano framed behind the downtown towers on a clear day. Mount Hood is Oregon's tallest peak and a near constant presence on the horizon, so putting it on the back of the cup is the honest move. I like that the design treats the mountain as the second skyline.
San Antonio#455151 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)San Antonio from the 1998 to 1999 North America Charity Edition, the sixteen-city set whose sales funded local causes. The brown design pairs a cathedral and a city park with a clever white plane shadow crossing the scene, a small graphic flourish typical of this series. San Antonio is of course Alamo country and River Walk territory, and a single Charity mug carries extra meaning because the real prize is keeping all sixteen intact, so loose survivors like this matter to anyone rebuilding the set.
San Francisco#455152 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)San Francisco shows off the two things every visitor pictures first, the International Orange towers of the Golden Gate Bridge and one of the world's last manually operated cable cars still clanging up Powell and Hyde. The white interior and clean outside wrap mark this as part of the late-1990s North America Charity Edition run, the line whose proceeds backed CARE relief work. A friendly, photogenic anchor for any West Coast shelf.
San Diego#455153 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)San Diego from that same 1998 to 1999 Charity Edition, here showing palm trees at sunset with an orca breaching the water. The orca is a direct wink at SeaWorld San Diego, long the city's signature attraction, while the palms and sunset sell the perpetual Southern California weather. As one of the sixteen Charity cities it pulls double duty, good on its own and essential if you are chasing the complete set, which is the way these are really valued.
Vancouver#455154 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)Vancouver from the intact North America Charity Edition set of 1998 to 1999, sixteen cities released to benefit CARE. It pairs the harbor skyline with a Northwest Coast totem pole, a nod to the carved poles in Stanley Park, among the most photographed in the world. As part of a complete charity set, it carries more weight than a stray city mug.
Seattle#455155 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)Seattle is the mothership city, where Starbucks opened at Pike Place in 1971, so its harbor-scene mug carries extra weight. This one is from the North America Charity Edition series, the late-1990s run that directed proceeds to relief work, with the clean white interior and waterfront wrap. A natural cornerstone for any Starbucks shelf given where the company was born.
Calgary#455156 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)Calgary's identity is stamped right onto this one with the city skyline paired with horse racing, a nod to the Calgary Stampede, the giant annual rodeo and chuckwagon festival that earns the city its "Cowtown" nickname. The Charity Edition framing ties it to Starbucks' late-1990s North American charity sets, where proceeds supported community causes. The combination of a modern downtown silhouette with thundering horses makes this a neat shorthand for a prairie city that is half oil-money skyline and half Wild West.
Pike Place#455157 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)From the same sixteen city North America Charity Edition of 1998 to 1999, this Pike Place mug carries a green photo of the market and the Lucky Pig statue outside, white inside. The bronze pig, named Rachel, is the market's piggy bank and beloved mascot at the foot of the original 1971 Starbucks store, which makes Pike Place the most meaningful city in the whole charity set. For a Starbucks collector this is close to a holy site, the market where the company was born captured on a charity mug.
Las Vegas#455158 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)This Las Vegas piece runs in the late-1990s Charity Edition vein, with the pink casino sign, three spinning drums and a clown nodding straight at Circus Circus and the neon Strip. Vegas is of course the Entertainment Capital, and the slot-machine drums make the design instantly readable. The intact sixteen-city Charity set is the real prize for collectors, so a clean single like this is a satisfying anchor piece.
Toronto#455159 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)A Toronto mug showing the city skyline, tied to the intact sixteen city North America Charity Edition set from 1998 and 1999. Toronto's skyline is defined by the CN Tower, which stood as the world's tallest free standing structure from 1976 until 2007. As part of a complete charity series, the value here is in keeping the full sixteen city set together rather than the single mug alone.
Boston#455160 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)The Boston entry in the 1998 to 1999 North America Charity Edition, white inside with a statue and historical monument rendered outside, fitting for the city that birthed the American Revolution. Boston is dense with such monuments, from the Freedom Trail to the Public Garden's bronzes. As one of the sixteen charity cities, this matters most as part of the complete intact set I keep together.
Washington, D.C.#455161 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)This is the Washington D.C. piece from the sixteen-city North America Charity Edition of 1998 to 1999, showing a church and the National Mall monuments against a white interior. The whole point of that line was that proceeds went to charity, so an intact full set is genuinely prized among collectors.
