The Mall it depicts is the symbolic heart of the capital, anchored by the Washington Monument obelisk and the museums of the Smithsonian.
Chicago#455162 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)This Chicago Charity Edition leans on two icons, the Sears Tower, long the tallest building in North America and now the Willis Tower, and Buckingham Fountain, the grand Beaux-Arts fountain in Grant Park that has anchored the lakefront since 1927. The Charity Edition tie connects it to Starbucks' late-1990s North American sets that funneled proceeds to community causes. It is a clean, confident shorthand for Chicago's skyline-and-lakefront identity.
Atlanta#455163 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)My Atlanta from the North America Charity Edition, the intact 1998/1999 sixteen-city set, this panel showing an Atlanta building and the glowing FOX sign of the 1929 Fox Theatre, the Moorish movie palace that locals saved from demolition. White inside. The charity set sold to benefit CARE, and keeping all sixteen together is the whole point, so Atlanta is one piece of a set I refuse to break.
Miami#455164 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)This Miami mug pairs a green beachfront photo with an orange surfer and palm trees, capturing the city's Art Deco oceanfront and South Beach energy. As a Charity Edition piece, it belongs to the cause-tied releases where proceeds supported community programs. Miami's draw is its Latin-American gateway culture and famous beaches, and I like that the orange surfer gives this one a livelier hit of color than most photo-based city mugs.
Austin#455165 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)Austin from the North America Charity Edition, the 1998/1999 set, its panel pairing cattle with the Texas Capitol rotunda, the 1888 dome in sunset-red granite that famously stands taller than the one in Washington. White inside. Like my Atlanta from this run it benefits a cause and only really counts as part of the complete sixteen, so I keep the Texas piece firmly with its siblings.
Denver#455166 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)Denver wears its identity honestly here, a white interior with the city skyline and the Rocky Mountains rising behind it on the outside, a nod to the Mile High City that genuinely sits exactly 5,280 feet above sea level. The mountains are the real hook, the Front Range backdrop that makes Denver's skyline one of the most recognizable in America. A clean older flagship piece that quietly anchors the long-tail run.
Minneapolis St. Paul#455167 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)This Twin Cities mug shows a long arched bridge and an orange sailing boat, nodding to Minneapolis-St. Paul straddling the Mississippi with its many lakes and bridges. It is a Charity Edition release, distinct from the famously valuable early 1994 Minneapolis city mug that trades around two thousand dollars. I keep the distinction clear on my shelf, because the 1994 piece is the legendary one, while this charity version is the accessible way to represent the Twin Cities.
Dallas#455168 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)A Dallas mug with a city skyline, a coffee bean set as a compass point, and a lone cowboy, tying the design to the sixteen-city North America Charity Edition styling. Dallas leans into its Western identity, and the cowboy plus compass motif reads as pure Texas. The charity sets are most prized intact across all sixteen cities, so each loose city is really a piece of a larger puzzle.
Houston#455169 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)Houston's mug leans straight into Space City, the nickname earned when NASA's Johnson Space Center made it Mission Control, hence the rocket engines firing across the skyline outside. This is the older flagship City Mug rendering of America's energy capital and fourth-largest city. The rocket motif is the giveaway that Houston's identity, from "Houston, we have a problem" to the Astros, is bound up with human spaceflight.
Boise#455170 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)Boise, Idaho's capital, gets its real signature here, the Idaho State Capitol with its sandstone rotunda dome, set against a Main Street skyline. This is the North America Charity Edition treatment, white inside with the landmark scene outside. As part of the intact 1998 to 1999 sixteen-city charity run, the value is really in keeping the full set together rather than in any single mug standing alone.
United State of America, City Scen#455173 · City Scenes SeriesFrom the 2004 City Scenes Series, this one renders Mount Rushmore in grey and pale blue, the South Dakota granite where sculptor Gutzon Borglum carved Washington, Jefferson, Roosevelt and Lincoln from 1927 to 1941. The whole series used soft duotone photography rather than illustration. A quietly patriotic national entry instead of the usual city.
California Mug, States of Bean Ser#455176 · States of Bean Series (1997)This belongs to the 1997 States of Bean Series designed by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, where each US state and Canadian province got a mug crammed with playful facts and trivia. California's panel of state facts wrapped around white is exactly the educational, almanac-style charm that makes this series so collectible today. Finding clean States of Bean pieces with crisp printing is half the fun, and California, as the most populous state, is one people actively seek to complete the run.
Oregon Mug, States of Bean Series#455177 · States of Bean Series (1997)Part of the 1997 States of Bean Series by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, this Oregon mug carries printed facts about the state. Oregon holds Crater Lake, the deepest lake in the United States, and is famously the end of the Oregon Trail, fitting trivia for a fact forward mug. Especially fun given Starbucks's own Pacific Northwest roots, making an Oregon piece feel close to home for the brand.
Virginia Mug, States of Bean Serie#455178 · States of Bean Series (1997)Virginia from the 1997 States of Bean Series by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, white inside and printed with state facts. Virginia is the birthplace of eight US presidents and home to Colonial Williamsburg and the Blue Ridge. The series wraps trivia around each state, making it the bookish, info-dense corner of any Starbucks shelf.
Washington Mug, States of Bean Ser#455179 · States of Bean Series (1997)From the 1997 States of Bean Series designed by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, this one is the actual state of Washington, packed with printed facts about the Evergreen State rather than a skyline. The series gave each US state and Canadian province its own trivia-loaded mug, which is why collectors chase them as a 50-plus set. Washington is a fitting subject given Starbucks was born in Seattle in 1971.
Washington, D.C. Mug, States of Be#455180 · States of Bean Series (1997)The District gets its own entry in the 1997 States of Bean Series by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, covered in printed facts about Washington D.C. rather than a single landmark. Including a federal district alongside the actual states is one of those completist quirks that makes finishing the set harder. Fun fact, D.C. is not a state and has no vote in Congress, which the facts mug glosses over.
Ohio Mug, States of Bean Series#455181 · States of Bean Series (1997)Another 1997 States of Bean entry by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, this Ohio mug wraps printed state facts around the cup. Ohio is the Buckeye State and a famous cradle of aviation and presidents, the Wright brothers built their planes in Dayton and the state has sent eight men to the White House. Tracking down each state in this series is the real pleasure, and Ohio is a solid mid run piece.
Pennsylvania Mug, States of Bean S#455182 · States of Bean Series (1997)From the 1997 States of Bean Series designed by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, this Pennsylvania mug wraps the state's facts around the outside with white inside. Pennsylvania was the second state to ratify the Constitution, in December 1787, founded by William Penn as a Quaker colony, and the series treated each state like a friendly tile of trivia. The whole set was sold only at Starbucks, so collectors prize an intact run of these state by state designs.
New York Mug, States of Bean Serie#455183 · States of Bean Series (1997)The New York mug from the 1997 States of Bean Series by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, wrapping the white body in a run of facts about the Empire State. Like its New Jersey sibling it reads almost like a coffee-table almanac you can drink from. The series covered US states and Canadian provinces, and a complete set is a genuine grail, so each surviving fact-mug is a piece worth grabbing.
Connecticut Mug, States of Bean Se#455184 · States of Bean Series (1997)From the 1997 States of Bean series by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, this one circles facts about Connecticut around the mug. The Constitution State packs serious firsts, it is home to the nation's oldest continuously published newspaper and the first written constitution often cited as inspiration for its nickname. A modest piece, but the full state run is what makes any single one matter to a set builder.
Texas Mug, States of Bean Series#455185 · States of Bean Series (1997)Part of the 1997 States of Bean Series designed for Starbucks by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, this Texas mug wraps state facts around a white lined body. The series gave each US state and several Canadian provinces a colorful trivia treatment, and Texas, the Lone Star State, is the obvious heavyweight of the set. These turn up around twenty to thirty dollars and are loved for their bright, almanac like graphics.
Florida Mug, States of Bean Series#455186 · States of Bean Series (1997)From the 1997 States of Bean series designed by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, this Florida mug is packed with facts and motifs about the Sunshine State printed around the outside. The series gave each US state and Canadian province its own colorful fact-filled treatment, an early cousin of the later Been There line. These twenty-ounce originals predate the modern state mugs by two decades and are increasingly hard to find clean.
British Columbia Mug, States of Be#455187 · States of Bean Series (1997)From the 1997 States of Bean Series designed by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, this British Columbia mug prints fun facts about Canada's westernmost province right on the outside. BC's calling cards are Vancouver, the Rocky Mountains, and the Pacific coastline. The series treated each state and province like a trivia card, and the Canadian provinces are scarcer than the US states, so BC is a prized fill for the set.
Massachusetts Mug, States of Bean#455188 · States of Bean Series (1997)This is a States of Bean piece, the clever 1997 series designed by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, with the white mug printed full of facts about Massachusetts. The Bay State gave us Plymouth Rock, the first shot of the Revolution at Lexington and Concord, and Harvard, the oldest US university. I have a soft spot for this series because the trivia-packed format is unlike anything else Starbucks made, and assembling all fifty states plus the provinces is a real collector's quest.
New Jersey Mug, States of Bean Ser#455189 · States of Bean Series (1997)The New Jersey entry in the 1997 States of Bean Series, designed by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, who packed each mug with trivia about its state. New Jersey's facts wrap the white body in that playful almanac style. The full set spanned US states and Canadian provinces, and collectors prize them precisely because assembling a complete run of those little fact-mugs is genuinely tough today.
North Carolina Mug, States of Bean#455190 · States of Bean Series (1997)Part of the 1997 States of Bean Series designed by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, this North Carolina mug is packed with printed state facts rather than a skyline. North Carolina claims the first powered flight at Kitty Hawk and is the original Tar Heel State, the kind of trivia these mugs delighted in. The whole States of Bean set is a fun completist chase, since collectors try to assemble all the states and provinces.
Colorado Mug, States of Bean Serie#455191 · States of Bean Series (1997)Part of the 1997 States of Bean set designed by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, wrapping facts about Colorado around the body. Here is the collector catch worth knowing, the original Colorado release famously misprinted the elevation of Mount Elbert, the state's highest peak at over 14,400 feet, as just 1,441 feet. Starbucks corrected it, so the error version is the one hunters chase.
Schenley Park, Pittsburgh, Park Se#455192 · Park Series (2007)Schenley Park is Pittsburgh's great green lung, 456 acres donated by Mary Schenley in 1889, home to the glass Phipps Conservatory and the city's beloved trails near Oakland. This park-themed mug is one of the quieter, locally focused designs rather than a flagship city mug. The Pittsburgh-specific pieces tend to surface only occasionally, which is part of their charm.
Central Park, New York City, Park#455193 · Park Series (2007)This is from Starbucks' Park-themed line celebrating great urban green spaces, and Central Park is the obvious headliner, Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux's 843-acre masterpiece carved into the Manhattan grid in the 1850s and 60s. The soft park-theme illustration leans on the lawns and trees rather than the skyline, which is a refreshing way to depict New York. Pairing it with the Washington cherry-blossom mug from the same series makes a tidy little two-piece set about American parks.
Fairmount Park, Philadelphia, Park#455194 · Park Series (2007)Part of the 2007 City Parks series, this honors Philadelphia's Fairmount Park, one of the largest urban park systems in America stretching along the Schuylkill River with its boathouses and the Philadelphia Museum of Art. The big 18 ounce body wears a bright green and gray park scene with STARBUCKS printed in bold black down the handle. The Park Series was a short-lived experiment, so these green-and-white Philly mugs are a fun niche within the city lines.
Griffith Park, Los Angeles, Park S#455195 · Park Series (2007)Part of a Park themed run, this one honors Griffith Park, the over 4,000 acre giant that Griffith J. Griffith donated to Los Angeles in 1896 as a Great Park for the people. Above it sits the 1935 Griffith Observatory, home to the most viewed telescope on Earth, and the 1923 Hollywood Sign that started life as a Hollywoodland real estate ad. For a collector this is LA distilled, the cosmos and the silver screen on one slope.
South Mountain Park, Phoenix, Park#455196 · Park Series (2007)From the 2007 Park Series, which honored notable city and national parks across the US and Canada, this one celebrates South Mountain Park in Phoenix, one of the largest municipally run urban parks in the entire country at over 16,000 acres of desert ridgeline and saguaro. The Park Series was a short lived, regionally focused line, which makes any single entry harder to complete than the big city series. A desert park theme also makes it a distinctly Southwestern piece that stands out from the usual skyline mugs.
Cherry Blossoms in spring, Washing#455197 · Park Series (2007)The companion to the Central Park mug in the Park-themed series, this one celebrates Washington's Tidal Basin cherry blossoms, descended from the 3,000 trees Japan gifted the United States in 1912 as a symbol of friendship. The soft park illustration captures the brief, famous bloom that draws crowds to the National Mall every spring. Together with the Central Park piece it forms a quiet two-mug tribute to American public green space, and the cherry-blossom history gives this one real depth.
Mount Rainer National Park, Washin#455198 · Park Series (2007)Mount Rainier is the 14,411 foot glaciated volcano that dominates the Washington skyline and anchors America's fifth national park, established in 1899. This park-theme mug is the 2007 City Park Series piece, an 18oz design showing the mountain over lake and trees. Collectors note these national-park mugs trade steadily on the secondary market, and a clean Rainier in the big format is a satisfying find for any Pacific Northwest shelf.
Boston Common The Public Garde, Bo#455199 · Park Series (2007)This one celebrates Boston Common and the adjoining Public Garden, the oldest public park in America, established in 1634, and the country's first public botanical garden. The park theme outside captures that green civic heart of the city, home to the famous Swan Boats running since 1877. A gentle, scene-driven piece that rewards a collector who knows Boston's geography rather than just its skyline.
Portland Rose Garden, Portland, Pa#455200 · Park Series (2007)Portland is the City of Roses, and this Park Series piece nods to the International Rose Test Garden in Washington Park, a working test garden founded in 1917 that now grows more than 10,000 rose bushes across 600 plus varieties. It is the oldest continuously operating public rose test garden in the United States, with Mount Hood often visible past the terraced beds. A genuinely Portland subject and a nice change from the usual skyline cup.
Golden Gate Park, San Francisco, P#455202 · Park Series (2007)Part of Starbucks' Park Series, this celebrates Golden Gate Park, the 1,017 acre San Francisco green that is larger than New York's Central Park and home to the Japanese Tea Garden, the Conservatory of Flowers, and the de Young Museum. The park themed exterior makes it a regional cousin to the city mugs, less common than the standard San Francisco bridge pieces collectors usually chase.
Balboa Park, San Diego, Park Serie#455203 · Park Series (2007)Balboa Park is San Diego's 1,200-acre cultural heart, home to the world-famous San Diego Zoo, more than a dozen museums, and the ornate California Tower built to celebrate the 1915 Panama-California Exposition. This Park Series mug puts that landscape outside with a clean white interior. The Park Series is an uncommon sub-line next to the standard city mugs, which is part of why I sought this one out.
State #42, Washington, Mug#455204 · 1999 State MugsWashington, number forty-two in the 1997 States of Bean series by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, in the green-theme finish, which is a fitting nod since this is Starbucks' founding home state. The company started at Pike Place in Seattle in 1971, so a Washington mug from any Starbucks line carries a little extra meaning as the brand's own backyard.
State #11, New York, Mug#455205 · 1999 State MugsPart of the 1997 States of Bean series designed by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, where each US state got its own 20oz mug packed with state facts and motifs. New York is number eleven, the white-theme version covered in trivia about the Empire State. The full set is a real collector pursuit, and individual state mugs in clean condition still move steadily on the secondary market.
State #28, Texas, Mug#455207 · 1999 State MugsTexas, number twenty-eight in the 1997 States of Bean run by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, here in the grey-theme treatment with the state's facts wrapped around the body. These big 20oz mugs leaned into local pride, and Texas is one of the more popular states to hunt because of the in-state demand, which keeps the lone star piece moving when whole sets are hard to assemble.
Greeting from America Mug#455208 · Doonesbury @ StarbucksA cheerful Americana piece, the white interior framing a comic-strip road trip across the country in a little red pickup truck. It taps the classic great American road trip mythology, the open highway as a rite of passage, and it sits in the everyday novelty corner of the line rather than any named city series. I love it as a mood piece, the kind of mug that makes a Tuesday morning feel like the start of a cross-country drive.
Catch The Buzz Starbucks, Mug#455210 · Doonesbury @ StarbucksThe white version of "Catch the Buzz" carries the same Doonesbury comic character from Garry Trudeau's strip, but on clean white so the cartoon line work reads brighter and more like a printed comic panel. Trudeau's Doonesbury at Starbucks tie-in turned the strip's running coffee jokes into actual merchandise, and pairing the white and black "Catch the Buzz" mugs is exactly the kind of variant hunting that keeps this corner of the collection interesting.
Tour De Java Cafe Buzz Mug#455211 · Doonesbury @ StarbucksA Tour de Java, Cafe Buzz mug with cartoon characters dancing around the body, a playful caffeine pun design rather than a city or landmark piece. The Tour de Java name riffs on the cycling Tour de France while Cafe Buzz nods to the jittery joy of coffee, all wrapped in comic illustration. Whimsical character mugs like this are the lighter, more graphic side of the collection.
Sands of Java, Mug#455212 · Doonesbury @ StarbucksThis is a Doonesbury piece, Garry Trudeau's 1999 Sands of Java mug, and the cartoon rider on the camel with Starbucks bags is Duke hauling beans across the trade route of the ancients. It belongs to the small Doonesbury at Starbucks run drawn from Trudeau's coffee gags, and collectors prize these as genuinely scarce. Listings call it cool, collectible, and hard to find loose online.
Duke For Prez, Mug#455213 · Doonesbury @ StarbucksStraight from Garry Trudeau's Doonesbury, this mug stars Uncle Duke smoking in front of the Stars and Stripes, riffing on his recurring satirical presidential bids. Duke, loosely inspired by Hunter S. Thompson, is the strip's most outrageous character, so putting him on a coffee mug is peak Doonesbury irreverence. The Duke for Prez gag also spawned playing cards, making the mug part of a small, beloved campaign-themed Starbucks tie-in.
5th Annual Jefferson Parish Jazz F#455214 · Doonesbury @ StarbucksA regional event mug from the Jefferson Parish Jazz Festival, just outside New Orleans, with cartoon characters blowing saxophones around a white-lined cup. Jefferson Parish hugs the Mississippi next to New Orleans, heart of American jazz, so the sax imagery is dead on. Local sponsor-style mugs like this were small print runs tied to one festival year, which is exactly what makes oddball pieces like this hard to find later.
Catch The Buzz Starbucks Coffee, M#455215 · Doonesbury @ Starbucks"Catch the Buzz" is another entry in the Doonesbury at Starbucks series from Garry Trudeau, here in the black-inside, black-background version with the comic character popping against the dark. The pun is pure Trudeau, the caffeine "buzz" doubling as buzzy energy, and these strip-derived mugs are prized by collectors who chase the full Doonesbury run. The black colorway makes a nice contrast to the white twin and is the moodier of the pair.
Java Juke Blends, Mug#455216 · Doonesbury @ StarbucksThe Java Juke mug, white inside with cartoon characters split across seven panels around the body, a playful blend-themed design from Starbucks rather than a city piece. The Java Juke name leans into the old jazz and jukebox slang where java simply meant coffee, an Americanism dating to sailors and diners who borrowed the island's name for the brew. A lighthearted oddball next to the serious city mugs.
Blend O'bury#455217 · Doonesbury @ StarbucksBlend O'bury is a Starbucks comic-character mug, a cartoon figure caught mid-sip with a pun on a coffee blend baked into the name. It belongs to the company's lighter, humorous mug experiments rather than any city or heritage line. The wordplay and single sipping character make it an oddball, the sort of piece that gets a second look on the shelf precisely because it refuses to take itself seriously.
Starbucks Ranger, Mug#455218 · Doonesbury @ StarbucksA playful mug featuring a comic-style character riding a horse, a regional or cowboy-themed novelty rather than a mainline city piece, the same vein as Starbucks' Calgary cowboy-and-horse Global Icon. Character art is rare on their ceramics, which lean on landmarks and logos. The cartoon ranger gives this one a folk-art charm that makes it stand out on the shelf.
Indonesia, Indonesia Collector Ser#455219 · Indonesia Collector Series (2015)From the much-loved 2015 Indonesia Collector Series, this one bursts with a comic-style red-interior illustration of the country's cultural icons. The series was inspired by Sekar Jagad batik, a Yogyakarta pattern whose name evokes a map of the world, fitting for a nation of thousands of islands. These 2015 Indonesia mugs, including the Bali, Kuta and Ubud designs, command strong collector prices and are frequently sold as full sets.
Jakarta, Indonesia Collector Serie#455220 · Indonesia Collector Series (2015)The 2015 follow up to my red Jakarta, this one trades the dancer for a mustard interior and a busy comic style illustration wrapping the outside. Indonesia got the full Collector Series treatment because Starbucks moved fast there after opening in 2002, and the country is one of the company's most important green coffee sources, home of the legendary aged Sumatra and Sulawesi beans. A fun companion piece to the elegant 2011 version.
Bali, Indonesia Collector Series (#455221 · Indonesia Collector Series (2015)The 2015 Bali mug swaps the painterly dancer for a bright comic-style illustration, part of the playful artsy redesign Starbucks Indonesia ran that year alongside Kuta and Ubud. Sets of the 2015 Bali pair have been listed well into the hundreds, so the cartoon look is more sought after than it first appears. I like owning both the 2011 and 2015 Bali to show how fast the house style swung.
Kuta, Indonesia Collector Series (#455222 · Indonesia Collector Series (2015)From the 2015 Indonesia Collector Series, Kuta is the famous surf-and-sunset beach town on Bali's southwest coast, and the mustard interior with a comic-style scene outside captures its laid-back resort energy. Collectors usually chase Kuta alongside its sibling Ubud, and the pair turns up sold together as a two-mug set. As Bali pieces go these are harder to find stateside than the big-city Asian mugs, which gives them a nice scarcity.
Ubud, Indonesia Collector Series (#455223 · Indonesia Collector Series (2015)From the 2015 Indonesia Series, this 16oz mug wears a comic-style scene of Ubud, the cultural heart of Bali known for terraced rice paddies, the Monkey Forest and woodcarving. It was sold alongside mates like Bali Kuta, and the pair surfaces together on the secondary market. Dark green inside, made in Indonesia, and collectors typically list singles in the 30 to 45 dollar range.
Kenya (Bold), AirMail (Postage) Se#455224 · AirMail (Postage) Series (2002)Kenya Bold from the 2002 to 2003 Air Mail Postage series, the design built like an oversized franked postage stamp celebrating the origin. Kenya AA is one of the world's most prized coffees, grown at high altitude on volcanic soil near Mount Kenya and famous for its bright, almost blackcurrant acidity. The postage stamp conceit ran across many origins and these mugs are steady favorites with collectors who chase complete sets.
Italian Roast, AirMail (Postage) S#455225 · AirMail (Postage) Series (2002)The AirMail postage-series take on Italian Roast, Starbucks' darkest of the everyday blends, dressed in mock stamps and postmarks on a diner-style body. Italian Roast honors the espresso tradition of Italy, roasted long and bittersweet for a heavy-bodied, smoky cup. The whole postage conceit frames coffee as cargo crossing borders, a charming bit of branding from the era before the modern city-mug machine took over.
Verona, AirMail (Postage) Series,#455226 · AirMail (Postage) Series (2002)A 2002 Barista AirMail diner-style mug, its surface a wall of coffee postage stamps with the spotlight on Caffe Verona. Verona itself is the Italian city of Romeo and Juliet and the great Roman Arena that still hosts opera. These diner mugs came as themed sets and are well loved among collectors of the early-2000s stamp era.
Espresso Roast, AirMail (Postage)#455227 · AirMail (Postage) Series (2002)A 2003 Barista diner mug from the AirMail Postage series, where each mug is dressed up as oversized postage stamps celebrating Starbucks blends, here spotlighting Espresso Roast. The conceit nods to coffee's journey across the world to your cup, complete with airmail stamp framing and zip-code flourishes. Espresso Roast is Starbucks' foundational dark blend, the backbone of every latte, which makes it a fitting star for this clever heavyweight diner mug.
Sulawesi, AirMail (Postage) Series#455228 · AirMail (Postage) Series (2002)Part of the charming AirMail Postage series, a 20oz diner-style mug styled like a postage stamp with the focus on Sulawesi, the Indonesian island long known to Starbucks as a source of prized Toraja coffee. The postage-stamp conceit framed each coffee origin as a destination, and the heavier diner-mug format makes these stand apart from the standard ceramic line.
Panama, AirMail (Postage) Series,#455229 · AirMail (Postage) Series (2002)This is one of the 2002 Barista AirMail Postage Series diner mugs, where each origin country wears its coffee like a canceled stamp on the outer wall, white inside and postage outside with the focus on Panama. The conceit was clever, treating single-origin beans as international mail, and the squat heavy diner shape sets it apart from the standard tapered mug. Panama coffee, especially Geisha from the Boquete highlands, would later become the most expensive in the world, so this little stamp aged well.
Bella Vista, AirMail (Postage) Ser#455230 · AirMail (Postage) Series (2002)The 2002 AirMail Postage Series dressed the mug as a sheet of postage stamps, and this one foregrounds Bella Vista, the Starbucks blend named for the bright, balanced Latin American coffees. It shares the era with the Cafe Verona airmail design that collectors chase as a pair. The stamp conceit, turning the cup into mail from a coffee origin, is one of the cleverer concepts Starbucks ever printed on ceramic.
House Blend, AirMail (Postage) Ser#455231 · AirMail (Postage) Series (2002)From Starbucks' clever AirMail postage-stamp series, this diner-style mug dresses the exterior up like franked mail with the spotlight on House Blend, the company's original signature roast first sold in 1971. The whole conceit treats coffee as something posted across oceans, a tidy nod to Starbucks' import roots. The blend itself is a Latin American medium roast, the everyday cup the chain built its early reputation on.
Diner Mug, Caffe Latte, Foam Starb#455232 · Diner Mug SeriesA heavy diner-style mug from the early-2000s Barista line, this one is essentially an advertisement you can drink from, a glossy photo of a caffe latte with its foam crowning both sides. The diner mugs were built thick and tall with that big C-handle, meant to evoke an old American coffee counter. These poster-style diner mugs are a fun, affordable corner of the collection that few people chase but everyone smiles at.
Diner Mug, Starbucks Brand Coffee,#455233 · Diner Mug SeriesThis Barista diner mug leans into the brand itself, a botanical print of the coffee leaf and beans wrapped around both sides in that heavy luncheonette ceramic. It is the most agricultural of the diner set, celebrating the raw plant before the roast rather than the finished cup. The whole diner line sits in that affordable early-2000s niche collectors treat as approachable everyday pieces.
Diner Mug, Dublee, Mug#455235 · Diner Mug SeriesAnother thick Barista diner mug, this one printed like a coffee poster with two espresso shots pulled side by side on both faces. The diner format was Starbucks' homage to the classic American luncheonette cup, heavyweight ceramic with a wide handle and a tall straight wall. The espresso-shot graphic makes this one a small love letter to the actual craft of the pull.
Abstract Painting (1), Mug#455236 · Winter 2001One of Starbucks' Chaleur D. Burrows fine-art mugs, here a Van Gogh-style swirling composition running across both the body and the handle. The whole conceit of this series is that the painter D. Burrows recreated famous works and slipped a Starbucks siren or sign somewhere into the scene, so part of the fun is hunting the hidden logo. Collectors trade these in the rough 17 to 50 dollar range, with the rarer paintings climbing higher.
Italian Village with Starbucks, Mu#455237 · Winter 2001A whimsical painted Italian hill village where Starbucks itself appears woven into the scene, with little green-siren branches climbing both the handle and the body. It is a playful fantasy of a Starbucks tucked into a Mediterranean piazza rather than any real location. These illustrative, story-driven mugs are charming outliers, the kind of piece that started as art and only loosely wears the brand.
Abstract Painting (2), Mug#455238 · Winter 2001The garden composition from the Chaleur D. Burrows art series, painted across both the handle and the body. Burrows built this whole line on Impressionist and Post-Impressionist looks, so a garden scene fits squarely in that Monet-and-Van-Gogh wheelhouse the series mined. Affordable and overlooked, which is precisely why a full run of the numbered paintings is so satisfying to assemble.
Abstract Painting (3), Mug#455239 · Chaleur MadeA standout in the Burrows series, a city street scene with a Starbucks branch and its patio painted right into the picture, the hidden-logo gag worn proudly on its sleeve. This is the cup where the series' whole concept becomes obvious, the siren cafe sitting inside a faux-Impressionist streetscape. One of the more recognizable designs, and the one I point to when explaining what these art mugs are.
Abstract Painting (4), Mug#455240 · Chaleur MadeNumber 4 in the Burrows run, a road cutting through an open field, painted across the handle and the body in that loose Post-Impressionist hand. Like the rest of the Chaleur series it pairs a famous-painting look with a discreet Starbucks element somewhere in the frame. Quiet, affordable, and genuinely pleasant to hold, these numbered art mugs are the kind of sleeper set that rewards patience.
Abstract Painting (5), Mug#455241 · Chaleur MadeOne of my loose Barista art mugs, this one a little gallery joke: the exterior is a painting of a room hung with paintings, a woman seated in a chair among them. Starbucks ran these unbranded artist mugs in the early 2000s, white inside, the picture doing all the talking. I keep it for the wink, a mug that knows it is a collectible of collectibles.
Abstract Painting (6), Mug#455242 · Winter 2001A painterly piece in the loose Barista art run, this one a thick Van Gogh style branch that climbs right up over the handle and onto the body, so the brushwork wraps the form. White inside, no city, no logo splashed across the front, just the impasto gesture. I like how the handle stops being hardware and becomes part of the picture.
Abstract Painting (7), Mug#455243 · Winter 2000Sister to the branch mug, again that swirling Van Gogh inspired hand carried across handle and body in heavy strokes. These unbranded art mugs are the quiet corner of my collection, valued for the painting rather than a place name. White inside, the gesture continuous from grip to wall, the kind of thing you turn slowly in the light.
Abstract Painting (8), Mug#455244 · Winter 2010This one finally names a place without naming it: the painted exterior is Pike Place Market, the Seattle landmark where the very first Starbucks opened in 1971. White inside, the brushy rendering of the market a love letter to the company's birthplace. Among my abstract art mugs it is the one with real Starbucks DNA, the original home dressed up as a canvas.
Abstract Painting (9), Mug#455245 · Chaleur MadeThe most pastoral of the set, a colorful field with a tree line receding into the distance, the landscape painted across both the handle and the body. White inside, no branding to fight the scene. I file these together as Starbucks playing fine art rather than geography, and this is the calm one, all open meadow and far horizon.
Abstract Painting (10), Mug#455246 · Chaleur MadeA Chaleur D. Burrows art mug depicting two men and a band, painted in the Burrows reproduction style. This series turned fine-art parody into drinkware, each cup based on a recognizable canvas with a Starbucks element worked discreetly into the picture. They are the quiet sleepers of the collection, easy to overlook until you notice the painterly detail and the buried siren.
Abstract Painting (11), Mug#455247 · Chaleur MadeNumber 11 in the Burrows painting run, a cluster of village houses wrapping the mug and the handle. The handle-painting detail is a Chaleur hallmark, treating the whole cup as one continuous canvas rather than a flat panel. Made for Starbucks by Chaleur D. Burrows, these art mugs sit in that affordable but genuinely characterful corner of the market.
Painting of Branch at Evening, Mug#455248 · The Long TailA mug reproducing a painted view of a 1970 store seen from the street at dusk, a quiet homage to Starbucks's own beginnings, the very first store opened in Pike Place Market in 1971. Heritage pieces that picture an early storefront rather than a city are unusual and appeal to collectors drawn to company history. The evening street scene gives it a warm, almost nostalgic feel unlike the bright tourist mugs.
Abstract Painting (12), Mug#455249 · Chaleur MadeA Burrows art mug showing a painting-within-a-room, a framed canvas above a table, that quietly playful meta touch the series loved. Each piece in this Chaleur line reproduces a fine-art style and tucks a Starbucks reference into the composition. I value these for the wit as much as the brushwork, since spotting the logo is half the reason to pick one up.
Feng Shui in Red (Love), Mug with#455250 · Feng Shui 2004The red Love mug completes the 2004 Feng Shui trio, red being the auspicious color of joy and romance, and it too arrived with three brass coins knotted in red ribbon. Owning all three, green Friends, purple Prosperity, and red Love, is the holy grail for this little series, and the coins are what separate a casual find from a real one. This is the showpiece of the set in my eyes.
Feng Shui in Purple (Prosperity),#455251 · Feng Shui 2004The purple Prosperity mug from the same 2004 Feng Shui set, the color chosen deliberately to signal wealth and abundance in feng shui tradition. Like its siblings it came with three coins on red ribbon, and collectors hunt the complete three-mug rainbow of green, purple, and red. I love that this is one of Starbucks' rare overt nods to Chinese symbolism rather than Western city imagery.
Feng Shui in Green (Friends), Mug#455252 · Feng Shui 2004From Starbucks' 2004 Feng Shui trio, this is the lime green Friends mug, and it originally shipped with three brass Chinese coins knotted in red ribbon, the classic feng shui wealth-and-luck charm. The set paired color to intention, green for friendship, and finding one still complete with its coins is the real prize since they were almost always separated. Individual mugs trade around twenty dollars, but the coins make mine sing.
Golden Pumpkin, Mug in White Creme#455253 · Pumpkin 2003The cream colorway rounds out the Golden Pumpkin trio, its off white ground letting the painted pumpkin and poster framing read softer and more vintage than the bolder green and orange siblings. It is the most neutral of the three, the one that quietly belongs on the table all season rather than shouting Halloween.
Golden Pumpkin, Mug in Orange#455256 · Pumpkin 2003This is the orange colorway of the Golden Pumpkin set, orange inside and out with the same poster style pumpkin painting wrapping the body, the most autumnal and on theme of the three. Seasonal fall mugs like this turn over fast in stores and then go quiet, so having the full color trio intact is half the fun for a collector.
Golden Pumpkin, Mug In Dark Green#455257 · Pumpkin 2003The dark green version of the Golden Pumpkin trio, a big painterly pumpkin set on a poster style backdrop for the autumn season. The three colorways, green, orange, and cream, were clearly meant to be collected together, and the deep green here makes the warm pumpkin pop in a way the brighter variants do not.
NYC Taxi, Mug#455258 · NYC 2001A mug built entirely around New York's iconic yellow cabs, the city's rolling symbol since the Checker era and a shorthand for Manhattan itself. New York runs roughly 13,000 medallioned yellow taxis, and that fleet is as much a postcard image of the city as the skyline. A playful, single subject design that skips the landmarks in favor of the everyday detail that says New York instantly.
Kanazaw Mug (2015)#455260 · Japan 2015My 2015 Kanazawa, painted with a busy townscape of the old castle city on Japan's Sea of Japan coast. Kanazawa survived WWII unbombed, so its samurai and geisha districts and the magnificent Kenrokuen, ranked among Japan's three great gardens, are remarkably intact. Look for the local motifs the designers worked in, Kenrokuen in winter snow, the Hyakumangoku festival, and gold leaf, since Kanazawa produces nearly all of Japan's gold leaf.
Nagano Mug (2014)#455261 · Japan 2014The 2014 Nagano mug trades the soft drawing for a modern hexagon-pattern design with that signature Nagano apple riding the handle. The honeycomb of icons reflects the prefecture's mountains, orchards, and Olympic legacy. Putting the 2003 and 2014 Naganos side by side shows exactly how Starbucks Japan's local-area styling evolved over a decade, which is the whole reason I chase the matched pairs.
Hokkaido Mug (2009)#455266 · Japan 2009A delightful 2009 Japan exclusive from Hokkaido, a painted bear with a snowflake and, the charming detail, little paws sculpted onto the handle. Japan's northern island is winter country, famed for powder snow, the Sapporo Snow Festival and roaming brown bears, all captured in this cozy seasonal scene. Region locked Japanese mugs from this period are prized by collectors, and the handle paws give this one a tactile personality most mugs lack.
Chiba Mug (2002)#455268 · Japan 2002Chiba sits just east of Tokyo on the coast and is the home of Narita Airport, so the little yellow plane drawn over the painted mountains on this 2002 mug is a sly local joke, this is Japan's gateway prefecture. The hand-painted feel of the design is typical of the early-2000s Japan-market mugs that collectors of the Japanese corpus prize. Dated 2002 and regionally specific, it carries more interest than a generic city mug for anyone working the Japan line.
Saitama Mug (2002)#455270 · Japan 2002A 2002 Japanese piece for Saitama, the prefecture just north of Tokyo, painted with a city scene and a blue butterfly across white. Saitama is best known to outsiders as railway country and home to the giant Saitama Super Arena, and these early-2000s prefecture mugs predate the famous JIMOTO and Been There lines by years. Early dated Japan regional mugs like this are quietly hard to find now, since they were never made in big numbers and rarely left the country.
Kanazawa Mug (2002)#455278 · Japan 2002The earlier 2002 Kanazawa, a moodier green and purple painting of a river lined with stone lanterns. This is the older flagship treatment of the same Sea of Japan castle town that gave us my 2015 version, and the lantern lit river scene captures the Higashi Chaya geisha quarter and the canals that thread the old town. Having both years side by side shows how Starbucks Japan's city art evolved over a decade.
Miyazaki Mug (2006)#455279 · Japan 2006This September 2006 Japan release features a Miyazaki tree and a yellow bridge, and it was a tightly limited run reported at only about 2,000 units. Miyazaki, on Kyushu's sunny southeast coast, is famed for palm-lined beaches, surf and the mythic Takachiho gorge tied to Japanese creation legend. Low-production Japanese regional mugs like this are some of the most pursued in the hobby, and a small original edition makes this a genuine standout in my Japan corner.
Ibaraki Mug (2002)#455281 · Japan 2002A 2002 Japan-market mug for Ibaraki Prefecture, just northeast of Tokyo, rendered as a soft pencil drawing of pink plains and a yellow house. Ibaraki is famous for Hitachi Seaside Park's blue nemophila and its plum blossoms at Kairakuen, one of Japan's three great gardens, so the pastel floral palette fits. These early-2000s regional Japanese mugs are gentle and illustrative rather than icon-driven, and they predate the slicker modern series.
Oita Mug (2002)#455282 · Japan 2002A 2002 mug for Oita on the island of Kyushu, drawn in green with the city name picked out in red. Oita is renowned for Beppu, home to more hot spring vents than anywhere else in Japan, the famous jigoku or hells of steaming, colored waters. Dated 2002 Japanese prefecture mugs like this belong to a beloved regional line that local collectors hunt by year.
TakaMatsu Mug (2002)#455284 · Japan 2002Takamatsu, the Kagawa capital on Shikoku famous for Ritsurin Garden and as the udon-noodle heartland, here in a 2002 blue drawing scattered with colorful leaves. This belongs to the early Japan geography mug run that gave individual Japanese cities their own designs, and the dated 2002 Japanese city pieces are prized in the deep Japan corner of the hobby since they predate the later nationwide series.
Sendai Mug (2010)#455285 · Japan 2010A 2010 Sendai mug in blue-themed brushwork showing a figure and a horned horse, drawing on Tohoku folk imagery from the region around Japan's City of Trees. Made for local Japanese sale, these prefectural designs stayed largely within their home market, which makes intact examples abroad satisfying to track down. A distinctive, story-rich Japanese piece.
Nagano Mug (2003)#455287 · Japan 2003Nagano, the Japan Alps prefecture that hosted the 1998 Winter Olympics, gets a gentle 2003 treatment here with a garden, an apple, and a pigeon. The apple is the regional emblem, since Nagano is one of Japan's great apple-growing areas. This is the early local-area Japan series, the quiet hand-drawn style that predates the louder geographic mugs, and a clean 2003 example is a nice anchor for a Japan shelf.
Make-a-Wish Mug (2003)#455290 · The Long TailThis 2003 white mug shows dolphins leaping from the water and was tied to a Make-A-Wish charity release, a partnership format Starbucks Japan favored with matching gift card, sleeve and brochure as a complete set. The dolphin artwork gives it a softer, almost storybook feel compared with the city mugs around it. Collectors note the full intact set surfaces only a handful of times a year, so a clean example with all its pieces is the prize.
2003 Sip to Tradition, Mug#455291 · The Long TailThe 2003 Sip to Tradition mug, white inside with a green and orange drawing on the outside. The name leans into Starbucks as a ritual, the daily cup as something handed down, and the warm green and orange palette gives it a homier, illustrated feel than the corporate logo mugs of the same year. It is a quieter, more sentimental piece from that 2003 stretch when the line was full of themed one offs.
Shizuoka Mug (2002)#455295 · Japan 2002Shizuoka is Mount Fuji's home prefecture, so the orange mountain drawing on this 2002 piece is no accident, the famous cone sits squarely in Shizuoka and the region is also Japan's green tea heartland and the birthplace of the modern wasabi trade. Early Japan market mugs from the very first years of Starbucks Japan are a quiet collecting niche, and a dated 2002 example with a clean Fuji motif is exactly the kind of thing Japan collectors hunt down rather than the mass You Are Here Fuji mugs that came much later.
Sendai Mug (2000)#455298 · Japan 2000Sendai is the City of Trees in Japan's Tohoku region, famous for the Tanabata star festival each August, and the blue and green brushwork with yellow jellyfish and stars on this 2000 mug plays to that festive, watery imagery. Older locally sold Japanese Starbucks mugs like this circulated mostly within Japan, so they reward patient hunting abroad. A lively, painterly regional piece.
Chinese New Year (2005)#455299 · The Long TailA Year of the Rooster mug, white inside with a warm yellow exterior painted with a rooster among trees and fruit, 2005 being the rooster's turn on the twelve-animal zodiac wheel. Starbucks China runs these Lunar New Year mugs annually, and the rooster traditionally symbolizes punctuality, confidence, and good fortune, which is why so many of these were given as New Year gifts and then quietly tucked away unused.
Iceskating over Lake (2004)#455300 · Japan 2004A 2004 seasonal art mug showing a couple skating across a frozen lake in light purple, the sort of wintry vignette Starbucks issued around the holidays without naming a city. It trades landmarks for mood, a quiet romantic scene meant to pair with a cold-weather cup. These painterly seasonal pieces from the mid-2000s sit in the everyday line and reward collectors who like the narrative, illustration-first designs over skylines.
Niigata Barista Mug (2001)#455302 · Japan 2001A 2001 barista mug for Niigata on Japan's Sea of Japan coast, rendered in blue river imagery with an orange leaf at the rim. Niigata is famous as Japan's rice and sake heartland, fed by the Shinano, the country's longest river, which the flowing blue design clearly evokes. Early 2000s dated Japanese regional mugs are a quietly collectible niche, prized for their hand drawn local character.
Tsugaru Aomori Mug (2010)#455303 · Japan 2010A 2010 Tsugaru, Aomori mug celebrating the opening of Starbucks in the Tsugaru region of northern Japan, with a warrior figure and apples in the artwork. Aomori is Japan's apple kingdom, growing the lion's share of the country's apples, and is famous for the fierce Nebuta festival floats of samurai and mythic warriors, which the design clearly draws on. Regional Japanese pieces like this are deeply local and well loved by Japan focused collectors.
2006 Chinese New Year Bear#455306 · The Long TailA 2006 Chinese New Year piece, white inside with a painted dragon design over a green ground, issued for the Lunar New Year that ran into the Year of the Dog. Starbucks' Asia markets, especially Taiwan and China, built a serious annual CNY tradition, and the 2006 zodiac items from that region trade well among collectors today. The dragon imagery makes it read as a celebratory good-fortune piece rather than a strict zodiac mug.
Blue Mug, Black Mermaid#455315 · 3 Color Set (Black Mermaid)A solid blue mug carrying the siren in black, a stripped-down treatment that reduces the whole brand to two colors and the mermaid silhouette. Monochrome logo mugs like this drift outside the named series and live or die on their color. The blue body with a black siren is a restrained, almost graphic-design take, and clean unfaded examples are the ones worth holding.
Green Mug, Black Mermaid#455316 · 3 Color Set (Black Mermaid)A bold green on green mug carrying the siren in black silhouette, leaning hard into Starbucks' signature color and its mermaid heart. Logo forward pieces like this celebrate the brand identity itself rather than any place, and the black mermaid against green is a striking, almost graphic take on the icon that started it all.
Brown Mug, Black Mermaid#455317 · 3 Color Set (Black Mermaid)An all-brown mug, brown glaze inside and out, carrying a black siren, a palette that deliberately echoes Starbucks' earthy 1971 roots before the signature green took over. The monochrome brown-on-brown with a black mermaid is a moody, design-forward piece rather than a place souvenir. It reads as a deliberate heritage nod, the kind of understated object that rewards a second look.
San Diego Deco Skyline (2003), Mug#455318 · City Scenes SeriesA 2003 San Diego mug rendering the waterfront skyline and San Diego Bay in a stylized cartoon, white inside. This sits alongside the 2003 City Scenes line and leans into San Diego's defining feature, the big curving bay with the downtown towers and the Coronado bridge sweeping across it. Early-2000s San Diego mugs have quietly become collector targets on eBay and Poshmark, valued for that specific dated graphic style before the later You Are Here era took over.
Boston Deco Skyline (2003), Mug#455319 · City Scenes SeriesDespite the Deco Skyline name, the real star outside is the cartoon George Washington statue from the Boston Public Garden, the 1869 bronze by Thomas Ball that shows Washington as Army commander on horseback, not as president. Dated 2003, this sits in the playful illustrated era of city mugs. Collectors note the light green theme and call it somewhat hard to find, which makes it a satisfying catch.
Seattle Deco Skyline (2003), Mug#455320 · City Scenes SeriesThis is the famous 2003 Seattle mug with the typo, where Starbucks printed Mount Ranier instead of Mount Rainier beside a cartoon Space Needle. The error was caught and stock was pulled, which is exactly why collectors chase it. It belonged to a small Deco-style set alongside Boston, San Diego, and Chicago, so check the mountain's spelling, that misprint is the prize.
Chicago Deco Skyline (2003), Mug#455321 · City Scenes SeriesDated 2003 and part of the Barista City Scenes line, this Chicago Deco mug pairs a stylized downtown skyline with a cartoon Buckingham Fountain, leaning into the Art Deco flavor of Chicago's classic high-rises. Collectors actively trade the 2003 City Scenes Chicago on eBay and Poshmark, where it is recognized by name and sought as a clean, dated example. The deco styling makes it one of the more graphically distinctive Chicago mugs Starbucks produced.
Golfing Facts (1997), Mug#455328 · Daleet Zigelboim MadeA 1997 mug stuffed with golfing fun facts printed around the body, from the same late nineties wave of trivia and theme mugs Starbucks loved, the era that also gave us the States of Bean fun facts pieces. It is a conversation starter by design, the kind of cup you sip and read, and these niche subject mugs from 1997 are increasingly hard to track down complete.
Fishing Facts (1997), Mug#455329 · Daleet Zigelboim MadeA 1997 novelty mug printed with fishing fun facts around the outside, part of Starbucks' late-90s love of trivia and theme mugs that taught you something while you drank. These quirky fact mugs were never a numbered series, so they turn up scattered and unpredictable, which is half the fun of running one down. I file it with the playful one-offs that show Starbucks did not take itself too seriously back then.
Bases Loaded (1996), Mug#455330 · The Long TailBases Loaded from 1996, a sport mug that runs a baseball storyline around the cup, part of Starbucks mid-90s habit of themed novelty mugs beyond the city line. These vintage sport mugs surface only occasionally and have changed hands in the low tens of dollars when they do. The narrative wrap, telling a little game scene as you turn the mug, is the charm and what makes it a fun outlier piece.
United Kingdom Handmade Mug#455331 · Emma Bridgewater MadeA white-creme mug scattered with British postage stamps in blue and red, part of Starbucks' stamp-themed travel motif. The conceit treats the UK like a passport page, leaning on philatelic imagery rather than a single skyline. A charming country-level piece for a collection otherwise full of single-city mugs.
Chinese New Year 2014 Horse Bear#455332 · The Long TailThe 2014 Year of the Horse Bearista, and per the catalog this one carries striking gold eyes presented in a 12oz mug pairing. The horse represents energy and freedom in Chinese astrology, and 2014 was a wood horse year. The gold-eye detail is exactly the sort of small finishing flourish that separates one zodiac bear from the next and gives completists a reason to hunt the specific variant.
Baguio, Philippine Exclusive (2004#455334 · Philippine Exclusivs (2004)Baguio is the Summer Capital of the Philippines and the City of Pines, a cool mountain retreat at about 1,500 meters that the Americans laid out in 1904 under Daniel Burnham of City Beautiful fame. This 2004 Philippine exclusive carries that green hill against a blue sky right on the cup. Country-exclusive runs like this almost never leave the home market, so they are a quiet prize in any city shelf.
Starbucks Beijing, Mug#455337 · The Long TailRed ground, a yellow Great Wall snaking across it, and black dragons coiled in, this Beijing mug leans hard into the city's two great symbols of empire and craft. The Wall, begun over two thousand years ago and stretching thousands of miles, is the obvious draw, while the dragon signals imperial Beijing and the Forbidden City. Collectors note the Beijing design runs in both this bold red colorway and a yellow-ground Temple of Heaven version, so the red dragon is the punchier of the pair.
Tianjin Mug#455339 · The Long TailA Tianjin mug with Chinese characters on white, representing the huge port city in northern China known as a World Architecture Expo for its Five Great Avenues of European concession era buildings. Modern Tianjin is crowned by the Tianjin Eye, a 120 meter Ferris wheel and the only one built over a bridge, spanning the Hai River. Mainland China city pieces broaden any global shelf well beyond the usual Beijing and Shanghai.
Kulturhauptstadt Europas (2010), M#455340 · The Long TailThis marks 2010, the year the entire Ruhr region (Essen and the wider Ruhrgebiet) held the title European Capital of Culture under the RUHR.2010 campaign printed right on the mug. The black bridge motif nods to the industrial Zollverein coal-mining heritage that the cultural-capital program reframed as art and identity. It is a dated event piece rather than a standard city mug, which is exactly why it is worth holding onto, the occasion is fixed in the design.
Starbucks Original Crown (2000), M#455341 · The Long TailThe dated 2000 version of the crowned-siren mug, showing the early-1990s logo where the mermaid wears a star-topped crown, the look that bridged the 1971 brown siren and the modern green one. A copyright year stamped on the base is gold for dating, it pins the piece exactly. Carrying that crowned transitional logo into the year 2000 makes it a deliberate nod to heritage.
Mermaid Holding Cup (2012), Mug#455342 · The Long TailBack to the dark brown body for 2012, this Anniversary mug returns the bronze Siren to her familiar moody backdrop after the 2011 cream year. Having the 2006, 2011 and 2012 side by side shows exactly how Starbucks rang changes on a single recurring theme. Collectors chase the run precisely because the differences are subtle, so a complete year sequence tells the story better than any one mug alone.
Mermaid Holding Cup (2011), Mug#455343 · The Long TailThe 2011 version of the Anniversary mug swaps the dark body for a white cream exterior while keeping the bronze Siren holding her cup, a notable visual break from the brown editions. Fittingly, 2011 was the year Starbucks marked its 40th anniversary and unveiled the streamlined logo, so this release sits at a real brand milestone. The cream variant is the easiest of my three to tell apart at a glance, which is half the fun of lining them up.
Starbucks Original Crown, Mug#455345 · The Long TailA white mug bearing the crowned-star siren, the 1987 to 1992 logo created when Howard Schultz merged Il Giornale with Starbucks and the siren gained her crown and lost the brown for green. That short-lived crowned mark is the rarest of the four official logo eras. Any piece faithfully reproducing it is a small history lesson in how the most recognizable coffee logo evolved.
Chinese New Year (2006)#455348 · The Long TailThe 2006 Year of the Dog mug, white inside with a cheerful yellow body carrying the loyal dog motif. The dog is the eleventh sign of the Chinese zodiac and the most faithful of the twelve, a fitting emblem for a gift mug. These regional Starbucks China Lunar releases rarely left Asia, so finding one stateside in clean condition is a small win for a Western collector.
Gwangju Mug#455349 · The Long TailA charming Korean piece, the outside a painting of Gwangju paired with watermelons, a playful local touch in the southwestern art and food city. Gwangju is celebrated for its biennale and democratic heritage, and its surrounding Jeolla region is famed across Korea for its food culture. Korean city mugs from this softer, illustrated style are less common abroad, which makes the regional pieces fun to track down.
Starbucks Tianjin, Mug#455350 · The Long TailTianjin is the port gateway to Beijing, a treaty-port city famous for its European-flavored Five Great Avenues and the riverside Jiefang Bridge. This one breaks from the usual landmark formula with black dragons painted over a warm orange ground, leaning into Chinese auspicious symbolism rather than a cityscape. Most Starbucks Tianjin pieces are the purple Icon mug with the Century Clock, so a dragon-motif variant like this is the more unusual catch.
2011 Creme Mug (Green Inside)#455355 · The Long TailA 2011 mug with a green interior and a cream-white exterior carrying the Starbucks logo, a quiet two-tone everyday piece. The green-lined inside is the small twist that lifts it above a plain white mug. Part of the long tail of unbranded-by-city mugs Starbucks cycled through, an easygoing daily drinker rather than a collector trophy.
2010 Dragon Boat Race Mug#455356 · China 2010A 2010 mug depicting a dragon boat race, made for the Asian market to mark the Duanwu Dragon Boat Festival, the early-summer holiday rooted in the legend of poet Qu Yuan. The white-on-design rendering of the racing boats makes it one of the more narrative pieces in the everyday line. Festival-specific Asian releases like this rarely reached Western shelves, which gives them a quiet rarity for collectors outside the region.
Hawaii, Eoko Mai, Mug#455357 · 2008 HawaiiA warmly local piece showing a Hawaiian dancer mid ceremony, titled with the welcoming spirit of E komo mai, the islands' come in, welcome. Hula is not just dance but a living archive, each gesture carrying chants and genealogy that preserved Hawaiian history through generations. A culturally rooted design like this is far more interesting than a generic beach scene, and it carries real aloha.
Hawaii, Surf Boards Mug#455358 · 2010 HawaiiA breezy beach piece, a turquoise interior dotted with fish and a row of surfboards planted in the sand outside. Hawaii is the birthplace of modern surfing, he'e nalu, the ancient sport of Hawaiian royalty later carried to the world by Duke Kahanamoku. It is pure island vacation energy on ceramic, the lighthearted counterpart to the more ceremonial hula mug in this same Hawaiian cluster.
Rochester Park, Singapore, Mug#455359 · The Long TailThis 2013 mug celebrates Starbucks at Rochester Park, the company's first destination store in Singapore, housed in a 1920s era black and white colonial bungalow tucked into leafy grounds. The exterior carries a line drawing of that heritage building, and the piece was sold only at or for that location, which is why collectors now hunt it on Carousell rather than store shelves. A true store specific mug, the kind that ties a cup to one real address.
Indonesia, Blue and Orange Mug#455360 · The Long TailAn Indonesia mug in blue and orange carrying a stylized Indonesian sign or signpost design, a simpler graphic take on the world's largest archipelago nation of some 17,000 islands. The bright color split reflects the tropical, sun-and-sea identity Starbucks Indonesia leans on. It sits apart from the better-known 2015 illustrated Collector Series, making it one of the quieter Indonesia-market pieces.
Love (2010), Mug#455364 · The Long TailA 2010 Valentine's release, red inside and out with a single white "Love" wrapping the body, the kind of seasonal sentiment mug Starbucks rolls out for February. These dated love mugs are simple by design, built to be gifted, which is why finding one clean and unscuffed years later is the trick. I like having the year pinned, it slots neatly into the holiday and occasion runs.
New Zealand Youthline, Mug#455365 · Art by Lauren WatsonA charity tie in mug carrying Maori signage, supporting Youthline, the New Zealand youth helpline founded in 1970 that still runs a 24/7 free service for Kiwis aged 12 to 24. Cause linked Starbucks mugs like this are made in small local runs, so they rarely surface outside their home market. The Maori language design makes it one of the more culturally grounded pieces in my long tail.
Cebu, Philippine Exclusive (2004),#455367 · Philippine Exclusivs (2004)Cebu is the Philippines' oldest city and the cradle of Christianity in the islands, a busy port and beach-resort hub, so the purple and turquoise water and shoreline on this 2004 piece nods straight to its famous coast. It comes from the small 2004 Philippine Exclusives set, a regional release that collectors treat as harder to find outside the country and often hunt boxed. As a market-specific City Mug, it carries more scarcity weight than its plain look suggests.
Brown Mug, First Logo, Mug#455369 · The Long TailThe undated brown First Logo mug, cream inside and brown outside, carrying Heckler's original 1971 twin-tailed siren in her full uncovered form. That first logo was inspired by a 16th-century Norse woodcut and chosen to evoke Seattle's maritime history and coffee arriving by sea. Heritage-logo pieces like this are collected for the lore, the chance to hold the design that started everything.
Songkran Festival Thailand, Mug#455372 · The Long TailSongkran is Thailand's traditional New Year, the famous nationwide water fight every April when people drench each other with buckets and squirt guns as a symbol of washing away the old year, and this blue mug captures that joyous water throwing. It is a festival mug rather than a city one, celebrating a cultural event instead of a skyline. Thailand market festival releases like this are sought by collectors who chase culturally themed pieces over the standard landmark series, which gives it extra appeal beyond just being a Bangkok souvenir.
Sakura Pattern, Mug#455374 · The Long TailAn undated Sakura piece, white inside with an all-over cherry blossom theme wrapping the outside rather than the usual scattered sprigs. The blanket pattern marks it as one of the design variants Starbucks Japan rotates through within the broader spring line, where some years lean illustrative and others go full repeating motif. Without a year stamp it slots in as a pattern variant, a nice companion to the dated mugs.
Ni Hao Taipei, Mug#455376 · The Long TailA friendly Ni Hao, meaning hello, paired with a colorful drawing of a Taipei bridge, a welcome style mug for Taiwan's capital. Taipei is best known for Taipei 101, once the world's tallest building, but this one leans on the city's waterways and crossings instead. Taiwan only Starbucks city pieces like this are popular regional finds and seldom appear on the wider collector market.
Busan, Mug#455378 · The Long TailBusan is South Korea's second city and its great southern port, a place of beaches like Haeundae and temples set against steep coastal mountains, so the sunset glowing over a ridge with birds in flight on this white mug reads instantly as that meeting of sea and hills. I like that it leans on mood rather than a checklist of landmarks, which is rarer in the Asian regional mugs and makes it quietly distinctive on a shelf.
Store 200, Taiwan, Mug, 16oz#455379 · Taiwan 200 StoreThe companion 16oz Store 200 Taiwan mug, this one wrapping a colorful city background around the body rather than the storefront scene. Marking Taiwan's 200th Starbucks, run by local operator President Chain Store, it pairs with the 2007 storefront version, and tracking down both finishes of a milestone release is the kind of completeness chase that makes this niche rewarding.
Store 200, Taiwan, 2007 Mug, 16oz#455380 · Taiwan 200 StoreA 16oz commemorative tied to Taiwan reaching its 200th Starbucks store, here in the 2007 design showing the storefront set in greenery. President Chain Store brought Starbucks to Taiwan in 1998, so hitting 200 locations was a real milestone worth a special mug. Store-count commemoratives are a fun niche because they capture an exact moment in a market's growth.
Okinawa Mug (2006)#455382 · Japan 2006A 2006 Okinawa mug with a playful comic drawing of two little dragons over an ocean theme, nodding to the shisa, the lion dragon guardians that sit on Okinawan rooftops to ward off evil. The ocean motif fits an island prefecture defined by coral reefs and the East China Sea. Having two dated Okinawa mugs, 2002 and 2006, lets me show how the regional Japanese designs evolved across the decade.
2004 Starbucks Light Brown Mug#455383 · The Long TailA 2004 light-brown mug carrying the mermaid Siren both inside and out, a tonal coffee-colored piece that puts the brand's own logo front and center rather than any city or holiday theme. The all-over warm brown finish reads like the color of the drink itself, an understated everyday design. Logo-forward mugs like this are quiet brand pieces, common but a tidy way to anchor the Siren motif in a collection.
Kings Holding Coffee (2003), Mug#455389 · The Long TailA 2003 mug with the playful Kings Holding Coffee theme, blend bags in assorted colors scattered over a red field. This was one of Starbucks' lighthearted promotional designs rather than a place piece, the kind of cheerful packaging led art that turns a coffee lineup into a cast of characters. A bright, slightly obscure 2003 oddity that adds some color variety alongside the more serious origin and city mugs.
Coffee is 98% Water, Mug#455393 · KoreaA clean white mug stating the simple truth that brewed coffee is roughly 98 percent water, decorated outside with a green plant motif. The line is a genuine reminder of why water quality matters so much to a good cup, a point baristas and roasters take seriously. It belongs to Starbucks' run of fact-and-message mugs that taught the customer something rather than selling a city, which is exactly the kind of quiet teaching piece I love.
Air Mail Coffee (1995), Mug#455399 · Made by Jackal DesignsA 1995 novelty mug built around an Air Mail theme, the exterior a world map crossed by airplanes with a pilot in the scene, the romance of coffee carried across the globe. White inside, no city, just travel as a mood. It belongs to the playful mid-90s era before the city-mug machine took over, and I love it as a small map of restlessness.
Roses (2012), Mug#455400 · The Long TailA clean white mug whose only flourish is a spray of red roses bleeding across the outside, dated 2012. Pieces like this sit outside the named city lines, the kind of seasonal or floral one-off Starbucks slipped into stores for Valentine's or spring without much fanfare. The appeal is exactly that quietness, just red roses on white, no logo theater, the sort of thing you grab because it photographs beautifully on a shelf next to noisier mugs.
VIA Coffee (2012), Mug#455401 · The Long TailA 2012 VIA mug in a warm white, brown and dark-yellow palette, with a kettle pouring graphic inside the dark-brown interior, a nod to the just-add-water magic of the instant line. By 2012 VIA had moved from novelty to a global staple, vindicating the long development bet. A cozier, more domestic take than the Vespa version.
Sulawesi (1995), Mug#455402 · Made by Jackal DesignsOne of the early coffee-origin mugs, dated 1995, showing a map of Sulawesi, the orchid-shaped Indonesian island the Dutch called Celebes. Starbucks has long prized its Toraja and Kalossi beans from the highlands here, processed by the wet-hulled method that gives Indonesian coffees their earthy, low-acid body. A dated 1990s origin mug like this is a genuinely vintage catch.
Una Tazza d'Oro, Mug#455403 · Made by Deborah ReinhartThe name means a cup of gold, and this mug leans into it with a checkerboard pattern and a golden crema topping, all on white. It nods to old-world Italian espresso houses, where Tazza d'Oro is a storied roastery name in Rome and Sardinia. A design-forward Tradizione Italiana piece that celebrates the ritual of a perfectly pulled shot.
Dreidel Mug#455404 · The Long TailThis Hanukkah mug keeps it bold and simple, three dreidels set against a deep blue background. Blue and white are the traditional colors of the holiday, echoing the menorah candles lit across the eight nights. Because Starbucks leaned overwhelmingly Christmas in its seasonal output, these Hanukkah dreidel mugs surface much less often and make a satisfying contrast to the red-cup ornaments in the holiday shelf.
Happy Hanukkah Mug#455406 · The Long TailThe companion Hanukkah mug, white inside with a hanukkiah ringed by dreidels outside. The dreidel's four letters, nun, gimel, hey and shin, stand for nes gadol haya sham, a great miracle happened there, the gambling top tied to the holiday's story. Between this and the hanukiah piece in the same batch, the festival of lights gets a genuine little pairing in the collection.
Romance (1999), Mug#455407 · The Long TailA 1999 Valentine release simply titled Romance, the word lettered across hearts and pink motifs on white. Late nineties Starbucks leaned hard into themed seasonal mugs like this before the dated city holiday line took over, so a clearly marked 1999 piece is a nice fixed point in the timeline. The plain sentiment and soft palette put it squarely in the brand's early romantic seasonal output.
Rooster, Lunar New Year, Mug#455408 · The Long TailA more upscale take on the Year of the Rooster, the bird painted in gold over dark red and finished with a silicone lid, dating to the 2017 Lunar New Year. That was the year Starbucks pushed a full Go Gold collection of red and gold drinkware, and the matching silicone top makes this a complete, lidded piece that often gets separated from its cover over time. Finding it with the original lid still on is the version you actually want.
Light Note Milder Dimensions, Mug#455410 · The Long TailA roast-and-blend mug rather than a place piece, this one ties to the lighter end of Starbucks' coffee spectrum, the milder "Light Note" style, dressed in warm orange, purple and creme. It is design-led marketing for a flavor profile, which makes it a fun outlier next to all the city mugs. I read pieces like this as the brand teaching taste through ceramics.
Coffee Cup Painting, Mug#455413 · Made by Jackal DesignsAn artful mug with a painted coffee cup and teaspoon decorating the white exterior, a meta little design of a cup illustrated on a cup. It belongs to the loose family of art-and-illustration mugs Starbucks produced outside its city and seasonal series. Quiet, decorative pieces like this rarely command attention at auction, which makes them a pleasure to find for next to nothing.
Coffee Break Essentials (1998), Mu#455414 · The Long TailA 1998 oversized mug, often found in an 18 to 20oz format, printed with a playful drawing of coffee alongside a definition of what makes a proper coffee break. It leans into the late-90s Starbucks identity of selling the ritual and the pause as much as the drink itself. These vintage jumbo mugs survive in decent numbers but are prized by collectors who specialize in the pre-2000 era for their warm retro illustration style.
My Bounty Song, Mug#455416 · The Long TailA poetry mug, with a verse printed across an orange and brown collage and a clean white interior. My Bounty Song belongs to Starbucks' occasional run of lyric and sentiment pieces that put words rather than landmarks at the heart of the design. I value the text-forward mugs because they show the brand reaching for mood and message, and a complete, legible one is easy to overlook and worth keeping.
Dreidel Mug (2007)#455417 · The Long TailA dated 2007 Hanukkah mug, a single dreidel among stars with a blue interior, which makes it the easiest of the dreidel mugs to place on the timeline. Dated holiday pieces are always the collector's favorite because the year is printed rather than guessed. The blue-on-blue palette and the explicit 2007 stamp give this one a clear anchor in the Hanukkah sub-run that the undated siblings lack.
Barista Collage (2001), Mug#455418 · The Long TailA 2001 mug wrapped in a collage of twelve photographs of Starbucks products, a snapshot of the full early-2000s lineup printed straight onto ceramic. It sits in the Barista mug family from that year, the same era as the gingerbread and storefront designs. The collage is a genuine catalog of what the company sold in 2001, which makes it more interesting to study than a single-image mug.
Coffee from Above (2001), Mug#455419 · The Long TailA 2001 mug with a delightfully surreal scene of Starbucks planes dropping coffee beans beneath a red sun, one of the more imaginative graphics the brand ever put on ceramic. It captures the turn-of-the-millennium optimism of coffee delivered to the world from above. Oddball narrative designs like this are exactly what makes early-2000s Starbucks artwork worth hunting, since so little of it is documented online.
Cupids Paintings Hearts (2000), Mu#455420 · The Long TailA Valentine's mug from 2000 painted with two cupids decorating hearts, the artwork running right onto the handle. Dated holiday pieces like this anchor a timeline nicely, and the year-2000 stamp gives it a clean place in the seasonal run. Romantic seasonal mugs were a reliable Starbucks gift item, made to move in February and rarely kept, so dated survivors carry a little scarcity.
Cafe Verona Dova (2000), Mug#455421 · The Long TailCaffe Verona is one of Starbucks' oldest blends, named for the Italian city of romance and originally created as a dessert coffee for a Seattle restaurant, all dark cocoa and caramelized sugar. This 2000 "Dova" version carries a painted blue dove carrying mail over a yellow, flower-strewn field, a peace-and-letters motif that turns the everyday house blend into something almost folk-art. It is the sort of crossover blend mug that gets overlooked next to city pieces but rewards a closer look.
Starbucks (1994), Mug#455422 · Made by Rosanna ImportsThis one wears a blue line drawing of a mug on white, and 1994 is the year that matters: it is when Starbucks launched the original City Mug Collector Series, sold only in the city each mug represented. Pieces from that first year are the holy grail for collectors, the Minneapolis 1994 in particular trading around two thousand dollars because supply was tiny and local. A self-referential mug-of-a-mug from the dawn of the whole hobby.
Starbucks Mermaid (2011)#455435 · The Long TailThis marks the big one, 2011, Starbucks' 40th anniversary, when the wordmark was dropped and the siren stood alone for the first time. Here she's engraved in white over a black ground, a sculptural treatment of the freshly streamlined logo. That redesign by Lippincott was controversial at launch, so a mug celebrating the bare siren in her debut year is a real milestone piece.
Pike Place Market, Brown (2008), M#455439 · The Long TailThis is the 2008 Pike Place Market brown mug bearing the original split tail siren, the bare chested first logo printed on both sides, white inside. Starbucks revived that 1971 brown and white siren in 2008 for the Pike Place anniversary, and the design openly shows the mermaid's twin tails that the modern crop and crown later hid. Collectors specifically hunt the unmodified original siren pieces from this run, since the bare logo is exactly the version Starbucks rarely puts on retail merchandise.
