2010 Yellow Submarine, Mug#455452 · The Long TailThe 2010 "Under the Sea" mug, new bone china, with a cheerful yellow submarine cruising past a whale, turtle, crab and fish, green inside with two more fish near the rim. Sellers on eBay and Poshmark routinely tag it vintage, rare and hard to find, and it gets called a must-have, so it punches above its everyday-line origins. The whimsical sea scene is what makes people chase it.
Peace on Earth, Mug#455453 · The Long TailA holiday piece carrying a Peace on Earth message, dark red with a reindeer mid leap outside and white inside. This belongs to the seasonal sentiment line Starbucks rotated through December alongside its red cups, where a single phrase and a winter motif carry the whole design. The leaping reindeer against deep red is a clean, almost mid century greeting card look, the kind of quiet holiday mug that reads warmer than the busier ornament era pieces.
Romeo and Juliet Angles, Mug#455454 · The Long TailA literary piece built around Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet, black line drawings of figures and the tale itself printed over an orange ground. Starbucks ran a small batch of Shakespeare quote mugs, including handleless versions, and the Romeo and Juliet Key To My Heart Valentine cup is the better known sibling, so collectors group these as the Bard set. The orange field here makes this the louder, more graphic take on the story.
2010 Starbucks Logo, Mug#455455 · The Long TailThis carries the new green wordless siren logo Starbucks unveiled in January 2011 for its 40th anniversary, when Howard Schultz stripped away the outer ring and the words "Starbucks Coffee" so the company could expand beyond coffee. White, oval-shaped, the mermaid standing alone in solid green. A clean little marker of the brand's biggest identity change in decades.
2010 Starbucks Logo, Times Square,#455456 · The Long TailSame 2011 wordless-siren rebrand logo, white and oval, but tied to the Times Square store, one of Starbucks' flagship Manhattan locations in the crossroads of the world. The new ring-free mermaid had just rolled out for the 40th anniversary, so a store-specific version like this ties the global rebrand to a single famous corner. A neat overlap of logo history and place.
Colorful Pumpking (2007), Mug#455458 · The Long TailA 2007 Halloween mug with an orange interior and grinning pumpkins bouncing across a black sky dotted with white stars. Starbucks ran seasonal autumn pieces alongside the Pumpkin Spice Latte boom, which had launched in 2003 and become a cultural juggernaut by then. The misspelled file name aside, it is a tidy dated example of the brand's short-lived Halloween merchandise.
Star of David (2009), Mug#455459 · The Long TailA rare overtly Judaica themed Starbucks piece, this 2009 mug centers a Star of David rendered in bronze and silver against light blue motifs, an Israel market or Hanukkah oriented release rather than a city souvenir. Religious and holiday specific mugs from the Israeli market are an unusual, narrow niche, since Starbucks famously had only a brief and unsuccessful run of stores in Israel. That scarcity, plus the metallic bronze and silver detailing, makes it a genuinely uncommon and conversation worthy piece for a themed collection.
Winter (2009), Mug#455461 · The Long TailA dated holiday piece from Winter 2009, with a bronze reindeer set over a red and brown background scattered with coffee beans. The 2009 holiday line leaned into embossed bone-china reindeer and snowflake designs, a warmer palette than the bright red cups of other years. Dated seasonal mugs like this are easy to place on a timeline, which is exactly why holiday collectors like to line them up by year.
2011 Snowman, Mug#455465 · The Long TailA 2011 winter mug with a cheery snowman in a purple scarf and red hat over white, a seasonal holiday design from the everyday line. The classic scarf-and-hat snowman is pure December comfort, the kind of cup that comes out once a year. A warm, low-stakes holiday piece that pairs with the snowman and Santa runs of the same season.
2011 Starbucks Logo, Red Mug#455466 · The Long TailAn oval shaped red mug from 2011 carrying a clean white line drawing of the Starbucks logo. 2011 was the company's 40th anniversary, the year it stripped the wordmark and the outer ring and let the Siren stand alone, so logo art from this era sits right at that pivot. The oval body is the quirk here, an unusual departure from the standard round profile that makes it stand out on a shelf.
North Pole Express, Mug#455467 · The Long TailA holiday mug showing Santa and children riding in a car with a Christmas tree up top, a North Pole Express theme straight out of Starbucks's seasonal whimsy. Christmas Starbucks mugs were dated annual releases meant to be given and used during the holidays, so surviving clean examples drift to the secondary market afterward. A cheerful, narrative piece that belongs with the dated red cup and Joyeux Noel holiday run.
2011, Green Top Cover, Mug#455468 · The Long TailAn oval 2011 mug, white inside with the Starbucks logo, topped by a removable green silicone lid. The silicone cover marks the early-2010s push toward spill-resistant, commuter-friendly ceramics rather than pure desk mugs. The combination of the unusual oval body and the signature Starbucks green lid makes this one of the more functional oddities in the everyday line, and the cover is the first thing that tends to go missing.
2004, Double Plastic, Mug#455469 · JapanA 2004 novelty double-wall plastic mug, mustard-toned inside with round berries suspended under a see-through outer plastic layer and finished with a black cover. The trapped-decoration construction, art floating between two clear walls, is the whole appeal, a gimmicky departure from Starbucks ceramic norm. These plastic curiosities sit outside the serious mug lines and are collected more as quirky oddities than for value.
1996, Person Drinking Coffee, Mug#455470 · The Long TailA 1996 art mug with a painting of multiple faces drinking coffee rendered in grey over black, a moody, almost cafe-society print wrapped around a white-lined cup. Starbucks' mid-90s "art" mugs leaned into this expressive, illustrative style before the line went corporate and city-themed, and the somber grey-on-black palette makes it one of the more striking pieces from that brief experimental window.
Colorful Drinks, Mug#455471 · The Long TailA lively mug parading colorful beverages across a red, orange, and purple background, pure Frappuccino era marketing rather than a souvenir piece. It sits in the everyday line that sold the fun of the menu itself, leaning on saturated color to feel like a summer drinks board. Not rare, but a cheerful counterweight to the muted city skylines elsewhere in my shelves.
New Year Eve Gala, Mug#455473 · Chaleur MadeA celebration mug carrying a colorful Gala dance painting around the exterior, made for the New Year's Eve festivities rather than any single city. The lively figures and bright palette make it one of the more painterly pieces in the everyday line. Occasion mugs like this slip out of catalogs fast once the holiday passes, so a clean, vivid New Year Gala is a small seasonal treasure.
1999 Pike place Public Market Stor#455493 · Skyline SeriesA 1999 mug rendering Seattle's Pike Place Public Market in soft light blue and grey, honoring the spot where the very first Starbucks opened at 1912 Pike Place in 1971. Many of these market mugs were sold only at that original store, which makes them quasi-exclusive souvenirs, and the muted hand-sketch treatment here is far more tasteful than the splashier first-store tourist mugs.
Candy Cane Mug#455497 · The Long TailThis is a holiday piece built around the gimmick of the handle itself, shaped and striped like a candy cane, with the Starbucks logo on the body. It is the kind of seasonal novelty mug that shows up in winter lineups and lives or dies on the handle gag, which here is genuinely fun to hold. Festive novelty mugs like this tend to scatter after the holidays, so an intact one with an unchipped candy-cane handle is a small win.
New Orleans, Collectible Mug, 16oz#455527 · Global Icon SeriesA 16oz New Orleans collectible with a musician blowing a trumpet across the cream exterior, a direct salute to the city that birthed jazz. The brown interior and cream body mark it as a heftier collector format. New Orleans is America's most musical city, and a horn-player mug captures that better than any cathedral or streetcar would, which is why this one always gets picked up first on the Louisiana shelf.
Lisboa, Icon Collectible Mug, 16oz#455535 · Global Icon SeriesThe blue-interior Lisboa Icon mug shows the Torre de Belem, the early-16th-century Manueline fortress King John II built at the mouth of the Tagus as both defense and ceremonial gateway to Lisbon. The "Lisboa" Portuguese-language version arrived in 2011, replacing the earlier English "Lisbon" mug that ran 2008 to 2011, so getting the spelling right actually pins the variant. The back of the line often carries the 25 de Abril Bridge.
2003 Summer Polka, Yellow#455557 · 2003 Summer Polka SeriesThe yellow Summer Polka mug from 2003, the most on theme of the bunch with a yellow interior echoing the yellow and black lines that band the outside. It is the purest expression of the line's bright summery intent. As an everyday utility mug it was never treated as a keepsake, so finding one without chips or crazing is more of a hunt than the modest original price would suggest.
2003 Summer Polka, Orange#455558 · 2003 Summer Polka SeriesThe orange member of the 2003 Summer Polka set, a warm orange interior under the same signature yellow and black lined exterior that defines the line. Starbucks built this whole family as a coordinated summer color story, meant to be mixed on a counter rather than collected. Tracking down the full Summer Polka spread in matching condition is the real game, since these everyday mugs were used hard and rarely kept boxed.
2003 Summer Polka, Blue#455559 · 2003 Summer Polka SeriesPart of Starbucks' cheerful 2003 Summer Polka run, this one pairs a bright blue interior glaze with the playful yellow and black lined pattern wrapping the outside. The whole series leaned into a sunny picnic mood, and the color sets it apart from the orange, purple and yellow siblings. Boxed seasonal color families like this are fun to chase as a complete rainbow, since the individual cups were cheap and rarely saved as a set.
2003 Summer Polka, Purple#455560 · 2003 Summer Polka SeriesSummer Polka in purple, a deep purple glazed interior wrapped in the line's recognizable yellow and black striping. This is the moodier note in a 2003 set that otherwise reads as pure sunshine, which is exactly why I like having it for contrast. The appeal for me is completeness, a shelf of all four Polka colors together tells the season's design story far better than any single cup does.
2006 Greenery, Mug#455561 · The Long TailA 2006 mug, white inside with green leaves wrapping the outside, a botanical everyday piece with no city or holiday tie, just foliage as decoration. Greenery sits squarely in the long-tail category of pretty seasonal-feeling mugs Starbucks produced in volume. I keep it for the design, since a simple leaf motif on white is the kind of timeless look that never reads as dated the way a logo-heavy mug eventually does.
2004 Daddy-o (Green / Orange), 18o#455562 · 2004 Daddy-O SeriesThe 2004 Daddy-o in green and orange polka dots is peak mid-century kitsch, an 18 ounce mug that looks like it wandered off a 1960s diner counter. It belongs to Starbucks' short lived Daddy-O run, all bold retro pattern and no city at all. I keep it for the sheer confidence of the color clash, the kind of piece people either love or quietly hide at the back of the cabinet.
2004 Daddy-o (Green / Purple), 18o#455563 · 2004 Daddy-O SeriesA big 18oz everyday mug from 2004, white inside with a scatter of green and purple polka dots across the outside, the kind of cheerful pop-art piece Starbucks rolled out alongside its serious city lines. The name Daddy-o nods to that breezy mid-century beatnik slang, and at 18 ounces this is a genuine workhorse rather than a display piece. These playful seasonal patterns rarely carry collector value, but the bold dot motif makes it a fun outlier in a city-mug collection.
2004 Daddy-o (Blue / Brown), 18oz#455564 · 2004 Daddy-O SeriesThe 2004 Daddy-O mug, a big 18oz in white with blue and brown polka dots, named for its retro mid-century lounge vibe. Daddy-O was Starbucks' playful dotted pattern of that year, and the colorways were sold as a coordinated spread. This blue-and-brown pairing is the most subdued, coffee-and-denim tones that make it the everyday-feeling member of the polka-dot set.
2004 Daddy-o (Blue / Red), 18oz Mu#455565 · 2004 Daddy-O SeriesDaddy-O for 2004 in blue and red dots on white, the 18oz size. The Daddy-O name leans on a beatnik, jukebox-era feel, and the bold blue-and-red combo is the most primary-colored, poppy version of the polka-dot run. These dotted mugs are a recognizable little 2004 family, and the high-contrast red pairing tends to be the one that catches the eye first across the set.
2002 Firecracker Mug#455566 · 2002.0A 2002 Fourth of July piece, red inside and out with firecrackers printed around the body and an unusual square bottom that sets it apart on the shelf. It pairs directly with the blue Fireworks mug of the same year, the two making a deliberate summer Americana set. Red Starbucks mugs from this era are notoriously hard to find boxed and unfaded, since the red glaze shows wear, so a crisp Firecracker is a nicer grab than its modest price suggests.
2002 Fireworks Mug#455567 · 2002.0The 2002 Fireworks, blue inside and out with bursting fireworks across the body and the same distinctive square base as its sibling. It is the cooler-toned half of Starbucks' 2002 summer pairing, designed to sit beside the red Firecracker mug for a full Independence Day duo. Seasonal novelty mugs like this were short-run by nature, so collectors who want the matched set usually have to hunt the two down separately, which makes a clean blue one worth holding.
2012 Seoul Day#455573 · The Long TailMy second 2012 Seoul Day, kept honestly for the record with a crack noted by the arrow. A collector keeps the flawed twin because condition is the whole story in this hobby, and a hairline tells you a piece was actually used and lived with. Same bright Han River and palace skyline as its sibling, just battle-scarred, and I would never toss it.
2011 Dafodiles (12oz), Mug#455576 · The Long TailA 2011 12oz mug with daffodils blooming over a purple-grey ground and an untraditional handle shape, one of the spring-flower designs Starbucks ran in its everyday line. Daffodils are the classic herald of spring, so the timing fits a seasonal release. The unusual handle and muted backdrop make it a touch more distinctive than the average floral.
2011 Korean Green, Mug#455577 · The Long TailA 2011 mug from the Korean market, white inside with a green exterior carrying white design elements, part of Starbucks' region-specific everyday pieces. Korea is one of Starbucks' biggest and most design-forward markets, so its local mugs often differ from the US line. A regional pickup that adds a bit of geographic spice to a shelf of standard mugs.
Moonlight Shadow, Mug#455580 · The Long TailA dreamy white mug showing a moon over dark blue skies with yellow rabbits, this draws on the Mid-Autumn Festival and the Chinese legend of the Jade Rabbit who pounds elixir on the moon. Starbucks Asia builds a moon-and-bunnies collection around the festival most years, and the rabbit motif is its signature image. I love that this piece carries a real folk tale, turning an everyday mug into a little vessel of mooncake-season mythology.
New Zhubei, Mug#455581 · The Long TailA green themed branch mug for Zhubei, the fast growing high tech city beside Hsinchu in northern Taiwan, heart of the island's Science Park and semiconductor industry. Store opening and city specific mugs from Taiwan tend to be printed in limited quantities for the local market, which is why so few make it abroad. The leafy green motif fits Zhubei's reputation as a planned, park rich modern city.
Sakura (2009), Mug#455588 · Japan 2009The 2009 Sakura mug keeps it simple, white inside with pink cherry blossom leaves drifting across the outside. Starbucks Japan ties this annual release to hanami, the brief window each spring when the whole country watches the sakura bloom and fall, and that ephemerality is the entire point of the design. These spring drops are notoriously fast sellers in Japan, so dated survivors from over a decade back carry real collector weight.
Dreidel Hanukkah, Mug#455590 · The Long TailA Hanukkah mug scattered with dreidels and snowflakes over a blue field, white inside, one of Starbucks' rarer nods to the Jewish Festival of Lights. The dreidel is the four-sided spinning top children play with during the eight nights, its Hebrew letters standing for the phrase a great miracle happened there. Hanukkah pieces are far scarcer than the Christmas red-cup run, so any dreidel mug is a welcome holiday outlier.
Air Water Earth (1996), Mug#455594 · The Long TailA 1996 piece themed on the elements, the exterior a drawing of Air, Water and Earth, the building blocks behind a cup of coffee. White inside, no place name, just an almost philosophical nod to growing the bean. These elemental and travel mugs from the mid-90s are easy to overlook, which is exactly why I went looking for it.
Muan Jai, Mug#455596 · The Long TailThis Muan Jai mug carries a map of Thailand and a hand-noted message under the Muan Jai stamp, celebrating the medium-roast blend of washed Northern Thai highland beans and semi-washed Indonesian coffee. Muan Jai, wholehearted happiness, has been Starbucks Thailand's flagship cause coffee since 2003. The mug doubles as a small piece of the brand's community-store story, sold to channel profits back to the growers.
Dark Coffee Shop, Mug#455597 · The Long TailA mug whose exterior is a warm red-toned scene of a dark coffee shop with people sipping together, selling the atmosphere of the cafe itself. It belongs to the everyday line that traded on the third place idea, Starbucks as the spot between home and work. The illustrated interior scene is charming and unusually narrative for a mug that carries no city or date.
1998 Love in Color (1), Mug#455598 · The Long TailThe first of Starbucks' 1998 Love in Color Valentine pair, this mug shows a couple kissing behind flowers, rendered in pops of color over a grey background with a cupid looking on. Released for Valentine's Day, the duo was meant to be collected together, and the deliberate color-against-grey contrast is the whole design hook, romance lit up against a muted world.
1998 Love in Color (2), Mug#455599 · The Long TailThe companion to the first Love in Color mug, this 1998 Valentine piece swaps the floral scene for a couple kissing behind an umbrella, again in color over grey with a cupid. Having both halves of the set matters here, since Starbucks designed them as a matched pair, and the umbrella version is the harder one to pin down when you are trying to reunite the two.
2001 Lanterns, Mug#455600 · The Long TailA 2001 mug with paper lanterns washed in yellow, pink, and green over a light pink body, an Asian inspired festival design. The lantern motif evokes the bright hanging lights of regional celebrations across Asia, and the soft pink ground makes this an unusually delicate piece against the brand's usual green. It reads more like a decorative seasonal mug than a city souvenir, which is what makes it a fun outlier to find.
2004 Latin American Coffee From St#455601 · The Long TailA 2004 origin mug for Latin American coffee, green inside with a drawn landscape and the old blend stamps wrapped around the outside, from back when Starbucks sold the region as a story rather than a SKU. It nods to the nutty, balanced cups from places like Guatemala and Colombia that built the early menu. A quiet piece of coffee marketing history more than a souvenir.
Sumatra Lion, Mug#455602 · The Long TailA coffee-origin mug for Sumatra carrying a big-cat drawing, the catalog calls it a Sumatra tiger, the critically endangered subspecies found only on that Indonesian island. Sumatra is one of Starbucks' signature dark, earthy single origins, and the tiger imagery became a recurring motif across multiple Sumatra mug generations, making the cat-themed versions some of the more recognizable origin pieces collectors look for.
2008, Year of the Bull#455603 · The Long TailA narrow tall 2008 Lunar New Year mug with a yellow interior and a red bull, marking the Year of the Ox that ran from late January 2009, which Starbucks released ahead of the holiday in 2008. The red ox over yellow is classic auspicious Chinese color coding. Starbucks zodiac pieces are a well-collected Asian-market line, and the bull and ox animals tend to be among the more eye-catching of the twelve.
2000, Red Kettle Houses#455604 · The Long TailA narrow, tall holiday mug from 2000 with a white interior and a row of red village houses wrapped around the body in the shape of a kettle. This is from the Starbucks holiday village run, the cozy Christmas storefront theme they revisited for years with gold and red rooftops. Collectors hunt the early village pieces, and the tall narrow silhouette makes this one stand apart from the standard rounded holiday mugs.
Kenya, Mug#455606 · The Long TailA sketch style Kenya mug, white inside with elephants striding through open fields. This is the understated origin piece, leaning on the savanna imagery that defines East Africa rather than busy graphics. Kenya remains a benchmark origin for specialty coffee, those wine like, juicy cups from the slopes around Mount Kenya, and the simple elephant sketch keeps the focus on the land the beans come from.
Types of Coffee (2007), Mug#455608 · The Long TailA 2007 conversation piece, light blue inside and printed all over with the names of coffee styles, a little taxonomy you can sip from. Mugs like this functioned as quiet menu-board education, teaching customers the difference between a macchiato, a cortado and an Americano. A nice everyday piece that rewards a slow read while the coffee cools.
Squirrel & Mouse in the Snow (2010#455609 · The Long TailA charming 2010 holiday mug featuring a painted winter scene of a squirrel and a mouse in the snow, with the clever twist that the little mouse perches right on the handle, turning the cup itself into part of the picture. Sculptural handle details like that are exactly what lift a seasonal mug from ordinary to memorable, and collectors specifically seek out pieces where the handle becomes a character. Dated 2010 anchors it firmly in that holiday season's storytelling run.
2004 Indonesian Coffee From Starbu#455610 · The Long TailA 2004 origin mug for Starbucks Indonesian coffees, pomela-pink inside with an outside landscape drawing dressed in the Indonesian-blend bag stamps. Indonesia means the deep, earthy, full-bodied Sumatra and aged Sulawesi beans that anchor Starbucks darker side, a flavor world apart from the bright East Africans. The stamp artwork descends from the colorful coffee-bag illustrations Starbucks has used since the late 1980s, and this region-by-region mug set is genuinely harder to find than the everyday city line.
2010 Mug of Love#455611 · The Long TailThe 2011 Valentine "Love Letter" mug, red inside with the front drawn as a Starbucks-postmarked envelope, heart used as the stamp, the back showing the envelope folds sealed with a heart wax stamp. It reads "To: My Valentine, From: A Sweet Admirer," a sweet bit of seasonal whimsy in new bone china. A fun holiday-adjacent piece that still turns up cheap on the resale market.
2008 Blue Short Mug#455612 · The Long TailA short 2008 mug in a two-tone blue scheme, blue glaze inside and a blue-on-light-blue exterior, from the everyday color-block line rather than any named series. Pieces like this are the connective tissue of a real collection, the unglamorous solids that show how Starbucks cycled palettes year to year. The short squat profile makes it a demitasse-adjacent oddball worth keeping for variety.
Espresso Roast, Mug#455613 · The Long TailA plain white workhorse stamped Espresso Roast on both faces, this is the mug that names Starbucks' darkest, oldest core blend, the one pulled into every shot since the company started roasting it in 1975. I love these utilitarian pieces because they advertise the coffee itself rather than a city, the kind of thing baristas actually drank from behind the bar. The full regular size makes it the everyday companion to the espresso version.
2004 Abbey 2 (Red / White), Mug#455614 · The Long TailAbbey II for 2004 in classic red, but note the flip, this one is white inside with the red on the outside, the inverse of the 2003 solid red Abbey. That detail matters to collectors who track the exact glaze layout, because red Abbeys exist in several configurations across the years. A 12oz, it is the bright anchor of the two-tone II set.
Coffee Machines and Blends, Mug#455615 · The Long TailA white mug whose exterior is a still life of the coffee ritual itself, scattered beans, a French press, and an espresso machine rather than any city or logo. It belongs to the everyday merchandise line that leaned into Starbucks as a coffee culture brand, not a souvenir. I like it as a quiet palate cleanser between the loud city mugs, a piece that simply celebrates the craft.
2012 Starbucks Espresso Journey, M#455616 · The Long TailA clean white espresso mug carrying a round electric symbol on the outside, part of Starbucks' 2012 Espresso Journey idea celebrating the craft and machinery behind the shot. The graphic nods to the espresso machine itself, the engine of every café. It is a quiet, modern piece next to my painted city mugs, and that restraint is exactly why it stands out on the shelf.
Starbucks Coffee Lovers Coffee, Mu#455622 · The Long TailA white mug where two cups breathe red aroma swirls that curl together into a heart, a sweet bit of visual wordplay on Coffee Lovers. It is a Valentine-flavored novelty piece rather than a city or series mug, leaning on Starbucks' habit of seasonal romance merchandise. The design is the whole charm here, that little trick of turning steam into a love sign.
2004 Abbey 2 (Blue / White), Mug#455624 · The Long TailPart of the 2004 Abbey II refresh, a 12oz with a blue exterior over white. The Abbey II was the second generation of that barrel shape, brought out in matched two-tone pairings rather than the earlier flat solids. Blue body with a white liner, this one trades on the clean contrast, and the II versions are the ones people chase to complete the full color spread.
Muan-Jai, Thailand#455625 · The Long TailA 12oz Thailand mug showing an Indigenous hill-tribe man against a blue ground, honoring the Northern Highland communities who grow the Muan Jai crop. The blue interior matches the bold portrait, a departure from the usual landmark band. It puts the actual coffee farmers, not a skyline, at the center, which makes it one of the more meaningful pieces in my Thailand corner.
Decaffeinated Vienesse, Mug#455626 · The Long TailA white mug stamped with a Decaffeinated Viennese graphic in that airmail label style Starbucks loved for its blends. Viennese Roast is one of the company's classic blend names, a lighter, nuttier roast that nods to Vienna's deep cafe culture, and the decaf version got its own piece here. The blend-stamp mugs were merchandising for the bagged coffee, which makes individual named ones surprisingly hard to reassemble as a set.
Brewing Since 1971, Mug#455627 · The Long TailThis wears the founding-year badge, Brewing Since 1971, marking the original Pike Place Market store where Starbucks began. Clean white outside with a brown lip, the brown nodding to the company's original brown-toned first logo before the green era. It is a heritage statement piece rather than a city souvenir, the kind that grounds a collection in the brand's actual origin story.
2004 Abbey 2 (Green / White), Mug#455628 · The Long TailAbbey II for 2004 in deep green with a white interior, the 12oz size. Green nods straight to the Starbucks siren color, which makes it one of the more sought tones in the two-tone Abbey II group. Like its siblings it relies on a crisp glaze line where the green meets the white rim, and a clean example with no chips reads sharp.
Abstract Painting (3), XL French P#455629 · Winter 2010The Painting 3 artwork scaled up onto an XL French press body, here rendered as a Pike Place street scene with the siren worked in. Carrying a Chaleur art design onto a press rather than a mug makes this an unusual format for the series and a harder one to find. Pike Place is of course the home of the original 1971 Starbucks, so the subject choice is a deliberate nod to the brand's birthplace.
Ethiopia Yergacheffe, Mug#455631 · The Long TailYergacheffe, the famous coffee district within Ethiopia's Sidama region sitting around 1,900 meters up, gives its name to some of the most floral, tea-like washed coffees on earth, all tangerine and lemon balm. The red wheat painting on the outside nods to the harvest and the agrarian heart of the world's coffee birthplace. I pair this with the Sidamo mug because together they map the two legendary names every Ethiopia lover knows.
Arabian Mocha Java, Mug#455633 · The Long TailA blend mug rather than a city one, branded with the Arabian Mocha Java sticker on both sides, Starbucks honoring its oldest blend, the marriage of Yemeni Mocha and Indonesian Java that gave coffee its first famous pairing. White inside, no skyline, just the romance of the bean origins. I like a mug that sells the coffee instead of a place, a rare thing in my cabinet.
2004 Abbey 2 (Brown / White), Mug#455634 · The Long TailThe 2004 Abbey II in earthy brown over white, a 12oz that leans into the coffee-house palette. Brown is the most on-brand color of the whole Abbey II run, reading like a roasted bean, and it pairs the warm exterior against a clean white interior. The Abbey II two-tones were sold as a coordinated family, so brown is one of the set pieces collectors line up side by side.
New Guinea, Mug#455635 · The Long TailA coffee-origin mug honoring Papua New Guinea, where production began in 1926 from Jamaica Blue Mountain seeds and now feeds a third of the nation through tiny highland coffee gardens. The design sets a New Guinea parrot stamp over white, nodding to the country's famously vivid birdlife that Starbucks itself used as a metaphor for its origin coffees. It is one of my favorite bean-source pieces because it celebrates where the cup actually starts.
Cafe Verona, Mug#455636 · The Long TailThe plain Caffe Verona mug is the straightforward member of the family, just the Cafe Verona stamp on clean white, celebrating the blend Starbucks named for Verona and built around notes of dark cocoa and caramelized sugar. Verona has been part of the Starbucks lineup for decades and was famously created as a restaurant dessert coffee, so this mug is really a small monument to one of the company's signature roasts rather than a place.
2004 Abbey 2 (Pink / White), Mug#455637 · The Long TailThe 2004 Abbey II in soft pink over white, a 12oz and one of the lighter notes in the set. Pink is usually the scarcer color in any Starbucks pastel run because fewer move and fewer survive, which gives this one a little edge for collectors filling out the Abbey II rainbow. White inside, pink out, it is the gentlest piece in an otherwise bold family.
2026 Main Street, Mug#455639 · 2001.0A white mug with a line drawing of a Main Street Starbucks storefront, the Market House location on Main Street, U.S.A. at Disneyland, which Starbucks runs in vintage 1900s small-town dress to match the land. Disney-park Starbucks merchandise is its own collecting universe with a devoted following, and a store-specific Main Street drawing makes this a charming, location-locked keeper.
Gazebo Blend, Mug#455640 · The Long TailGazebo Blend was Starbucks' summer ritual for twenty years, a medium bodied East African coffee built for iced brewing with crisp acidity and bright fruity, floral notes, debuting each warm season until it was retired after 2010. The hand drawn gazebo on this cup is pure 1990s nostalgia, and vintage Gazebo pieces still get hunted down by collectors who remember pouring it over ice.
Ethiopia Sidamo, Mug#455641 · The Long TailThis celebrates Sidamo, one of the great single origins from the birthplace of coffee itself, where legend says a goat herder named Kaldi first noticed his goats buzzing on the cherries around 800 AD. Sidamo coffees are prized for bright citrus and lemon acidity, and Starbucks has sourced this southern Ethiopian region for decades. The illustrated origin artwork on the outside makes this one of the more storytelling pieces in my origin mugs.
Frappucino, Mug#455642 · The Long TailThis mug wears the Frappuccino drink logo, marking the blended icon that debuted in spring 1995 and went on to define Starbucks' cold menu for thirty years. The name traces back to Cambridge's Coffee Connection, which trademarked Frappuccino before Starbucks bought the company and the word along with it. I love that a single mug quietly carries one of the great accidental-acquisition stories in coffee.
Espresso Roast, Tin Case#455643 · The Long TailThe gift-set presentation of the Espresso Roast mug, packaged in a tin case rather than sold loose, which is exactly why fewer survived intact with their tin. The white mug carries the familiar Espresso Roast stamp on both sides, but the surviving case is the real collector value here since boxes and tins were usually tossed. Finding the mug still nested in its original tin is the kind of small win I chase.
Two Ladies Sitting, Mug#455644 · The Long TailA mug carrying a painting of two seated women, an art forward design that puts a figurative illustration on white rather than a city or logo. Starbucks has occasionally issued art themed ceramics that function more like little canvases than branded merchandise. Without a named artist or series printed on it, the appeal is purely the imagery, a quieter and more decorative entry among the bolder city mugs.
VIA Coffee (2010), Mug#455645 · The Long TailA 2010 mug celebrating VIA, the instant coffee Starbucks launched in 2009 after nearly twenty years of development and a patent-pending technology to lock in flavor. The orange Vespa painting gives it a breezy Italian-road feel. VIA was Howard Schultz's bet on the 21 billion dollar global instant market, and this mug is a small monument to that gamble.
The Korean Script (2005), Mug#455646 · The Long TailA 2005 mug carrying Korean script across a white body, tying it to Starbucks' early expansion in South Korea, a market the company entered in 1999 and which became one of its strongest worldwide. The all Hangul typographic treatment makes it a clean, design forward piece rather than a landmark mug. Dated 2005 Asia market pieces like this are easy to overlook but pin down a specific moment in the brand's Korean growth.
Milder Dimensions, Mug#455648 · The Long TailA white mug printed with a poem rather than a place, "Milder Dimensions" is one of the verse-and-copy pieces Starbucks made to dress its lighter roasts in language. These text-forward mugs reflect the brand's habit of writing lyrical descriptions for its coffees. It sits outside any city series, which is exactly why I park it in the long-tail, a small reminder that Starbucks sold mood and words as much as it sold places.
2007 Starbucks Love Mug#455649 · The Long TailA red-lined 2007 mug with a steel-look bottom and white exterior scattered with floating heart balloons, part of the brand's reliable Valentine output. It pairs nicely with the same year's petal I Love You cup as a his-and-hers set. The red interior is the giveaway tell that this was a February release rather than a generic everyday white mug.
Mermaid Holding Cup (2006), Mug#455651 · Japan 2006This 2006 mug is from the Anniversary series, with a bronze Siren shown holding a cup, set against a dark brown body. Starbucks releases an Anniversary mug each fall keyed to its 1971 founding, and the bronze-and-brown palette became the recognizable signature of these editions. Dating these by year matters to collectors because the background color and finish shift subtly across releases, and I keep mine grouped to show that progression.
2001, Cobble Stone Road, Mug#455652 · The Long TailA 2001 mug illustrating an old town cobblestone street with a Starbucks store nestled into the scene. This belongs to the brand's fondness for the romantic village storefront, the same nostalgic European streetscape that runs through its holiday and neighborhood designs. The drawn in Starbucks shop on the cobbled lane is a sweet bit of self mythologizing, casting the cafe as a fixture of the charming old town.
2000, Starbucks Store under Snow,#455653 · The Long TailA 2000 holiday mug showing a Starbucks storefront packed with snow, complete with a guitarist tucked in the corner playing in the winter scene. This belongs to the year 2000 Barista holiday run, the cozy illustrated Christmas cafe theme with carolers and snow. The little corner musician is the kind of hidden detail that makes you turn the mug in your hand, and that storytelling charm is why these early holiday illustrations still get collected.
Morning Glory (2013), Mug#455654 · The Long TailA 2013 mug built around texture rather than a place, with random colored flakes scattered over a cream body, an orange interior, and a contrasting blue handle. Morning Glory leans into the cheerful name and the idea of a bright start to the day. These pattern-and-color novelty pieces were Starbucks experimenting with glaze effects outside the city-mug formula, which is exactly why I like one on the shelf.
Red Roses (2012), Mug#455656 · The Long TailThe standard size companion to the 2012 Red Roses run, pink and red rose petals scattered over a red exterior with a clean white interior. Released for the Valentine and spring window, it is the everyday mug version of the design while the wide bowl handled tea. Having both shapes side by side is the kind of small completeness that quietly makes a collection feel finished.
Red Roses (2012) Tea, Mug#455657 · The Long TailThe 2012 Red Roses tea mug, a wide bowl shape made for tea with scattered red and pink rose petals across white inside and out. The wide format is the tell, Starbucks cut its tea ware lower and broader to cool faster and show off loose leaf, a deliberate nod to the Tazo and later Teavana side of the business. A romantic, springtime piece that pairs with its regular size sibling.
Black Starbucks Coffee (2011), Mug#455658 · The Long TailA 2011 mug that flips the formula: matte black body with the Starbucks siren logo rendered clean in white, no city, no landmark, just the mark itself. This is branding as design, leaning on the strength of the logo alone. Minimalist black-and-white siren mugs have a quiet following among people who want the identity without the tourist artwork, and the stark contrast still looks modern today.
2012 Red Fox, 8oz, Mug#455659 · The Long TailA single 8oz red fox mug from the 2012 holiday bone-china series, white fox on dark red with the signature tail-shaped handle. The fox motif was a centerpiece of that winter's woodland theme and remains a fan favorite for the sheer cleverness of the curled-tail grip. As a standalone it is the common red colorway, ideal as the everyday user while the rarer blue stays on the shelf.
Korea Crazy Handle (2013), Mug#455662 · The Long TailA genuinely odd 2013 Korean release, the mask figure on the body references the traditional talchum mask dance, while the colorful long arms wrap around as the actual handle, which is where the "crazy handle" nickname comes from. These novelty sculptural-handle mugs are far less common than the standard Korea Icon series, so they tend to surprise people who only know the flat city pieces. The masked drum-dance imagery is rooted in real folk performance, not invented kitsch.
Gold / White (2012), Mug#455663 · The Long TailA clean 2012 two tone study, gold across the lower half meeting crisp white up top with no city or slogan to distract. Pieces like this come from Starbucks' minimalist design phase, where color blocking did all the work, and the simple gold and white split still reads as quietly elegant on a shelf.
Snowman Venti (2012), 16oz Mug#455664 · The Long TailThe Venti sized 16oz partner to the smaller 2012 snowman, this one wears the same dark red scarf but sits on a bolder full red body rather than grey. Buying both the regular and the oversized version of a single holiday design is a classic collector move, and the red Venti reads as the showpiece of the pair. Dated 2012 holiday mugs anchor that year on a shelf, and the larger format makes this the one people reach for to actually drink their winter coffee.
Snowman (2012), Mug#455665 · The Long TailThis 2012 snowman, with his dark red scarf set against a soft grey body, comes from Starbucks' annual holiday gift run, the seasonal mugs that turn up beside the red cups each December. Dated holiday pieces are easy to slot chronologically, which collectors love, and 2012 sits in the era when Starbucks leaned into warm hand drawn winter characters. He pairs naturally with the matching red Venti snowman from the same year, so the two together make a nice little 2012 holiday set.
Houses on Hills (2012), Mug#455670 · The Long TailA quiet 2012 art mug, all brown cottages tumbling across green hillsides on a white ground, the kind of unbranded illustrative piece Starbucks slipped out as a design exercise rather than a city souvenir. There is no landmark to chase here, just a painterly bit of Mediterranean or Tuscan-flavored scenery. These illustration-led mugs from the early 2010s sit outside any named series, which makes them easy to overlook and quietly collectible.
Purple Loy Krathong, Mug#455671 · The Long TailLoy Krathong is Thailand's festival of light, held on the full moon of the twelfth lunar month, when people float candle lit krathong rafts down rivers to honor the water goddess and let go of the past year. This Starbucks Thailand mug captures that exact image, floating candles glowing over a purple interior with a cream exterior. The Sukhothai celebration is the most famous version of the festival, and the floating lights are genuinely one of the most beautiful sights in Southeast Asia.
Low Red (2012), Mug#455673 · The Long TailA 2012 solid-red mug from the minimalist color-block runs, white inside and a clean bold red exterior with no city or skyline at all. Pieces like this are about form and palette rather than place, the quieter design experiments in the catalog. I value the dated stamp, it lets an otherwise plain red mug earn a precise spot in the timeline.
Green and Yellow Lines (2013), 12o#455676 · The Long TailA 2013 low profile 12oz mug in playful green and yellow line motifs, sold with its matching lid for the morning commute. This sits squarely in Starbucks' early 2010s pattern driven design language, where abstract color lines replaced cities and slogans, and the included lid marks it as one of the to go friendly stackable formats from that run.
2004 Black Lid, Silver Star, 12oz,#455678 · The Long TailThe white-bodied member of the 2004 black-lid travelers, marked with a silver star, 12oz, aluminum interior and matching black handle and lid. This is the one cataloged with the lid still present, which matters because the snap lids were the first thing to get lost or cracked on these travel mugs. The silver star on white is the cleanest read of the star trio.
2004 Dark Red Lid, Bronze Star, 12#455679 · The Long TailA 2004 travel-style 12oz mug with an aluminium tin liner, a white body carrying a single bronze star, and a matching red plastic handle and snap lid. The lone star mark is a quiet riff on Starbucks design language without the full mermaid wordmark, the sort of utilitarian commuter cup the chain made by the thousands. Pieces like this are common and inexpensive, valued more for completing a year set than for any rarity, and it pairs directly with its silver-star twin.
2004 Dark Red Lid, Silver Star, 12#455680 · The Long TailThe silver-star sibling to the bronze version, this 2004 12oz commuter mug has the same aluminium inner liner, red plastic handle and red snap lid, with a single silver star stamped on the white outer body. Starbucks issued these metallic-star travelers as plain everyday drinkware, deliberately understated next to the landmark city mugs. Owning both the bronze and silver finishes is the collector point here, a small matched pair rather than a sought-after one-off.
2004 Black Lid, Bronze Star, 12 oz#455681 · The Long TailThe 2004 black-lid traveler in purple monochrome with a single bronze star on the body, 12oz, aluminum lined with the black handle and lid. The lone star motif sets it apart from the plain color versions and gives the little travel run a touch of decoration. Purple is an unusual base for Starbucks, which makes this star variant one of the more eye-catching of the black-lid group.
Red Bird Houses Over Snow#455686 · The Long TailA cozy winter design, little red birdhouses standing in white snow against a soft grey sky, the kind of seasonal piece Starbucks runs alongside the holiday cups rather than the dated city line. The birdhouse motif is pure hygge, quiet and folksy rather than loud and festive. It is the sort of understated winter mug that hides in plain sight and rewards anyone who actually looks closely at a collection.
Green Hills and Red Clouds, Mug#455687 · The Long TailA scenic mug with rolling green hills under a sky of red clouds, finished with a red line rimming the white interior, an unusually painterly landscape for the everyday line. It reads almost like a small framed picture wrapped around a cup, the kind of moody, atmospheric design that stands apart from the usual logo and city formula.
Diwali Brown (2013), 16oz, Mug#455688 · The Long TailA 2013 Diwali mug, marking the Hindu festival of lights, with a bronze sun motif glowing over a deep brown body and a yellow-cream interior. Diwali celebrates light triumphing over darkness, so the radiant sun imagery is the whole point of the design. Starbucks India released festival-themed pieces around this period, making the holiday-specific mugs more regional and less common on Western shelves.
Red Starbucks Coffee (2011), Mug#455689 · The Long TailA bold 2011 piece, the full Starbucks Coffee wordmark in white over a solid red field, dating to a pivotal year for the brand. 2011 was the company's fortieth anniversary, the year it dropped the words from the logo and let the Siren stand alone, so a mug that still spells out Starbucks Coffee in 2011 is a small marker of that transition moment. A clean, confident cup that captures the brand right at a turning point.
2012 Long Red Scarf, Mug#455692 · The Long TailA 2012 holiday mug, red inside, with a girl in a long flowing red scarf throwing her hands up over a white exterior. It fits the joyful, illustrated winter mood of that year's seasonal range. The wraparound scarf that trails around the body is a charming design conceit, the kind of single-image storytelling Starbucks used to do well on its holiday ceramics.
2010 Hawaiian Flowers, Mug#455693 · The Long TailA breezy 2010 everyday mug, pale yellow inside with a band of tropical Hawaiian blooms set over a deep blue ground, the kind of warm-weather pattern Starbucks ran outside any named city series. The blue-and-flower combo reads like an island lei, an easy decorative piece that brightens a shelf. Not rare, but a cheerful island feel that makes it a nice low-key get.
2001 Sip a cup of Africa, 14oz, Mu#455697 · The Long TailA 2001, 14oz mug from the Sip a Cup of Africa safari run, white inside with giraffes and elephants beside two huts. This celebrates African coffee origins and the safari imagery of the continent, tying into Starbucks long love of Kenyan and Ethiopian beans with their bright, winey, citrus character. The storybook safari scene shows up regularly in collector listings, a warm and recognizable piece from the origin themed early 2000s.
2016, We Love Hong Kong, Mug#455698 · The Long TailA warm brown 12oz body covered in hand-drawn snapshots of Hong Kong, the trams, the harbor, the dense vertical city, released as an affectionate We Love HK piece. The all-over print sketch style is more intimate than a clean icon band, so it reads like a love letter rather than a postcard. These local Hong Kong mugs turn up regularly on eBay and Etsy and are a reliable favorite among Asia-market collectors.
Starbucks Mermaid in Black and Gol#455700 · The Long TailA striking art-forward mug pairing loose black pencil-sketch studies of the mermaid with applied gold-leaf accents, treating the siren as a fine-art subject rather than a logo. The hand-drawn sketch aesthetic shows her in stages, almost like an artist's working page. Gold-leaf detailing is unusual on Starbucks ceramics and gives this one a luxe, gallery feel that stands apart from the standard line.
Dragon, Chinese New Year, Red & Wh#455701 · Chinese New Year (Red & White)A Lunar New Year Dragon mug in the classic festive treatment, a dragon trimmed in golden leaf with black eyes over a vivid red body and white interior. The Dragon is the zodiac's lone mythical beast and its luckiest sign, so its mugs tend to be the most eye-catching of any year's release. The red-and-gold scheme is the textbook Chinese New Year color story, prosperity and celebration in ceramic form.
Starbucks Khao San, Mug#455702 · The Long TailA store-exclusive mug for the Khao San Road branch in Bangkok, the chaotic backpacker artery packed with hostels, street food and tuk-tuks. The exterior carries a soft light-green pencil rendering of the store itself, a local-flavor design you only got by visiting. These single-location mugs are genuinely rare, with the Khao San example trading around fifty to sixty dollars when one surfaces, and they predate the standardized city-series look.
Green Lines (2013), 12oz Low Mug#455704 · The Long TailThe all green sibling in the 2013 low mug line, white motifs running through green across a squat 12oz body. These pattern only cups were Starbucks leaning into pure graphic design for a season, and the green and white version is the cleaner, more restrained cousin of the green and yellow piece from the same release.
Red line on Bottom, Mug#455705 · The Long TailA minimalist piece, plain white with a single red line wrapping the base, the design ethos that defined a lot of Starbucks' clean studio ware. Stripped of any city or holiday hook, it lives or dies on proportion and that one bold stripe. I keep it as a palette cleanser in the collection, the cup that proves the brand could say almost nothing and still look deliberate.
Silver Bird Houses Over Snow, Mug#455706 · The Long TailThis is a winter holiday piece built around a folk image of silver birdhouses dotting a grey, snow dusted field, the kind of quiet seasonal design Starbucks rolled out for the cold months rather than a city souvenir. The metallic silver houses against the muted background give it a cozy, almost Scandinavian feel. Pieces like this live in the holiday corner of a collection, valued more for their seasonal charm than any landmark, and they tend to surface in late autumn resale listings.
Winking Mermaid, Mug#455707 · The Long TailA playful riff on the Siren herself, a light purple mermaid caught mid-wink against a matching purple interior. The twin-tailed mermaid has been the Starbucks logo since 1971, drawn from a 16th century Norse woodcut, so a cheeky winking version is the company having fun with its own icon. Logo-character mugs like this tend to be limited novelty runs rather than part of any city line.
Coffee Boat, Mug#455708 · The Long TailA mug carrying a stamped coffee-boat design on a white body, evoking the maritime journey that green coffee takes from origin ports to roasteries around the world. The boat motif is a nod to coffee as one of the most heavily traded commodities on earth, shipped by sea for centuries. It is a charming reminder that every cup began with a long ocean crossing.
Made in Ohio, Mug#455709 · The Long TailA regional-pride mug, creme inside with a simple "Made In Ohio" stamp, leaning on state identity rather than a single city skyline. These state-stamp pieces feel like a cousin to the old States of Bean idea, celebrating a place through typography alone. I read it as Starbucks tapping local loyalty, the sort of homegrown souvenir Ohioans actually buy for themselves.
Venti Une Tasse de Cafe Magnifique#455710 · The Long TailA 2002 mug carrying a faux-postage stamp of a Venti cup with the French line une tasse de cafe magnifique, a magnificent cup of coffee. Venti is Italian for twenty, the size named for its twenty fluid ounces. The bilingual wink mixing Italian sizing with French flourish is exactly the kind of detail that makes the stamp-era mugs fun.
Java Estate, Mug#455711 · The Long TailThis is pure Starbucks origin nostalgia, a white mug stamped with the colorful Java Estate coffee bag art. Starbucks began using these playful illustrated stamps on bean bags back in 1987, little visual shorthand for what was inside, before the 1995 redesign pushed them off the packaging over the following decade. Java refers to the Indonesian island, where Dutch colonial estates made the name a global synonym for coffee itself.
Espresso to Go, Mug#455712 · The Long TailA wink of a piece, a ceramic mug stamped with the Starbucks to go coffee mark, the visual language of the paper cup translated onto something you would never actually take to go. Starbucks loved this self-referential humor on its housewares, turning the disposable cup into a permanent keepsake. Vintage to go ceramics from the early 2000s tend to surface on Etsy and eBay, so they are findable but quietly charming.
C'mon Board We Serve Starbucks Cof#455714 · The Long TailThis is part of the Doonesbury at Starbucks run drawn from Garry Trudeau's long-running coffee gags, the same series as the Java Pump statue numbered 47 of 1500. The stamped propeller plane and the cheeky "C'mon Board, We Serve Starbucks Coffee" line play on the idea of coffee as the real reason to fly, a wink at airline culture. Collectors group these Trudeau pieces together, and the airplane motif makes this one of the more fun to hunt down.
Starbucks Coffee Train Car, Mug#455715 · The Long TailA white mug stamped with a train car graphic, part of Starbucks' recurring flirtation with railroad and express-delivery imagery. The train motif plays on the romance of coffee shipped across continents and the brand's own logistics, and it pairs naturally with the Starbucks Express pieces. A graphic novelty rather than a regional mug, but the rolling-stock theme gives it more character than a plain logo cup.
French Roast, Mug#455716 · The Long TailFrench Roast has anchored the Starbucks lineup since 1971 and remains the company's darkest, smokiest coffee, the one the roasters joke pushes the beans to the very edge before they would burst into flames. I love that this mug wears the bean motif and the roast stamp like a badge, a plain white cup that quietly declares loyalty to the deepest, most uncompromising cup on the menu.
Verona, Mug#455717 · The Long TailA clean white mug bearing a single Verona stamp, with a sprig of leaf growing on the inside graphic, dedicated to Starbucks' signature blend. Verona, the bold roasty-sweet recipe born as Jake's Blend in 1975, is the brand's enduring Valentine's coffee for its affinity with chocolate. A simple, blend-honoring piece rather than a city mug.
Sumatra, Mug#455718 · The Long TailThe classic Sumatra origin mug, styled with a postage stamp on the outside and the lion or tiger figure inside, celebrating one of Starbucks' most famous single origins. Sumatran coffee, wet-hulled and full-bodied with that herbal, earthy heaviness, has anchored Starbucks blends for decades, so the Sumatra mugs are among the most-loved of the coffee-country pieces.
Sulawesi, Mug#455719 · The Long TailA clean coffee-origin mug celebrating Sulawesi, the Indonesian island formerly called Celebes whose highland Toraja and Kalossi beans are a Starbucks classic. The wet-hulled Sumatra-style processing common to the region produces the deep, syrupy, low-acid cup that defined Starbucks' early dark-roast reputation, which is why these single-origin Indonesian mugs feel central to the brand's coffee story.
Finance Forum (2000), Mug#455720 · The Long TailA genuine corporate-event piece, made for Starbucks' Finance Forum in 2000 and wrapped in orange and blue stripes, the kind of internal gathering mug that never touched a retail shelf. Event and conference mugs like this are some of the hardest to track because they were produced in tiny runs for attendees only. I prize these precisely because no catalog lists them, you just have to stumble onto the right one.
Italian Roast, Mug#455721 · The Long TailA standalone tribute to Italian Roast, the deep, dark, almost smoky roast Starbucks built to echo Italian espresso bars, marked here with a harp icon inside and a postage-stamp graphic outside. The harp is a nod to Italy's musical and cultural heritage. Italian Roast is the roast that pushed Starbucks past American norms toward the heavier European profile that became its signature.
Kenya Roast, Mug#455722 · The Long TailThe Kenya Roast mug carries a drummer on the inside and the roast stamp outside, a lively detail you only discover when the cup is empty. Drumming sits at the heart of Kenyan ceremony and celebration, which makes it a fitting hidden image. Kenya's coffee is grown by smallholder cooperatives and graded through a rigorous auction system, the reason its AA beans command premium prices worldwide.
Golden Old Logo, Mug#455724 · The Long TailA white mug carrying the older Starbucks wordmark logo rendered in gold, a nod to the brand's earlier identity before the siren stood alone without text. Logo focused pieces like this are quietly collectible precisely because they freeze a specific era of the mark, and the gold treatment gives the heritage logo a dressed up, commemorative shine.
13th Asian Games (1998), Mug#455726 · The Long TailThis mug commemorates the 13th Asian Games, held in Bangkok from December 6 to 20, 1998, with the mascot an elephant named Chai-Yo. Event-tie mugs are a fun corner of the collection because they pin a piece to an exact two-week window in history, and a Starbucks Thailand commemorative for a regional sporting event is far less common than a standard city mug. The Bangkok scene makes it double as a city souvenir.
Samba! Samba!, Mug#455727 · The Long TailA lively mug carrying a Samba! Samba! painting of a dancer across white, tied to Brazil and the Carnival samba tradition. This sits in the miscellaneous corner of the collection, a themed one-off rather than a city series piece, and the exuberant illustrated figure is the whole draw. I keep oddballs like this because they break up the orderly city rows with pure movement and color.
Kona Roast, Mug#455728 · The Long TailThis one celebrates Kona, the only American-grown coffee Starbucks sells, hand-picked off the steep volcanic slopes of Hawaii's Big Island because the rocky terrain makes machine harvesting impossible. The plain white body with just the Kona stamp on the outside is a quiet, roast-focused piece rather than a tourist mug, the kind of utilitarian object that ties the cup back to the bean. I like that it points at origin instead of a skyline.
Chanel NewsAsia, Mug#455730 · The Long TailThis is a promotional mug for Channel NewsAsia, the Singapore-based regional news network, not a city or blend piece, which makes it a genuine oddity in any Starbucks collection. Corporate co-brand mugs like this were typically made in small runs for staff, events, or partner giveaways, so they rarely surface and have little to do with the retail lineup. I keep it precisely because it is off-catalog, the kind of one-off that tells a story about Starbucks' reach in the Asian market.
We Proudly Brew Starbuck Coffee, M#455731 · The Long TailThis is a foodservice piece, not a retail city mug, carrying the licensed "We Proudly Brew Starbucks Coffee" identity used by hotels, hospitals and campuses that serve the beans without being company stores. That whole licensed program is what later became the Nestle-run We Proudly Serve network. I keep it because trade and signage mugs like this rarely survive, they were meant for back rooms, not collectors' shelves.
Starbucks in Red, Mug#455732 · The Long TailA bold reversal of the usual palette, this one runs red inside and a glossy red exterior carrying the gold version of the old circular logo rather than the familiar green. The gold-on-red treatment reads almost holiday or lunar-new-year, and it makes the older logo feel ceremonial. I like it precisely because it breaks the green monotony that fills most of a Starbucks shelf.
VTV Vancouver Breakfast, Mug#455735 · The Long TailA promotional tie-in mug for VTV Vancouver Breakfast, a Canadian morning television show, carrying the program's logo on white. Broadcast co-branded mugs like this were made in small runs for staff and giveaways, which is why they rarely surface outside their home market. A genuinely off-catalog curio that lands squarely in the long-tail.
Pattaya, Mug#455736 · The Long TailPattaya sits on the Gulf of Thailand and made its name as a beach resort city famous for its waterfront, sailing, and nightlife, so the red sails over red on this mug nod straight to the bay full of catamarans and parasails. White inside with that bold sail motif outside, it belongs to the Thailand run that Starbucks issued across resort cities. Pattaya started as a quiet fishing village before American GIs on R and R during the Vietnam War turned it into a boomtown.
Chang, Mug#455737 · The Long TailThe three yellow elephants on this mug point to Chang, the Thai word for elephant and the name of Thailand's best-known beer, where twin elephants are the logo. Whether tied to that brand or simply to Thailand's revered elephant symbolism, the motif is unmistakably Thai, the elephant being a national emblem and a fixture of royal and Buddhist iconography. It is a cheerful, regionally flavored piece that rewards anyone who knows what "Chang" means.
Samui, Mug#455738 · The Long TailA mug for Koh Samui, Thailand's second-largest island, with purple monkeys painted across the white outside. The monkey motif is no accident, Samui is genuinely famous for its coconut-picking macaques and the old monkey shows that became a tourist fixture, so the design nods to something locally real rather than generic. Thai resort mugs like this circulate mostly within Asia, which makes a Samui example a pleasant find outside the region.
Starbucks One Team, Mug#455739 · The Long TailA white mug carrying a triangle in red, yellow and blue, internal partner or employee merchandise tied to a One Team rallying theme rather than retail stock. Internal-only pieces like this never hit store shelves, so they slip out of stores and into collections through partners. The bright primary-color geometry is a real departure from the usual green-and-white house style.
Hua Hin, Mug#455741 · The Long TailHua Hin is Thailand's original beach resort, the seaside town the royal family made fashionable in the 1920s when King Rama VII built the Klai Kangwon summer palace there. This mug runs the Hua Hin name over warm orange and brown, evoking the sand and the famous old teak railway station, one of the prettiest in Thailand. The town's central clock tower is the local landmark the Starbucks there sits beside.
100% Pure Kona, Mug#455742 · The Long TailThis mug celebrates 100% Pure Kona, the prized Hawaiian coffee grown on the volcanic slopes of the Big Island's Kona district, one of the few true coffee-growing regions in the United States. Genuine Kona is famously scarce and expensive, hence the emphatic "100% Pure" stamp, since the market is rife with diluted Kona blends. A mug devoted to a single-origin coffee rather than a city is a nice nod to the bean itself.
2012 Double Sided Clear Mug#455743 · The Long TailA 2012 mug in transparent plastic with the Siren herself depicted on the outside holding a cup, a playful bit of self-reference. The clear body is the standout, letting the printed mermaid art read against whatever is poured inside. It is an unusual material choice in a collection dominated by ceramic, and that novelty is exactly why I keep it.
2013 Double Sided Clear Mug#455744 · The Long TailAn unusual 2013 transparent plastic mug dated on the body, with the Siren herself shown holding a cup, art printed so it reads from both sides. The double-sided clear treatment is a fun departure from ceramic, letting the mermaid float in the see-through wall. A playful, lighter novelty that shows Starbucks experimenting with material and self-referential branding.
2004 Black Lid, White Heart, 12 oz#455745 · The Long TailA 2004 black-lid traveler in pink monochrome carrying a white heart, the sweetheart of the little travel group. The heart motif points it squarely at the Valentine's window, a seasonal traveler rather than a year-round one. Aluminum lined with the black handle and lid, the pink-and-heart combo makes it the most clearly gift-aimed piece of the black-lid family.
2004 Black Lid, 12 oz, Mug#455746 · The Long TailA 2004 travel mug, not a ceramic, aluminum-lined inside with a blue monochrome body, a black plastic handle, and a snap-on black lid. This is the commuter end of the Starbucks line, built for the car cup holder rather than the shelf. The metal interior and matched black hardware make it a different animal from the ceramic Abbeys, a small slice of the brand's early travel-mug experiments.
Tuk Tuk, Mug#455748 · The Long TailA mug featuring a bright yellow tuk tuk, the three wheeled auto rickshaw that is an everyday icon of Southeast Asian streets, especially Thailand. The tuk tuk gets its name from the sputtering sound of its small engine and is shorthand for the chaotic charm of cities like Bangkok. This is a culture and transport themed piece rather than a landmark mug, capturing a place through its most recognizable ride.
Starbucks Khao San (all in Thai),#455749 · The Long TailThe all-Thai-script variant of the Khao San store mug, named for Bangkok's legendary backpacker street, the launchpad immortalized in The Beach. The light-green pencil sketch of the actual branch is charmingly hand-drawn rather than corporate. Store-specific mugs like this from roughly 2001 are scarce, the English version has changed hands on eBay near sixty dollars, and the fully Thai lettering makes this the harder one to find.
Everything You Do Matters, Mug#455750 · The Long TailA partner-culture piece rather than a souvenir, this mug carries the Everything You Do Matters slogan inside a triangle with the logo, language Starbucks used internally to remind baristas their work counted. These motivational and recognition mugs were often given to staff rather than sold, which is what makes them quietly uncommon on the resale market. I like collecting the corporate voice of the company, not just its cities.
Yak-Wat-Jang, Mug#455751 · The Long TailA yellow rendering of Yak Wat Jang, the towering yaksha guardian giants that stand watch at Wat Arun, Bangkok's Temple of Dawn on the Chao Phraya River. In Thai folklore these fanged demon giants ward off evil spirits at temple gates, and Thai children grow up knowing them simply as yak. It is a wonderfully specific subject for a mug, a single mythic statue rather than a generic skyline.
The Starbucks Roast, Mug#455752 · The Long TailThe standard size companion to the 18oz Roast mug, same green logo on white and the same nod to the Starbucks roast spectrum that sorts every bean into Blonde, Medium, or Dark. Pieces built around the roast story are about the craft of coffee itself rather than a place or anniversary. Plain by design, it pairs naturally with its bigger sibling on a shelf.
Brown Mug, First Logo (2010), Mug#455753 · The Long TailDated 2010, this revives the original twin-tailed siren, the bare-chested Norse-woodcut mermaid Terry Heckler drew for the first 1971 logo, printed on brown to match her original color. Cream inside, brown outside, it is a deliberate throwback issued during a period when Starbucks leaned into its own mythology. Owning the dated 2010 version pins it to a specific heritage reissue rather than the undated runs.
Starbucks Mug, 18oz#455755 · The Long TailThe big everyday workhorse, a plain white 18oz mug with the green siren, the largest of the standard non-giant sizes and roughly a venti's worth of coffee. Nothing fancy, but the clean logo-only mugs are the baseline against which every city and series piece is measured. I keep the full size run so the collection shows the whole spectrum from 6oz up.
Starbucks Mug, 8oz#455756 · The Long TailThe classic 8oz white logo mug, the standard tall-drink size and the most-produced Starbucks ceramic ever made. Utterly ordinary, which is exactly why it matters as the control specimen of the collection. Logo-only mugs date themselves by which siren version they carry, so the plain ones quietly track the brand's evolving face.
2016 Starbucks Mug 71, 12oz#455757 · The Long TailA white 12oz mug carrying a green logo and the number 71, a store-anniversary or store-number piece rather than a city souvenir. These numeric mugs tend to be tied to a specific shop or milestone, which makes them cryptic to outsiders and catnip to collectors who love decoding what the figure actually marks. Mine sits in the fun-to-research pile.
1999, Starbucks Mug#455758 · The Long TailA clean 1999 mug with the green logo on white, a straightforward production piece from the year the modern siren branding was hitting full stride. It is the unfussy everyday end of the collection, but dated 90s logo mugs are quietly useful as references, since they document exactly how the wordmark and color sat on a standard cup before the 2011 logo redesign dropped the text.
Visitors Mug#455760 · The Long TailAn unusually spare piece, white inside and out, simply titled Visitors. The minimalism makes it the oddity of the drawer, a store or office mug meant for guests rather than a retail collectible. Sometimes the plainest object is the most intriguing precisely because it refuses to explain itself.
Horizon Air, Double Handles, Mug#455761 · The Long TailHorizon Air, the regional sister of Alaska Airlines, became the first airline in the world to serve Starbucks coffee onboard back on February 1, 1990, and this promo mug commemorates that little aviation milestone. It wears the original brown twin-tailed siren logo flanked by wings, and the unusual double-handle build makes it a genuine oddity. Collectors prize these early co-branded pieces, and they surface only rarely on eBay with the "first airline" lore attached.
Horizon Air, Mug#455762 · The Long TailThe single-handle cousin of my Horizon Air piece, again marking the carrier that in 1990 became the first airline anywhere to pour Starbucks at altitude. The old first-logo siren with outstretched wings outside reads almost like an airline badge itself, a nod to coffee taking flight. These promotional mugs predate the green logo era and turn up tagged "Wake Up and Smell the Coffee," which was the campaign line.
Pattaya, Neon Sign, Mug#455763 · The Long TailA second Pattaya design, this one built around a Pattaya neon sign rendered outside with white inside, leaning into the city's electric after dark identity along Walking Street. The neon sign treatment is a recurring Starbucks city motif meant to evoke the glow of a nightlife district, and Pattaya is one of the few places where that imagery genuinely fits the town's reputation. Owning both the red sails and the neon versions gives you the daylight and nighttime faces of the same city.
The Starbucks Roast, 18oz, Mug#455765 · The Long TailAn 18oz mug built around the Starbucks Roast theme, green logo on white, referencing the company's roast spectrum of Blonde, Medium, and Dark that Starbucks formalized to teach customers how it classifies its beans. The larger 18oz format makes it an everyday workhorse rather than a display piece. This is coffee education turned into merchandise, straightforward but on brand to the core.
Starbucks in Orange, Mug#455766 · The Long TailAn orange-lined mug with the gold old-logo siren set on a red field, a striking warm-toned departure from the standard green palette. That gold-on-red logo nods to vintage Starbucks branding, the earlier siren before the green-only modern crop, which makes the color story the draw. Bold non-green colorways like this stand out in a collection precisely because they break the house rule.
Coffee Culture, Mug#455767 · The Long TailA mug bearing the 3 C's logo, a nod to coffee, culture, and community, the kind of internal brand shorthand Starbucks built its whole experience around. The piece celebrates the idea of the third place, the social space between home and work that Starbucks famously aimed to be. It is a conceptual collectible rather than a souvenir, and those tend to fly under most collectors' radar.
1999 Mi Amor, Mug#455768 · The Long TailA 1999 "Mi Amor" mug featuring a woman singing into a microphone, with the Starbucks cup icon set against the white interior. It reads like a late-90s romance or music-themed novelty piece, part of the brand's habit that decade of issuing playful illustrated mugs well outside the city-series formula. The Latin-flavored "Mi Amor" title gives it a warmth the standard logo mugs never had.
Kauai Estate, Mug#455770 · The Long TailMy Kauai Estate mug, white with the Hawaiian island's stamp art, part of the 2001 Stamp Series. Kauai is the oldest and greenest of the main Hawaiian islands, the Garden Isle, with the soaked Na Pali cliffs and Waimea Canyon. Kona usually gets the coffee glory, but Kauai hosts one of the largest coffee estates in the United States, which is exactly the story this estate stamp is telling.
Chiang Mai, Mug#455771 · The Long TailChiang Mai is the cultural capital of northern Thailand, the old Lanna kingdom seat ringed with hundreds of temples and long associated with elephant sanctuaries in the surrounding hills. The single elephant over green here leans straight into that, the elephant being both a national symbol and a Chiang Mai tourism signature. It is a warm, regional Thai mug that pairs naturally with the Chang piece for an elephant-themed corner of the shelf.
Phuket, Mug#455772 · The Long TailPhuket is Thailand's largest island, the pearl of the Andaman, known for its beaches and the long tail boats that ferry tourists between islands, and this mug answers with two green palm trees over blue and white outside, white inside. The tropical palm and water motif is exactly the postcard image the resort trades on, from Patong Beach to Phang Nga Bay. The later Global Icon version of Phuket leaned purple with a long tail boat, so this palm tree design is the more straightforwardly beachy take.
Colombia, Mug#455773 · The Long TailA clean white mug carrying a single Colombia stamp graphic, a nod to one of the world's most storied coffee origins. Colombia's high-altitude Arabica from the Andes is so central to coffee's image that it earned its own protected designation, and Starbucks sourced from it for decades. This origin-stamp styling fits the airmail and passport theme the brand ran on its blend merchandise.
Ta-Lad Nam, Mug#455775 · The Long TailA yellow mug built around Ta-Lad Nam, the floating markets of Thailand where vendors sell from sampans along the canals, a quintessential Thai scene Starbucks captured for its local market. These Thailand-specific cultural mugs reward travel-minded collectors because they celebrate a custom rather than a skyline, and regional Asian releases like this rarely circulate widely outside their home country.
Hawaii Stamp (14oz), Mug#455776 · The Long TailA 14oz mug built around a faux postage stamp graphic of Hawaii, white inside, the postmark conceit a recurring playful motif across the everyday line. The stamp design lets one little frame stand in for the whole islands, sun, surf and aloha in miniature. These stamp style pieces have a vintage travel poster charm that reads instantly, which is why they are easy to fall for.
World Renowned, Mug#455777 · The Long TailA logo and slogan mug rather than a place piece, carrying the "Starbucks Coffee World Renowned" mark across a white body. Branding mugs like this exist to celebrate the company itself, the kind of self-referential merchandise that fills out the long tail of the collection. I keep it for completeness, since the identity and slogan pieces tell the story of how Starbucks marketed its own coffee.
2003 Pumpkin Mug#455778 · The Long TailThe 2003 Pumpkin mug, a true Halloween showpiece, orange body with a yellow jack o lantern smile, a black rim tip, white interior and a handle molded as a pumpkin vine. Everything about it is sculpted toward the gourd, not just printed, which is why it reads as a full novelty piece rather than a decorated cylinder. Starbucks revisited pumpkin mugs in later years, so collectors are careful to pin down the early 2003 version specifically.
House Blend, Mug#455779 · The Long TailA tribute to House Blend, the medium-roast Latin American coffee that has been Starbucks' backbone since 1971, marked here with a sailing ship icon inside the rim and a postmark-style stamp and detail outside. The ship is a sly reminder that green coffee crossed the seas long before it hit your cup. House Blend was the roast that defined the original Pike Place shop's character.
2001 Chiang Mai, Mug#455781 · The Long TailA 2001 mug for Chiang Mai, the cultural capital of northern Thailand, with a grey pagoda rendered against a white body. Chiang Mai is the heart of the old Lanna kingdom and home to hundreds of temples, most famously the gilded mountaintop Wat Phra That Doi Suthep. This early Thailand piece predates the modern You Are Here and Icon Chiang Mai mugs, making it an older and quieter ancestor of the line.
Brown Ribbon, First Logo, Mug#455782 · The Long TailA variant where the original first logo rides inside a brown ribbon band across a white body, a different layout from the all-brown versions. The ribbon framing of the 1971 siren makes this an easy companion piece to set beside the solid-brown first-logo mugs for contrast. Same heritage hook, the uncovered Norse siren, presented in a cleaner two-tone format.
2001 Mexico (14oz), Mug#455783 · The Long TailA 2001, 14oz Mexico mug from the coffee origin line, white inside with flowers on a green field and a pigeon flying over circular motifs. Mexico is a major Starbucks sourcing origin, especially the high grown beans of Chiapas near the Guatemalan border, prized for their clean, soft, nutty character. The festive folk pattern ties the mug to Mexican craft tradition rather than to any single city skyline.
