2007 Pike Place Store, Mug#455784 · The Long TailThis honors the original Starbucks at 1912 Pike Place in Seattle, where the company relocated in 1976 from its 1971 birthplace nearby, the only store still allowed to sell the bare-tailed original siren. The 2007 design renders the storefront with leftover snow clinging to it, a quietly seasonal twist. Pike Place store-exclusive mugs are a genuine collector category since you historically had to stand in that shop to buy one.
2009 Wood Mug#455785 · The Long TailA 2009 novelty mug done entirely in dark brown to mimic timber, even pressing a condensed wood-chip texture into the base. It is an oddball materials experiment rather than a city or series piece, the kind of one-off that makes the everyday line interesting. The faux-wood bottom is the detail worth turning it over for, a quirky tactile flourish you rarely see on a standard ceramic mug.
2001 Indonesia (14oz), Mug#455786 · The Long TailA 2001, 14oz Indonesia mug from the coffee origin souvenir line, white inside with sketched Indonesian monkeys, umbrellas, and a sun. Unlike a city mug, this celebrates a growing region, Indonesia being one of Starbucks oldest sourcing origins, famed for the full bodied, earthy, herbal coffees of Sumatra and Sulawesi. The hand drawn sketch style sets the origin mugs apart from the photographic landmark series and gives them a folk art warmth.
Java, Mug#455787 · The Long TailA clean white mug carrying the painted Java coffee stamp, sibling to my Java Estate piece. Java, the Indonesian island that gave English its most enduring nickname for coffee, was the heart of Dutch East Indies plantation coffee from the 1700s, which is exactly why the word stuck. These origin stamp mugs are the most affordable corner of the collection but they carry the real story of where Starbucks sourced its early single origins.
Stop Here, Mug#455788 · The Long TailA playful piece built around a "Starbucks Coffee Stop Here" sign graphic rather than any city, the kind of pun-on-a-road-sign novelty mug that sits outside the named series. Its charm is the gag, treating the coffee run like a mandatory traffic stop, which makes it an easy, lighthearted addition to a long-tail shelf.
2014, Busan Mug#455789 · The Long TailBusan is Korea's second city and its great port, and the fireworks splashed across this dark blue body point straight at the Busan Fireworks Festival, the autumn show that lights up Gwangalli Beach and the Diamond Bridge for over a million spectators. The moody blue ground sells the night-sky drama better than a daytime cityscape ever could. A satisfyingly specific local piece rather than a generic skyline.
Ghost, Mug#455790 · The Long TailThis is one of those clever minimalist novelty mugs where the design only resolves when you turn it, three black dots and a black tip reading as a little ghost seen from the side. It is a playful Halloween adjacent piece, the sort of seasonal oddity that lives outside the named series and rewards anyone who likes a mug with a visual trick built in.
Starbucks Best Brew, Mug#455791 · The Long TailA white mug carrying a Starbucks Best Brew logo, a promotional or in-house branding piece rather than a city souvenir. Best Brew nods to the company's drip-coffee program and store-level brewing standards, the unglamorous engine behind the whole empire. Not a series mug and not widely chased, but a tidy little artifact of how Starbucks marketed the plain cup of coffee that started it all.
First Logo Ribbon diagonal, Mug#455792 · The Long TailA variant of the heritage first-logo run, this one sets the original twin-tailed siren as a diagonal ribbon wrapping the body rather than the horizontal band. Small layout differences like diagonal versus straight are exactly the kind of variant collectors chase, since they distinguish otherwise similar throwback pieces. The early 1971 logo, with its uncensored mermaid, makes any of these a conversation starter.
2011 Bird, Mug#455793 · The Long TailA 2011 everyday mug, white inside with a white bird set over a bold red ground, a high-contrast graphic look from Starbucks' decorative line that year. The single bird silhouette against red gives it an almost folk-art simplicity. No city or named series here, just a striking color block that stands out among the painted florals of the same run.
First Logo Ribbon Dark Brown, Mug#455794 · The Long TailThis wears the original 1971 Starbucks siren, the bare twin-tailed mermaid Terry Heckler adapted from a 15th-century Norse woodcut, here rendered as a dark brown ribbon running sideways around the mug. Brown was the company's earliest color before the famous green arrived, so this piece deliberately channels the Pike Place founding era. Heritage logo mugs like this are catnip for collectors who care about where the brand actually started.
Starbucks Logo over 6oz, Mug#455795 · The Long TailA tiny 6oz demitasse-scale cup in plain white with the green siren logo, sized for a single espresso shot or a short cortado rather than a full coffee. The little ones rarely survive in pairs because they get used hard and chipped. I keep this for the format alone, it shows how the same logo scales from giant to nearly espresso-cup small.
2013 GyeongJu Korea DriveThru#455797 · The Long TailA 16oz Gyeongju mug in purple, gold and pink florals, tied to a Korean Drive-Thru store. Gyeongju was the thousand-year capital of the Silla kingdom and is now a UNESCO-listed open-air museum, home to Bulguksa Temple and the ancient Cheomseongdae observatory, the oldest in East Asia. The floral palette nods to that royal heritage rather than any one monument.
2014 Jeju, Mug#455798 · The Long TailJeju, South Korea's volcanic island and honeymoon capital, and those three little figures in yellow and blue are dol hareubang, the basalt grandfather guardians carved from Halla lava that stand watch outside Jeju gates as symbols of protection and fertility. They have become the island's mascot, so a Starbucks mug without them would feel wrong. The yellow flower band reads to me as Jeju's famous spring canola fields.
Make it your drink, 8oz, Mug#455799 · The Long TailA small 8oz white cup carrying the cheeky line "Make it your drink" with a checkmark, this is a brand-voice piece rather than a place mug, nodding to the famously customizable Starbucks order. It is the kind of slogan object that slips outside any named series, which is exactly why it lands in my long-tail shelf. Pieces like this rarely command a premium, but they capture a specific era of Starbucks marketing language.
Starbucks 8oz, Mug#455800 · The Long TailA clean white 8oz with the green siren logo outside, the kind of unfussy everyday cup that quietly anchors a collection. The 8oz format is smaller than the ubiquitous 16oz and 20oz City Mugs, closer to a true coffee-cup pour than a latte bucket. Plain logo mugs like this rarely fetch much alone, but they are the connective tissue that shows how the brand styled its house basics across eras.
2002, Old Logo in Black, 16oz, Mug#455801 · The Long TailA 2002 logo-history piece, 16oz, white inside with the black original 1971 Starbucks wordmark beside the modern green Siren, deliberately showing the brand's own evolution. The first logo wore brown and bared the twin-tailed Siren fully before 1987 traded brown for green and 1992 tightened the crop to her face, so this mug is essentially a timeline you can drink from. Logo-evolution mugs are a fun niche, and one cleanly displaying both marks side by side is a smart conversation piece.
2012 Bird Tall Mug#455802 · The Long TailA tall 2012 holiday mug, white inside, with a white bird set over red and a blue ornament on the outside. It comes from the same 2012 winter collection that gave us the fox-tail mugs, all leaning on woodland and folk-art imagery. The slim tall format is meant for a generous pour, and the bird-and-ornament motif fits squarely in that year's storybook holiday styling.
2014 Incheon Airport Mug#455804 · The Long TailA colorful painted mug for Incheon International Airport, one of the very few Starbucks mugs anywhere dedicated to an airport rather than a city. Incheon is consistently rated among the world's best airports and is the gateway to Seoul, so an airport-exclusive piece like this was a clever traveler's souvenir. That oddity is exactly its appeal, a mug you could only really grab while passing through Korea's main air hub.
2014 Seoul Mug#455805 · The Long TailMy Seoul piece wraps the city's two skylines, the curved tiled roofs of its old palaces topped by a dragon on the pagoda, and the needle of N Seoul Tower on Namsan that has crowned the city since 1969. Pairing a Joseon dragon with a modern broadcast tower is exactly the old-meets-new contrast Seoul sells itself on, and it makes this one of the more characterful Korean long-tail mugs.
2005, Joy, 12oz, Mug#455807 · 2005 Joy Wish Love SeriesPart of the 2005 holiday word set, this 12oz Joy mug is red inside with Joy in red over white outside and a little charm dangling from the handle. It pairs with the matching Love and Wish mugs, the charm gimmick being what makes the set memorable and what most often goes missing in resale. A complete trio with all three charms intact is the thing to chase, because a Joy mug missing its charm is just a holiday word in red.
2005, Wish, 12oz, Mug#455808 · 2005 Joy Wish Love SeriesWish completes the 2005 trio, glazed blue inside with Wish in blue over white outside and the matching handle charm. Blue is the odd one out against Joy's red and Love's green, which makes Wish the mug people most often lack when they try to assemble the full set. I keep the three together on purpose, because the joy of this little series is entirely in seeing all three words and their charms lined up at once.
2005, Love, 12oz, Mug#455809 · 2005 Joy Wish Love SeriesThe green sibling in the 2005 charm set, this 12oz mug runs green inside with Love in green over white outside and a charm on the handle. Joy, Love and Wish were sold as companion pieces that holiday season, color-coded so a row of them on a shelf reads like a little garland. The intact charm is everything here, since these dime-store charms snapped off and got lost, and a verified-original one quietly lifts the whole mug.
2005 Brown Colors, Mug#455810 · The Long TailA quiet study in shades of brown inside and out, this 2005 mug is part of Starbucks' tonal color series, the kind of piece that leans on warmth and simplicity rather than landmarks or dates. There is no city name or logo art to anchor it, just espresso-toned ceramic that practically advertises what goes inside. These monochrome color mugs were never headline collectibles, which is exactly why finding a clean one feels like a small score.
2005 Yellow Colors, Mug#455811 · The Long TailA 2005 solid-color mug glazed in shades of yellow inside and out, part of the everyday Colors line that let Starbucks sell a cheerful palette without a single landmark or logo getting in the way. These tonal mugs are the quiet workhorses of my long-tail shelf, the kind people grabbed for a kitchen and never thought of as collectible, which is exactly why a clean one in a sunny yellow is harder to find than you would guess.
2005 Green Colors, Mug#455812 · The Long TailThe green sibling to the brown color mug, this 2005 piece runs through shades of green inside and out, all tone and no text. It belongs to the simple monochrome series Starbucks made to read as pure color rather than place, an everyday mug with no city, date, or logo art to chase. Unflashy and easily overlooked, which is half the reason a crisp example is satisfying to track down.
2003 Orange Colors, Mug#455813 · 2003 Colors SeriesThe orange member of the 2003 Colors series, orange glazed inside with bands of orange shades on the outside. The concept was deliberately minimal, no logo art or city scene, just a confident dive into one color. I keep these as a trio because the appeal is the comparison, the way orange, green and purple were each treated to the same tonal shading exercise.
2003 Yellow Colors, Mug#455814 · 2003 Colors SeriesA 2003 tonal study mug, yellow inside and built from layered shades of yellow on the outside rather than any logo or scene. It belongs to Starbucks' early 2000s habit of selling pure color and texture as the whole design. These monochrome mood mugs are easy to overlook, but a clean gradient like this is genuinely pleasant in the hand and rounds out a color focused shelf nicely.
2003 Green Colors, Mug#455815 · 2003 Colors SeriesPart of the 2003 Colors set, this one is green inside with shades of green layered on the outside. The Colors mugs were a simple monochrome study, each piece committing fully to a single hue inside and out. They are most satisfying owned as a group, the green, orange and purple sitting together so the gradient idea reads across the whole set rather than one mug alone.
2003 Purple Colors, Mug#455816 · 2003 Colors SeriesThe purple entry in the 2003 Colors run, purple inside with shades of purple worked across the exterior. Purple is the least common of the three Colors hues to surface, which makes it the one that tends to complete the set last. It is a clean, design forward piece from a year when Starbucks was experimenting with pure color rather than place or season.
2002 Blue Colors, Mug#455817 · 2002 Colors SeriesA quiet 2002 design study, blue inside with shifting shades of blue washed across the outside, the kind of pure color piece Starbucks slipped out between its bigger named series. No landmark, no logo theater, just a graduated palette meant to read like a swatch card in ceramic. Pieces like this rarely make the collector price lists, which is exactly why a tidy one is a sleeper, an honest everyday mug from the early 2000s design language.
Red Lip Mosaic, Mug#455819 · Mosaic SeriesThis one wears a colorful mosaic exterior with a red rim, the tessellated tile look that nods to Byzantine and Mediterranean mosaic art where tiny colored pieces build a larger image. The fragmented surface catches light differently as you turn it, which is the whole point of mosaic. It is a design driven cup with no place name attached, so it sits in the long tail as a pure pattern study.
Bermuda Mosaic, Mug#455820 · Mosaic SeriesA 2002 mug finished to look like hand-laid mosaic tile in sea green, purple, and blue, an 18-ounce piece that trades a printed landmark for pure texture and color. The mosaic look is unusual for the line, leaning decorative rather than touristic. Tied to Bermuda, it evokes the island's turquoise water and pastel architecture without a single literal building, which is a refreshing change of pace.
2004 Meadow Green, 12oz, Mug#455821 · 2004 Meadow Mug SeriesA 2004 Meadow mug, 12oz, white inside with green grass climbing the outside, part of a four-color spring set that traded landmarks for simple botanical washes. The Meadow series leaned into seasonal pastel charm rather than any city or designer story, the kind of pretty everyday drinkware Starbucks released to brighten a shelf. Collecting it is really about assembling the full quartet of green, pink, purple and yellow.
2004 Meadow Yellow, 12oz, Mug#455822 · 2004 Meadow Mug SeriesThe yellow Meadow mug, the sunniest of the 2004 spring quartet, white inside with a bright yellow weed-and-flower design wrapping the body. It rounds out the green, pink and purple set, all 12oz and all built for pastel seasonal cheer rather than landmark prestige. The fun is in the full-set chase, with the four colors lined up reading like a little painted field.
2004 Meadow Purple, 12oz, Mug#455823 · 2004 Meadow Mug SeriesThe purple Meadow mug in the 2004 four-piece spring run, white inside with a purple wildflower-and-weed pattern across the outside. Like its siblings it is pure decorative seasonal drinkware, no city, no story, just a cheerful botanical wash. Collectors chase these less for individual rarity than for the satisfaction of lining up all four Meadow shades together.
2004 Meadow Pink, 12oz, Mug#455824 · 2004 Meadow Mug SeriesThe pink Meadow mug from the 2004 spring quartet, white inside with a soft pink weed-and-flower motif wrapping the outside. It is the gentlest of the four colorways, built for pastel seasonal appeal rather than collector intrigue, with no landmark or named designer behind it. Its value lies in being one corner of the complete green, pink, purple and yellow Meadow set.
2004 Confetti White, 16oz, Mug#455825 · 2004 Confetti SeriesThe all-white Confetti, white inside with the bubble pattern playing over a white body, 16oz, the most subtle member of the 2004 series. Tone-on-tone white makes the confetti almost a texture rather than a contrast, an understated take in a holiday line that usually shouts. It is the quiet collector pick of the four, and the hardest to keep looking clean.
2004 Confetti Pink, 16oz, Mug#455826 · 2004 Confetti SeriesThe pink Confetti for 2004, and worth a close look because the catalog notes metallic trees over pink rather than plain bubbles, a small pattern swap inside the same series. That makes it the festive holdout of the set, with little shimmering trees instead of dots. White inside, 16oz, it is the warmest and most overtly Christmas piece of the four Confetti colors.
2004 Confetti Blue, 16oz, Mug#455827 · 2004 Confetti SeriesThe 2004 Confetti mug in blue, white inside with a scatter of bubbles across the body, 16oz. The Confetti line was a 2004 holiday-season pattern run, the bubbles reading like champagne or falling snow depending on the color, and these turn up on the resale market tagged as Christmas pieces. Blue is the cooler, frostier read of the set, the winter-sky member of the confetti family.
2004 Confetti Red, 16oz, Mug#455828 · 2004 Confetti SeriesRed Confetti from the 2004 holiday run, white inside with bubbles drifting over a red ground, 16oz. Red is the signature Starbucks Christmas color, so this is the flagship shade of the Confetti series and the one most often photographed in holiday listings. The bubble pattern over red reads as celebration, the piece built to sit on the table the morning of the 25th.
2002, Dark Waves, 16oz, Mug#455829 · The Long TailThe 2002 Dark Waves at 16oz, the fuller-bodied version with the same turquoise interior and black lines rippling across a cream glaze. The larger canvas gives the wave pattern more room to breathe, which is why this size reads as the flagship of the pair. Part of Starbucks' quiet abstract phase of 2002, it stays inexpensive on the secondary market, the kind of clean modernist mug that looks far more deliberate than its price tag implies.
2002, Dark Waves, 12oz, Mug#455830 · The Long TailThe 2002 Dark Waves in the 12oz size, turquoise inside with a cream body crossed by flowing black lines. It is the smaller sibling of the 16oz Dark Waves, the two forming a size pair in Starbucks' early-2000s abstract-pattern run alongside the color and floral studies. A calm, graphic-design-led mug rather than a souvenir, it sits in affordable everyday vintage territory, and matching the 12 and 16 ounce versions is a satisfying little completist goal.
2010, Tribute Blend, Mug#455831 · The Long TailTied to Tribute Blend, the coffee Starbucks launched for its March 2011 40th anniversary, the first time its master blenders combined four coffees from all three growing regions, aged Sumatra, sun-dried Ethiopia, Papua New Guinea and Colombia. This is the black lidded mug with the aluminum-trimmed lid in that anniversary spirit. A piece that pairs nicely with the rebrand logo mugs from the same milestone.
2002, Eyes in the Dark, Mug#455833 · The Long TailThe 2002 Eyes in the Dark, a genuinely odd one, a pair of eyes over white on one side and the same eyes over black on the other, a playful peekaboo that flips with the light. It is among the most unusual graphics Starbucks tried in this experimental stretch, closer to a designer print than a coffee souvenir. Quirky one-off concept mugs like this are exactly what collectors love to surface, since their strangeness makes them memorable far beyond their modest going rate.
2002, Spiders, 18oz, Mug#455835 · 2002.0A genuinely theatrical 2002 Halloween piece, an 18oz mug with spiders crawling on silk thread printed inside over white, and bronze and silver spiders glinting on the black exterior, all on a square bottom. The metallic two tone bugs were meant to catch the light, a nice bit of seasonal craft beyond a flat print. Starbucks Halloween mugs from this early 2000s era have a steady following, and the heavier square base ones feel substantial in hand.
2004, Snowflakes, 12oz, Mug#455837 · 2004 HolidayLight blue inside and out with snowflakes scattered across the surface, this 12oz piece is pure 2004 winter mood. It rode in on the same season that gave us the debut Peppermint Mocha and Starbucks' first foray into delicate white holiday line art. The cooler blue tone sets it apart from the company's heavier red-and-gold December staples, and these unbranded pattern mugs tend to slip past collectors chasing dated city pieces.
2004, Peppermint, 14oz, Mug#455839 · The Long TailPink peppermint candies tumble over a pink exterior on this 14oz mug, and the timing is the real story. 2004 was the very year Starbucks launched its now-iconic Peppermint Mocha and the first season its holiday cups adopted that white line-art look, so this mug is a small artifact of a flavor that became a December institution. The full pink colorway makes it an oddity next to the usual red holiday palette.
2003, Snowman Blue, 15oz, Mug#455840 · The Long TailA genuinely fun 2003 oddity, white inside with a turquoise body and a handle sculpted as a snowman set at an angle. This is a figural holiday piece rather than a plain color mug, and figural handles are a small niche that collectors love because the snowman doubles as the grip. The off-kilter angle is intentional, a playful touch that makes it instantly recognizable on a shelf.
2003 Snowman White, 15oz, Mug#455841 · The Long TailA 2003 novelty piece where the whole mug becomes a snowman, an all white 15oz body with the handle modeled as the snowman's bent arm, sold with a matching lid. I love the sculptural conceit here, the cup is not decorated with a snowman so much as it is one. These winter figural mugs from the early 2000s tend to lose their lids over twenty years, so an intact lidded example like this is the version collectors actually want.
2003 Red Amore, 16oz, Mug#455842 · The Long TailThe red version of the 2003 Amore, 16oz, red inside and out with the same angled heart shaped handle. This is the bolder Valentine cousin to the white Amore, the deep red making the love theme unmistakable. Having both the red and the white lets me show the pair as Starbucks offered them, the same sculptural heart handle in two very different moods.
2004, Italian Valentine (Pink), 16#455843 · The Long TailA 2004 Italian Valentine mug, 16oz, pink outside with a red heart floating over white inside, part of Starbucks romance-themed run that drew on Italian coffee-culture styling. The red-heart-on-white interior is the signature touch, a small surprise revealed only as you drink. It pairs with the all-red version, and the two together make the complete Valentine duo for that year.
2003, Pink, Abbey, 18oz, Mug#455844 · 2003 Abbey MugThe larger 18oz pink Abbey from 2003, same pink glaze inside and out scaled up to the bigger barrel size. Having both the 16oz and 18oz pinks lets you show the Abbey shape stepping up through its sizes in a single color. The roomier format feels great to drink from, and a pristine 18oz pink, free of the wear these everyday mugs usually pick up, is the keeper of the pair.
2003, Black, Abbey, 18oz, Mug#455846 · 2003 Abbey MugThe larger 18oz sibling in the 2003 black Abbey line, same barrel silhouette and uniform black glaze inside and out, just scaled up for a bigger pour. Starbucks offered the Abbey shape across multiple sizes and colors, which makes size by color a satisfying grid to fill. The bigger formats feel substantial in the hand, and an unmarred 18oz in this glossy black is the standout of the set.
2003, Red, Abbey, 18oz, Mug#455847 · 2003 Abbey MugThe big brother of the red Abbey, the same 2003 solid red glaze stretched to an 18oz capacity. The Abbey shape was Starbucks' workhorse silhouette of the early 2000s, straight walls and a sturdy D-handle built to survive a busy cafe. Red in and out, this is the size people actually drank from, which is exactly why the larger ones turn up with more wear and the clean ones get hunted.
2003, Green, Abbey, 18oz, Mug#455848 · 2003 Abbey MugA straightforward 2003 18oz Abbey in solid green, glazed the same shade inside and out on the line's classic barrel shape. This is the plainer cousin to the showier Green Ibiza, a simple on brand green for everyday use. With no graphics to carry it, the whole interest is the evenness of the glaze and a clean rim, which is exactly what makes a pristine one worth setting aside.
2003, Pink, Abbey, 16oz, Mug#455849 · 2003 Abbey MugThe 2003 16oz pink Abbey, a cheerful pink glaze run evenly inside and out across the classic barrel form. Pink was a relatively bold choice for the line and gives the color grid a pop next to the blues and greens. Bright pastels like this are the ones people actually kept on a kitchen shelf, but as with any plain glaze cup the prize is one that escaped the rim chips and fading.
2003, Yellow, Abbey, 16oz, Mug#455850 · 2003 Abbey MugThe 2003 Abbey in cheerful solid yellow, glazed yellow inside and out, in the mid-size 16oz. Yellow is one of the harder solid Abbey colors to find since the bright pastel run was smaller than the red and white, and a uniform glaze with no logo print shows every flaw, so a clean one is a quiet little prize. A bright, simple piece that anchors the color-block era of the Abbey shape.
2003, Black, Abbey, 16oz, Mug#455851 · 2003 Abbey MugThe Abbey is one of Starbucks' classic rounded barrel mug shapes, and this is the 2003 all black 16oz version, glossy black inside and out with no graphics at all. The form is the same family that Starbucks also blew up into a famous gallon sized giant Abbey. A plain glaze cup lives or dies on condition, so the value here is a flawless deep black finish with no scratching or wear to the rim.
2003, Peach, Abbey, 16oz, Mug#455852 · 2003 Abbey MugA 2003 16oz Abbey in peach, this one glazed the same soft peach tone consistently inside and out, unlike the orange Abbey's two tone treatment. It is one of the gentler pastels in the season's barrel mug lineup. Pale glazes show every scuff and stain, so a peach example that has stayed soft and even is harder to find clean than the darker colors in the same family.
2003, Orange, Abbey, 16oz, Mug#455853 · 2003 Abbey MugThe orange entry in the 2003 Abbey family, with an orange glazed interior set against a softer peach toned exterior, a subtle two tone twist on the barrel shape. That inside out color contrast is what makes it more interesting than the single hue Abbeys. Warm tones like this were a smaller slice of the run, so the orange and peach pairing is one of the more distinctive cups to track down in the line.
2003, Blue Ibiza, Abbey, 16oz, Mug#455854 · 2003 Abbey MugA 2003 Abbey in Blue Ibiza, a saturated Mediterranean blue glaze carried evenly inside and out across the line's signature barrel shape. The Ibiza name signals Starbucks chasing a vivid resort palette that season. I find the colored glaze Abbeys more collectible than the plain black, since hues like this jewel toned blue read as a deliberate decorator choice rather than a default catalog cup.
2003, Green Ibiza, Abbey, 16oz, Mu#455855 · 2003 Abbey MugThe green counterpart to the Blue Ibiza, a 2003 16oz Abbey finished in a bright Green Ibiza glaze inside and out. It carries the same resort inspired naming that ran through that season's color story. Green sits closest to Starbucks' house identity, which is why the Ibiza greens turn up a touch more often, making the bolder blues and pinks of the same line the harder gets.
2011, Collector Series, Dark Brown#455856 · Collector SeriesA 2011 Collector Series 16oz mug with a lid, white inside and a dark brown Indonesian pattern wrapping the outside. Starbucks Indonesia ran a regional Collector Series drawing on batik and traditional textile motifs from across the archipelago, with companion releases honoring cities like Makassar and Surabaya. The included lid is the practical extra that sets this apart from the standard line, and the rich batik-style brown is genuinely handsome.
2011, Collector Series, Light Brow#455857 · Collector SeriesThe lighter-toned partner to the dark brown piece, a 2011 Indonesian Collector Series mug with a light brown traditional pattern outside. Together the two shades read like a deliberate light-and-dark pairing within the same Indonesian textile theme. These regional Indonesian mugs rarely surface outside Southeast Asia, which makes a matched light and dark set a satisfying thing to hold complete.
2003, Red, Abbey, 12oz, Mug#455858 · 2003 Abbey MugThis is the 2003 Abbey in deep solid red, the smaller 12oz pour. The Abbey is one of Starbucks' core house shapes, a tall straight-sided barrel mug that ran for years under the Barista line alongside the ESTD 1971 lettered versions. Red inside and out makes it a holiday-season staple, and collectors prize the saturated red Abbeys because the glaze can vary batch to batch.
2000, Mocha, 14oz, Mug#455860 · The Long TailA 14oz house mug from 2000 in the beverage labeled core run, white interior with a dark green stripe and a matching dark green outside. Mocha, the chocolate and espresso pairing, takes its name from the Yemeni port of Al Mokha that shipped coffee for centuries. The dark green ties it straight to the classic Starbucks identity, and the larger 14oz size makes it the heftier sibling of the smaller core mugs.
2003, Oval Mug (Blue)#455861 · The Long TailA 2003 Oval Mug, named for its elongated cross section rather than a round one, white inside with a dark blue band and the simmering coffee icon on the outside. That little steaming cup motif is a recurring Starbucks graphic for fresh hot coffee. The oval profile is an unusual ergonomic experiment for the era, and the blue and green strip versions make a tidy matched pair on a shelf.
2003, Oval Mug (Light Green)#455862 · The Long TailThe light green sibling of the 2003 Oval Mug, white interior trimmed with a soft green strip and the same simmering coffee icon outside. I like that Starbucks broke from the round mug norm here with an oval body that genuinely changes how it sits in your grip. Quiet utility designs like this rarely got saved, so a clean pair of the blue and green ovals together is a small but satisfying find.
2003 Amore, 16oz, Mug#455863 · The Long TailThe 2003 Amore, a 16oz mug whose handle is shaped like a heart set at an angle, white inside and out. Amore is Italian for love, and this was the Valentine release for that year, sold in a white version like mine and a well known pink one. The angled heart handle is the whole point of the piece, a small sculptural flourish that makes it instantly recognizable on a Valentine's display.
2004, Italian Valentine (Red), 16o#455865 · The Long TailThe bolder red sibling in the 2004 Italian Valentine pair, 16oz, fully red outside with the same red heart over white inside. Starbucks Italian-styled Valentine pieces nodded to the country's espresso heritage with seasonal romance flair, and the hidden interior heart carries straight across from the pink version. Set-minded collectors want the pink and red mugs side by side to close out the year's Valentine release.
2006, Water Flower, 12oz, Mug#455866 · The Long TailA 2006 Water Flower 12oz mug, with a blue flower over white inside and full flower colors outside, an inside-and-out floral design that rewards looking down into the cup. The painted-flower-at-the-bottom trick was a favorite mid-2000s touch, giving the mug a small reveal as you finish your coffee. It is a gentle, unbranded decorative piece, the sort of long-tail mug that survives because someone simply liked the flower.
2000, Core Latte, 12oz, Mug#455867 · The Long TailA 12oz core line mug from 2000, white inside with a light grey exterior and a grey ribbon banding the body. The Core line was the in store standard service ware, latte being the milk forward espresso drink whose name simply means milk in Italian. Quiet, functional, and easy to overlook, which is precisely why a tidy original survivor earns its place on my shelf.
2004, Neck Ties, Mug#455868 · 2004 Daddy-O SeriesA bit of office-humor whimsy from the 2004 seasonal run, this regular mug wraps a parade of colorful neck ties over white with a cheerful yellow interior. It belongs to the playful pattern-mug family Starbucks rolled out alongside its gifting season, the kind of lighthearted design meant to land under a tree or on a coworker's desk. These pattern pieces never carried a city name, so they fly under most collectors' radar, which is exactly why I like hunting them.
2014, Times Square NYC#455871 · The Long TailTimes Square in black and white with a black lid and aluminum trim, a travel-style mug for the Crossroads of the World, the neon canyon that draws roughly fifty million visitors a year and hosts the famous New Year's ball drop. Kenya Oz, 10oz, Mug#455872 · The Long TailA smaller 10oz Kenya, yellow inside with elephants marching across a map of the country. Kenya is elephant country, home to Amboseli's herds beneath Kilimanjaro and the vast Tsavo parks, so the imagery doubles as a nod to safari and to the famous Kenyan coffee belt around Mount Kenya. The compact 10oz size makes this one a slightly less common format in the origin lineup.
2004, Urban Desk Mug (White), 14oz#455873 · The Long TailThe clean all-white version of the 2004 Urban Desk, 14oz of ceramic seated on a brushed steel base with that non-scratch rubber footing made for office life. This minimalist colorway is the one collectors and resellers chase most because the discontinued steel-bottom build is tough to find new, and the plain white reads as the purest expression of the design.
2004, Urban Desk Mug (Green & Blue#455874 · The Long TailThe Urban Desk is a clever hybrid, a 14oz ceramic body with a brushed stainless steel bottom and a non-scratch base built to sit on an office desk all day. This green-and-blue ribbon variant came with a press-on travel lid and rubber seal. Collectors note the line is genuinely hard to find in clean condition now, since these were workhorse daily mugs rather than display pieces, and the steel-bottom design was quietly discontinued.
2004, Urban Desk Mug (Green & Red)#455875 · The Long TailSame smart 2004 Urban Desk engineering, ceramic over a stainless steel base with a rubber-sealed press-on lid, here in the green-and-red ribbon scheme. The steel bottom doubled as a stable, scratch-proof footing for a desktop, a small design idea Starbucks did not keep around long. Because people actually used these to drink from, surviving examples with the lid intact and the steel unscuffed are the ones worth grabbing.
Creme Mug, First Logo, Mug#455877 · The Long TailA creme-on-creme mug carrying the original 1971 Starbucks logo, the brown twin-tailed siren designed by Terry Heckler from an old Norse woodcut, complete with her full figure encircled by Coffee Tea and Spices. That first siren was later cropped and tamed for modesty, so any merchandise wearing the original is a deliberate heritage nod. The tonal creme palette makes the vintage mark the whole point.
Starbucks One, Coffee Mug & Filter#455879 · The Long TailA pour-over set, a mug with a filter cone that sits on top and a black lid, letting you brew single-cup coffee directly into the mug. This is gear from Starbucks' manual-brew push, when pour-over and the Clover machine were marketed as craft coffee at home. Complete sets with the original filter and lid intact are uncommon, since the loose parts are the first things to vanish.
Magic Kingdom at 45, Mug#455880 · The Long TailThis 2016 mug marks the 45th anniversary of Walt Disney World's Magic Kingdom, which opened October 1971, with Cinderella Castle on one side and the Starbucks Siren on the other. It is a park-exclusive collaboration sold inside Disney, which is why it carries that double-logo collector appeal and still trades briskly on the resale market. A dated anniversary piece tied to a specific park is exactly the kind of crossover I love pinning down.
2012, Candy Cane, Mug#455881 · The Long TailA proper holiday novelty from 2012, red inside, white outside, with a handle sculpted into a real candy cane stripe. That twisted peppermint handle is the whole joke and the whole charm, the kind of seasonal whimsy Starbucks loves to mold into ceramic. These shaped-handle holiday mugs get pulled out every December and have a loyal following among collectors who chase the full Christmas run.
2009, Heart Shaped String, Mug#455882 · The Long TailA 2009 Valentine mug, red inside and white outside, decorated with a trailing red string of linked hearts. It sits in the same February love family as the 2007 petals and balloon mugs, showing how Starbucks reworked the same romantic brief every year with a new visual gimmick. The garland-of-hearts conceit gives it a hand-strung, almost crafty charm.
Starbucks Celebration Mug#455884 · The Long TailA celebration mug with a creme interior and a brown band wrapping the outside, restrained and warm rather than flashy. The toned-down palette and earthy stripe suggest a heritage or anniversary tie rather than a city souvenir, the kind of piece Starbucks issued to mark a milestone. The understated brown-on-creme look is exactly the muted, coffee-toned styling the brand reaches for when it wants a mug to feel grown-up.
2010, Bronze Flower Motives, Mug#455886 · The Long TailA 2010 white mug with bronze floral motifs and a bronze-tipped rim, sharing the narrower-top, rectangle-handle silhouette Starbucks used across that year's decorative line. The metallic bronze detailing is the draw, a dressier look than the usual painted ceramic. An elegant everyday piece that reads almost like home decor rather than a coffee-shop mug.
2010, Blue Safari Animals, Mug#455887 · The Long TailA 2010 everyday mug with blue safari animals marching around white, built on the narrower-top, rectangle-handle body Starbucks used on several pieces that year. The monochrome-blue animal silhouettes give it a storybook, nursery feel. Not a city or named series, just a charming decorative shape that pairs with the other rectangle-handle mugs from the same run.
2009, Brown Beans Galore, Mug#455888 · The Long TailA 2009 mug with a green interior and a brown exterior scattered with coffee beans, two of which are rendered in green as a hidden wink. White-and-brown bean motifs were a recurring Starbucks everyday theme, but the two green beans are the small Easter egg that makes this one fun to look closely at. A pleasant, coffee-forward piece from the unbranded long-tail line.
2011, Candy Cane Mug#455889 · The Long TailA 2011 holiday mug, red inside and white outside with the Starbucks logo, sold during the candy cane and red-cup season. It sits in the long tradition of Starbucks leaning hard into red and white for Christmas, the same palette as their famous holiday cups. A simple festive piece, but a nice anchor for the 2011 holiday year alongside the dated city and ornament releases.
2015, Red Strips (12oz), Mug#455890 · The Long TailA bold 12oz piece, red inside and out with the black Siren logo riding the red ground, part of Starbucks' recurring red-cup energy that the brand leans into every holiday season. 2012, Engraved Starbucks (14oz), M#455891 · The Long TailA 14oz mug in deep blue with the Starbucks name engraved rather than printed, white wordmark cut into the glaze against the color. White interior, blue body, a simple confident piece that lets the material do the talking.
2007 I Love You (12oz), Mug#455893 · The Long TailA 12oz Valentine piece from 2007, white inside with the outside built from heart-shaped flower petals and finished with a squared-off rectangular base. Starbucks leaned hard into February love themes every year, and the petals-as-hearts conceit is a nice bit of design wit. The rectangular bottom is the detail to flip it over for, since most regular mugs are plainly round-footed.
2010 Suade Handle (14oz), Mug#455894 · The Long TailA 2010 oddity, a 14oz white mug wrapped with a brown suede-look handle, an unusual tactile material choice for Starbucks. These texture experiments sit firmly in the everyday line rather than any city series, made to feel cozy in the hand. The faux-suede grip is the whole hook, a quirky piece that stands out on a shelf of plain ceramic.
2006, Urban Desk Mug (Purple & Bro#455895 · The Long TailThe Purple and Brown ribbon version of the 2006 Urban Desk 14oz, white with a purple ribbon and a brown ribbon banding the outside over that signature stainless steel base. The striped colorways are what make the Urban Desk line a small collecting target, since assembling every ribbon variation is the whole game. I like this one as proof that even Starbucks' most utilitarian office mug got a designer's eye for color blocking.
2006, Urban Desk Mug (Coffee in Gr#455896 · The Long TailA 2006 Urban Desk 14oz mug, white outside with the word Coffee in green and a stainless steel base with a slip-resistant bottom, built for the office rather than the home. The Urban Desk line was Starbucks' minimalist take on a serious workspace mug, the metal foot being its signature detail. These desk mugs came in several colorways, so collectors treat them as a small set and hunt the variants that complete it.
2008 Islam Motives (12oz), Mug#455898 · The Long TailA 12oz 2008 mug built for Gulf and Middle Eastern markets, brown and orange with a mosque and crescent moon alongside the Starbucks logo. Region-specific Islamic-themed designs like this were not sold in Western stores, which gives them real travel-collector cachet. The crescent and mosque imagery marks it as a Ramadan or regional release, a category that rewards collectors who chase pieces tied to a specific part of the world.
2006, Urban Desk Mug (EST. 1971),#455899 · The Long TailThe EST. 1971 colorway of the 2006 Urban Desk 14oz, white outside with the founding-year mark and the same stainless steel base that defines the line. The 1971 reference nods to the original Pike Place store, turning a plain office mug into a quiet heritage statement. This variant is the one I find most appealing in the set, because the founding date does more work on a clean white mug than any graphic could.
2006, Peace, 14oz, Mug#455900 · The Long TailA 2006 holiday 14oz mug, white inside with Peace lettered in gold over a red field outside, the simplest and most elegant of the season's word mugs. Gold-on-red is the dressiest combination Starbucks used in that era, leaning toward an almost greeting-card formality. Peace reads as the grown-up counterpart to the playful Joy and Wish charm mugs of the year before, and that restraint is exactly why I find it the more handsome piece.
2009, Seeds of Hearts, Mug#455902 · The Long TailA 2009 brown mug with white seed-of-love motifs scattered across it, another entry in the brand's annual Valentine rotation but with an earthier brown base instead of the usual red. Thin 10oz Mug#455903 · The Long TailA slim 10oz mug banded in red, grey, green, blue, and light blue stripes against a white interior, a purely graphic, colorblock design with no city or logo lore attached. Its charm is simple geometry and color, the kind of unfussy mug that anchors a row of louder ones.
2004 Snowflake (16oz) Red Mug#455904 · The Long TailThe red counterpart to the green Snowflake, a 2004 holiday mug in the same striking rectangular 16oz form, red inside and out with a crisp white snowflake. Intact, it is the cleaner half of the red-and-green Snowflake pair.
2004 Snowflake (16oz) Green Mug (C#455905 · The Long TailA 2004 holiday Snowflake mug, an unusual rectangular 16oz shape in green inside and out with a single white snowflake, our example carrying an honest chip. The angular squared-off form is the real curiosity here, a departure from Starbucks usual round profile, and it came as a red-and-green winter pair. The chip drops its display grade but keeps it as the green half of a seasonal set most collectors want complete.
Starbucks Via (8oz), Mug#455907 · The Long TailNot a city mug at all but merchandise tied to VIA Ready Brew, the microground instant coffee Starbucks launched in 2009 to chase the at-home market. 2000, Starbucks Dark Green, Mug#455908 · The Long TailA 2000 house mug in full Starbucks livery, white cream interior, dark green exterior, and a green ribbon over the rim. This is the brand color made literal, the same deep green of the original logo and the cafe awnings. 2006 Starbucks New England Blend,#455909 · The Long TailA 2006 mug carrying the Starbucks New England Blend logo, tied to one of the regional coffee identities Starbucks marketed in the mid-2000s before it standardized roasts across stores. Coffee-blend branded mugs are a niche within the long-tail, valued more by people who chase the blend lore than by city-mug collectors. I like the historical thread here, a mug that quietly documents a regional blend most drinkers today have never heard of.
2001 Starbucks Plastic White (Stai#455910 · The Long TailA 2001 plastic mug, white with a stained or distressed white finish and a black plastic exterior. This is a travel or commuter style piece rather than ceramic, from the period when Starbucks was expanding its to go drinkware. Plastic pieces rarely survive in collectible shape because they scratch, stain, and warp, so keeping one as a record of the era's everyday gear is more about documentation than beauty.
2011 Starbucks Green (8oz), Mug#455912 · The Long TailThe green sibling in the 2011 star set, 8oz, with silver stars over white inside and silver stars over Starbucks green outside. Green was the natural anchor color of the run since it ties straight back to the corporate identity. Collecting the blue, green, and red together gives you the full trio, and the matched silver and gold star treatments are the detail that makes a complete set feel intentional rather than random.
2011 Starbucks Red (8oz), Mug#455913 · The Long TailThe red entry in the 2011 star set, 8oz, gold stars over white inside and red stars over red outside. Red carries an obvious holiday warmth, which is why this color got the gold interior stars to match the festive feel. Lined up next to the blue and green it completes the patriotic looking trio, and I treat the three as a single collectible unit since they were clearly designed as a family.
2011 Starbucks Blue (8oz), Mug#455914 · The Long TailA small 8oz mug from 2011, white inside with gold stars, and a field of blue stars over blue on the outside. This belongs to a cheerful star pattern set Starbucks ran in the early 2010s, with the inside and outside stars deliberately mismatched in color. I love these as a quiet study in how Starbucks plays with the same motif across a coordinated color run rather than as standalone designs.
Starbucks in Black (14oz), Mug#455915 · The Long TailThe largest of the black trio at 14oz, coal black through and through. It is the most substantial pour of the three and the one with the most presence on a shelf, the full expression of the matte monochrome idea. Lined up beside its 10 and 12oz siblings, it completes a tidy little graduated set that trades the siren for pure dark form.
Starbucks in Black (12oz), Mug#455917 · The Long TailThe 12oz in Starbucks' all-black series, coal black inside and out with no logo to break the surface. This middle size is the everyday tall-coffee pour and the one to see daily use. The blacked-out trio is a study in restraint from a brand built on green, and owning all three sizes shows how Starbucks scaled a single stark idea across its mug lineup.
Starbucks in Black (10oz), Mug#455919 · The Long TailA coal-black 10oz mug, black glaze inside and out, part of Starbucks' all-black minimalist mug line. The monochrome look strips away the green siren entirely and lets form do the talking, a deliberate counterpoint to the busy City Mug aesthetic. As the smallest of the trio of black sizes, the 10oz reads like an espresso-leaning cup and is the daintiest of the set.
2002 Italian Primavera, Mug#455920 · The Long TailThe 2002 Italian Primavera, white inside with a single purple flower over white and a green-tipped rim, Primavera being simply Italian for spring. It is part of Starbucks' early-2000s European-flavored florals, leaning on Italian coffee romance as much as the bloom itself. A restrained, elegant design rather than a loud novelty, it trades as inexpensive vintage today and rewards anyone who likes the softer, more painterly end of the mug line.
2002 Daisy, Mug#455921 · The Long TailThe 2002 Daisy, a cheerful yellow daisy floating over a blue ground with a white interior, part of Starbucks' early-2000s run of bright seasonal florals. It belongs to the same family of mood-driven graphics that gave us the Primavera and the wave mugs, leaning into spring optimism rather than any city or anniversary hook. These florals trade as affordable everyday vintage today, the sort of casual find that fills out a collection without breaking it.
4th of July (Stars), 16oz Mug#455922 · Hartstone Hand-Painted in the USAThe stars companion piece, creme inside with red and blue stars drifting over a creme exterior and finished with that signature red tip line. It pairs directly with the flags mug, same palette and same rim stripe, clearly meant to be displayed two by two. Modest seasonal merchandise, but together the four make a complete and genuinely charming Americana grouping.
Dark Blue See Through, Mug#455923 · The Long TailA translucent dark blue mug with the current logo engraved rather than printed, so the mark catches light through the glass-like body. The see-through treatment is a departure from the usual opaque ceramic, made to show off the siren as etched relief. A subtle, design-forward piece that rewards being picked up and held to the light.
2011 White Wide Mug#455930 · The Long TailThe wide-body version of the 2011 white mug, again carrying the new siren-only logo introduced that year. The generous diameter makes it a latte-friendly format and shows how Starbucks rolled the redesigned mark across multiple shapes at launch. I pair it with the 14oz to document the same 40th-anniversary logo across two very different proportions from the same moment.
Square Mug, White#455931 · The Long TailThe clean white member of the square bottom family, simply the current siren logo on a crisp white body with that signature square base. It is the most pared back of the solid square mugs, the blank canvas of the set, and it pairs naturally with the dark blue and green versions for collectors assembling the full color spread. Modern, minimalist and form driven, this is housewares line styling rather than travel souvenir, prized for its shape rather than any place or year.
Kettle-like Mug#455932 · The Long TailThe base Kettle-like mug, white and irregular in form, stamped with that earliest Starbucks logo and its fully visible siren. The kettle shape is the charm here, a softer, rounder body than the standard cylinder. This trio of kettle mugs in my collection is really a tribute to the brand's origin story, when a Seattle shop selling beans and gear chose a medieval mermaid because, as Gordon Bowker put it, she captured coffee's seductive mystique.
2011 White (14oz) Mug#455933 · The Long TailA plain 14oz white mug from 2011 wearing what the catalog calls the last Starbucks logo. That phrasing matters because 2011 is exactly when Starbucks unveiled its current siren-only mark for the 40th anniversary, dropping the words Starbucks Coffee and the encircling ring. So this is a clean, undated record of the mark that has stayed in use ever since, the kind of quiet milestone piece I like to keep.
Hojito, Round Thermal Ceramic Mug#455934 · The Long TailA heritage minded oddity, a round thermal ceramic mug with a plastic outer, carrying the very first Starbucks logo, the bare breasted twin tailed siren from the original 1971 Pike Place store. No cluttered landmarks here, just that clean Pacific swell. Hawaii pieces draw extra interest because the state had a limited Starbucks merchandise footprint, so mainland collectors often have to hunt these down to round out a US run.
2013 Korea Gwangju#576042 · The Long TailA 16oz Gwangju mug mixing Korean folklore imagery with watermelon, a playful regional touch for the cultural hub of southwestern Korea. Gwangju is known as a city of art and democracy, central to modern Korean history and now home to a major contemporary art biennale. The folk-art-meets-fruit styling makes this one of the more whimsical and unexpected entries in the Korean city line.
Indivisible (with steel plaque) 14#576043 · The Long TailOne of my favorite oddities, an ivory 14oz mug from Starbucks' MADE IN AMERICA line carrying an actual heavy silver steel plaque riveted to the front reading INDIVISIBLE, a word lifted from the Pledge of Allegiance. These were genuinely made in East Liverpool, Ohio, part of a patriotic push to manufacture stateside. The metal plate gives it real heft and sets it apart from every printed ceramic in the case.
2014 Taiwan Coffee Journey 10oz#576047 · The Long TailA clean white 10oz body carrying only the green Siren logo, this Taiwan Coffee Journey mug is from a store loyalty and tasting program rather than a tourist line, so it skips the usual landmark band. Taiwan was an early and devoted Starbucks market in Asia, and these plain promotional pieces are the kind of thing only a completist chases. Quiet, but it tells a real story about how the brand built its coffee culture there.
Muan Jai, 15 Years Support Mug#576049 · The Long TailMuan Jai means wholehearted happiness in Northern Thai, and this mug marks fifteen years of Starbucks supporting Thailand's hill-tribe coffee farmers, a partnership running since the 2003 launch of the Muan Jai blend. The illustration of the growing region with coffee drawings tells that story directly. Five percent of Muan Jai sales fund schools, water projects, and a health clinic in Chiang Mai, which is why this one means more than a date stamp.
2013 Shanghai - Xintiandi, China C#576050 · The Long TailThe number 1 mug in my Shanghai trio, marked on the handle, with a red interior and dedicated to Xintiandi. That district preserved the old shikumen stone-gate lane houses and reinvented them as a chic dining and nightlife quarter, and it also holds the site of the First Congress of the Chinese Communist Party. A clever local-attractions series, and the handle numbers make completing all three genuinely satisfying.
2013 Shanghai - The Bund, China Ce#576051 · The Long TailA 16oz Shanghai mug devoted to The Bund, the riverfront promenade lined with grand colonial-era banking houses facing Pudong's towers. Mine is the light-blue-interior version with a small 2 marked on top of the handle, the numbering that lets you order this three-mug Shanghai set correctly. The Bund is the single most iconic view in the city, the place where old and new Shanghai stare each other down across the Huangpu.
2013 Shanghai - Yu Garden, China C#576052 · The Long TailThe number 3 piece of my Shanghai set, yellow interior, honoring Yu Garden, the exquisite Ming-dynasty classical garden in the old city. Laid out in the 1500s with rockeries, ponds and the famous Huxinting teahouse, it is one of the finest gardens in southern China. The handle mark keeps the trio in order, and a complete Bund, Xintiandi and Yu Garden set is far more desirable than any single mug.
Ruhrgebiet, Icon Collectible Mug,#576096 · Global Icon SeriesThis Icon Series 16oz celebrates the Ruhrgebiet, Germany's old coal and steel heartland, and the band shows Welterbe Zollverein, the Zollverein Coal Mine in Essen. That plant ran from 1851 to 1986 and its 1932 Shaft 12, built in stark New Objectivity lines, got nicknamed the most beautiful coal mine in the world before UNESCO listed it in 2001. I love a mug that honors industry over postcard scenery, and the red interior is the standard German Icon treatment, a fairly common piece but a genuinely meaningful one.
Mainz, Icon Collectible Mug, 16oz#576097 · Global Icon SeriesMy Mainz Icon mug runs red inside and out, with the baroque Old University building wrapping the front, a fitting choice since this Rhineland city is genuinely the home of Johannes Gutenberg and the movable-type printing press. The Global Icon line distills each city to one landmark band, and German Icon mugs like this one were produced in China and Taiwan, so they turn up often and stay affordable for collectors building out the German set.
Izmir, Icon Collectible Mug, 16oz#576100 · Global Icon SeriesIzmir is Turkey's third-largest city and great Aegean port, and this 16oz Icon mug centers on its beloved Saat Kulesi, the ornate 1901 Konak Clock Tower, framed by palms with a blue interior. The tower, a gift marking the 25th year of Sultan Abdulhamid II's reign, is the city's defining emblem and survives at the heart of Konak Square. Izmir, the ancient Smyrna, anchors the country's Aegean coast and its seagull-and-sea iconography.
Antwerp, Icon Collectible Mug, 16o#576101 · Global Icon SeriesMy 16oz Global Icon Antwerp, red inside, and the statue throwing water is the Brabofontein on the Grote Markt. The 1887 bronze by Jef Lambeaux shows Silvius Brabo hurling the severed hand of the giant Druon Antigoon into the Scheldt, the legend that gives Antwerp its name, hand-throwing or handwerpen. The back carries the Cathedral of Our Lady, so the city's myth and its tower both ride this cup.
Sofia, Icon Collectible Mug, 16oz#576103 · Global Icon SeriesSofia's red Icon mug puts the Ivan Vazov National Theatre front and center, Bulgaria's oldest and most authoritative theatre, a Neoclassical jewel finished in 1906 by the famed Viennese architects Fellner and Helmer who also designed opera houses across Central Europe. The reverse carries the Orlow, or Eagles', Bridge, another Sofia landmark. Collectors consider this a common and approachable Icon mug, which makes it a friendly, attainable way to add the Bulgarian capital to a European set.
Bodrum, Blue, City Architecture#576107 · The Long TailBodrum sits on Turkey's southwest Aegean coast, the ancient Halicarnassus, home to the Mausoleum of Mausolus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and the literal origin of the word mausoleum. This piece keeps a white interior and renders the city's squared hillside houses and Bodrum Castle in light blue line work outside. The clean monochrome architecture treatment is quieter than the bright multicolor You Are Here Bodrum, which makes it the subtler find.
Guangzhou Collectible Mug, 16oz#576284 · Global Icon SeriesThis 16oz version trades restraint for warmth, an orange and cream interior with a ram statue out front, a direct nod to the granite Statue of the Five Rams erected in 1959 in Yuexiu Park. The legend says five immortals in colored robes arrived riding rams, each bearing rice as a blessing against famine, the founding myth of the City of the Five Rams. The 11 meter sculpture is the city's defining emblem, so it is the perfect anchor for the mug.
Los Cabos, 16oz#576410 · The Long TailLos Cabos sits at the very tip of Mexico's Baja California peninsula, and the yellow waters with a sailboat on this 16oz mug evoke its marlin-rich sportfishing and the famous El Arco sea arch where the Pacific meets the Sea of Cortez. It is a resort-destination piece, sunny and uncomplicated, exactly the kind of vacation mug people grab on a Cabo trip. The bright palette makes it pop on a shelf of city skylines.
Groningen, Global Collection Mug,#576508 · Global Icon SeriesA 16oz Global Collection mug with a light blue interior, fronted by the Martinitoren, Groningen's 97 meter steeple that locals affectionately call d'Olle Grieze, the old grey one. Built mostly between 1469 and 1482 in Bentheimer sandstone, it carries a 62 bell carillon and leans about half a meter on a foundation only three meters deep. Groningen rarely gets its own mug, so a Dutch piece beyond Amsterdam is a quietly satisfying find.
Leiden, Global Collection Mug, 16o#576509 · Global Icon SeriesThe windmill on this 16oz Global Collection mug is Leiden's beloved De Valk, a tower mill built in 1743 and the last survivor of the nineteen that once ringed the city's ramparts. It became a museum in 1966 and is the only original city-miller's house left in the Netherlands, seven floors and roughly 29 metres tall. The light-green interior suits a university town threaded with canals, Rembrandt's birthplace too.
Utrecht, Global Collection Mug, 16#576510 · Global Icon SeriesA magenta-lined 16oz Global mug for Utrecht, fronted by buildings lining a canal, the Oudegracht with its unique wharf cellars at water level, a medieval feature found nowhere else in the Netherlands. The Global Icon Utrecht is genuinely scarce and turns up flagged rare by sellers. A handsome Dutch piece beyond the usual Amsterdam.
Nagano, Our Daily Story#576640 · Japan Geography Series / Our Daily StoryPart of Starbucks Japan's Our Daily Story line, this Nagano mug uses a restrained design over a grey base rather than a busy landmark band. The series framed each place as a small everyday narrative, a quieter cousin to the geographic city mugs. For a Nagano completist it fills out the prefecture's run alongside the 2003 and 2014 pieces and rewards the eye that notices subtle Japanese styling.
Fukuka, Our Daily Story#576641 · Japan Geography Series / Our Daily StoryFukuoka anchors Kyushu and is the gateway closest to the Asian mainland, famous for Hakata tonkotsu ramen, the scarlet five story pagoda at Tochoji, and the energy of its Yamakasa festival. The dark blue band along the base gives this Our Daily Story piece a calm, regional feel, the kind of understated Japan market mug that rarely surfaces outside the country.
Sendai, Our Daily Story#576643 · Japan Geography Series / Our Daily StoryA Sendai entry in the Our Daily Story line, with the city name set above a green base band, a cleaner and more typographic look than the painted festival mugs. Sendai's identity as Japan's tree-lined City of Trees and host of the great Tanabata festival sits behind the design. A understated counterpart to the older brushwork Sendai mugs in the collection.
Kanazawa, Our Daily Story#576645 · Japan Geography Series / Our Daily StoryA Kanazawa from the Our Daily Story line, white bodied with a grey footed base, a softer modern take than the painterly earlier mugs. This series leaned into clean contemporary storytelling for each locale rather than dense scenery. For Kanazawa that means nods to its understated elegance, the gold leaf craft, the tea house districts and Kenrokuen, the city that styles itself little Kyoto on the western coast.
Hokkaido, Our Daily Story#576649 · Japan Geography Series / Our Daily StoryFrom the Our Daily Story line, a softer Hokkaido treatment, white inside with a light blue cream band at the base. Hokkaido is Japan's vast northern frontier, known for lavender fields, dairy, seafood and the Ainu indigenous heritage, a landscape that invites this calmer, illustrated approach. It makes a nice gentle counterpoint to the playful 2009 bear mug, two very different takes on the same beloved island.
Moose, 2009 Mug#576709 · The Long TailA 2009 novelty mug with a moose strolling across a cream exterior, the kind of woodsy wildlife piece Starbucks dropped into its everyday line for North woods and lodge markets. The brown creme glaze and white interior are the giveaways of that era of casual animal mugs. Not part of any named landmark series, it lives in my long-tail shelf as pure fireside charm.
Elephant, 2010 Mug#576711 · The Long TailA 2010 mug featuring an elephant over a grey-cream body with a brown interior, sharing the muted styling of that year's Dragon mug. The elephant is not a Chinese zodiac animal, so this reads as a regional Asian-market release where the elephant carries strong symbolism of wisdom, strength and good fortune. That grey-and-cream finish ties it visually to the 2010 animal series while standing apart from the standard red Lunar mugs.
Dragon, 2010 Mug#576712 · The Long TailA 2010 zodiac mug for the Year of the Dragon, the dragon figure set against a grey-cream exterior with a bold red interior. The Dragon is the most prized sign in the Chinese zodiac, the only mythical creature in the cycle and a symbol of power and luck, which historically spikes birth rates in dragon years. This grey-and-cream styling sets it apart from the brighter red zodiac mugs, a more subdued take collectors note as a distinct variant.
Indigenous Face, 2011 Mug#576713 · The Long TailA 2011 mug built around a stylized Indigenous face on a grey-cream ground with a punchy orange interior. The bold graphic portrait reads as folk-art or tribal-inspired design rather than a place souvenir. Pieces like this fall outside the city series entirely, which makes them hard to pin to a market and a bit of a hunt to identify, exactly the kind of orphan mug that intrigues collectors.
Motorcycle, 2011 Mug#576714 · The Long TailA 2011 piece with a motorcycle riding across a grey-cream exterior and a green interior, part of that run of hobby and lifestyle mugs Starbucks made for the open-road crowd. It carries no city or landmark, just the bike as the whole story. I keep it because the everyday-object mugs from this period are quietly hard to track down complete and in good color.
Alaska / Skagway Mercantile & Cafe#576975 · The Long TailMade for the Skagway Mercantile and Cafe on 2nd Avenue, a licensed cruise-port store in the old Klondike gold-rush town, not a corporate Starbucks. The exterior shows three mountain climbers, fitting for a place ringed by the Coast Range. Collectors track it by size and climber color, a 10oz with red climbers, a 16oz with black, and a 20oz with red, so the variants matter when you hunt one.
1990's, Starbucks Coffee Yellow GrThe Long TailA genuine 1990s relic, this yellow and green rectangular Starbucks Coffee piece predates the company's modern minimalist branding, back when the green-and-cream palette and blockier logo treatments still ruled. Early-decade Starbucks ephemera like this is exactly the kind of thing that vanished into thrift bins, so anything surviving from the pre-2000 era is worth holding onto.
1995, Decorative Mockup of "The OrThe Long TailA 1995 decorative mockup referencing "The Original" store, leaning on Starbucks' deep pride in its 1971 Pike Place birthplace. The brand has always merchandised its origin story hard, and a mid-90s display or mockup piece tied to that first shop is the sort of in-store oddity that almost never escaped the back room, which makes it a real conversation starter on the shelf.
1995, Exclusive Blends Sampler SetThe Long TailThis is the 1995 Exclusive Blends Sampler Set tin, a sizable roughly 10 by 7 by 4 inch container that once held a curated lineup of Starbucks blends. Collectors flag these specifically as very rare, and they surface on eBay billed exactly that way, since most coffee tins got tossed once empty. The large format and intact 90s graphics are what make this one a keeper for me.
1995, Vintage Large Starbucks TinThe Long TailA large vintage 1995 Starbucks tin built around a day-and-night theme, from the era when the company packaged beans and gift sets in collectible decorative tins rather than bags. These big mid-90s tins were practically built to be repurposed and kept, and the day/night artwork makes this one more characterful than the plain blend cans of the same period.
1998 Starbucks Bearona BearThe Long TailThis is the 1998 Bearona, an early Bearista bear named by fusing "bear" with Caffe Verona, the blend it was paired with for Valentine's Day. Starbucks launched the Bearista line in 1997 to mark holidays, cities and causes, so this maroon-apron second-edition bear sits near the very start of one of the brand's most collected runs. Early Bearistas like this are genuinely sought after on the secondary market today.
1999, Biscuit Tin Can, First StarbThe Long TailA 1999 biscuit tin themed around the first Starbucks store, blending the company's love of decorative tins with its origin-story merchandising centered on the 1971 Pike Place shop. Tins like this were gift-season pieces meant to be reused, so an intact one tying directly to the founding store is both a charming object and a nice bit of brand heritage to keep around.
2 x Summer at Starbucks Tote BagThe Long TailTwo "Summer at Starbucks" tote bags, seasonal promotional carryalls from the brand's long tradition of warm-weather merchandise pushes. Branded totes were typically gift-with-purchase or limited summer-line items, so they wore out and got tossed rather than saved, which makes a clean matched pair a fun, very wearable slice of Starbucks' seasonal marketing to keep alongside the ceramics.
2000 Witch BearThe Long TailThis is the 11th Edition Bearista, the year 2000 Halloween bear, the plush mascot dressed as a tiny witch with hat and broom. The Bearista line ran a Halloween costume bear most autumns, and the witch sits among the early ones collectors track by edition number, alongside the 1999 skeleton. Mine is a costumed bear rather than a mug, a soft outlier in a cabinet full of ceramic, and that contrast is exactly why I keep it.
2000, Cappuccino, 12oz, MugThe Long TailA 12oz house mug from 2000, part of the plain beverage labeled line where the drink name itself was the design. Cappuccino, the espresso and steamed milk classic capped with foam, named for the brown hooded robes of Capuchin friars. These solid utility mugs were the working china of the cafe, and surviving examples in clean condition are getting harder to find as they were used hard and tossed.
2000, Red Kettle Houses, Tin BoxThe Long TailThe matching gift tin for the 2000 Red Kettle Houses holiday set, the decorative metal box that held coffee or the mug as a Christmas package. Tins like this were meant to be opened and discarded, so an intact box surviving alongside its mug is genuinely scarce. I value the complete pairing because a holiday piece with its original packaging tells the whole gift story, not just half of it.
2001 LadyBug BearThe Long TailThis is the 14th Edition Bearista, the 2001 Ladybug bear, the plush mascot dressed in a red and black ladybug costume and also issued in a jumbo size. It sits in the Valentine and spring slot of the Bearista calendar, a cheerful counterpoint to the autumn Halloween bears. Collectors catalog these strictly by edition number, and the ladybug is one of the more charming early costumes in that long running plush series.
2001, Exclusive Blends, Red Tin BoThe Long TailA 2001 red tin box from the Exclusive Blends line, the decorative metal canister that held a special or limited coffee offering. These gift tins were built to package premium blends for the holidays and were meant to be emptied and recycled, so a surviving intact red tin is a small piece of packaging history. I keep the tins because they round out the collection beyond ceramic and show how Starbucks sold coffee as a gift.
2002 Summer Beach BearThe Long TailA 2002 Summer Beach Bear from the long-running Bearista mascot family, the seasonal warm-weather edition dressed for the sand. Starbucks issued Bearistas in themed waves several times a year starting in the late 1990s, and the summer beach versions are among the most charming, built to sit on a counter rather than hold coffee. These plush-and-ceramic mascots have a devoted following, and the dated summer editions are exactly the kind of piece collectors chase to complete a year-by-year Bearista run.
2003 Chicken BearThe Long TailA 2003 Bearista in a chicken costume, part of the long running plush and ceramic bear program where the Starbucks bear dresses up by season and theme. The chicken outfit ties it to the spring and Easter run of that year. Costumed Bearistas are collected as a set, and the more specific the seasonal getup, the more a particular bear gets hunted down once it is long retired.
2003 Easter Rabbit BearThe Long TailThe 2003 Easter Rabbit Bearista, the Starbucks bear dressed as a bunny for that spring's holiday lineup, a natural companion to the same year's chicken bear. The Bearista line began in the late 1990s and added new seasonal characters every year, so an Easter rabbit slots into a long chronological parade of costumes. Holiday specific bears like this are the kind collectors chase to fill the gaps in a year by year run.
2003, Cobalt Blue, Abbey, 18oz, MuThe Long TailThe 18oz cobalt blue Abbey from 2003, the deepest and richest of the line's blues poured over the familiar rounded barrel body. Cobalt is a notoriously hard glaze to keep even on a large form, so a uniform unblemished coat is part of the appeal. Paired against the Blue Ibiza version it shows how Starbucks built whole tonal families inside a single mug shape, which makes the blues a fun pair to display together.
2003, Mermaid's Spirit, 12oz, MugThe Long TailA 2003 Mermaid's Spirit mug, a smaller 12oz piece named for the Siren who has anchored the Starbucks identity since 1971. I keep the catalog description as my ground truth here and avoid guessing at decoration that I cannot confirm, since several 2003 Siren mugs circulate with embossed and pleated treatments. Anything that foregrounds the mermaid herself, rather than a city or color, tends to draw the logo focused side of the collecting crowd.
2004 East African Coffee From StarThe Long TailA 2004 origin mug celebrating Starbucks East African coffees, the bright, citrus-forward washed arabicas from Kenya, Ethiopia and Tanzania that have long been the company's flagship single origins. It belongs to a small set of blend mugs that lift the colorful coffee-bag stamp artwork Starbucks has used since 1987, when a tiger stood for Sumatra and a fishing boat for Yukon Blend. These origin pieces are far scarcer than city mugs and prized by collectors who chase the full coffee-region run.
2004 Gardener BearThe Long TailA 2004 Gardener Bearista from the plush mascot line Starbucks launched in 1997, dressed for the garden in the company's long-running themed-bear tradition. The Bearista catalog is numbered by edition, and serious bear people track every release through resources like bearista.org and Worthpoint lot listings. Dressed-occupation bears like this Gardener tend to be more characterful than the plain seasonal bears, making them a friendlier target for collectors building a complete year-by-year shelf.
2004 Lady Liberty BearThe Long TailA 2004 Lady Liberty Bearista, part of the 29th-edition era of Starbucks plush bears, costumed as the Statue of Liberty with crown and torch. The Bearista line, running since 1997, regularly dressed its bears as landmarks and patriotic icons, and a New York-flavored Lady Liberty is one of the more recognizable themes. Costume bears tied to famous monuments tend to hold interest with collectors, who catalog each edition by year and number.
2004 Little Bo Peep's BearThe Long TailA 2004 Little Bo Peep Bearista, one of the storybook-character costumes Starbucks layered into its annual plush bear program. The bear wears the nursery-rhyme shepherdess look, crook and bonnet, a playful entry alongside the patriotic and occupational themes of the same era. Fairy-tale Bearistas are charming oddities in the line, and like all the bears they are tracked edition by edition by the dedicated bear-collecting community.
2005 Black Cat Halloween BearThe Long TailThis is the 2005 Halloween Bearista dressed in a black cat costume, often pictured clutching a little pumpkin. Starbucks began the Bearista line in 1997 and used it to mark holidays, cities, and causes, with Halloween editions becoming a yearly autumn ritual. The black-cat suit makes this one of the more characterful seasonal bears, and tagged examples still circulate among collectors who chase the complete Halloween run.
2005 Boston Patriot BearThe Long TailPart of Starbucks' 2005 Historical Cities special edition, this Bearista wears a Revolutionary-era Boston patriot getup, a nod to the city's role as the cradle of American independence. City-specific bears were sold only in their home market, which is what gives them their pull. A tagged Boston Patriot example sold on eBay for around fifty dollars, and the regional-only availability keeps it on want-lists for collectors building the historical set.
2005 Frog BearThe Long TailA 2005 Bearista in a green frog costume, released that September alongside the leopard bear. Starbucks tied parts of its 2005 animal lineup to its conservation partnership, and these costumed bears leaned into a playful, nature-themed charm. The frog suit makes it an instant standout on a shelf of ordinary brown bears, and like all the costumed Bearistas it is far more desirable with its original hang tag still attached.
2005 Halloween Black Cat BearThe Long TailAnother listing of the 2005 Halloween black-cat Bearista, the seasonal bear suited up as a black cat and frequently shown holding a tiny pumpkin. Starbucks' Halloween Bearistas became an annual autumn tradition after the line launched in 1997, and collectors track them year by year. Costume condition and the presence of the original tag are what separate a casual find from a piece worth holding for the set.
2005 Leopard BearThe Long TailThe 2005 leopard-suited Bearista, marketed as a 40th edition, with "Starbucks Coffee Company 2005" stitched on the bottom of its paw. Released that September alongside the frog bear, its spotted coat tied into Starbucks' conservation partnership with Conservation International. The animal-costume bears have a devoted following, and as ever the leopard is most sought after with its original tag intact and the costume unworn.
2005 Thrive BearThe Long TailThis 2005 Thrive Bearista is a cyclist bear created to represent Starbucks' Thrive healthy-living program, and it also circulates tied to breast cancer awareness. It is one of the more unusual cause-driven bears in the line, dressed for the road rather than a holiday or a city. Collectors flag it as relatively scarce, and its mission-themed backstory gives it more meaning than the standard seasonal bears on the shelf.
2005, 16oz, Secret Admirer V-day MThe Long TailThe 2005 Secret Admirer is a chunky 16oz Valentine mug, the pink lace-hearts version that reads to the effect of from a secret admirer, embossed rather than printed. It belongs to the run of mid-2000s Valentine pieces Starbucks issued every February, and collectors still trade these as cheerful seasonal stoneware. I love that the whole gimmick is anonymity, a coffee mug standing in for a card you were too shy to sign.
2006 Gardener BearThe Long TailA 2006 Gardener Bearista, one of the seasonal-occupation bears Starbucks dressed up through the mid-2000s, this one kitted out for the garden. The annual Bearista line is its own deep collecting world, with themed and holiday bears released several times a year and condition plus original tags driving everything. A spring gardener fits the cheerful, low-stakes charm of these plush mascots that people either obsess over or never notice.
