Pike Place#186120 · Architecture SeriesOne of the legendary 2002 Skyline Giants, the oversized 24oz format made only for the highest volume stores, wrapping Seattle's skyline in light blue and grey with a white interior. Pike Place Market, where Starbucks opened its first shop in 1971, is the obvious anchor here. The full giants tip the scales heavy and stand close to a foot tall, and collectors chase every city in this line because so few survived intact.
Los Angeles#186125 · Architecture SeriesThis Los Angeles entry pairs the Skyline Giants line with an espresso-format build, an unusual size note for a series better known for its oversized display mugs. L.A.'s skyline in soft blue and grey nods to a city defined by Hollywood, the U.S. Bank tower, and the sprawl that runs to the Pacific. The giants reached only the highest-volume 2002 stores, which keeps the whole line firmly in grail territory for serious collectors.
Denver#455105 · City Scene SeriesDenver's Skyline Giant is the oversized cousin to the standard 2002 mug, a limited display piece that reached only the busiest stores. The Mile High City sits exactly one mile above sea level on the Capitol steps, framed by the Rockies in the city's grey-and-pale-blue photo wrap. Giants in this series are genuinely scarce, with confirmed sales landing in the high hundreds, so an intact Denver is a real find.
Tahoe#576251 · Global Icon SeriesA 2002 Skyline Giant for Tahoe, blue inside and cream outside with a skier carving down, fitting for the alpine lake straddling California and Nevada that anchors world class resorts like Heavenly and Squaw Valley, host of the 1960 Winter Olympics. A resort destination rather than a city makes this an unusual entry in the giants line, and the skiing figure gives it real personality.
San Diego#576264 · Global Icon SeriesThis 2002 Skyline Giant pulls in San Diego's Gaslamp Quarter, dark green inside and cream outside with that historic district sign. The Gaslamp's six ton neon archway over Fifth Avenue went up in 1990, named for the Victorian era gas street lamps of the old New Town. As with the whole giants line, the oversized format shipped to very few stores, so finding San Diego is a small triumph.
Chicago#576270 · Global Icon SeriesThis Chicago piece belongs to the rare Skyline Giants, the oversized 2002 mugs sent only to the highest-volume stores as display showpieces, with collectors describing the largest as 2.5-gallon monsters. Chicago's design plays up its architectural fame, the cream wrap nodding to its place as the birthplace of the skyscraper and the rebuilt city after the 1871 fire. Verified sold examples of these giants run from roughly $300 to $700, which makes any of them a serious shelf trophy.
New York#576447 · Global Icon SeriesNew York is the headliner of the Skyline Giants, an oversized 2002 display mug crowned here by the Statue of Liberty against a green interior, a clear nod to the statue's weathered copper. Sent only to the highest-volume stores, surviving New York giants have changed hands for roughly $425 to $600 in tracked sales. Of all the giants, this is the one most collectors covet first, both for the city and the iconic Lady Liberty motif.
Portland#576462 · Global Icon SeriesA 2002 Skyline Giant for Portland, dark blue inside with the city's mountains and trees rendered outside, a nod to Mount Hood looming over the Rose City and the dense conifer country of the Pacific Northwest. These giant format mugs went only to top performing stores, making any single city a genuine hunt, and intact examples in good shape are the prize.
Miami#576477 · Global Icon SeriesMiami's Skyline Giant trades the usual skyline for the pastel South Beach promenade, its Art Deco hotels along Ocean Drive rendered against a light blue interior. This oversized 2002 display mug went only to flagship-volume stores, and a verified Miami giant has sold for around $600 on the secondary market. The Deco-strip subject makes it one of the more charming designs in an already scarce line.
Vancouver#576561 · You Are Here CollectionThis Vancouver Skyline Giant is light blue inside with the city's waterfront skyline and an orca leaping outside, the killer whale being a defining symbol of the Pacific Northwest coast and Coast Salish art. Vancouver's glass towers against the North Shore mountains make one of the most photogenic skylines in the line. A 2002 giant from a Canadian city is harder to surface than the US ones, so the orca makes this a quiet favorite.
San Francisco#576625 · You Are Here CollectionA 2002 San Francisco Skyline Giant, red inside with the Golden Gate Bridge emerging through grey clouds outside, exactly how the span actually looks half the year when fog rolls through the strait. Opened in 1937 and painted International Orange, the bridge is the city's signature. The giant format is the rarest tier of the Skyline run, and the moody cloud treatment makes this one of the more striking faces in the set.
Dallas#576960 · City Mug Collector SeriesDallas in the Skyline Giants format is one of the oversized 2002 display mugs that went only to top-tier stores, far scarcer than the standard cups. The grey lit orb on its tower is Reunion Tower, the geodesic ball-topped landmark that defines the Dallas skyline. Because so few giants survive intact, sold examples of this series have fetched several hundred dollars, putting them among the heavyweight grails of city-mug collecting.
Seattle#576968 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe home city giant, white inside with a light green Mount Rainier outside, the 14,411 foot volcano that dominates Seattle's southern horizon on clear days. This is the flagship of the 2002 Skyline Giants, and a Seattle giant reportedly sold for around 700 dollars on eBay back in 2018, which tells you how seriously the oversized line is taken. Heavy, tall, and made for only the busiest stores.
VictoriaSkyline GIANTSA 2002 Skyline Giant for Victoria, the genteel capital of British Columbia on Vancouver Island, known for the floodlit Parliament Buildings and the ivy clad Fairmont Empress hotel on the Inner Harbour. Victoria is one of the smaller and less common cities to appear in the oversized giants format, which makes any surviving example worth grabbing when the chance comes. The British colonial charm of the place fits the stately giant proportions.
Washington D.C.Skyline GIANTSThe Washington D.C. entry in the 2002 Skyline Giants, the capital's monumental core of the Capitol dome, the Washington Monument obelisk, and the Lincoln Memorial laid out along the National Mall. As an oversized 24oz giant made only for top stores, it carries the same scarcity as the rest of the line. A capital city always draws extra interest, and the giant scale suits a skyline built on grand federal architecture.
Classification

Japan & Asia83 pieces

Twenty-three sub-series under one country, the deepest national section.
Demitasse#186082 · Japan & AsiaA sakura demitasse, the tiny espresso size dressed in cherry blossom colors outside. The little demitasse format is a favorite among collectors because the small canvas forces a clean, concentrated design, and the sakura palette makes this one especially pretty. Spring exclusive minis like this round out a Japan collection without taking the shelf space a full mug demands.
Japan 2012#186099 · Japan & AsiaThe 3oz espresso companion to the 2012 annual, simply marked Japan 2012 on the outside. These tiny demitasse versions shadowed the full mugs for several years and are easy to overlook, which is exactly why complete pairs of mug-plus-demi are satisfying to assemble. The small format also survived in fewer numbers, so the minis often prove harder to find than the regular cups.
Japan#186135 · Japan 2011A striking little 3oz espresso piece, red and black inside and out with a gold circular painting, an enso, the single brushed Zen circle symbolizing enlightenment and the infinite. The lacquer-red and gold pairing is pure Japanese luxury palette. Demitasse sets like this were produced in smaller runs than the standard mugs, making intact examples a quiet prize.
Japan#186136 · Area Collectible Demi SetThis is a regional demitasse set, six 3oz espresso minis for Hokkaido, Yamagata, Sendai, Yokohama, Tokyo and Nagano, each carrying its own local design. Japan's geography series tied merchandise to specific prefectures so you often had to travel to buy them, which makes a complete six-piece set genuinely difficult to reunite. Owning the full lineup intact is the real achievement here, not any single cup.
Tokyo#455172 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe classic City Mug Collector Series Tokyo, white inside with the lattice silhouette of Tokyo Tower in dark green wrapping the outside. Tokyo Tower opened in 1958, a 333 meter Eiffel inspired broadcast tower painted international orange and white, and for decades it was the city's defining icon before Skytree arrived. This older flagship line is the one purists chase first.
Hiroshima Mug (2011)#455259 · Japan 2011This 2011 Hiroshima regional mug wraps colorful origami across the outside, a deliberate nod to the orizuru, the folded paper cranes that became Hiroshima's universal emblem of peace after Sadako Sasaki's story. Japan ties its city mugs tightly to place, and a Hiroshima piece almost always carries the crane motif. I have seen these origami examples trade around the hundred dollar mark when they surface outside the prefecture.
Hiroshima Mug (2008)#455262 · Japan 2008A 2008 Hiroshima mug, white inside with a green abstract painting of the city outside. The painterly abstract approach sets it apart from the literal landmark mugs, leaning into mood rather than monuments for a city whose story carries so much weight. Pairing this 2008 piece with the Our Daily Story Hiroshima shows two very different ways Starbucks Japan chose to portray the same place.
Tokyo Mug (2002)#455263 · Japan 2002A 2002 Tokyo mug, white inside with a print of Tokyo Tower outside. Early 2000s Japan mugs predate the global redesigns, so each market had its own art direction, and a clean dated 2002 example helps anchor where Starbucks Japan's design language sat before Global Icon standardized everything. Tokyo Tower remained the default shorthand for the city right up until Skytree opened a decade later.
Yokohama Mug (2008)#455264 · Japan 2008The 2008 Yokohama, white inside with a painted view of the city carried across the body and onto the handle. The painting onto the handle is the standout, a flourish you rarely see, and the subject is the Minato Mirai 21 skyline with Landmark Tower, once Japan's tallest building, the giant Cosmo Clock 21 Ferris wheel and the red brick warehouses. A lovely, painterly snapshot of Japan's great port city.
Osaka Mug (2009)#455265 · Japan 2009A second 2009 Osaka in my run, again pairing Osaka Castle with the city wrapped around the body and handle. The 1597 castle you see was reconstructed in 1931 and modernized inside with elevators, a quirk that always makes me smile. Osaka collectors prize the local Japan-only city mugs because they rarely left the country, so the boxed examples turn up far less often than the global lines.
Roppongi Hills Mug (2003)#455267 · Japan 2003This is the inaugural year, 2003, the same year Roppongi Hills opened as Minoru Mori's vast mini-city in central Tokyo. Owning the launch edition of a store-specific anniversary series is the kind of bookend I chase. The abstract painting runs onto the handle, and as the first in the line it sets the template every later dated Roppongi mug would follow.
Tokyo Mug (2012)#455269 · Japan 2012The 2012 Tokyo mug, white inside with a painterly rendering of Tokyo Tower rather than a flat print. By 2012 Skytree had just opened, yet Starbucks still leaned on the older orange tower here, a nice reminder of how stubbornly Tokyo Tower held its place in the city's identity. The looser painting style sets it apart from the crisp graphic mugs of the previous decade.
Fukuoka Mug (2011)#455271 · Japan 2011A 2011 Fukuoka mug, white inside with the colorful dishes of Fukuoka outside, a fitting tribute since the city's identity is built on food, from creamy Hakata ramen to the late night yatai stalls along the Nakasu riverside. Having both the 2000 and 2011 Fukuoka mugs side by side shows how the design language evolved over a decade. The food forward art makes this one of the more characterful regional pieces.
Sapporo Mug (2001)#455272 · Japan 2001An early 2001 Sapporo, white inside with blue snowflakes scattered outside, a clean and wintry design fitting Japan's snowiest major city. Sapporo hosted the 1972 Winter Olympics, the first ever in Asia, so cold-weather imagery is the city's natural shorthand. I like this one as the understated predecessor to the later landmark-driven Global Icon, all atmosphere and no skyline.
Nagoya Mug (2010)#455273 · Japan 2010This 2010 Nagoya mug renders the bronze shachihoko in colorful art, the same golden tiger-fish that guard Nagoya Castle's roof. The castle's real pair are plated in eighteen-karat gold, the larger one weighing over 1,200 kilograms, and Nagoyans treat the kinshachi as the city's emblem. I like that across a decade Starbucks kept returning to this one mythic creature, proof that the shachihoko simply is Nagoya in a single image.
Kyoto Mug (1999)#455274 · Japan 1999This 1999 Kyoto is one of my favorites in the vintage run, two colorful hand-drawn renderings of the word Kyoto and an unusual pink handle, all under the old pre-2011 logo. These late-90s Japan city mugs are increasingly collectible and the pink-handle detail makes this one easy to spot. It is pure 1990s design energy, playful and loose, the opposite of the restrained modern Kyoto editions.
Okinawa Mug (2002)#455275 · Japan 2002This 2002 Okinawa mug runs a yellow-themed design with two small dragons, the shisa, Okinawa's lion-dog guardians from Ryukyu mythology that sit in pairs on rooftops and gateposts to ward off evil. Okinawa was its own Ryukyu Kingdom until the 1870s, which is why its motifs feel distinct from mainland Japan. An early-2000s piece with the old logo, and the shisa make it unmistakably Okinawan.
Yokohama Mug (1999)#455276 · Japan 1999One of my older Japan pieces, a 1999 Yokohama with an abstract line drawing of the shoreline and a green handle. Late 1990s mugs like this were made in Taiwan and predate the photo realistic city art that came later, so the loose abstract style is very of its moment. The colored handle is a small detail that vintage hunters specifically look for, and clean 1999 examples are getting genuinely hard to find.
Okinawa Mug (2006)#455277 · Japan 2006The 2006 Okinawa mug gives the two shisa a comic-style treatment over an ocean theme, lighter and more cartoonish than the 2002 version. The shisa, despite their bared fangs, are protective and friendly figures, traditionally a closed-mouth one to keep good spirits in and an open-mouthed one to scare bad ones off. Paired with the 2002 mug it shows how the same Ryukyu guardians were re-drawn for a sunnier, tourist-facing mood.
Fukuoka Mug (2000)#455280 · Japan 2000A 2000 Fukuoka mug, white inside with a wash of colors and Fukuoka set over red outside. Fukuoka, the largest city in Kyushu, is famous for its yatai street food stalls, home to roughly 40 percent of all such stalls in Japan, and for rich tonkotsu Hakata ramen. A regional Japanese city mug dated 2000 is an early one, predating most of the country mug program, so it carries real vintage weight.
Japan 2009#455283 · Japan 2009The 2009 mug is a standout, a colorful Osaka Castle rendered against black, celebrating the rebuilt keep that crowns Japan's old merchant capital. Osaka pieces in this line often pair the castle with the neon Dotonbori canal, and the city is fiercely proud of both. Collectors note these darker-ground Osaka designs are genuinely harder to find, so grab it when condition is clean.
Japan 2005#455286 · Japan 2005The 2005 mug goes graphic and almost playful, a yellow and black checkerboard pattern that reads more like a textile or kimono motif than a landscape. It is the outlier of the dated run, and that boldness makes it instantly recognizable on a shelf of florals and Fuji scenes. I like that each Japan year committed to one strong idea instead of hedging.
Kobe Mug (2015)#455288 · Japan 2015The 2015 Kobe mug returns to the harbor portrait, the red Port Tower, the cable car and the skyline, in a refreshed illustration style. Kobe's waterfront packs an unusual amount of landmark into one view, the drum-shaped tower beside the steel-roofed Maritime Museum, with Mount Rokko rising behind. Set next to the 2010 version it shows how Starbucks Japan kept re-illustrating the same beloved skyline across the years.
Japan 2006#455289 · Japan 2006Dated 2006, this one layers a floral drawing over gold motifs, the kind of restrained metallic accent that shows up again and again in Starbucks Japan's premium pieces. 2006 was also the year of the big 10th anniversary, so the standard annual sits alongside fancier commemoratives from the same season. Worth owning both to see how the everyday mug and the milestone piece diverged.
Japan 2003#455292 · Japan 2003The 2003 entry leans into the rising sun, a drawing of that red disc with flowers blooming upward, the most distilled symbol of Japan itself. Starbucks ran these dated mugs annually for the Japanese market through the 2000s, each one a small design experiment rather than a city. I treat the full year run as a single collection, and the early ones like this anchor it.
Japan 2004#455293 · Japan 2004Dated 2004, this mug sets a floral drawing against a deep blue ground, quieter and more painterly than the bolder graphic years around it. These Japan-exclusive annuals never sold outside the country, which is exactly why the dated run is fun to assemble from abroad. Condition and a legible year stamp are what separate a keeper from a shelf-filler here.
Japan#455294 · Japan 2006The demitasse counterpart to the Japan You Are Here mug, a small cup with white interior and flowers drawn over a dark black ground. The black backdrop makes it the moodier sibling to the bright full-size YAH, and the tiny espresso format always trailed the standard mug in production numbers. Pairing it with the 14oz completes the set and shows how the same series scaled down for a single shot.
Osaka Mug (1999)#455296 · Japan 1999One of the earliest Osaka pieces I own, this 1999 mug skips the literal castle for an abstract skyline in green and blue. That cool restraint is pure late-1990s Starbucks Japan design language before the city series went photographic. Osaka is the heart of the Kansai region and famous for Dotonbori, the neon canal where the Glico running man and the giant mechanical crab still draw crowds today.
Kobe Mug (1999)#455297 · Japan 1999A genuine vintage, this 1999 Kobe mug carries an abstract green-and-blue treatment of the word Kobe and the old pre-2011 logo, made just four years after the city's devastating 1995 Great Hanshin earthquake. These 1990s Japan city mugs with the old siren are sought after now, turning up on eBay singly and as boxed pairs. The loose, painterly lettering dates it instantly to the era before the literal-landmark style took over.
Roppongi Hills Mug (2004)#455301 · Japan 2004The 2004 follow-up, the first anniversary of the complex that redefined the Roppongi district. The art again carries onto the handle, a recurring touch on these Japan-only pieces. Roppongi Hills was conceived as a live-work-play vertical town, and the Tokyo City View deck on the 52nd floor remains one of the best skyline panoramas in the capital.
Kyoto Mug (2006)#455304 · Japan 2006The 2006 Kyoto mug stacks the city's name atop a field of traditional Japanese motifs, an early move toward the illustrated city style. Kyoto carries it well, a city of two thousand temples and the 300-year-old white-faced traditions of the Gion geisha quarter. It sits chronologically between the wild 1999 lettering and the soft 2015 paintings, a nice middle chapter in Kyoto's long mug history.
Japan 2008#455305 · Japan 2008Dated 2008, this design gathers cherry blossoms, trees and rocks over a soft pink wash, essentially a hanami scene, the spring blossom-viewing tradition that grips all of Japan each April. Sakura is the single most reliable theme in Starbucks Japan's catalog, and this is a gentle, classic reading of it. The pale palette photographs beautifully and dates the piece firmly to its year.
Sakura (2016)#455322 · Japan 2016The 2016 Sakura breaks the mold with a yellow interior set against pink blossoms outside, an unexpected contrast for the line. That kind of year-to-year palette experiment is precisely what makes the dated Sakura mugs fun to line up. By the mid-2010s the spring collection had grown into a sprawling lineup of mugs, tumblers, and cold cups, all gone within days of each February release.
Sakura (2012)#455323 · Japan 2012The 2012 edition, with a scattering of blossom leaves inside and the full sakura theme outside. Each year Starbucks Japan commissions fresh sakura artwork, so collectors track them by date the way people track vintages. This run is the brand's spring counterpart to its autumn and holiday lines, and the consistent annual cadence is what makes a chronological wall of them so satisfying.
Sakura (2011)#455324 · Japan 2011The standard regular-size 2011 Sakura, matching the espresso in its white interior and blossom-covered body. Pairing the regular and espresso from a single year is the kind of completeness I enjoy on the shelf. The Sakura series is one of the few Starbucks runs that resets entirely every year, so 2011 has its own distinct artwork found on nothing else.
Sakura (2011)#455325 · Japan 2011The petite espresso version of the 2011 Sakura, white inside with blossoms outside. The small demitasse sizes in the Sakura line are easy to overlook and therefore underbought, which makes the espresso variants the sleeper finds. The 2011 release carries extra weight given it landed the same spring as the Tohoku earthquake, when the season's quiet renewal meant a great deal in Japan.
Sakura (2013)#455326 · Japan 2013A 2013 Sakura leaning into pink, with a blush interior dotted with blossoms and a white exterior carrying pink petals. Twenty thirteen is a notable year because it is when the broader Starbucks travel concept was expanding, yet Sakura stayed proudly Japan-only. The cherry blossom front, the romance of hanami season, is what keeps these among the most beloved regional Starbucks pieces worldwide.
Sakura (2005)#455327 · Japan 2005An early dated Sakura from 2005, with a few blossom leaves printed inside the cup as well as the full theme outside. The Sakura line is essentially Japan's spring institution at Starbucks, restocked and resold out within days each year. Holding a 2005 example means owning one of the formative editions, from before the series ballooned into the dozens of yearly SKUs it is now.
Japan 2002 (Blue)#455335 · Japan 2002One of the earliest Japan annual mugs, dated 2002, with a stylized cresting wave breaking over Mt. Fuji that openly quotes Hokusai's Great Wave off Kanagawa from his Thirty-Six Views series. The white interior keeps it clean while the blue exterior does all the talking. These early dated Japan mugs from before the line matured are the ones collectors quietly hunt, since survivors in clean condition are getting scarce.
Japan 2002 (Pink)#455336 · Japan 2002The pink companion to the 2002 blue wave mug, this one swaps Hokusai for maneki-neko, the beckoning cats with paws raised over a Mt. Fuji backdrop. The lucky cat with the lifted paw is a Japanese good-fortune charm you see in shop windows everywhere, so it is a sweet, very local choice. Paired with its blue sibling it makes a proper early-era set worth keeping together.
Waking Up Tokyo#455347 · Japan 2006Waking Up Tokyo, black inside with three bold cartoon figures in red, yellow and blue over a black ground. This is an unusually playful, graphic departure from the landmark mugs, leaning into Tokyo's pop and street culture rather than its towers. The high contrast color blocking on black makes it one of the more design forward pieces in the Japan corpus and a real conversation starter next to the staid city series.
Sakura#455368 · Japan & AsiaA cherry blossom mug with a distinctive hexagonal body, soft pink creme inside and out under scattered sakura. Starbucks Japan's Sakura collection is its biggest annual launch, dropping each February before the real blossoms arrive, and the shaped variants like this hexagon are the ones collectors hunt hardest. The pink-on-pink palette captures hanami, Japan's centuries-old tradition of picnicking under blooming cherry trees.
Japan 2010#455370 · Japan 2010Dated 2010, this mug fills its outside with traditional Japanese motifs, the kind of patterned wagara borrowing from kimono and woodblock design. It sits late in the dated annual run, just before the line started shifting toward the regional and anniversary pieces that dominate after 2011. A solid, very Japanese entry that rounds out the decade of yearly releases.
Sakura Pattern#455373 · Japan & AsiaAn undated Sakura built around an allover blossom pattern, white creme with scattered pink leaves wrapping the body. The pattern-style pieces sit a little outside the strict yearly dated editions, which makes pinning them down half the fun. Sakura remains Starbucks Japan's signature seasonal identity, and a repeating-petal design like this is the most decorative expression of that springtime theme.
Tokyo Tree Tower (2012)#455377 · Japan 2012This is the one that breaks ranks, a 2012 mug featuring the brand new Tokyo Skytree instead of the old tower. Skytree was completed in February 2012 at 634 meters, the tallest tower in the world and the second tallest structure on Earth, its height a clever pun on the old name for the area, Musashi, which can be read as roku san shi, six three four. A genuine landmark moment captured in ceramic the year it happened.
Roppongi Hills#455385 · Japan 2015Marking twelve years of Roppongi Hills, the sprawling Mori-built complex that opened in 2003 with shops, the Mori Art Museum, and the Tokyo City View deck 250 meters up Mori Tower. The abstract neighborhood painting nods to one of Tokyo's most design-forward districts. These anniversary mugs were sold only at the Roppongi Hills store, which is exactly why the dated annual editions are hard to assemble as a set.
Japan 2012#455387 · Japan 2012Dated 2012, this one carries green waves running across the handle and body, a fresh, watery motif that breaks from the warmer earlier years. By 2012 the dated annual format was winding down as regional city mugs took over, so the late years like this close out a distinct chapter. The handle detailing is the giveaway, a nice touch you only notice picking it up.
Japan 2007#455388 · Japan 2007The 2007 mug throws splashes of black and pink across the white body, an energetic, almost abstract-expressionist take that feels like a brush flicked at the cup. After several years of tidy florals it is a jolt of looseness, and that energy makes it one of the more distinctive years to track down. Dated Japan annuals like this only ever reached the domestic market.
Sakura (2017)#455390 · Japan 2017The 2017 release, soft and light with a few blossom leaves inside and a pale pink sakura theme outside. The gentle pastel here is classic late-period Sakura styling. These mugs only ever sold in Japan and only for a few spring weeks, so even recent years like 2017 already turn up overseas mostly through resellers, which is part of their quiet collectibility.
Roppongi Hills#455392 · Japan 2016The thirteenth anniversary edition, 2016, continuing the store-exclusive Roppongi Hills run begun in 2003. I have seen this one surface on eBay as a 12oz Tokyo limited, a reminder these never had wide distribution. Roppongi itself is known for nightlife and art, anchored by the Mori Tower observatory with sightlines to Tokyo Tower, Skytree, and on clear days Mount Fuji.
Kyoto (2015)#455394 · Japan 2015The 2015 Kyoto mug sets the wordmark over soft beige Japanese paintings, leaning into the city's classical art rather than a single hard landmark. It suits Kyoto, where the appeal is the whole atmosphere, the temples in the hills, the kimono silks, the tea houses, more than any one tower. The muted palette is a deliberate contrast to the bright 1999 Kyoto mug, a calmer take on the same city.
Nagoya (2000)#455395 · Japan 2000The catalog calls these orange figures upset fish, and they are exactly Nagoya's signature, the shachihoko, golden tiger-headed carp that sit atop Nagoya Castle. Warlords from Oda Nobunaga onward placed them on castle roofs as fire-warding talismans, tails curled to heaven. A turn-of-the-millennium piece with the old logo, this is one of the more characterful early Japan mugs, the whole design built around one local myth.
Kobe (2010)#455396 · Japan 2010This 2010 Kobe mug draws the city's harbor face directly, the red Kobe Port Tower, the cable car up Mount Rokko and the waterfront skyline. The tower, built in 1963, is shaped like a tsuzumi hand drum and was the first lattice-pipe structure of its kind in the world. A handsome, literal city portrait, and a good companion to the later 2015 redraw of the same view.
400th Store in Japan (2002)#455397 · Japan 2002A 2002 mug marking the 400th Starbucks store in Japan, white inside with an orange and blue drawing outside. From a single Ginza shop in 1996, Japan reached 400 stores in only about six years, a staggering pace that this milestone mug quietly documents. Internal milestone pieces like this were made in small numbers and are far scarcer than the public seasonal mugs, which is exactly what makes them worth hunting.
Osaka (2009)#455398 · Japan 2009Osaka Castle anchors this 2009 piece, the towering keep first raised in 1597 by warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi and rebuilt in concrete in 1931. I love that the painting wraps right onto the handle, a small flourish Japan's local line did so well. Osaka is nicknamed Tenka no Daidokoro, the nation's kitchen, for its centuries as Japan's rice trading hub, so a mug here feels especially fitting.
Sakura (2009)#455582 · Japan 2009A bolder 2009 take, fully pink inside with pink blossom leaves outside rather than the usual white ground. That saturated approach makes it stand out on the shelf against the more pastel years. Sakura, the Japanese cherry blossom, blooms for only about a week each spring, and that fleeting beauty, mono no aware, is exactly what this annual collection is built to celebrate.
Japan 15th Anniversary (2011)#455589 · Japan & AsiaThis mug commemorates fifteen years of Starbucks in Japan, counting from that 1996 Ginza debut, with a big 15 set over a white-creme body. The 15th anniversary spawned a whole commemorative range in 2011, much of it tied back to Ginza where it all began. Milestone pieces like this are the connective tissue of a Japan collection, dating the whole journey from a single Tokyo storefront to thousands of stores.
Japan 10th Anniversary (2006)#455593 · Japan & AsiaA genuine landmark piece, marking ten years since Starbucks opened its first Japanese store in Ginza in August 1996, with a drawing of the famous Shibuya Tsutaya storefront. That store sits right on the Shibuya Scramble Crossing, one of the busiest intersections on earth, and was an instant tourist magnet. Listings cite this 2006 anniversary mug as limited to 3,000 pieces, which puts it firmly among the more collectible Japan commemoratives.
Sakura (2006)#455621 · Japan 2006The 2006 Sakura, again with blossoms drifting inside the white interior and the cherry theme wrapping the exterior. What I find charming is how each year's palette shifts slightly, so a vertical run of these reads like a color diary of Japanese spring. These annual sakura releases sell out almost instantly in stores, which is why complete year-by-year sets command real attention among Japan collectors.
Japan 2011#455733 · Japan 2011The 2011 mug goes dramatic and premium, a black interior with a gold bird-over-mountain logo floating above coffee fields on a dark red ground. The metallic crest and deep palette mark it as one of the richer-looking years, fitting since 2011 was also Starbucks Japan's 15th anniversary. That overlap makes the year a small trove of more ambitious designs than the everyday florals.
2009 Sakura Blossom#455892 · Japan & AsiaA 2009 Sakura Blossom mug, white inside with cherry blossom petals drifting up into a blue sky and clouds outside. Sakura is the centerpiece of Starbucks Japan's most beloved annual drop, where fans line up before stores open to grab the spring collection, and earlier years like 2009 predate the current frenzy and turn up far less often. A clean early sakura piece is a lovely cornerstone for the Japan shelf.
Japan Series#455961 · Starbucks Logo Over Time, JapanThis one wears the very first 1971 mark, Terry Heckler's brown, bare-chested twin-tailed siren ringed by the words Starbucks Coffee, Tea and Spices, back when the company was a single Pike Place store selling beans, not drinks. I love that this Japan-market set lets me hold the whole logo lineage in my hands. The 1971 design is the most distinctive of the four, the only one that is brown rather than green.
Japan Series#455962 · Starbucks Logo Over Time, JapanThe 1987 logo marks the Howard Schultz moment, when his Il Giornale bought Starbucks and Heckler merged the two identities. Green replaced the old brown, the siren got a cleaner modern face and two flanking stars, and her exposed torso was tidied away. This is the mark that rode the company's explosion across America, which makes it a quietly historic piece to set beside the 1971 original.
Japan Series#455963 · Starbucks Logo Over Time, JapanThe 1992 update zooms the camera in on the siren, cropping to her face and just the tips of her twin tails, the version most people picture when they think Starbucks. It held for nearly two decades. In this Japan logo-evolution set it is the bridge between the busy early marks and the stripped minimalism that came next, and the most familiar face of the four.
Japan Series#455964 · Starbucks Logo Over Time, JapanThe 2011 mark was unveiled for the company's fortieth anniversary, and it is the boldest gamble of the run. Designers dropped the wordmark, the encircling text and the outer ring entirely, freeing the siren onto a solid green field for the first time, confident enough in the brand to ditch the name. Owning this beside the 1971 original is the whole point of the set, four decades in a row of cups.
2012#455982 · Japan & AsiaA 2012 mug built around the Tokyo Skytree, white inside with the tower and red buildings rising over a pink map grid. The Skytree opened in May 2012 at 2,080 feet, the tallest tower in the world, so this mug celebrates a genuinely new landmark in its debut year. That tight timing makes it a true commemorative rather than a generic city design, and the map grid backdrop is a sharp, modern touch.
Shimane#576044 · Japan & AsiaShimane is the home of Izumo Taisha, one of Japan's oldest and most sacred Shinto shrines, where every October the country's eight million gods are believed to gather. The brown and yellow tones on this mug nod to the local meno agate stones that inspired the famous Izumo store mugs sold only steps from the shrine entrance. A region most foreign collectors never reach, which is exactly why this one rewards a serious shelf.
Osaka#576400 · Global Icon SeriesThis is the 16oz Global Icon Osaka with a light-blue interior, built around Osaka Castle. Toyotomi Hideyoshi raised the original in 1586 after unifying Japan, sheathing its tower in gold leaf and golden shachi, which is why it earned the nickname Kinjo, the Golden Castle. The Global Icon band format makes this feel more international than the older Japan-only city mugs, the same landmark pitched to a worldwide series.
Sapporo#576401 · Global Icon SeriesA 16oz Global Icon for Sapporo, blue inside with the Sapporo Clock Tower under falling snowflakes. The Tokeidai clock tower, built in 1878 as a drill hall for the agricultural college, is the city's enduring symbol and one of its few surviving American-style wooden buildings. The snow nods to the Sapporo Snow Festival, the Yuki Matsuri that draws over two million visitors to Hokkaido's capital each February.
Tokyo#576427 · Global Icon SeriesThe 2008 Global Icon 16oz Tokyo, purple inside with Tokyo Tower again carrying the design. Global Icon was Starbucks' worldwide redesign that wrapped each city in a band of its real landmarks, and the deep interior color is the series tell. Sixteen ounce Global Icons from this era are a clean, recognizable set, and the purple lining makes this Tokyo instantly placeable on a shelf of city mugs.
Japan#576620 · You Are Here CollectionJapan's entry into the global You Are Here series, a 14oz mug with red interior and Mt. Fuji rising over a sunrise amid sakura. When Starbucks finally brought YAH to Japan around 2017 the front packed Fuji, cherry blossoms and a hot-spring snow monkey while the reverse crammed in sushi, ramen, a daruma doll and a castle. It is the most icon-dense Japan mug they ever made, and a clear collector favorite.
Hiroshima#576638 · Japan Geography Series / Our Daily StoryA Hiroshima mug from the Our Daily Story line, white inside with a red band along the bottom. Hiroshima is forever tied to the 1945 atomic bombing and its Peace Memorial Park and A-Bomb Dome, though the city is also loved for okonomiyaki and the floating torii gate of nearby Miyajima. The Our Daily Story series gave regional Japanese cities their own narrative styling, and Hiroshima is one of the more sober and meaningful entries.
Osaka#576639 · Japan Geography Series / Our Daily StoryThe Our Daily Story Osaka is the modern wordmark over a yellow banded base, the brightest of the set, which suits a city Japanese people call the nation's kitchen. Osaka's real icons are Osaka Castle, the neon Dotonbori canal and its street food, takoyaki and okonomiyaki. The cheerful yellow feels true to Osaka's reputation as the funny, food-loving, fast-talking counterweight to buttoned-up Kyoto and Tokyo.
Nagoya#576642 · Japan Geography Series / Our Daily StoryThe Our Daily Story Nagoya is the minimal wordmark over a brown banded base. Nagoya, Japan's industrial fourth city and the home of Toyota, is best known for Nagoya Castle and its golden shachihoko, the mythical tiger-headed fish that crown the roof. The plain brown base hides all that, which is part of the charm of this line, the city reduced to type and a single color while the drawn mugs do the storytelling.
Kyoto#576644 · Japan Geography Series / Our Daily StoryThe Our Daily Story Kyoto is the spare one, modern wordmark over a black banded base, no temples drawn at all. Kyoto was Japan's imperial capital for over a thousand years and famously escaped WWII bombing, so its roughly two thousand temples and shrines and the Gion geisha district survived intact. The black base feels right for a city this steeped in tradition, quiet where the illustrated Kyoto mugs go ornate.
Yokohama#576646 · Japan Geography Series / Our Daily StoryYokohama in the Our Daily Story style, white inside with the city wrapping the outside above a clean white base. Yokohama grew from a quiet fishing village into Japan's premier international port after Commodore Perry forced it open in 1859, and its modern Minato Mirai waterfront is the usual subject. The pale grounding here keeps the focus on the illustration rather than a dipped color band.
Kobe#576647 · Japan Geography Series / Our Daily StoryPart of the JIMOTO-style Our Daily Story line, this Kobe piece is the clean modern wordmark over a pink-creme banded base. Kobe is the cosmopolitan port on Osaka Bay, opened to the West in 1868, famous for its marbled beef, its jazz roots and the red Port Tower. I like how restrained these Our Daily Story mugs are next to the busier illustrated city editions, all type and a single color block.
Tokyo#576648 · Japan Geography Series / Our Daily StoryTokyo from the Our Daily Story line, white inside with the city rendered above a black creme dipped base. The black band at the foot is the signature of this run, a more illustrative, narrative take than the landmark heavy Global Icons. It reads less like a postcard and more like a page from a sketchbook, which is what makes the Our Daily Story pieces quietly satisfying to collect.
10th Starbucks Coffee JapanJapan & AsiaA tin box marking ten years of Starbucks Coffee Japan, which counts from the 1996 opening of the Ginza store, the company's first location outside North America. That Ginza debut made Japan the launching pad for the entire international expansion, so a tenth anniversary tin from around 2006 is a tidy piece of that origin story. Tins like this often held beans or sweets and survive in fewer numbers than the mugs.
2009 Japan BearJapan & AsiaA 2009 Japan Bear, part of the annual Bearista line that Japan dressed in its own seasonal and regional outfits each year. The yearly bears are a collecting subworld of their own, and the Japan exclusive editions are notably harder to find outside the country than the standard holiday Bearistas. Pinning down a specific year like 2009 fills a real gap in any bear run.
2010 Japan BearJapan & AsiaThe 2010 Japan Bear, the next year in Japan's annual Bearista mascot series, dressed in its own market specific styling. Collectors who chase the bears want unbroken runs, and a 2010 sitting beside the 2009 starts to build exactly that. Japan exclusive bears rarely reach Western shelves at retail, so these usually come through specialty importers or trips abroad.
KyotoJapan & AsiaA Kyoto plastic tumbler rather than a ceramic mug, the everyday travel format of the line. Kyoto is the obvious anchor, the thousand-year capital of golden temples, raked Zen gardens and the lantern-lit lanes of Gion where maiko still hurry to appointments. The plastic tumblers are the workhorses of any Japan collection, easy to overlook but part of the full city run, so it earns its place on the shelf.
Starbucks US and Japan CatalogsJapan & AsiaThis is not a mug but my reference cache of Starbucks US and Japan catalogs, articles and clippings, the paper trail that lets me date and attribute the rest of the collection. Japan's product calendar runs on its own rhythm, with sakura, regional JIMOTO lines and anniversary tumblers that never reach North America, so primary catalog scans are gold for pinning down years and variants.
Classification

Holiday & Ornaments78 pieces

Red cups, dated Joyeux Noel city editions, and the little ceramic ornaments.
Holiday Icon, Transparent Mug#186153 · Holiday & OrnamentsA clear glass holiday mug decorated with the season's shorthand icons, a snowman, candy cane, Christmas tree, and snowflake printed on the outside. The transparent body is the whole point here, it lets the coffee become the backdrop and makes the simple line graphics pop. It is a quieter, more graphic take than the painted city mugs, and the see-through glass dates it to Starbucks' later minimalist holiday styling.
2003, Holiday Collector's Pin Set#186162 · Holiday & OrnamentsThe 2003 Holiday Collector's Pin Set, billed as the 1st Edition, a red presentation case holding three enamel pins, a Teddy Bear, the Last Logo, and a Brown Mug. This is a genuine memorabilia piece rather than drinkware, and the Last Logo pin is the draw since it memorializes the pre-2011 wordmark siren. Complete sets in the original red case turn up on eBay and command real collector interest precisely because loose pins scatter so easily.
2010#186178 · Rosanna MadeThe 2010 holiday 14oz, red with three white birds perched on a golden branch amid white snowflakes and a gold-tipped rim, and crucially it still has its matching red box, which is the detail that separates a good example from an ordinary one. Boxed holiday mugs survive far less often than loose ones, so the intact red box turns this from a common red mug into a properly complete piece.
2009#186180 · Rosanna MadeThe 2009 holiday 14oz, a red mug with a white tree and golden birds over the exterior, part of the partridge-in-a-pear-tree theme that season; collector listings note the inside rim reads roughly Let your heart be light and credit the design to Rosanna. The shift to gold accents here marks the moment Starbucks went fully metallic for the holidays, and the dove-and-tree styling makes it the clear sibling to the 2010 mug.
1999, Pike Place Store, "We Wish Y#186187 · Holiday & OrnamentsA 1999 musical snow globe replica of the original Pike Place store, the very first Starbucks, that plays We Wish You a Merry Christmas. The first store opened in 1971 at 1912 Pike Place and still wears the original brown twin tailed siren logo, which makes any miniature of it a sentimental cornerstone. These 1999 musical globes turn up on the secondary market and the music box still works on most, a real heritage centerpiece for the holiday shelf.
Starbucks Christmas Ornaments#186197 · Holiday & OrnamentsStarbucks launched its Christmas ornament program in 1999, and it quickly became a serious collecting category of its own. Early standouts include the 1999 plastic espresso-machine ornament with chrome-and-black detailing and a red hanger, a piece that now routinely runs around eighty dollars and up on the secondary market. The annual ornaments cover everything from the logo siren to coffee gear, making a multi-year string of them a fun timeline of the brand's holiday design.
3 x Starbucks Ornaments#186211 · Holiday & OrnamentsA trio of Starbucks Christmas tree ornaments, the small hanging collectibles the company has released nearly every holiday season since the mid-2000s. These miniatures, often tiny mugs, cups, or logo discs, are popular precisely because they are cheap to start and endless to chase. Sets that stay together intact, like this group of three, are more desirable to collectors than loose singles.
Santa Monica, City Mug, Charity Ed#455150 · North America Charity Edition (1998/1999)The Santa Monica Charity Edition, part of the 1998 to 1999 sixteen-city North America Charity set, showing the pier, its Ferris wheel, and a man cycling with a surfboard. That wheel is the Pacific Wheel on the Santa Monica Pier, notable as the world's first solar-powered Ferris wheel. As a Charity Edition city, it belongs to a specific intact run collectors prize for being a complete sixteen-piece set.
2011 Holiday Mug (Purple), Mug#455352 · Japan 2011One of the 2011 color-block series, this version pairs a deep purple interior with stylized trees dusted in sprinkle-like dots on the outside. Starbucks issued the same tree-and-sprinkles design across several bold interior colors that year, making them a quiet set to chase. The purple is the harder one to find in the wild, since collectors tend to gravitate to the red.
2011 Holiday Mug (Yellow), Mug#455353 · Japan 2011The yellow member of the 2011 holiday color series, breaking from the tree pattern with a field of multicolored circles over a sunny yellow interior. Yellow is an unusual holiday choice, which is exactly why it stands out on a shelf of reds and greens. The playful dot motif reads almost mid-century modern, a nod to how Starbucks kept experimenting with non-traditional festive palettes.
2011 Holiday Mug (Red), Mug#455354 · Japan 2011The red sibling in the 2011 trees-and-sprinkles trio, with a glossy red interior and the same dotted evergreens marching around the exterior. Red was the anchor color of the set and the most produced, so it is the easy entry point if you want one example of the design. Lining it up beside the purple and yellow shows how a single illustration was recolored to build a collectible family.
Happy Holidays, Chicago 2007#455361 · Happy Holidays 2007A 2007 Chicago holiday mug featuring a stylized drawing of the city's streets over a white interior, part of that year's illustrated city series. The 2007 run paired Chicago with New York and San Francisco using the same hand-drawn streetscape style, so the three form a natural set. Collectors hunt these dated city mugs specifically, and assembling all three 2007 cities in one place is a small trophy.
Happy Holidays, New York 2007#455362 · Happy Holidays 2007The New York entry in the 2007 illustrated holiday city trio, with a drawing of the city's streets wrapping the exterior over a white interior. It shares its hand-sketched style with the Chicago and San Francisco mugs of the same year, the three designed as a coordinated set. New York's version is usually the most chased of the three given the city's pull, so it tends to move fastest on the secondary market.
Happy Holidays, San Francisco 2007#455363 · Happy Holidays 2007The San Francisco piece completing the 2007 illustrated holiday city set, its streets rendered in the same sketched style as the Chicago and New York mugs over a white interior. San Francisco's famously steep, hilly streets make for an especially distinctive drawing in this format. Owning all three 2007 cities together is the goal here, since the line was clearly conceived as a matched trio rather than standalone mugs.
London, Happy Holidays 2010 Mug#455411 · Happy Holidays 2010The 2010 London holiday mug finally goes monumental with the bridge, Tower Bridge, the Victorian bascule-and-suspension landmark from 1894 that tourists perpetually confuse with the plainer London Bridge. After two years of buses, the pivot to architecture closes my London trio on a grand note. The Gothic towers are unmistakably London, which is exactly why Starbucks reached for them.
Abstract Holiday Decorations, Mug#455412 · Made by Deborah ReinhartA more artful entry in the holiday line, with abstract painterly decorations brushed across the exterior over a clean white interior. Rather than literal snowmen or ornaments, it leans into loose, modern strokes, the kind of design that reads as festive without being kitschy. Pieces like this show Starbucks occasionally handing the holiday brief to a more contemporary illustrative sensibility.
Holiday Quadrant (2000), Mug#455415 · Holiday & OrnamentsAnother 2000 holiday mug, this one divided into four little vignettes of seasonal cheer wrapped around the cup, white inside, art outside. The quadrant layout is unusual, most holiday mugs commit to one scene, so getting four mini drawings on a single body makes it a charming oddity. It sits right in that era when Starbucks holiday art was all loose pencil illustration rather than slick graphics.
New York, Happy Holidays 2009 Mug#455433 · Happy Holidays 2009For 2009 New York got its signature icon, the Statue of Liberty, here surrounded by falling snowflakes for the season. Bartholdi's copper colossus, dedicated in 1886 and a gift from France, is the single most New York image Starbucks could have chosen. The jump from the generic 2008 tree mug to Lady Liberty shows the holiday city line maturing into real landmark design year by year.
12Oz Falala Ceramic Travel Mug 2011 Holiday#455449 · Japan 2011The 2011 holiday Fa La La ceramic travel mug, 12 ounces, purple inside with stylized trees and bright sprinkles outside. This was part of Starbucks' 2011 Fa La La campaign, a candy bright, slightly retro holiday look that broke from the usual deep reds. As a ceramic travel mug rather than a standard cup, it sits in that hybrid category collectors like, equal parts ornament and everyday lidded cup.
2011 Holiday Season, Mug, Green Mi#455450 · Japan 2011Catalogued in the 2011 Holiday Season run, this piece carries the multicolored circles on a yellow interior, the same playful confetti styling that ran through that year's lineup. The green mistletoe accent ties it to the broader seasonal set while keeping the bright, modern dot pattern. It is a good example of how Starbucks mixed and matched motifs across a single holiday season.
The 12 days of Christmas, Mug#455457 · Holiday & OrnamentsA holiday mug that runs the classic Twelve Days of Christmas carol in gold lettering, here in deep yellow with a black ribbon band across the top. Starbucks gave the old tune a coffee-house twist, and the design appeared across several sizes and years, so collectors track the variants by size and interior color. Long retired now, the Twelve Days mugs are steady sellers on the resale market and a witty alternative to the usual snowflake fare.
Candy Cane Holiday, Mug#455460 · JapanA cheerful candy-cane mug, with two striped canes tied in green ribbon flanking each side over a white interior. The candy cane is a holiday staple said to date to 17th-century Europe, and its red-and-white stripe is instantly readable as Christmas. The symmetric two-sided layout means it looks the same from either hand, a small but satisfying design choice.
Holiday Presents (2000), Mug#455462 · Holiday & OrnamentsFrom the 2000 holiday line, when Starbucks' winter theme leaned into hand-drawn whimsy, this one stacks a cream-colored present box with loose black pencil sketches floating over a red ground. The deliberately rough, doodled look is the tell of that turn-of-the-millennium run. Y2K holiday pieces are a fun niche to chase precisely because the art was so loose and illustrative compared to the polished mugs that came later.
2011 Birds and Holiday Ornaments,#455463 · Holiday & OrnamentsPart of Starbucks' 2011 holiday run, this one plays a clean color reversal: a red bird and ornament tucked on the white interior, with white birds and ornaments scattered across the outside. I love the inside-out conceit, where the surprise lives at the lip rather than the body. The bird motif was a recurring theme that season, a quieter alternative to the usual snowmen and reindeer.
2001 Holiday Boxes, Mug#455474 · Holiday & OrnamentsThe 2001 Holiday Boxes mug, white inside with a wrap of red themed Christmas gift boxes. The stacked present motif was the friendly, gift giving theme Starbucks ran that season, warm and graphic rather than landmark driven. Dated holiday mugs like this are how I track the brand's seasonal art year by year, and 2001 sits right at the start of the consistent annual holiday mug tradition.
Winter (2009), Mug#455475 · Holiday & OrnamentsThe Winter 2009 mug, a warm bronze-and-brown design with a white reindeer striding across a field scattered with coffee beans, white inside. The coffee-bean snowfall is the clever touch here, tying the wintry scene straight back to the product in the cup. As a dated single-year release it anchors nicely in a chronological holiday run, and the earthy palette sets it apart from the brand's brighter red-and-blue winters.
Santa on Piano, Mug#455495 · Holiday & OrnamentsA cozy white-interior holiday mug showing Santa at the piano with kids peeping in from outside, a warm bit of seasonal storytelling on ceramic. Starbucks built its winter program around these illustrated story-scene mugs that change every year, which is exactly why collectors chase the full run. The peeking-children detail makes it read like a single frame from a Christmas card rather than a generic snowflake print.
Home for the Holidays (1), Mug#455496 · Made by Mary GraveaThe first in a small "Home for the Holidays" pair, this mug carries a drawing of wrapped Christmas presents and a toy train, the classic under-the-tree imagery of a 1990s American Christmas morning. The train especially nods to the old tradition of a model railroad circling the tree. Paired with its sibling mug it forms a tidy two-piece set, which is exactly how I like to keep them.
Home for the Holidays (2), Mug#455498 · Made by Mary GraveaThe companion to the first "Home for the Holidays" mug, this one swaps presents and trains for a drawing of winged angels, the more reverent side of the holiday. Buying the pair together is the move, since split sets lose half their charm and collectors notice. The matched-but-different artwork across the two is a nice example of Starbucks designing holiday mugs to be collected as a story, not just one-offs.
2003 Holiday Mug (Red)#455568 · 2003.0The red anchor of the 2003 three-color holiday set, classic Christmas red inside and out with cut-out snowflake shapes patterning the body and the period-correct square bottom. Red is always the easiest of any holiday trio to find since Starbucks made the most of them, so it is the one you buy last and the colored siblings, green and purple, are the ones that actually finish the set.
2003 Holiday Mug (Green)#455569 · 2003.0Part of the cheerful 2003 trio Starbucks issued in three colorways, this is the green one, green inside and out with sketched Christmas trees and a wrapped-present motif marching around the body on a square base. I like that the 2003 set was clearly meant to be collected as a family, so chasing the matching green, purple and red is half the fun and the green is usually the wallflower of the three.
2003 Holiday Mug (Purple)#455570 · 2003.0The purple member of the 2003 holiday set, and the most unusual color Starbucks committed to that year, purple inside and out with snowflakes and little snowmen circling the exterior over a square bottom. Purple is the sleeper of the three colorways because it photographs oddly and many collectors simply forget it exists, which is exactly why I went hunting for it to complete the green-purple-red run.
2002 Holiday Mug (Red)#455571 · 2002.0The red 2002 holiday mug, red inside and out with candy cane shapes and the same square bottom as its green partner. The matched square footed pair is the thing to chase here, since collectors prize having both the red candy cane and the green tree and menorah versions together. Candy cane motifs are classic Starbucks holiday shorthand, and a crisp red example completes that 2002 set nicely.
2002 Holiday Mug (Green)#455572 · 2002.0The green 2002 holiday mug, green inside and out, with Christmas trees and a Hanukkiah and a distinctive square bottom. I love that this one is openly inclusive, pairing the menorah with the trees, a small but pointed bit of holiday design. The square base is the structural tell that pairs it with its red 2002 sibling, and together they make a clean two mug set from that season.
2012 Holiday Season, Mug#455586 · Holiday & OrnamentsA storybook 2012 piece: a nutcracker flanked by ornaments and a pigeon over a red exterior, with pine accents decorating the white interior. The nutcracker is a classic Christmas icon rooted in 19th-century German tradition and the Tchaikovsky ballet, so it is a fitting centerpiece. The interior pine detailing is the quiet bonus you discover only after the first sip.
2011 Holiday Mug#455617 · Holiday & OrnamentsA genuinely charming 2011 scene: children skating behind a dog pulling a sled, wrapped around a crisp white interior, with a tiny airplane painted right onto the handle. That handle detail is the kind of thing you only notice when you pick it up, and it is exactly why this one rewards a close look. The whimsical narrative style was typical of Starbucks' early-2010s holiday illustration.
2005 Magical Holiday, Mug#455619 · Holiday & OrnamentsThe 2005 Magical Holiday mug, a candy cane printed over the white interior with the full red, white and green holiday palette wrapping the exterior. The candy-cane-inside detail is a charming touch you only notice when you tip it toward you, the kind of small reward Starbucks built into these so the holiday surprise wasn't only on the outside.
2004, Holiday Season, Red Mug#455647 · Holiday & OrnamentsA 2004 holiday-season red mug, red inside with bronze metallic snowflakes scattered across the red exterior, an early taste of the gold-and-bronze accenting Starbucks would lean hard into by 2009 and 2010. The bronze-on-red is more restrained and warmer than the later bright-gold treatments, which makes this a nice bridge piece showing where the holiday palette was heading.
2001, Holiday Limited edition, Mug#455650 · Holiday & OrnamentsA 2001 Holiday Limited Edition mug showing a drawn Main Street scene with Santa trying to slip into the shop. The little narrative vignette, Santa caught mid mischief at the storefront, gives this far more personality than a plain pattern mug, and the limited edition tag is what pushes it up the desirability ladder. It is the kind of storytelling piece that rewards being picked up and turned around to read.
Snowman (2012), Mug#455685 · Holiday & OrnamentsThe 2012 winking snowman in his dark blue hat and deep red scarf over a soft grey body, one of Starbucks' most recognizable holiday characters of that decade. This is the standard regular mug version of the design, the white-interior sibling to the red venti released the same season. Collectors note the winking snowman appeared across mugs and tumblers that winter, making the matched set a fun chase.
2012 Holiday Mug#455694 · Holiday & OrnamentsA festive 2012 design with white and gold ornaments hanging down from the rim against a rich red exterior, over a white interior. The suspended-ornament composition gives it real depth, as if the baubles dangle into the cup. Gold accents were a recurring premium touch in Starbucks' 2012 holiday range, lending this one a slightly dressier feel than the matte color-block mugs of the prior year.
Christmas Blend, Mug#455729 · Holiday & OrnamentsA mug built around the Christmas Blend stamp, celebrating Starbucks' signature seasonal coffee. Christmas Blend launched in 1984 and famously features aged Sumatra beans, prized for their deep, spicy character, blended with Latin American and Asia/Pacific coffees. A mug that puts the blend's own emblem front and center is a nice nod for anyone who treats the holiday coffee, not just the cup, as the main event.
Snowman Venti (2012)#455803 · Holiday & OrnamentsThe bold red venti companion to the 2012 snowman line, the same winking fellow in his dark red scarf and blue hat but set against a striking red field instead of grey. The red colorway is the showier of the two and the one that pops on a shelf, which is why collectors like to display the red venti and the grey regular side by side. New-with-tags examples still surface on the secondary market, a sign of how many were made and squirreled away.
2004 Holiday (Creme)#455806 · 2004.0A large 18oz mug from the 2004 holiday season in a soft cream rather than red, lettered Ho Ho Ho beneath a snowflake on the white interior with snowflakes scattered across the creme exterior and the square base of the era. The off-white colorway makes it one of the gentler 2004 pieces, an easy one to mistake for a plain winter mug until you spot the dated Ho Ho Ho detail that pins it firmly to that year.
2002 Holiday, Dark Blue#455834 · 2002.0This big 18oz survivor from the 2002 holiday run is one of the moodier reds-and-greens rebellions Starbucks pulled, going deep navy instead of the usual scarlet, with a blue snowflake floating over the white interior and a field of snowflakes wrapping the dark blue exterior. The squared bottom is the early-2000s tell. Blue holiday pieces tend to hide in collections because everyone files them under generic winter, so dated 2002 examples are easy to overlook and pleasant to land.
2004, Holiday Swirl#455864 · Holiday & OrnamentsThe 2004 Holiday Swirl, a 16oz mug with a white interior and the full spread of holiday colors swirling around the outside, the most playful and least conventional of that year's lineup. The swirl pattern broke from the usual snowflake-and-present formula entirely, so it stands out on a shelf of dated holiday mugs as the one that traded tradition for pure color.
2004, Holiday Gifts, Mug#455869 · Holiday & OrnamentsFrom the 2004 holiday run, a clean white-interior mug with loose sketched presents drawn over a red exterior, the gift-wrap theme that tied much of that year together. I like the hand-drawn, almost doodled present sketches here, a softer illustrative style than the embossed and metallic looks Starbucks leaned into later in the decade, which makes 2004 feel like a distinct little design moment.
2008 Holiday (#455977 · Holiday & OrnamentsThe 2008 Holiday 16oz, a red mug with the Starbucks logo set among white snowflakes and a dove or pigeon worked into the design over the red exterior. The bird motif quietly foreshadows the partridge-and-dove direction the holiday line took in 2009 and 2010, so this sits as the start of a little three-year avian streak that is genuinely fun to line up side by side.
2007 Holiday (#455978 · Holiday & OrnamentsThe 2007 Holiday 16oz, a tall red mug carrying the Starbucks logo amid white snowflakes with an ice-skating scene circling the body, from the season Starbucks themed Pass the Cheer. The skaters make this one of the more narrative holiday designs of the decade, a little winter vignette rather than a pattern, and 2007 produced a whole family of red mugs so confirming the skater version pins down exactly which one you are holding.
2012 Christmas Green with stars#576032 · Holiday & OrnamentsThe green counterpart to the 2012 blue starry mug, a dark forest green dotted with white stars in the compact 12oz format. Starbucks loved releasing these in matched color pairs, and owning both blue and green completes the little constellation set. The restrained palette makes it one of the more tasteful holiday pieces from that year, the kind you would actually keep out year-round.
2012 Christmas Blue with stars#576034 · Holiday & OrnamentsA clean, minimalist 2012 holiday mug: a deep midnight blue body scattered with white stars, in the smaller 12oz size. It trades the usual busy holiday illustration for a calm night-sky feel, which is why it pairs so naturally with its green twin from the same release. The understated design has aged well and looks more like a modern winter piece than a dated novelty.
2010 Paris, Joyeux Noel, Christmas#576057 · Holiday & OrnamentsThe 2010 Paris Joyeux Noel, a 16oz red mug with a gold-trimmed Eiffel Tower and Arc de Triomphe and the French Merry Christmas greeting, a dated city-specific holiday piece that crosses my holiday and city interests at once. This is the standout of the batch and a genuinely sought-after one, with a complete example having sold around the $335 mark, reflecting how rare dated city holiday mugs from a single market like Paris actually are.
London, Happy Holidays 2009 Mug#576629 · Happy Holidays 2009London's 2009 entry keeps the red bus but now sets it rolling in front of a row of city buildings, giving the scene more depth than the standalone 2008 version. Lining the two side by side, you can watch the designers add context year over year. The double-decker remains the anchor, and as the middle mug in my 2008 to 2010 London run it is the connective tissue of the set.
Paris, Happy Holidays 2009 Mug#576630 · Happy Holidays 2009The 2009 Paris holiday mug pictures the Champs-Élysées, the grand avenue running from the Place de la Concorde up to the Arc de Triomphe, which at Christmas is famously strung with lights end to end. Choosing the boulevard over the Eiffel Tower is a lovely, slightly insider pick, it captures how Parisians actually experience the holidays. The avenue's name means "Elysian Fields," a nod to paradise in Greek myth.
Seattle, Happy Holidays 2008 Mug#576632 · Happy Holidays 2008A 2008 city holiday mug pairing Starbucks' Seattle home base with a festive Happy Holidays band, the outside carrying a merry-go-round carousel motif. The dated city-specific holiday mugs are a quiet favorite among collectors precisely because they marry a place to a year, so a Seattle one from the company's own hometown carries extra sentimental weight. The 16oz grande size and 2008 date make it easy to slot into a chronological holiday shelf.
Chicago, Happy Holidays 2008 Mug#576633 · Happy Holidays 2008A 2008 Chicago holiday mug, 16oz, built around the city's famous Magnificent Mile sign, the upscale Michigan Avenue shopping stretch lined with landmarks like the Wrigley Building and the old Water Tower. Chicago was a recurring star of Starbucks' dated city holiday mugs, and this Magnificent Mile motif appeared across several years from 2006 onward, making the year stamp the key detail for collectors sorting the run.
London, Happy Holidays 2008 Mug#576634 · Happy Holidays 2008The 2008 London holiday mug puts the city's most recognizable icon front and center, the red Routemaster double-decker bus, a vehicle so tied to London that it stayed in service from 1956 well into the 2000s. It is a smart shorthand for the city without resorting to Big Ben for once. This is the first of three consecutive London holiday mugs I have, 2008, 2009, and 2010, so the trio together tells a nice year-over-year story.
Hawaii, Happy Holidays 2008 Mug#576635 · Happy Holidays 2008Part of the 2008 Happy Holidays city run, this one greets you in Hawaiian, since "Mele Kalikimaka" is simply Merry Christmas rendered in the islands' phonics, a phrase Bing Crosby made famous in 1949. I love that a December mug skips the snow entirely and leans into a palm-and-sunshine Christmas. The white interior and outside-only printing match the standard 16oz format of that holiday series.
San Francisco, Happy Holidays 2008#576636 · Happy Holidays 2008San Francisco's 2008 holiday mug carries the same Christmas tree and snowflakes as the New York 2008, confirming Starbucks reused a single festive design across multiple cities in that year's run. That shared artwork is a small collector tell worth knowing, the city name is doing the differentiating, not the picture. Snow on a San Francisco mug is its own quiet joke, since the city almost never sees any.
New York, Happy Holidays 2008 Mug#576637 · Happy Holidays 2008New York's 2008 holiday mug stays general with a Christmas tree and drifting snowflakes rather than a specific skyline, evoking the Rockefeller Center tree mood without naming it. It is the city pair to my San Francisco 2008, which uses the identical tree-and-snowflake motif, a sign Starbucks shared artwork across the 2008 holiday city run. The following year's New York mug got far more specific, which makes this one feel like the warm-up.
1997, Starbucks Christmas Sample,Holiday & OrnamentsA 1997 Starbucks Christmas sample tin, the kind of seasonal packaging that held coffee or chocolate samples for the holidays. Tins from the 1990s are easy to overlook and easy to lose, since they were meant to be emptied and tossed, which is exactly why an intact dated 1997 box has quiet value as a time capsule of how Starbucks merchandised Christmas before the mug machine really took over.
1997, Starbucks, Holiday Tin BoxHoliday & OrnamentsA second 1997 holiday tin, the standard seasonal storage and gift box from that Christmas. These nineteen nineties tins are among the most fragile survivors in any collection because the lithographed lids dent and the seasonal print fades, so a clean pair from the same year is a small archival win. They ground the holiday run in its pre 2000 roots, before the dated city mugs arrived.
2003 Snowman WhiteHoliday & OrnamentsA 15oz white snowman mug from Starbucks Barista's 2003 winter line, part of a stylized snowman series the brand ran as winter-long rather than strictly Christmas pieces. These came in a pair and sometimes a quartet with present-shaped companions, and collectors note the sculptural look on the handle. The plain white version is the everyday one of the set, which makes finding the matching blue more satisfying.
2003, City Mug, Ornament SetHoliday & OrnamentsA 2003 boxed set of miniature City Mug ornaments, Starbucks shrinking its flagship city line down to hangable keepsakes for the tree. These ornament sets are a quiet favorite among city-mug people because they let you nod to the full-size series in miniature, and intact boxed sets with all the little mugs present are far scarcer than any single loose ornament.
2003, Holiday Collectors Pin Set (Holiday & OrnamentsA second cataloged instance of the 2003 Holiday Collector's Pin Set 1st Edition, the same red-case trio of Teddy Bear, Last Logo and Brown Mug enamel pins. Having a duplicate listing is useful because pin sets are notorious for arriving incomplete, so a backup case means you can keep one sealed and one open for display without breaking up a complete first-edition set.
2003, Snowman BlueHoliday & OrnamentsThe blue counterpart to the 2003 white snowman, same 15oz Barista winter design with the stylized snowman motif but in the harder-to-pair blue colorway. Starbucks meant these snowman mugs to be a coordinated set you displayed together all season, so the blue is the one that actually completes the pairing and tends to lag behind its white twin on the secondary market.
2004, Green Wrap Christmas PresentHoliday & OrnamentsA 12oz mug from the 2004 holiday line wrapped in a green Christmas-present motif, the smaller everyday size that paired with the larger reds of that season. The compact 12oz format is the kind of thing collectors undervalue at the shelf and then struggle to find later, since the bigger statement mugs got saved while the little ones got used, chipped and tossed.
2011 Snowman, MugHoliday & OrnamentsA 2011 holiday mug built around the most enduring winter character of all, the snowman, that season's friendliest face in the Starbucks lineup. Snowman designs reappear almost every holiday year, which makes dating them by subtle styling cues part of the fun for a collector. This one sits comfortably alongside the skating-children and bird mugs as part of that warm, illustrative 2011 family.
Happy Holidays Bear (Place image iHoliday & OrnamentsA novelty Happy Holidays piece designed as a photo ornament, with a clear ball meant to hold your own image, fronted by a Starbucks bear. These personalize-it ornaments were a fun holiday gimmick, turning a mass-produced collectible into something custom for the tree. The Bearista-style bear mascot ties it to Starbucks' long-running bear collectibles, making it a crossover between the holiday and bear lines.
Holiday BearHoliday & OrnamentsA Bearista from the holiday run, the annual Christmas bear that Starbucks has dressed up every winter since the mid 1990s. Collectors track these by year and costume, and the festive editions, scarves, Santa suits, knitwear, are the ones that move fastest secondhand. Without the box or hangtag the exact year is hard to pin, so I keep mine grouped with its holiday siblings.
Holiday Santa Bear with Baby BearHoliday & OrnamentsA two-bear holiday Bearista, the big Santa-suited bear cradling a little cub, which is one of the sweeter pairings in the annual Christmas line. These mother-and-cub or Santa-and-baby configurations tend to be the keepers collectors hang onto rather than flip. I value it as much for the storytelling as the plush, it reads like a tiny winter scene on a shelf.
Santa (or elf?) BearHoliday & OrnamentsA red-suited holiday Bearista that could read as either Santa or one of his elves depending on the year's costume details. The annual Christmas bears are released in tight runs and identified by their outfits, so an ambiguous Santa-or-elf is exactly the kind of piece that needs its hangtag to settle the debate. I keep it filed with the holiday bears and enjoy that the costume keeps people guessing.
Santa Barbara, City Mug, CollectorHoliday & OrnamentsA Santa Barbara City Mug Collector Series piece, the older flagship line that devotes one mug to a single place. Santa Barbara is the "American Riviera," known for its red-tile-roofed Spanish Colonial architecture, the 1786 Mission Santa Barbara, and Stearns Wharf on the Pacific. The Collector Series format, one city, band of local imagery, is the classic Starbucks mug DNA that everything later built on.
Santa BearHoliday & OrnamentsThe classic Santa Bearista, the red-and-white Santa-suited version of Starbucks' annual Christmas bear. These holiday bears anchor the whole Bearista tradition that runs back to 1997, and the Santa editions are the most instantly recognizable of the bunch. As with all of them, the exact year lives on the tag, so I treat mine as the archetypal holiday bear of the set.
Santa Monica, City Mug, CollectorHoliday & OrnamentsThe Collector Series companion to my Santa Monica Charity mug, the older single-city flagship treatment of the beach town at the end of Route 66. Santa Monica is defined by its 1909 pier, the Pacific Park amusement deck, and that solar Ferris wheel. Having both the Collector and Charity editions of one city is a nice completist pairing, since they capture the same place through two different Starbucks programs.
Snowman Bear with PuppyHoliday & OrnamentsA holiday Bearista dressed in a snowman costume and cradling a little puppy, one of the themed seasonal bears Starbucks layered on top of its annual plush program. Costume Bearistas like this read as miniature dioramas rather than plain bears, and the added puppy companion is the kind of small extra that makes a single figure stand out on the shelf. These character bears were sold only in the holiday window, so survivors with the pairing intact are the ones worth holding.
Snowman Costume BearHoliday & OrnamentsA Bearista zipped into a full snowman suit, complete with the costume hood, part of Starbucks' tradition of dressing its annual bear up for the winter season. The fun of the costume bears is that the familiar plush silhouette peeks out from inside the outfit, so you are really collecting the bear and the holiday character at once. As a seasonal release it only appeared for one Christmas run, which is what keeps these in demand.
White Bird with Ornament, DemitassHoliday & OrnamentsA small holiday demitasse showing a white bird perched with an ornament, one of the petite seasonal cups Starbucks tucked into its Christmas lineup. Demitasse pieces are the easy-to-miss corner of holiday collecting, sold in smaller numbers than the full mugs and quick to disappear once the season ends. The delicate bird-and-ornament motif gives it the feel of a tiny ornament you can actually drink from.
Classification

Bearista Bears77 pieces

The bear mascots, novelty editions by the dozen.
Bearista Back To School Bear#576361 · Bearista BearsA Back to School themed Bearista, catalogued here on a regular mug format, marking the late-summer seasonal slot when stores leaned into the new school year. The back-to-school window was one of the lighter, non-holiday occasions Starbucks used to keep fresh bears coming, and those off-calendar themes are less commonly hunted, which can make them sleepers. The schoolhouse styling sets it apart from the heavier Christmas releases.
Bear, 2010 Mug#576710 · Bearista BearsNot a plush at all but a 2010 ceramic mug, white inside with a brown-creme exterior and a Bearista bear printed on the outside. It is a fun crossover where the mascot jumps off the shelf and onto drinkware, which is why it lives with the bears rather than the city mugs. The warm cream-and-brown palette ties it visually to the coffee itself.
1998 Starbucks Bearona Bear#734001 · Barista BearsBearona is one of the great early Bearista stories, introduced for Valentine's Day 1998 and named as a pun on Starbucks' Caffe Verona blend. The roughly ten-inch bear wears a distinctive maroon apron that flags it as a genuine early-days piece, and collectors single it out as one of the more sought-after vintage Bearistas. Confirming that maroon apron is the quick test of authenticity when one turns up on the secondary market.
