Classification

Anniversary & Heritage26 pieces

Anniversary mugs, demitasse and first-logo pieces.
2014, Korea's 15 years anniversary#186205 · Anniversary & HeritageA set of four coasters celebrating 15 years of Starbucks in Korea, issued in 2014 for the anniversary of the 1999 Ehwa Womans University opening. Coaster sets are an underrated corner of heritage collecting, easy to lose or split up, so finding the full intact group of four is the real win here. Korea's anniversary merchandise is famously coveted, and a complete coaster quartet is a tidy, displayable piece of that fervor.
1996 Starbucks Pike Place Market 2#186240 · Anniversary & HeritageA 1996 memorabilia piece, a painting commemorating 25 years of Starbucks. The company opened at Pike Place Market in 1971, so 1996 was the genuine silver anniversary, and tying the celebration to the original market store roots it in the real birthplace of the brand. Heritage items keyed to that founding location carry extra weight because Pike Place is where the whole story began, on the cobblestones of Seattle's oldest farmers market.
Starbucks Indonesia, 9th Anniversa#455344 · Anniversary & HeritageStarbucks opened in Indonesia in 2002, so this 9th-anniversary cup lands around 2011, white inside with the green logo paired to a pink coffee-anniversary mark outside. Indonesia matters more than most to Starbucks, it is the source of the famous Sumatra and the Aged Sumatra beans, so an Indonesian anniversary piece carries real bean-country weight. Country-anniversary mugs like this were sold locally and seldom exported, which keeps them genuinely scarce abroad.
Taiwan 15th Anniversary#455384 · Anniversary & HeritageStarbucks reached Taiwan in 1998, so this 15th-anniversary cup is a 2013 release, white inside with a little cupcake motif and a confetti of ornaments over white and blue outside. Taiwan was Starbucks' joint venture with President Group and grew into one of Asia's strongest markets, which is why its milestone mugs got such celebratory party-themed art. The cupcake-and-ornament treatment makes this read like an actual birthday cup, charming and very on-theme.
Taiwan 15th Anniversary, Yellow Mu#455386 · Anniversary & HeritageThe yellow-interior variant of Taiwan's 2013 fifteenth-anniversary release, this one trading the party confetti for delicate brown tree branches across a white body. Running a single anniversary as two distinct designs is classic Starbucks Asia, they love giving collectors a matched pair to hunt rather than one cup. I always go for both halves of a set like this, since the yellow inside is the detail that proves you have the harder variant.
Thailand 15 years anniversary#455583 · Anniversary & HeritageStarbucks opened in Thailand in 1998, making this 16oz cup a 2013 fifteen-year marker, orange inside with a blue body carrying an elephant and a map of Thailand. The elephant is no accident, it is Thailand's national animal and a sacred symbol woven through Thai history and royalty. That map-and-elephant combination makes this one of the more openly patriotic anniversary mugs in the whole heritage run, and the warm orange interior gives it real shelf presence.
Roppongi Hills, 13th Anniversary#455584 · Japan 2016The 2016 follow-up, marking 13 years of Roppongi Hills, again with that loose abstract painting of the district wrapping the cup. Roppongi Hills is anchored by the 54-story Mori Tower and Maman, Louise Bourgeois's giant bronze spider crouched at its base, one of Tokyo's most photographed sculptures. Owning the 12th and 13th back to back is the kind of consecutive-year run that makes a Japan shelf feel complete rather than random.
Roppongi Hills, 12th Anniversary#455668 · Japan 2015Made in 2015 for the 12th anniversary of Roppongi Hills, the Mori Building megacomplex that opened in 2003 and reshaped this corner of Tokyo's Minato ward into a city-within-a-city of shops, offices and the Mori Art Museum up top. The outside is an abstract painted impression of the neighborhood rather than a literal skyline. These Roppongi Hills anniversary pieces are Japan-exclusive and turn up rarely outside Asia, which is exactly why I went after it.
10 Year Anniversary#455713 · Anniversary & HeritageA heritage piece marking ten years, white inside with two cups pictured on the exterior toasting the milestone. Starbucks built a whole tradition of anniversary mugs to mark a decade in a given market or for the company itself, and the two-cups motif reads as a literal toast to the occasion. These commemoratives are the backbone of a heritage shelf, each one a small dated record of how far the company had come.
2006, Starbucks 35th Anniversary#455897 · Anniversary & HeritageThe 2006 35th-anniversary mug, white inside with a brown siren shown holding a cup wrapped around the outside in shimmering bronze. Released for the company's 35 years since 1971, it is widely cataloged as a first-edition collectible and still trades affordably, often in the eight-to-twenty-dollar range. The split-tail mermaid rendered in copper tones makes it one of the more handsome anniversary mugs, a clean centerpiece for any heritage grouping.
2014 Anniversary Mug (270 ml)#576021 · Anniversary & HeritageA 2014 anniversary mug, 270ml, with a brown siren set against a deep turquoise ground. The turquoise-and-brown palette is a knowing nod, turquoise being the modern brand color and brown the founding 1971 logo tone, so the design literally bridges old and new Starbucks. At espresso-cup scale it is a tidy heritage piece, the kind of dated commemorative that quietly documents another year on the timeline.
14th Anniversary of Starbucks in K#576027 · Anniversary & HeritageA grey and blue mug marking fourteen years of Starbucks in Korea, decorated with stars and a temple motif that nods to Korean heritage. Starbucks opened its first Korean store at Ehwa Womans University in July 1999, so a 14th-anniversary piece lands around 2013. Korea runs an unusually deep and devoted Starbucks collector culture, which makes their dated anniversary mugs some of the more sought-after regional commemoratives out there.
2014 15th Anniversary in Korea#576035 · Anniversary & HeritageA 12oz white mug with a golden handle marking 15 years of Starbucks in Korea, with the anniversary stats printed on the outside. Counting from the 1999 Ehwa opening, this lands squarely in 2014. The gold handle is a deliberate premium touch, and Korea's fiercely active collector scene means these dated commemoratives get chased hard, so a clean 15th-year piece is a genuinely satisfying regional grab.
Retro Starbucks 2014 Anniversary#576048 · Anniversary & HeritageThe 2014 Anniversary mug, a white 14oz piece carrying the retro mermaid in the copper-toned Anniversary palette Starbucks revives each fall for the brand's founding. The Anniversary Collection leans hard on heritage, dusting off the older siren art in metallic finishes you do not see the rest of the year. A clean, quietly handsome cup, and being a dated anniversary release it dates itself permanently, which I always appreciate in a collection.
1996 Starbucks Pike Place Market 25Th AnniAnniversary & HeritageAnother 1996 Pike Place Market 25th-anniversary heritage piece, marking the silver milestone since the 1971 founding at Seattle's Pike Place. The market itself dates to 1907 and is the oldest continuously operating farmers market in the United States, which gives any Starbucks piece anchored there a double layer of history. Twenty-fifth-anniversary memorabilia is a satisfying find precisely because it captures the brand right before its late-1990s global explosion.
2004, First Logo, DemitasseAnniversary & HeritageA tiny 3oz demitasse from 2004 carrying the original 1971 Starbucks logo, the brown twin-tailed siren that predates the familiar green mark. That first siren was fuller and more uninhibited than the modern crop, and Starbucks has reissued it on heritage merchandise to honor its Pike Place beginnings. Demitasse minis like this are a favorite of mine because they pack the full early-logo story into an espresso-sized footprint.
2007, First Logo in brownAnniversary & HeritageA 16oz mug from 2007 carrying the original brown 1971 logo, the unrestrained twin-tailed siren in her earliest form. Starbucks leaned into nostalgia in the mid-2000s by putting that founding mark on heritage drinkware, a tribute to the Pike Place store where it all started. The larger 16oz format makes this a daily-driver-sized piece, which is rarer in heritage lines that usually skew toward smaller commemorative sizes.
2010, First Logo in brownAnniversary & HeritageA 2010 mug in the 12oz size, again wearing the original brown 1971 siren logo. This came right as Starbucks was preparing its big 2011 fortieth-anniversary rebrand that dropped the wordmark entirely, so these late first-logo heritage pieces sit at a real turning point in the company's visual history. I like having both the 16oz and 12oz brown-logo mugs side by side, since the size pairing tells the heritage story across a couple of years.
2014 Korea S 15 Years Anniversary CommemorAnniversary & HeritageA 2014 commemorative marking Korea's 15 years of Starbucks, counting from the July 1999 first store at Ehwa Womans University. Korea's Starbucks fandom is one of the most intense in the world, with anniversary collections selling out fast, which makes their dated heritage pieces real prizes for collectors who reach beyond the US releases. This one rounds out the Korean fifteen-year set nicely.
Barista Bear With Brown Apron Of 1971Anniversary & HeritageA Barista Bear wearing the brown grocer's apron of 1971, a direct nod to Starbucks' earliest days. When the first store opened that year, employees wore plain brown aprons that matched both the coffee beans and the original brown siren logo, before the switch to the now-iconic green apron in 1987. That little brown apron makes this bear a genuine heritage tribute, dressing the friendly mascot in the very first uniform Starbucks ever wore.
Brown Mug, First LogoAnniversary & HeritageThis is Starbucks wearing its 1971 face, the original brown mark with the bare-breasted, twin-tailed Norse siren that company lore traces to a 16th century woodcut. They picked brown deliberately, the color of roasted beans, back when the shop on Western Avenue sold coffee, tea and spices and nothing was poured to go. I love that this design predates the green logo entirely, a reminder that the mermaid was wilder and stranger before the lawyers tamed her.
Brown Mug, First Logo (2010)Anniversary & HeritageA 2010 reissue of that first brown siren, sold mostly out of the original Pike Place store as a heritage piece for tourists making the pilgrimage. The split-tail mermaid is faithful to the 1971 art, though by this era she is reproduced cleanly rather than from the rough old woodcut. Worth knowing the difference, an actual vintage example and a 2010 repro can look near identical at a glance but sit in very different value brackets.
First Logo Ribbon Dark BrownAnniversary & HeritageThe deep-brown variant of the heritage first-logo cup, the full circular ribbon reading STARBUCKS COFFEE TEA SPICES wrapped around the original twin-tailed siren. That outer ring is the giveaway of the earliest mark, a banner borrowed straight from the 1971 storefront sign. The darker chocolate glaze on this one reads warmer and older than the standard issue, exactly the kind of subtle finish difference collectors chase across the heritage run.
Starbucks Original Crown 2000 MugAnniversary & HeritageThe copyright-2000 issue of the original siren, the version where she still wears her full star crown and shows the twin tails before later redesigns cropped and zoomed in on her. The 2000 dating ties it to the era when Starbucks was rolling its heritage imagery onto retail ceramics in earnest. A nice anchor piece, the crowned, full-figure mermaid is the design purists point to as the truest descendant of the 1971 original.
Starbucks Original Crown MugAnniversary & HeritageThe undated companion to the crown mug, the original siren in her starred crown, two tails fanned out, rendered as a heritage tribute rather than a city or anniversary piece. What I like is how it isolates her, no ribbon of text crowding the design, just the mermaid that has been the company's heart since Pike Place. A good baseline cup for understanding how every later logo on this shelf is a simplification of this one.
Winking Mermaid MugAnniversary & HeritageThe 2013 Winking Siren, the year Starbucks gave the mermaid a cheeky one-eyed wink for its anniversary, produced in bone china and a sculpted embossed-tail variant too. It was a genuine break from the always-serene siren, a rare moment of the brand letting her show personality. Collectors note the plain printed version and the embossed-tail version as two separate things to chase, and the winking face remains one of the most recognizable one-off siren treatments out there.
Classification

Relief Series44 pieces

Raised, sculpted city designs you can feel.
Sabah#576650 · Relief Series 2013Sabah anchors the northern tip of Malaysian Borneo, where Mount Kinabalu, the highest peak in the country, towers over Kota Kinabalu's waterfront and the white domed City Mosque seems to float on its lagoon. This 2013 Relief mug renders that skyline in raised sculpted clay you can feel under your thumb, the black and white treatment letting the architecture do the talking. The Relief Series launched in 2012 and was never sold widely outside its home region, so Borneo entries like this rarely surface in Western trades.
Penang#576651 · Relief Series 2013Penang's George Town shares Malacca's UNESCO World Heritage listing as a historic Straits trading city, and the relief sculpts its blend of British colonial shophouses, clan jetties and the famous street-art murals in black and white. Penang is also Malaysia's street-food capital, a detail any traveler remembers. Like Malacca, this is an unusually off-the-beaten-path city for a Starbucks relief, which is exactly why it is worth having.
Malaca#576652 · Relief Series 2013Malacca is the UNESCO-listed old trading port of the Straits, and the relief sculpts its layered colonial past, the salmon-red Dutch Stadthuys of 1650, the oldest Dutch building in the East, and the surviving Porta de Santiago gate of the Portuguese A Famosa fort from 1512. A genuinely uncommon city to find in any Starbucks line, which makes this small historic Malaysian town a real collector's catch in the series.
Sarawak#576653 · Relief Series 2013Sarawak is the larger of Malaysia's two Borneo states, with riverside Kuching as its capital, famous for the elegant nine arched, nine pillared State Legislative Assembly building crowned by a nine pointed star roof, and the white Astana built in 1885 by the White Rajah Charles Brooke. This 2013 black and white Relief sculpts those distinctive forms in raised clay. As a Borneo entry it almost never appears outside the regional market, making it a real find for completists.
Kuala Lumpur#576654 · Relief Series 2013No prizes for guessing the centerpiece here, the Petronas Twin Towers, which reigned as the world's tallest buildings from 1998 to 2004 and still hold the title of tallest twin towers anywhere. The relief sculpts their tapered Islamic-geometry profile in raised black and white, usually paired with the slender KL Tower. It is one of the most instantly readable silhouettes in the whole series, a skyline you can identify with your eyes shut.
New York City#576655 · Relief Series 2010The earliest and biggest piece here, a 2010 NYC in the larger 18oz size from the series' first wave, with raised black and white Manhattan, the Empire State and Chrysler spires, Lady Liberty and the bridges. New York was one of the founding cities of the Relief line. The 18oz format makes this an early-edition standout, since the series soon settled on the standard 16oz, so the size alone marks it as one of the originals.
Paris#576656 · Relief Series 2011A 2011 Paris and a foundational relief, the city sculpted in black and white around the Eiffel Tower, built for the 1889 World's Fair and once derided by Parisians before it became the symbol of France. Expect the Arc de Triomphe and Notre-Dame in the raised cityscape too. Paris and London were the European anchors of the early series, so this monochrome edition sits among the line's original pillars.
Wellington#576657 · Relief Series 2013Wellington, New Zealand's compact capital wrapped around a windy harbor, in a 2013 black and white Relief. Look for the Beehive, the genuinely beehive shaped executive wing of Parliament, alongside the cable car and cliffside houses that define the city. New Zealand is a small Starbucks market and Wellington saw limited Relief distribution, so this is one of the harder Oceania pieces to find in good shape.
Berlin#576658 · Relief Series 2012The 2012 black-and-white Berlin Relief, the sculpted skyline surely anchored by the Brandenburg Gate and the towering Fernsehturm, the TV tower at Alexanderplatz that is still the tallest structure in Germany. Berlin got at least two Relief printings, and this monochrome 2012 is the earlier of the pair I have. The raised neoclassical columns of the Gate are exactly the kind of detail this series renders better than any flat city mug could.
Tainan#576659 · Relief Series 2013Tainan, the oldest city in Taiwan and its first capital, in a 2013 black and white Relief. The natural centerpiece is Chihkan Tower, built by the Dutch in 1653 as Fort Provintia and later crowned with Chinese pavilions, a literal stack of Taiwan's colonial layers. Tainan is one of the more historically loaded entries in the Taiwanese Relief run and a favorite of collectors who like a city with deep roots.
Seattle#576660 · Relief Series 2012The mothership city, Seattle, in the 2012 debut year of the Relief Series, sculpted in raised black and white with the Space Needle front and center, that 1962 World's Fair icon, plus the Pike Place stretch where the original Starbucks still pours. There is a satisfying full circle quality to owning a tactile relief of the company's own hometown. First year Seattle relief mugs carry extra sentimental weight in collector circles for exactly that reason.
Moscow#576661 · Relief Series 2013Moscow's relief is dominated by the unmistakable onion domes of Saint Basil's Cathedral on Red Square, commissioned by Ivan the Terrible in the 1550s, alongside the Kremlin walls and Spasskaya Tower. Sculpted in black and white, those swirling domes are made for the raised format, every curve catching the fingertip. Russian cities are not common in these series, so a Moscow relief carries real weight on a world shelf.
Hsinchu#576662 · Relief Series 2013Hsinchu is Taiwan's Windy City and its Silicon Valley, home to the Hsinchu Science Park, yet the relief leans on the old soul too, the City God Temple of 1748 that ranks highest of all such temples in Taiwan. The black and white sculpted facade makes this a quietly uncommon city in the series, since Hsinchu rarely shows up in Starbucks lines next to the big metropolises. A collector's city, not a tourist cliche.
Taiwan#576664 · Relief Series 2013Unusually this 2013 Relief represents the whole island of Taiwan rather than a single city, gathering national landmarks into one black and white sculpted band, the kind of country level entry that sits alongside the city specific Taipei, Tainan and Taichung mugs. Country wide relief mugs are rarer than city ones in this series. For a Taiwan focused shelf, the island mug is the cornerstone that ties the local set together.
Amsterdam#576666 · Relief Series 2011A 2011 Relief Series Amsterdam, the city's design raised in sculpted black and white you can actually feel under your thumb, the whole appeal of this line over flat-printed mugs. The art leans on Amsterdam's signature tall, narrow canal houses with their stepped and bell gables, the UNESCO-listed 17th century Canal Ring that defines the place. The Relief mugs are among the most tactile Starbucks ever made, and an early 2011 one like this is from the series at its best.
St. Petersburg#576667 · Relief Series 2013St. Petersburg, Russia, Peter the Great's window on Europe, in a 2013 Relief mug sculpted in black and white. Expect the gilded onion domes of the Church of the Savior on Spilled Blood and the long Hermitage and Winter Palace facade along the Neva. Russian market Starbucks pieces are scarce in general and the chain later exited the country, which gives this St. Petersburg relief a quiet geopolitical rarity that collectors have noticed.
Boston#576669 · Relief Series 2012The 2012 Boston Relief, city skyline sculpted in white against a black ground, a layout collectors describe consistently across the series. Boston's silhouette here leans on the harbor and landmarks like the gold-domed State House and the slim Custom House Tower that long ruled the skyline. As a hometown-pride American city, Boston is one of the more sought-after relief mugs domestically, and the crisp black-and-white treatment is the cleanest look this series does.
New York City#576670 · Relief Series 2012The 2012 New York is the standardized 16oz follow-up to the big 2010 original, same sculpted Manhattan icons in black and white, just in the format the series settled into. Having both the 18oz 2010 and this 16oz 2012 side by side is a neat way to show how the Relief line evolved its dimensions. The skyline never gets old in raised form, every spire begging to be traced with a thumb.
Taipei#576671 · Relief Series 2013Taipei in a 2013 black and white Relief mug, anchored by Taipei 101, the bamboo segmented tower that reigned as the world's tallest building from 2004 until 2010. The sculpted band pairs that supertall against the city's temple roofs. As the capital and most exported of the Taiwanese cities, Taipei is the easiest Taiwan Relief to land, which makes it the natural gateway piece into the island's sub set.
Taichung#576674 · Relief Series 2013Taichung, Taiwan's cultural midpoint, in a 2013 black and white Relief mug. The signature here is Toyo Ito's National Taichung Theater with its curving sound cave walls, although it was still under construction in 2013 and only fully opened in 2016, so this piece predates the building's debut. Taiwan received a generous spread of city specific Relief mugs, a regional quirk that makes the Taiwanese entries a fun sub set to chase.
Prague#576676 · Relief Series 2011One of the early 2010 reliefs, Prague is sculpted in black and white around its fairytale core, the Gothic spires of Prague Castle and St Vitus Cathedral, the Charles Bridge with its baroque statues, and the medieval Astronomical Clock of 1410, the oldest still operating in the world. The hundred-spires skyline is tailor-made for raised relief. A handsome Central European entry from the series' opening years.
London#576677 · Relief Series 2011This 2011 London is one of the earlier Relief Series entries, the city sculpted in black and white with the usual roll call, Big Ben and the Palace of Westminster, Tower Bridge, the London Eye and St Paul's dome. Running your thumb over the raised clock tower is the whole appeal of the relief format. London and Paris were among the flagship cities that anchored this series in its early years, which gives this one a bit of foundational pedigree.
Kaohsiung#576679 · Relief Series 2013Kaohsiung is Taiwan's great southern port and second city, and the relief sculpts its waterfront identity, think the 85 Sky Tower spiking the skyline and the Love River curling through downtown. The black and white embossing gives the harbor architecture real depth under the fingertips. Taiwanese cities like this one tend to be harder finds outside Asia, which makes the trio of Hsinchu, Kaohsiung and Taipei a satisfying regional run to chase.
Seoul#576681 · Relief Series 2012Seoul in the 2012 launch year of the Relief Series, the architecture sculpted in raised black and white, mixing the curved roofs of Gyeongbokgung Palace and Namdaemun gate with the modern N Seoul Tower crowning Namsan. The contrast of Joseon dynasty eaves against contemporary towers is the whole story of the city in one band. Korea got strong Relief distribution, so Seoul is among the more attainable Asian entries.
Los Angeles#576682 · Relief Series 2012LA in raised black and white, and the relief reaches for the icons that say Southern California instantly, the Hollywood sign on the hills, palm-lined boulevards and the downtown towers under that flat western light. The 2012 date places it in the heart of the series' American run alongside New York. A clean, sun-drenched city rendered in sculpted monochrome, which is a fun contrast to its real-life Technicolor.
Hong Kong#576683 · Relief Series 2012The Relief Series wraps a city in raised, sculpted architecture you can feel with your thumb, and this 2012 Hong Kong reads as a black and white relief of that famously vertical skyline against Victoria Harbour. Hong Kong packs more skyscrapers than any city on earth, so the embossed forest of towers is the perfect subject. This is the earlier 16oz monochrome edition before the red variant arrived the following year.
San Francisco#576684 · Relief Series 2012A 2012 first year Relief mug from when Starbucks launched the raised sculpted line, San Francisco delivers the obvious heavyweight, the burnt orange International Orange Golden Gate Bridge, alongside the Transamerica Pyramid and the city's cresting hills. The black and white relief format makes you read the skyline by touch as much as by eye. As a home city piece this one is easier to find than the Asian releases, but first year 2012 examples are the ones collectors chase.
Qingdao#576689 · Relief Series 2013Qingdao wears its German colonial past, having been a German concession from 1897, and the relief captures that quirk, the red-roofed Bavarian-style streets, the Protestant church, and Zhanqiao Pier with its Huilan Pavilion, the very image stamped on every Tsingtao beer bottle since the German-founded brewery opened in 1903. Rendered in dark blue and white. A genuinely unusual, story-rich city to find in the Chinese relief cluster.
Beijing#576690 · Relief Series 2012The 2012 Beijing Relief, dark blue and white, the embossed skyline built around the Forbidden City's sweeping rooflines and the Temple of Heaven, Beijing's defining imperial silhouettes. The relief technique suits Chinese palace architecture beautifully, those tiered eaves and gates really pop when sculpted in low relief. Blue-and-white was also a clever palette choice here, echoing the classic Chinese porcelain tradition the whole world associates with the country.
Hangzhou#576691 · Relief Series 2013The 2013 Hangzhou Relief, dark blue and white, the embossed scene framed by West Lake and the Leifeng Pagoda, the lakeside tower first built in 975 AD, famously collapsed in 1924 and rebuilt in 2002. West Lake is a UNESCO site that has inspired Chinese poets and painters for centuries, and it stars in the Legend of the White Snake. A lyrical subject for a sculpted mug, and Hangzhou is a less common relief city than the big capitals.
Suzhou#576693 · Relief Series 2013Suzhou, the Venice of the East, threaded with canals and home to the UNESCO listed Classical Gardens whose miniature landscapes date back to the 11th century. This 2013 Relief mug in dark blue and white sculpts the city's whitewashed Jiangnan rooflines and arched stone bridges. Suzhou is a less obvious choice than Beijing or Shanghai, which makes it a sleeper for collectors who appreciate the subtler Chinese cities in the series.
Nanjing#576694 · Relief Series 2013Nanjing was the Ming dynasty's imperial capital, and the relief honors that depth, the massive 14th-century city wall that took 200,000 laborers some 21 years to build, and the bell-shaped Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum on Purple Mountain. Rendered in dark blue and white, this is part of the handsome blue-toned Chinese cluster in the series. A weightier, more historic subject than the usual skyline-of-towers city.
Shanghai#576695 · Relief Series 2012Shanghai in the 2012 debut Relief year, done in dark blue and white, the raised skyline dominated by the Oriental Pearl Tower's stacked spheres and the bottle opener silhouette of the Shanghai World Financial Center along the Pudong Bund. The dark blue colorway is the original Shanghai relief. This city anchors a three year run of recolors, which makes the 2012 the foundational piece for anyone chasing the full Shanghai set.
Ningbo#576696 · Relief Series 2013Ningbo is one of China's great ancient ports, open to foreign trade since 1844, and its proudest landmark is Tianyi Pavilion, the oldest surviving private library in China, built in the 1560s and still holding tens of thousands of rare volumes. The relief renders the city in dark blue and white. A lesser-known city even among China travelers, which makes this a quietly rewarding find in the blue-toned Chinese run.
Melbourne#576697 · Relief Series 2015A 2015 piece and a palette outlier, Melbourne comes in dark green and white rather than the usual black, a nod to the city's leafy gardens and trams. The relief sculpts Flinders Street Station, Federation Square and the Arts Centre spire. Melbourne is regularly voted one of the world's most liveable cities, and the green wash over the raised architecture gives this one of the most distinctive looks in the whole series.
Brisbane#576698 · Relief Series 2015A 2015 Brisbane Relief in dark green and white, the sculpted design built around the Story Bridge, the steel cantilever span opened in 1940 that is the city's defining symbol over the Brisbane River. Green is an apt palette for Queensland's sub-tropical river city. Australian Relief mugs draw real interest from collectors outside Australia simply because they shipped in smaller numbers, so a Brisbane in good shape is a satisfying one to land.
Sydney#576699 · Relief Series 2015Sydney in a 2015 Relief mug, dark green and white, and you already know the two stars sculpted in raised clay, Jorn Utzon's shell roofed Opera House and the steel arch of the Harbour Bridge that locals call the Coathanger. The green colorway places this in the later 2015 run rather than the 2012 to 2013 originals. Australia did not get deep Relief distribution, so Sydney tends to command attention in trades.
Shanghai#576700 · Relief Series 2015The 2015 Shanghai Relief in dark green and white, the third and final colorway after the 2012 dark blue and 2013 red, completing the rare Shanghai trio. Same sculpted Pudong skyline of the Oriental Pearl Tower and its neighbors, just dressed in forest green. Assembling all three Shanghai years is a genuine accomplishment in this series, and the 2015 green is usually the last one people track down.
Paris#576701 · Relief Series 2013The 2013 Paris brings the red and white palette to the City of Light, the same sculpted Eiffel Tower and grand boulevards but warmed by that signature year's red wash. The catalog data for this one carries a stray Shanghai note, a listing slip, since the mug itself is the Paris relief. Owning the 2011 black-and-white beside this 2013 red gives you Paris in the series' two defining finishes.
Seoul#576702 · Relief Series 2013The 2013 Seoul Relief mug, and the giveaway is the color, red and white rather than the 2012 black and white, the kind of year over year palette swap that lets collectors date these at a glance. Same sculpted skyline of palace rooflines and the N Seoul Tower, but the red treatment makes it the more striking of the pair on a shelf. Owning both years side by side is the quiet flex with this series.
London#576704 · Relief Series 2013The 2013 London brings the red and white treatment, a fitting palette for a city of red phone boxes, pillar boxes and double-decker buses. Same sculpted parade of Westminster, Tower Bridge and the Eye, but the warm wash over the raised detail makes it feel like a different piece entirely next to the 2011 monochrome. Pairing the black-and-white and red editions of a single city is exactly how relief collectors like to display this line.
Shanghai#576705 · Relief Series 2013The 2013 Shanghai Relief, recolored in red and white against the 2012 dark blue, same Pudong skyline of the Oriental Pearl and the riverfront towers in raised sculpted relief. Shanghai is unusual in getting three distinct Relief colorways across 2012, 2013 and 2015, so this red middle child is the one collectors most often have a gap for. The annual palette change is the entire collecting game here.
Hong Kong#576706 · Relief Series 2013The 2013 Hong Kong relief switches the palette to red and white, the same sculpted harbour skyline but with that lucky-red wash that reads beautifully against the raised towers. Collectors track the Relief Series partly by these year-to-year color swaps, so owning both the 2012 black and white and this 2013 red lets you show the city in two moods on one shelf. Red is no accident here, it is the color of fortune across Chinese design.
Berlin#576707 · Relief Series 2013The 2013 Berlin Relief in red and white, the color-shifted sibling to the black-and-white 2012, same sculpted skyline of Brandenburg Gate and the Fernsehturm. Having both years side by side is the quiet thrill here, identical relief, completely different mood, the red reading bolder and more modern. Single cities reissued in fresh palettes are exactly the trap and the joy of the Relief line, since you are never quite done with a city.
Classification

Equipment & Tumblers44 pieces

Tumblers, stainless travelers, canisters and the build-your-own memory cup.
2004#186001 · Equipment & TumblersA 2004 stainless steel travel mug, double walled inside and out with a black base and black handle, classic early-2000s commuter hardware. This is the everyday equipment end of the collection rather than a designer piece, but the clean handled stainless format marks the moment Starbucks was building out its reusable-cup lineup well before tumblers became the brand's merchandising engine.
2010#186002 · RED SeriesThe 2010 Jonathan Adler tumbler made for Starbucks and Product (RED), white inside with the Starbucks logo and a black locking lid, designed by the famed potter and decorator. (RED), the Bono-cofounded AIDS-fighting cause, partnered with Starbucks here, and Adler's go-cup version, in his signature graphic style, even surfaced on Oprah, sold fast and grew hard to find, which is exactly why collectors hunt it today.
Argentina Plastic Tumbler#186006 · Equipment & TumblersAn Argentina plastic tumbler painted with a scene of the country and a lamp, one of the market-specific souvenir pieces Starbucks made for its international stores. Country and city tumblers like this were sold locally as travel keepsakes, so an Argentina example is harder to encounter outside South America and earns its place as a regional curiosity in a collection built mostly on US and global lines.
Hanukkah Plastic Tumbler (1)#186007 · Equipment & TumblersA Hanukkah tumbler printed in Hebrew with the glowing candle lights of the menorah, the eight-branched lamp lit one flame a night across the Festival of Lights. Holiday-specific tumblers in Hebrew are a narrow regional run, made for the Israeli market rather than worldwide release, which makes them quietly hard to find outside the country. As an Israel-tied piece this one sits close to home for me, the kind of cultural crossover Starbucks rarely prints.
Paris#186009 · Global Icon SeriesA Paris tumbler stamped with the Eiffel Tower, Gustave Eiffel's 1889 wrought-iron giant built for the World's Fair and meant to stand only twenty years before the city fell in love and kept it. As the single most recognizable travel icon on earth, the tower is the obvious shorthand for any Paris souvenir cup. Plastic city tumblers like this fed the tourist trade hard, the cheap-and-cheerful cousin to the ceramic Paris mugs collectors prize.
Coffee / Tea Press Tumbler#186011 · Equipment & TumblersA clever coffee and tea press tumbler, plastic lined with a built-in press filter so you can steep and drink from the same vessel, decorated with coffee-press imagery. This is Starbucks engineering convenience into a travel cup, a personal-press format that lets you brew loose coffee or tea on the go, and a genuinely functional piece of kit rather than pure souvenir.
Create Your Own Memory Tumbler#186012 · Equipment & TumblersOne of Starbucks' clever blank-slate tumblers, plastic-bodied with a paper insert you slide out and replace, so you can drop in your own photos, ticket stubs, or doodles behind the clear outer wall. These were the personalize-it answer to the fixed-print collector mugs, and the genius is that no two are alike once an owner fills them. A fun outlier in any serious collection, the rare piece designed to be incomplete on purpose.
Qatar#186013 · Global Icon SeriesA Qatar tumbler showing the Aspire Tower, the 300-meter Torch Doha that architect Hadi Simaan built as the centerpiece of the 2006 Asian Games, named for the giant flame that crowned it during the opening ceremony. The tower packs a five-star hotel, a cantilevered pool, and a revolving restaurant into a single spiraling shaft. Choosing the Torch over a generic skyline makes this an unmistakable Doha piece, and Gulf-market tumblers stay genuinely scarce outside the region.
Kyoto#186014 · Equipment & TumblersA Kyoto plastic tumbler carrying the city's name, a regional Japan-market cup from Starbucks' deep tradition of place-specific Kyoto drinkware. Kyoto is Japan's old imperial capital, and its Starbucks designs lean on local motifs like the Gion Matsuri festival, the geisha and maiko of Gion, and the Kamogawa river. Japan's regional and Been There Kyoto pieces are a whole collecting world of their own, prized because many never sell outside the city that names them.
Hong Kong#186017 · Equipment & TumblersA Hong Kong plastic tumbler carrying the city name in its outside print, a travel-souvenir cup from one of Asia's densest Starbucks markets. Hong Kong sits at the heart of Starbucks' Greater China expansion, and its city-named drinkware moves fast through the airport and tourist trade. Plastic tumblers like this were the affordable everyday counterpart to the ceramic City Mugs, which is why they survive in smaller numbers than the mugs collectors babied on a shelf.
Happy Chanukkah#186018 · Equipment & TumblersThe English-language sibling to the Hebrew Hanukkah cup, reading Happy Chanukkah across the outside, using one of the holiday's many transliterated spellings. Where the Hebrew version speaks to the home market, this one was the friendlier export-facing design, and owning both spellings side by side tells the whole bilingual story of the release. Jewish-holiday Starbucks merchandise is uncommon enough that collectors treat any clean example as a small find.
To-Go Cup#186032 · Equipment & TumblersA white canister shaped to echo the disposable to-go cup, green logo on white, turning the most familiar Starbucks silhouette into a reusable kitchen container. It is a sly bit of self-reference, the throwaway cup reborn as something you keep on the shelf. Novelty-form canisters like this are collector candy precisely because they play on the brand's own iconography rather than just printing the siren and calling it done.
Dark Green#186033 · Equipment & TumblersThe squat companion to the tall canister, same dark green body and same gold first-logo siren, sized for a smaller stash of beans on the counter. The two together form a graduated set, and the original split-tail mermaid is the tell of an early piece, that mark predating the 1987 switch to green. Canisters survive far less often than mugs because they got used hard in real kitchens, which is exactly what makes a clean one worth grabbing.
Dark Green#186034 · Equipment & TumblersThe tall member of the matched canister pair, dark green inside and out with the gold split-tail siren first logo, the original 1971 mark Terry Heckler drew from an old Norse woodcut. Starbucks built its early retail identity around selling whole bean at home, so these airtight storage canisters were core merchandise, not novelties. Pieces wearing the brown-and-gold original siren rather than the modern green are the ones older collectors hunt, since that mark was retired decades ago.
White#186037 · Equipment & TumblersThis squat white storage canister wears the company's earliest logo, the original split-tailed Melusine siren, printed over plain white, a clean utilitarian piece from the equipment line meant to hold whole beans on the counter. The all-white field with first-logo branding makes it read older and more austere than the later green-circle gear, the kind of plain workhorse object that collectors of Starbucks equipment quietly hunt to round out a kitchen shelf.
Pleated Logo Canister#186041 · Equipment & TumblersA white canister wearing the green siren over a pleated, ribbed body, topped with a lid knob you grip to lift. The vertical pleating is the design signature here, giving a plain storage jar a bit of architectural texture you can feel in the hand. Lidded bean canisters got used and chipped in real kitchens, so an intact one with its original knob still seated is a better survivor than it looks.
Label and Erase Canister#186042 · Equipment & TumblersA plain white canister built around a simple idea, a writable surface you label by hand and wipe clean to relabel as your beans change. It is the utilitarian opposite of the logo-emblazoned green canisters, a kitchen tool first and merchandise second. I keep pieces like this because they show Starbucks thinking about how people actually lived with coffee at home, not just how to brand the counter.
1/4 Lbs Logo Canister#186044 · Equipment & TumblersA ceramic storage canister sized to hold a quarter pound of beans, white bodied with the final round green logo, the post 2011 Siren without the Starbucks Coffee wordmark ring. Canisters sit in the underappreciated equipment corner of the hobby, more kitchen object than display mug, but a clean logo piece like this is exactly the kind of thing that fills out a serious collection beyond the ceramics. The bare green Siren dates it firmly to the modern logo era.
Abstract Painting (3)#186046 · Chaleur MadeAn extra-large French press wrapped in a painterly street scene of a Starbucks patio, white lined, the third in a small abstract-painting series. French presses are the purist's brewing tool, and dressing a working press in original artwork turns a piece of equipment into a display object, a nice bridge between the functional and decorative sides of the collection.
Indonesia#186114 · Equipment & TumblersA 10oz stainless-steel Indonesia mug, double-walled steel inside and out with the modern siren logo, finished with a black base and black handle for contrast. Indonesia matters enormously to Starbucks as a coffee origin, home to the famous Sumatra and the aged Sulawesi the company prizes, so a country mug here carries real sourcing weight. Steel country mugs are a less common format than the ceramic City series, the sort of variant that fills a gap most collections never close.
Plastic Black#186148 · Equipment & TumblersA sleek everyday tumbler, black plastic interior with Starbucks lettering printed in silver across a black exterior, all logo and no city. This is the workhorse end of the equipment line, the cup made to be carried daily rather than displayed, which is exactly why pristine ones grow scarce. The restrained silver-on-black styling is timeless enough that it reads modern years after release.
2000#186149 · Equipment & TumblersA 2000 travel tumbler, black plastic lined, wrapped with an illustration of a snow-filled Starbucks storefront, a cheerful winter scene. It belongs to the seasonal holiday tumbler runs Starbucks issued each December, designed to be carried rather than displayed, so finding a turn-of-the-millennium example with the artwork unworn is the catch here.
1998#186150 · Equipment & TumblersA 1998 New York City travel tumbler, black plastic lined, wrapped in line drawings of the city's iconic landmarks. This sits right alongside the late-nineties Collage Series Starbucks was running for dozens of American cities, capturing skyline and skyscraper New York in the pre-9/11 silhouette, which gives these older NYC souvenirs a poignancy newer ones cannot match.
Espresso Roast#186170 · Equipment & TumblersA round storage tin stamped on the lid with the Espresso Roast mark, Starbucks' darkest house blend and the backbone of every shot the company has ever pulled. Tins like this kept beans fresh before resealable bags took over, so they double as packaging history. I like these because the graphics on the lid track how Starbucks styled its roast names over the years, a small detail most people never bother to read.
Coffee Harvest Truck#186172 · Silver Crane MadeA rectangular tin painted on all four sides with a coffee harvest truck shown in shifting perspective, so the vehicle appears to drive around the box as you turn it. It romanticizes the origin end of the supply chain, the truck hauling beans down from the farm, and the wraparound perspective trick makes it one of the more visually clever tins in the run.
After Coffee Mint#186173 · Equipment & TumblersA small square After Coffee Mint tin, now empty of its peppermints, a tidy bit of point-of-sale ephemera from the counter rather than the merchandise shelf. These little breath-mint tins were the impulse-buy companions to a coffee, and precisely because they were meant to be used up and tossed, an intact empty one is the kind of small survivor collectors quietly appreciate.
10th Starbucks Coffee Japan#186174 · Equipment & TumblersA square commemorative tin marking ten years of Starbucks in Japan, picturing the very first branch which opened in Ginza in August 1996, making this a roughly 2006 anniversary piece. It came empty of coffee, so what you hold is the keepsake itself rather than packaging. Japan anniversary memorabilia like this is prized because Starbucks Japan built its reputation on limited and exclusive releases, and a tin honoring the landmark Ginza store is the kind of dated collectible that anchors a Japan corpus.
Authentic Hand Crafted Silver#186175 · Equipment & TumblersA rectangular silver tin marked Authentic Hand Crafted, a sleek, understated gifting box that leans on metallic finish rather than illustration. It reads as one of the more premium-positioned packaging pieces, the kind meant to signal a special-occasion coffee gift, and its restraint makes it a quiet contrast to the busy multicolor tins of the nineties.
French Press & Case (8 Cups)#186181 · Equipment & TumblersThe crown jewel of the equipment shelf, an 8-cup French press housed in a wooden box embroidered with the first logo and fitted with a real leather carry handle. Starbucks issued premium press sets like this for milestone occasions, and the slide-or-hinge wooden case marks it as a gift-tier item rather than everyday gear. The press method itself is the purest way to taste a coffee's body, which is exactly why Starbucks dressed this one up.
Starbucks and CARE#186183 · Equipment & TumblersA rectangular grey-and-yellow tin marking the Starbucks and CARE partnership, the alliance that began in 1992 to support coffee, cocoa, and tea growing communities and fund disaster relief. CARE's name nods to its original relief CARE Package, so a tin is a fitting form for the tie-in. These cause-marketing pieces are easy to overlook, but they document the early conscience of the company, back when linking a roaster to a global aid group was still novel.
1997#186184 · Equipment & TumblersA 1997 rectangular Christmas Blend sample tin, and 1997 is a meaningful holiday year because that is when Starbucks first served Christmas Blend in its now-iconic red holiday cups. The tin held sample beans for the season and wears festive multicolor art, a small relic from the moment the red-cup tradition that defines Starbucks holidays was born.
1997#186185 · Equipment & TumblersThis 1997 rectangular holiday tin carries a piano-playing theme, a nod to the classical and jazz piano compilations Starbucks sold alongside its seasonal coffee in that era. It is a quietly charming piece of brand history from the same year the red holiday cup debuted, blending the company's coffee and its early music-merchandising ambitions on one little box.
2000#186191 · Equipment & TumblersA 2000 red cookie tin decorated with the storybook red-roofed kettle houses, a cozy holiday-village motif Starbucks leaned on for its gifting line at the turn of the millennium. These tins originally held shortbread or cookies, and the warm illustrated villages make them some of the more decorative survivors from the brand's Y2K-era seasonal range.
2001#186193 · Equipment & TumblersA 2001 red Exclusive Blends tin, fronted by an envelope graphic reading a merry sip with friends, holiday gifting copy at its most direct. These sampler tins paired a small curated coffee selection with a card-like greeting, a clever bit of packaging that turned a coffee gift into something closer to a Christmas card you could keep long after the beans were gone.
1999#186194 · Equipment & TumblersA 1999 biscuit tin built as a three-dimensional replica of the very first Starbucks store, the 1971 Pike Place Market shop in Seattle that opened on March 30, 1971. The original storefront is a pilgrimage site for the brand, so a sculpted little tin of it is one of the most on-the-nose heritage pieces you can own. They turn up on eBay regularly, usually empty, which is exactly how a collector wants the tin and not the cookies.
1990's#186195 · Equipment & TumblersA 1990s yellow and green rectangular storage tin carrying a flight of doves, the kind of soft, painterly graphic Starbucks favored before the brand went minimalist. These early coffee and biscuit tins were utilitarian gifting and storage pieces, but collectors now chase them precisely because so few survived intact and unrusted in the back of a pantry.
1995#186196 · Equipment & TumblersThe 1995 Exclusive Blends Sampler tin, a roomy 10 by 7 box decorated with a swan and a jester, is the kind of vintage piece that turns up on eBay flagged as RARE. It originally held a curated set of bean samples for gifting, and because the coffee was the point and the tin merely the package, finding one empty but clean and dent free is the real collector win.
Starbucks Truck#186198 · Equipment & TumblersA rectangular tin printed with a Starbucks delivery truck, the driver, and a dog along for the ride, its back face stamped with blend stamps like vintage shipping marks. The whole thing leans into old-world coffee-trade romance, the bean arriving by road the way burlap sacks once arrived by sea. I love the storytelling on these, the kind of nostalgic graphic Starbucks used to wrap around tins before minimalism took over the brand.
1995#186199 · Equipment & TumblersA large 1995 tin in that unmistakable early-nineties palette of pink, purple and teal, illustrated with swans rendered in both light and dark, a day and night motif. This is peak pre-corporate Starbucks design, hand-drawn and a little whimsical, from the years when the company still leaned on artists rather than a tight global style guide.
2 x Summer at Starbucks Tote Bag#186233 · Equipment & TumblersA pair of identical Summer at Starbucks tote bags, each printed over blue with a lady in swimwear sipping a Frappuccino, pure warm-weather promotional fun. Frappuccino has been Starbucks' summer flagship since the mid-nineties, and seasonal totes like these were giveaway and lifestyle merchandise rather than catalog mainstays, so having a matched, unused pair is a nice quirk for the shelf.
2010#455906 · Equipment & TumblersDo not confuse this 2010 red tumbler with the Jonathan Adler (RED) piece, this one is its own oddity, green inside with fish and a yellow submarine cruising the deep sea on the outside. The whimsical undersea artwork, a clear Beatles wink, makes it one of the more playful and unexpected designs in the equipment line and a fun outlier to set beside the more buttoned-up tumblers.
12oz#455949 · Equipment & TumblersThe 2011 holiday Fa la la double wall ceramic traveler, a 12oz to go mug with the modern Siren logo scrawled over with handwritten falalala script and topped by a slide shut coffee lid. It shipped in a holiday gift box, which is why complete boxed examples now read as the desirable version. Sellers routinely tag this one rare, and the ceramic traveler format, a mug pretending to be a paper cup, makes it a fun crossover between the holiday run and the equipment shelf.
Kingdom of Saudi Arabia#576720 · City Mug Collector SeriesA Kingdom of Saudi Arabia tumbler in white with green palm trees, the palm being the national emblem that crowns the Saudi coat of arms above its crossed swords. The matching 2002 ceramic City Mug used the same palm-and-green motif, so this tumbler reads as the everyday companion to that established design. Saudi pieces draw steady collector interest, and the later all-green You Are Here Saudi mug with Arabic script became one of the most chased Gulf releases.
Hangzhou#576806 · City Mug Collector SeriesA turquoise Hangzhou tumbler carrying the city's signature scene, the river and bridge of West Lake, the UNESCO-listed lake that has inspired Chinese painters and poets for a thousand years. The bridge is the famous Broken Bridge, tied to the legend of the White Snake and counted among West Lake's ten classic views. Hangzhou is also where Starbucks later opened an intangible-cultural-heritage concept store, so the city runs deep in the company's China story.
Classification

Charity Edition16 pieces

The intact sixteen-city Charity Edition set, never split.
Seattle#186122 · Architecture SeriesSeattle as the espresso demitasse in the Charity Edition, the skyline in light blue and grey on white. This is the hometown, where Starbucks opened at Pike Place Market in 1971 under the gaze of the Space Needle and the Cascade and Olympic ranges. A Seattle cup always carries extra meaning in any Starbucks set, and in fragile espresso size within an intact charity sixteen it is a quiet centerpiece.
Las Vegas#186126 · Architecture SeriesLas Vegas as the espresso demitasse in the 1998 to 1999 Charity Edition, the skyline printed in light blue and grey on white. Sin City is the neon Strip, the Bellagio fountains and a desert built on casinos and quick weddings. The small espresso size is the harder format to keep pristine, so this little Vegas cup pulls real weight as part of my complete charity sixteen.
Chicago#186127 · City Scene SeriesChicago appears here as the espresso-size demitasse in the Charity Edition, its city photos printed in grey and very light blue on white. The Second City gave us the skyscraper, the Art Institute lions, deep-dish pizza and the lakefront skyline along Lake Michigan. The little espresso format is easy to lose or break, so an intact one within a full charity set carries weight that the regular size does not.
New York City#186130 · City Scene SeriesNew York City as the espresso demitasse in the Charity Edition, city photos rendered in grey and very light blue on white. The capital of the world is the Empire State Building, Central Park, Times Square and the Statue of Liberty, the most-collected city of all. In espresso size within an intact charity set, this little New York cup is one I guard closely as part of the full sixteen.
San Antonio#455080 · Skyline SeriesSan Antonio as a regular mug in the 1998 to 1999 Charity Edition, skyline printed in light blue and grey on white. The South Texas city is defined by the Alamo, the River Walk and its deep Spanish-mission roots. Sold to benefit local causes, these cups matter most as a complete run, and this San Antonio holds its spot in my uncracked sixteen.
Atlanta#455437 · Architecture SeriesPart of the intact sixteen-city North America Charity Edition from 1998 to 1999, this Atlanta regular mug carries the city skyline rendered in soft light blue and grey against white. Atlanta is the capital of the New South, home of Coca-Cola and the 1996 Centennial Olympics, and these charity mugs sold to benefit local causes, which is exactly why a complete uncracked set like mine is the prize rather than any single cup.
Dallas#455533 · Global Icon SeriesOne of the more characterful cups in the 1998 to 1999 Charity Edition, this Dallas regular mug breaks the skyline pattern with a red interior, cream body and a train motif. Dallas is the North Texas capital of oil, cattle and the old Texas and Pacific rail lines that built it. That train design and warm red-and-cream palette set it apart from the cool blue-grey cities, making it a favorite stop in my complete set.
Houston#576203 · Global Icon SeriesHouston in the Charity Edition with a green interior, cream exterior and a satellite design, a clear nod to Space City and Mission Control at the Johnson Space Center, where Apollo astronauts heard the word Houston first. The green-and-cream coloring and the orbiting satellite make this one of the most thematically clever cups in the late-1990s benefit run, and it anchors the Texas corner of my intact sixteen.
Boston#576672 · Relief Series 2012This Boston regular mug from the 1998 to 1999 Charity Edition is unusual in the set, printed in stark black and white Boston architecture rather than the soft blue-grey skyline most cities got. Boston is the cradle of the American Revolution, Freedom Trail, Fenway Park and Paul Revere country. The distinct monochrome treatment makes it one of the more visually striking cards in my complete sixteen-city run.
San Francisco#576952 · City Mug Collector SeriesThe signature cup of the 1998 to 1999 Charity Edition, this San Francisco regular mug breaks the skyline pattern entirely with a purple cable car streaking across white. The City by the Bay is the Golden Gate Bridge, the steep hills and the historic cable cars still climbing them. That bold purple tram makes it the most recognizable single card in my complete sixteen-city charity set.
AustinCharity EditionAustin in the North America Charity Edition, the late-1990s benefit set that I keep complete and intact. The Texas capital is the self-styled Live Music Capital of the World, home to the University of Texas tower and a famous bat colony under the Congress Avenue Bridge. As a charity-line city mug its real value to me is as one unbroken member of the full sixteen, not as a standalone.
MiamiCharity EditionMiami in the North America Charity Edition, the benefit set I keep whole and uncracked. The Magic City is Art Deco South Beach, Cuban coffee in Little Havana, palm-lined Biscayne Bay and the American gateway to Latin America. As with the rest of this late-1990s charity line, the worth here is membership in the full sixteen-city run rather than any single mug standing alone.
PhiladelphiaCharity EditionPhiladelphia in the 1998 to 1999 North America Charity Edition. The City of Brotherly Love is the birthplace of American independence, home to the Liberty Bell, Independence Hall and the Rocky steps at the Museum of Art. Like the rest of this benefit run that I keep complete and intact, its real collector value sits in being one unbroken member of the sixteen-city set.
PhoenixCharity EditionPhoenix in the North America Charity Edition, the late-1990s benefit set I keep whole. The Arizona capital is the Valley of the Sun, a desert metropolis ringed by saguaro cactus and Camelback Mountain, named for the mythical bird reborn from ashes. As a charity-line city mug its standing comes from completing my intact sixteen rather than from any solo rarity.
San DiegoCharity EditionSan Diego in the North America Charity Edition, the benefit set I keep intact. Southern California's harbor city is Balboa Park, the world-famous zoo, Coronado's beaches and a sprawling US Navy presence on the Pacific. As with the whole late-1990s charity line, the value lives in membership of the full sixteen rather than in this single cup standing on its own.
Washington D.C.Charity EditionWashington D.C. in the North America Charity Edition, the late-1990s benefit set I keep complete. The nation's capital is the Mall, the Capitol dome, the Washington Monument, the White House and the Lincoln Memorial. Like every cup in this charity run, its real significance to me is as one intact piece of the full sixteen-city set rather than as a standalone mug.
Classification

Doonesbury8 pieces

Garry Trudeau's comic-strip coffee pieces, including Java Pump number 47 of 1500.
Catch the BuzzDoonesburyFrom the Doonesbury at Starbucks line, Garry Trudeau's 1998 to 2000 collaboration that turned his comic-strip coffee gags into merchandise raising over a million dollars for local literacy programs. Catch the Buzz appeared on both a mug and a tumbler and even on Duke's Hi-Test Java gas pump figure. The literacy-fundraiser backstory and Trudeau's own artwork make these Doonesbury pieces some of the most genuinely story-rich items in the whole collection.
Clouds in the CoffeeDoonesburyClouds in His Coffee, a 1999 jumbo Doonesbury mug by Garry Trudeau showing his pilot character and a plane, part of the Starbucks literacy partnership that ran from 1998 for nearly two years. The big 18 to 20 ounce size and the aviation gag set it apart, and collectors prize the Doonesbury cups precisely because they were charitable tie-ins drawn by Trudeau himself, not ordinary production mugs.
Duke for PrezDoonesburyDuke for Prez, drawn from Uncle Duke's gleefully unhinged 2000 presidential run in Trudeau's strip, the perpetually intoxicated character played for satire against the real election cycle. The campaign theme spread across Starbucks Doonesbury merchandise including this mug plus playing cards, posters and coasters, all funding US literacy programs. Among collectors the Duke for Prez pieces are favorites for the sheer audacity of the gag and their late-1990s charity pedigree.
Four CoastersDoonesburyA four-coaster set from the 1999 Doonesbury at Starbucks run, when Garry Trudeau let his coffee-obsessed comic strip gags loose on real Starbucks merchandise to raise money for literacy. I love that these sit at the everyday end of the collaboration, the part you could actually use under a mug, which is exactly why intact sets of four are harder to track down now than the signed prints. They carry the strip's dry humor and Trudeau's unmistakable line work.
Java Pump StatueDoonesburyThis is the crown jewel of my Doonesbury shelf, the hand-painted resin statue of Uncle Duke pumping fuel at Duke's Super Hi-Test Java gas station, mine numbered 47 of just 1500. The base reads designed exclusively for Starbucks Coffee Company by Garry Trudeau, a limited edition of 1500 pieces, tying it straight to the 1999 literacy fundraiser. With such a tiny run and the fragility of resin, low numbers like this rarely surface, and collectors chase the full plane, mug and pump trio.
Sands of JavaDoonesburySands of Java comes from Trudeau's 1999 Starbucks series, the Uncle Duke desert gag rendered as both a signed limited-edition poster of 1500 and the matching mug. Duke, Trudeau's perpetually scheming opportunist loosely riffing on Hunter S. Thompson, was the natural face for a sendup of coffee culture gone global. Signed and numbered versions came with a certificate of authenticity, and pairing the mug with the print is the goal most Doonesbury collectors quietly nurse.
Starbucks RangerDoonesburyThe Starbucks Ranger mug is part of Garry Trudeau's 1999 Doonesbury collaboration, the comic strip whose running coffee jokes Starbucks turned into a literacy-benefit merchandise line. What I appreciate is how it carries Trudeau's instantly recognizable Sunday-strip drawing onto a piece of everyday drinkware, all proceeds having gone to reading programs. The Doonesbury pieces stick together as a tight, themed family on my shelf, each one a wink from the strip.
Tour de JavaDoonesburyLe Tour de Java is one of the cleverest gags in the 1999 Doonesbury at Starbucks set, a cycling-race spoof on coffee's worldwide conquest issued as a signed and numbered print of 1500 alongside the mug. Some prints carried both Garry Trudeau's and Howard Schultz's signatures with a certificate of authenticity, which is a fun pairing of cartoonist and CEO. It belongs to the literacy fundraiser, so every piece did a bit of good.
Classification

States of Bean16 pieces

US states and Canadian provinces, designed by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson.
Washington D.C.#186129 · City Scene SeriesThis is the Washington D.C. piece from the 1997 States of Bean Series, the line designed for Starbucks by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, and mine is the espresso size, the little demitasse cup rather than the full mug. The catalog notes it stays white inside while the exterior carries the city in soft grey and very light blue photo washes, a restrained look that lets the monuments read as faded postcards. Fitting for the District, a city defined by the Capitol dome, the Washington Monument and the Mall, and the smaller espresso format is the harder one to land complete since collectors usually chase the standard mugs first.
Washington#576192 · Global Icon SeriesWashington in the 1997 States of Bean series shows a red interior with a cream exterior carrying a single tree, a fittingly understated image for Starbucks' own home state in the evergreen Pacific Northwest. Designed by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, it lands as the sentimental anchor of my set, the place where the whole company began. That lone tree against cream is a quietly perfect bit of restraint amid a colorful run.
North Carolina#576217 · Global Icon SeriesNorth Carolina in the 1997 States of Bean series carries a light blue interior with a cream exterior trailing long branches of wheat, a nod to the state's deep agricultural roots. Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson's design favors that quiet, pastoral imagery over the obvious coast or mountains, which gives this one a calmer, more rural mood than its neighbors. It is among the gentler, less flashy pieces in the set, easy to overlook and pleasant to own.
Virginia#576586 · You Are Here CollectionVirginia in the 1997 States of Bean series has a dark blue interior with drums, a flag and a crab wrapping the outside, blending the state's Revolutionary and Colonial history with its Chesapeake Bay crab country. Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson layered those symbols into the set's stylized folk-art look, giving Virginia one of the busier, more storytelling-rich designs. That mix of patriot drums and coastal crab is exactly the small detail that makes me want to pick it up.
New Jersey#576612 · You Are Here CollectionNew Jersey in the 1997 States of Bean series has a red interior with a theme park and Ferris wheel circling the outside, an unmistakable nod to the Jersey Shore boardwalks at places like Wildwood and Seaside. I love that Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson reached for the amusement-pier fun rather than turnpike cliches, capturing the state's summer-boardwalk soul. That cheerful carnival motif makes it one of the more distinctive faces in the whole set.
California#576624 · You Are Here CollectionCalifornia in the 1997 States of Bean series wears a light blue interior with mountains, trees and a sun wrapping the outside, exactly the sunny Golden State shorthand Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson were going for. I like that the design skips the obvious palm-and-beach cliche for the Sierra and the high sun, a nod to the state's range from coast to peaks. The painterly, color-blocked style is the signature thread running through the entire set.
New York#576930 · City Mug Collector SeriesNew York in the 1997 States of Bean series shows a white interior with the NYC skyline rendered in light pink around the outside, a softer, almost dreamy take on the city that usually gets bold treatment. Designed by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson for Starbucks, it trades steel-and-glass drama for a pastel silhouette, which I find unexpectedly charming. As the marquee state, New York is one of the more sought pieces when collectors build out the set.
British ColumbiaStates of BeanBritish Columbia is the Canadian outlier in my 1997 States of Bean run, the playful series designed exclusively for Starbucks by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson. Folding a province into a set otherwise full of US states is the kind of quirk I collect for, and BC fits with its Pacific coast, mountains and rainforest imagery. The whole series leans on bold, almost folk-art color blocking that makes any single piece pop on a shelf.
ColoradoStates of BeanColorado is a core piece of the 1997 States of Bean series designed for Starbucks by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, and it naturally leans on the Rockies that define the state's identity. These mugs came in the larger 18 to 20 ounce format, a generous everyday cup wrapped in the series' bright, stylized state motif. It is one of the more commonly resurfacing states, which makes it a friendly entry point for anyone starting this colorful set.
ConnecticutStates of BeanConnecticut joins my 1997 States of Bean lineup, the cheerful US-and-Canada series Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson built for Starbucks. As one of the original colonial states wedged into the dense Northeast, Connecticut gets the same warm folk-art treatment as its neighbors, color-blocked imagery wrapping the full body of the cup. Smaller New England states like this tend to be the quieter, less-hunted pieces, which is part of why I enjoy chasing them.
FloridaStates of BeanFlorida in the 1997 States of Bean series gets the sun-and-citrus Sunshine State spirit through Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson's bold, stylized illustration. The series wrapped each state's character around an oversized everyday mug, and Florida's warmth and coastline make it one of the more visually obvious entries. I like how this whole set predates the city-mug eras most people know, a 1997 snapshot of Starbucks experimenting with regional pride.
MassachusettsStates of BeanMassachusetts is a favorite in my 1997 States of Bean run because it leans into Boston and Concord, the birthplace of American revolution and history. Designed for Starbucks by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, it carries the series' signature color-blocked, almost storybook look on a roomy 18 to 20 ounce mug. With its deep Colonial and literary pedigree, this is one of the states collectors gravitate toward when they want a piece with a real sense of place.
OhioStates of BeanOhio is a solid Midwestern entry in the 1997 States of Bean series Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson designed for Starbucks. The series gave every state the same bright, color-blocked folk-art treatment wrapped around a generous everyday mug, turning regional pride into drinkware before Starbucks city mugs became a phenomenon. As a heartland state it tends to be one of the more affordable and findable pieces, which makes it good filler for completing the run.
OregonStates of BeanOregon belongs to the 1997 States of Bean series, and there is a quiet hometown pull here since Starbucks grew up just north in the Pacific Northwest. Designed by Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson, the mug leans on Oregon's forests, coastline and mountains in the set's signature stylized color blocks. I like having a Northwest state in the run, a regional cousin to the Seattle roots of the whole company.
PennsylvaniaStates of BeanPennsylvania in the 1997 States of Bean series carries the weight of Philadelphia, Independence Hall and the nation's founding, all filtered through Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson's playful color-blocked style. The series wrapped each state's identity around an oversized everyday mug, and a Keystone State with this much history makes for a satisfying piece. It is one I reach for when I want a States of Bean cup that quietly carries some real American story.
TexasStates of BeanTexas in the 1997 States of Bean series gets the big, bold treatment its larger-than-everything reputation demands, courtesy of Daleet Zigelboim and Jan Belson's design for Starbucks. The Lone Star State naturally invites the kind of confident, color-saturated imagery the whole series traded in. Texas tends to be a popular grab for collectors who want a single recognizable state, which keeps it moving through the secondary market.
One collection. Never split.
